author: Jessica Corbett
title: Armed Conflict Hinders Efforts to Contain Deadly Ebola Outbreak in the Congo
content:
The outbreak has killed more than 5,900 people, while fighting prevents health workers from reaching affected communities.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Three months after the United Nations senior Ebola coordinator warned that the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo was “growing exponentially,” government data showed Thursday that confirmed cases have topped 12,000 and left over 5,900 people dead.

The epidemic’s figures still rank behind the 2014-16 West African outbreak — which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 — but it is “the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll” from a decade ago, according to The Associated Press, which published a series of graphs demonstrating how fast-growing this crisis is.

Since the outbreak — caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus — was declared in May, it has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces. Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data recently revealed that just 15% of new cases come from contacts known to health authorities, and a Reuters analysis of satellite ⁠imagery found the death toll may be underestimated in two hard-hit areas.

Dozens of residents in eastern Congo say they have been unable to locate the bodies of relatives who died in the ongoing Ebola outbreak, while others say loved ones have been buried without their knowledge https://t.co/o5tKFPtRTS pic.twitter.com/PdCpb9Wa6R

The World Health Organization (WHO) said last Friday that “no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria; and no new country has reported confirmed cases,” but “the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection, and coordinated preparedness and response measures.”

The response in the DRC has been hindered by lack of community trust in authorities, poor infrastructure, and armed conflict, particularly between the army and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) — one of dozens of militant groups in the resource-rich eastern part of the country, and led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted⁠ of conscripting child soldiers by the International Criminal Court in 2012.

Summarizing remarks from Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s incident manager in the DRC, the AP reported Wednesday that “the fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus, and left some treatment centers with fewer staff.”

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

WHO temporarily moved its Mongbwalu team and partner staff to Bunia after fighting disrupted road access, Smallwood said. Mongbwalu, a mining town northwest of Bunia, is where the outbreak was first detected in May.

The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) said Wednesday that “the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities” due to clashes between DRC forces and the CRP, and Bangladeshi peacekeepers helped with that evacuation of health workers.

UN peacekeepers faced “significant logistical challenges,” including “difficult terrain, poor road conditions, and the fragile state of a wooden bridge,” before they reached the healthcare workers, who were evacuated by air to Bunia, MONUSCO noted.

“These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement,” the mission said. “This intervention is part of MONUSCO’s support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.”

.@WHO staff, @MinSanteRDC and other colleagues have been safely evacuated from the hospital in Akwe, Ituri Province, where they were sheltering amid fierce conflict for over three days. They have been brought to safety thanks to combined efforts across health, government and…

After the evacuation, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus thanked all those involved and stressed that “healthcare, health workers, Ebola responders, and humanitarian [aid] must be protected at all times!”

author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
title: Genocide, Displacement and Malnutrition Threaten Pregnancies in Gaza
content:
Doctors in Gaza report rising congenital abnormalities as pregnant women face exposure to bombs and toxic substances.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Faiqa al-Arini, 33, gave birth to her first child on October 19 at Al-Awda Maternity Hospital in central Gaza. She was forced to deliver early, at the beginning of her ninth month of pregnancy, after developing high blood pressure.

Al-Arini gave birth to a baby girl through a cesarean section. They named her Nour. After the delivery, the new mother remained in the intensive care unit while the newborn was transferred to the neonatal ward. Al-Arini did not see her daughter at all that first day.

Whenever she asked, “Where is my baby?” the nurses and her family members reassured her that the infant was in the neonatal ward.

The following day, Al-Arini began to feel that something was wrong. She recalled not hearing her daughter cry when she was born. She started questioning her family and was determined to get up and look for the baby herself if the nurses did not bring her. Eventually, her husband, Muhammad Abdel Jawad, 37, confronted her with the news.

“You know it is better to hear this from us than from someone else,” he told her. “Our baby has a congenital deformity. She was born without hands.”

Abdel Jawad had seen his daughter immediately after her birth. When he had asked the doctors about the main factors that could cause such abnormalities in newborn babies, the doctors pointed to the dust from missiles, toxic chemicals, and the unhealthy environment where displaced people are forced to live across the Gaza Strip.

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the number of recorded congenital abnormalities among newborns has been increasing year after year. The ministry confirmed that 260 cases of congenital abnormalities had been recorded among newborns by the end of September 2026, compared with 184 cases in 2022. The number of recorded cases reached 322 in 2025, representing a 75% increase over a three year time period. However, the Ministry of Health says these figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital abnormalities among newborns or determine their causes.

Ashraf Qeshta, an obstetrics and gynecology specialist at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, says that the number of cases of miscarriage and congenital abnormalities among pregnant women has exceeded normal levels. He attributes this to several factors produced by the genocide, most notably the inhalation of toxic gases, exposure to missile remnants, living in an unhealthy environment, malnutrition, and other hardships imposed by war.

“We are seeing a significant number of congenital abnormalities. For example, babies are being born without skulls, others without limbs, and some with serious health problems, such as non-functioning or damaged kidneys, or heart defects,” Qeshta told Mondoweiss.

Even in cases where doctors believe that the congenital abnormality is caused by exposure to bombs and toxic substances, proving this requires advanced medical testing, sophisticated equipment, and qualified specialists. According to Qeshta, these are precisely the resources the Ministry of Health lacks, making it difficult to investigate and establish the different causes with scientific certainty.

Al-Arini said her pregnancy was extremely difficult. She was repeatedly displaced from one place to another and faced severe economic hardship, including famine, as her pregnancy began during the final months of the famine in 2025.

“Like all women in the Gaza Strip, we live under the same conditions,” al-Arini said. “We are displaced, we go hungry, we live in fear, and we narrowly escape death almost every day. Bombs and missiles explode beside us, and shrapnel flies over us. This is the reality for all women in Gaza.”

“But the effects of all these things are now beginning to show on us. I am happy that I gave birth to a girl, and I love her very much. I had indeed wished she would be born with limbs, but their absence does not make her any less my daughter, nor does it change anything about my feelings toward her. However, it makes me think deeply about the condition of our homeland, and about how even giving birth here has become fraught with danger. A baby can be born with congenital abnormalities because of the conditions we are living in,” she said.

A report published by Human Rights Watch on January 28, 2025, documented the grave health and humanitarian risks that pregnant women in the Gaza Strip are facing as a result of the siege, destruction of healthcare facilities, shortages of food, water, and medicine, and Israel’s genocidal war.

The report noted that pregnant women in Gaza face a severe shortage of medical care before, during, and after pregnancy, in addition to malnutrition, dehydration, and anemia. They also struggle to reach hospitals and obtain the medical examinations, vitamins, and supplements necessary for a healthy pregnancy.

The report added that the deterioration of maternity and childbirth services had increased the risks of complications, including bleeding, preeclampsia, and infections, amid shortages of incubators and medical supplies. These conditions threaten the lives of mothers, fetuses, and newborn babies alike.

In addition, a report issued by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) on August 7, 2026, presented the findings of a survey conducted between June 2 and June 16. The survey covered a sample of 1,335 children and found that 12.2% suffered from stunting relative to their age as a result of chronic malnutrition and inadequate access to sufficient food.

Farah Abu Mustafa, 25, lives in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis with her nine-month-old daughter, Zainab. Abu Mustafa’s pregnancy was fraught with unexpected hardships, repeated displacement, daily bombardment, witnessing people die, and exposure to gases and missile remnants.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter, Zainab, was born under difficult circumstances marked by deprivation of food and a lack of medical services during pregnancy. Since her birth, she has spent almost as much time in the hospital as she has in the tent of their displacement camp.

Zainab is suffering from malnutrition, brain atrophy, delayed neurological and muscular development, and recurrent seizures. When she’s in the hospital, her weight and health improve because of the care she receives. But as soon as the family returns to the tent in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, her condition deteriorates again.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter requires specialized medical care and strict adherence to medications and treatment. But in the tents, she can barely provide her with something to sleep on, let alone a clean and suitable place to recover.

“This is the life of displacement,” Abu Mustafa said. “Even the simplest things require a miracle for us to obtain them. Everything around us is crushing and grinding down displaced people.”

Abu Mustafa also points out that even preventive treatments intended to reduce the risk of congenital abnormalities are not available in pharmacies or easily accessible.

“Our Israeli occupier is waging war on the very air we breathe,” she said. “It is creating an environment conducive to diseases, congenital abnormalities, and miscarriages. Every woman I know has experienced a miscarriage, and I know many women who have given birth to babies with congenital abnormalities.”

“The occupation wants to eliminate generations, not just leave them with deformities,” she said.

author: Julia Conley
title: The FCC Approves SpaceX’s Plan for 1 Million Space Satellites
content:
Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Federal Communications Commission’s approval on Wednesday of SpaceX’s plan to deploy one million orbital data center satellites into space by 2040 was not “just irresponsible,” said one environmental advocate.

“It’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.”

Whitehouse was among the critics who noted that the approval had been granted without an environmental review, which is required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the deployment of one million “orbital space modules,” which SpaceX has said would form a new data center constellation called “Starmind,” would open “a bold new frontier” and allow the U.S. to lead “the world into the era of super intelligence.”

The satellites would process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, according to SpaceX, the space exploration company led by Republican megadonor Elon Musk.

The environmental legal group Earthjustice said they also risk “changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky,” and denounced the commission for releasing the decision as families across the U.S. were preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The number of satellites in space has already grown rapidly in the last several years, with 15,000 satellites in orbit in 2026 — up from 1,400 just over a decade ago.

Satellites cause emissions as they are placed in space through rocket launches, and other environmental impacts include debris from potential collisions — especially as the number of satellites grows — degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution.

Astronomers spoke out against SpaceX’s plan earlier this year, saying it would prevent scientists from studying the night sky with modern telescopes, as well as disrupting ecosystems and humans’ biological clocks due to extreme light pollution.

On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s licensing of Musk’s plan.

“The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” said the group. “The intended and unintended radio emissions from a constellation of such unprecedented size would imperil radio astronomy research, and the waste heat generated by the data centers would produce a thermal signature that would increase the infrared background of the sky and threaten the efficacy of sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research. In addition, atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”

“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” the AAS added.

Earthjustice emphasized that the approval came as Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the permitting reform bill that would prevent future administrations from revoking licenses for projects including data centers and would block courts from enforcing environmental review laws for such projects if they had been violated previously.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of [President Donald] Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: After Nearly 50 Years in Prison, Leonard Peltier Says the Struggle Continues
content:
The longtime Indigenous activist discusses his conviction, childhood in boarding school and commitment to Indigenous sovereignty.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In September 2025, Democracy Now! host Amy Goodman sat down with longtime political prisoner and Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier for his first extended television and radio broadcast interview since his release to home confinement in February 2025. Before his commutation by former President Joe Biden, the 82-year-old Peltier spent nearly 50 years behind bars. Peltier has always maintained his innocence for the 1975 killing of two FBI officers. He is expected to serve the remainder of his life sentences under house arrest at the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Nation in Belcourt, North Dakota. In a wide-ranging conversation, we spoke to Peltier about his case, his time in prison, his childhood spent at an American Indian boarding school and his later involvement in the American Indian Movement (AIM) and more.

“We still have to live under that, that fear of losing our identity, losing our culture, our religion,” Peltier says about his continued commitment to Indigenous rights. “The struggle still goes on for me. I’m not going to give up.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: In this special broadcast, we spend the hour with longtime Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier. Last February, he was released from a federal prison in Florida after spending nearly half a century behind bars for a crime he says he did not commit. President Biden, on his last day in office, commuted Peltier’s life sentence to home confinement. Biden’s decision followed mounting calls by tribal leaders and supporters around the world in a decadeslong, community-led campaign fighting for his freedom.

In the 1970s, Peltier was involved with the American Indian Movement, known as AIM. In 1975, two FBI agents and one young AIM activist were killed in a shootout on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Two AIM members were later arrested for killing the agents. At the trial, the jury acquitted them. Leonard Peltier was arrested later, tried separately and convicted. Peltier has always maintained his innocence.

Notable supporters of Leonard Peltier over the years have included South African President Nelson Mandela, Pope Francis and Amnesty International. Supporters of Peltier say his trial was marked by gross FBI and federal prosecutorial misconduct, including the coercion of witnesses, fabricated testimony and suppressed exculpatory evidence.

After being released in February, Leonard Peltier returned home to live on the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Reservation in Belcourt, North Dakota. On September 12th, Leonard Peltier celebrated his 81st birthday. People gathered throughout the day, visiting him and calling from around the world to celebrate. That night and the next day, we spoke to Leonard Peltier in his living room in his first extended TV/radio broadcast interview since his release from prison.

AMY GOODMAN: Hi. I’m Amy Goodman, host of Democracy Now!, in the home of Leonard Peltier, just recently freed from prison after 49 years. LEONARD PELTIER: Plus two months. AMY GOODMAN: Plus two months. LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah. AMY GOODMAN: I’ve spoken to you so many times, Leonard, in prison, in various prisons, several of them supermax prisons. It is quite astonishing to be here with you in person. Tell us where we are. Where are we sitting? LEONARD PELTIER: We’re sitting in my home, that was given to me by my supporters. This was not given to me by the tribe, or the government had nothing to do with it. I was released by Biden under a commutation of my sentence and home confinement. Actually, what happened was, I was — I was taken out of one prison cell and really put into another type of prison. But this is my home now. This is my home. So it’s a million times better. AMY GOODMAN: Wait, what do you mean when you say you were taken out of your prison cell after more than 49 years, and you’re saying that you’re not completely free? LEONARD PELTIER: No, no, I’m on very restrictive restrictions. Even to go to the post office, I got to call my — I call her my handler. I have to call her to go to the post office. Then, when I get back, I have to call her and tell her I’m back. Or if I go anything, if I go shopping or whatever, I have to do that. If I have to go a hundred miles past the nation — I don’t call my place a “reservation,” either; we’re nations of people — I have to get a pass, usually from Washington, D.C., to go to medical, usually medical, or religious ceremonies on different nations, Indian Native nations. AMY GOODMAN: So, let’s go back to that moment when you were in that prison cell in Coleman, in Florida, and you got word that President Biden had commuted your sentence. It was just hours before he was leaving office? Can you tell us about that process, how it took place? LEONARD PELTIER: Well, as I went through the years filing for pardons and stuff, Ronald Reagan was the first one to promise to leave me — pardon me. Somebody in Washington stopped it. There’s only one organization that could have stopped it, and didn’t have the power to stop it, but still, somehow, were in power, enough to where they can override a president of the United States, our Congress. It’s the FBI. And Reagan promised to let me go. And the FBI intervened, and that was stopped. And Bill Clinton and Obama, and, finally, we get to Biden. And Biden, there was pressure put on him from all over the world. Almost every tribal nation here in the United States filed for my release, demanding my release. The United Nations — the United Nations did a full report on my case, and they demanded that I be released immediately and to be “paid,” quote-unquote. Hundreds of Congress and senators and millions of people — AMY GOODMAN: And the pope. LEONARD PELTIER: And the pope, two popes, the last pope and the current pope. And world leaders, many world leaders, demanded my release. AMY GOODMAN: The Nobel Peace laureate, bishop — Archbishop Desmond Tutu? LEONARD PELTIER: Yes. I was also nominated for — and nominated four times, because of my work from prisons, for a Nobel Prize. And the board and everything granted it, but somebody intervened again. So, four times, I lost that. I think somebody was pushing Biden to stop any — any possibility of signing a pardon. So, he didn’t sign it until the last moment. And actually, a day and a half before he actually signed it and he was — his term was completed, I just took the position that, “Nah, he’s not going to do this.” And I just kind of laid back in my cell, and I thought to myself, “Well, I guess I die here, and this is the only ultimate sacrifice I can make, and I have to accept it. I have no other choice.” And as I laid there and thinking about it, other people came by — even guards would tell me, “Don’t give up, Leonard. Don’t give up.” And other prisoners, and some of them prisoners were telling me that, “Leonard, he’s got to know that if he doesn’t sign this, this is political suicide for the Democratic Party, because there’s millions of people that are going to break away from this if he doesn’t.” And so, I was laying there, and I was thinking, “Well, let’s try one more thing.” So I called a representative of mine that was working closely with the Biden administration. We got — we have Native people — we had Native people in his administration who were communicating with Biden. And I said, “Tell him to give me a commutation on my sentence and home confinement.” So, she called and did this, and that’s what I ended up with. And that’s what I’m — that’s what I’m living under right now. AMY GOODMAN: How did you hear that you were going to be free? LEONARD PELTIER: Well, it was kind of unbelievable in the immediate moment. I thought somebody was just playing games with me. And I thought, “Ah, I’m going to wake up, and this is all a dream, and I’m in the cell, and I’ll be in there.” And I really didn’t believe it until, actually, I walked in the house here. AMY GOODMAN: What was it like to leave Coleman? LEONARD PELTIER: Wow! Imagine living in a cubicle larger than some people’s closets for all those years, and then you finally are able to walk out of there. I mean, it was just — for me, it was unbelievable that this was actually happening to me. But, I mean, the feeling of, wow, I can go — I’ll be home. Is this really over for me? Is this really going to be over for me? And it was disbelief. A lot of it was disbelief, really. LEONARD PELTIER: No. Two months ago, I think now, I lost 80% of my vision. And I’m in the process of, hopefully, getting my eyesight returned, treated and returned.

I was there with my grandmother, Hazel, and my little brother, Waha. And I remember sitting beside my grandma, waiting for my dad to come out those doors for the first time ever. And I remember asking my grandma, I said, “Do you think my dad’s gonna like me?” And she’s like, “Yeah, he’s gonna love you.” And I said, “Is it OK if I hug my dad?” You know? And she was like, “Yeah, of course. Go hug him.” And she kind of pushed me in that door, towards the door. And when it opened and he came out, he just smiled, and I ran to him. And I just remember him hugging me, and I was like, “That’s my dad. That’s my dad,” you know, because I hadn’t — I don’t have any memories prior to that. They said we lived together in Oregon, but I don’t remember that. They said we saw him in Canada when he — before they extradited him, but I don’t remember that.

AMY GOODMAN: How old were you when you saw him in Marion?

MARQUETTA SHIELDS-PELTIER: I think I was around 7 or 8 years old, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: So, what was it like through those years? I mean, it’s the only thing you knew, but to visit him only behind bars?

MARQUETTA SHIELDS-PELTIER: When I was young, it was really confusing. It was hard to understand why, you know, because he kind of protected me, probably because I was so young and I didn’t understand what was going on. But it was bittersweet, because I loved going there. And, like, for me, that was normal, you know, to see my dad there. Even though there’s dads around me with my other friends and stuff, I just — for me, that was normal.

But as I got older and started to understand what was going on, why he was there, I started to resent it, you know, because every time 3:00 came around, I hated it, because I knew I was going to have to leave my dad, and I wouldn’t see him again, especially that last day of the visit. We would usually spend about a week. And that last day of visits, I would just, like, “Man, I’m not going to see my dad again for six, seven months,” you know? And then, as I got older, it was just like, “Oh my god, what if I don’t get to see him again next time?”

You know, so, eventually I packed up my kids and moved to Kansas so I could be closer to him. And then that worked out for about three years. And then, from there, they moved him again across the country. So, yeah, we didn’t get to have the relationship I thought we would during that time, just because he was way over in Pennsylvania, then Florida, and I was stuck in Kansas.

AMY GOODMAN: And what was your understanding from early on, and did it change, of why he was behind bars?

MARQUETTA SHIELDS-PELTIER: Yeah, I just — like, I knew things had happened that were, you know, not — I’ve always been told and taught that my dad was there because he wanted better for me as his daughter, as a Native person. He wanted people to respect me, not only as his daughter, but just as a Native person, you know, to understand that we are not property or we are not animals or savages, that we are human beings, just like everybody else.

And as I got older and started understanding his case and what was, you know, the details of it, then it went from, you know, resenting — I never resented my dad, but I resented the government, and I resented — you know, but it went from not knowing the extent of it to knowing the full extent of it and just being proud of — like, even though I prayed for him to get out all the time, I knew what he stood for, and I was proud. And I had to, you know, keep fighting for him, because I knew that someday, someday, he would get out, you know? And he did. He did, which is unbelievable to me still.

AMY GOODMAN: When did you hear that Biden had commuted his sentence and sentenced him to home confinement?

MARQUETTA SHIELDS-PELTIER: I don’t remember the date exactly, but it was sometime at the end of January. It was just crazy, because I was planning on leaving. I was going to leave the country and just disappear, because I — after his parole was denied in June of ’24 — I think it was ’24 — I basically thought my dad was going to die there. So I had given up on everything, and I was getting ready to disappear into Canada and just disappear.

But I was sleeping on my mom’s couch that morning, and I heard the phone ring. And then I heard my mom, and she said, “What?” And I thought the worst, of course, that they called to tell me my dad was dead. And then my cousin was crying, and she said, “Marquetta, I’m so happy.” So I was like, “What are you talking about?” She’s like, “Your dad’s getting out of prison.” I was like, you know, like — I cussed in my mom’s house. And I usually — unless I’m joking with her. I just was like, “You’re lying. You’re lying to me. You’re lying to me. My dad’s” — She’s like, “They’re — Joe Biden” — and, you know, this, that and the other. And I just — I couldn’t — I didn’t know what to do. I just — I froze. And I still can’t remember if I called my nephew or if I called my brother, who I called, but I called somebody, and I asked them. I was like, “Is it true? My dad’s getting out of prison?” And they’re like, “Yeah.”

I’m so thankful to millions of people for the last 49 years of my life that helped pray for him, that helped write letters, that helped make phone calls, that sent signed petitions. You know, that’s all those people in it and to help bring my dad home.

But the thing of it is, is people don’t understand that, you know, when my dad went to prison, so did we. You know, we were out here free, but we weren’t free. We were out here struggling when he was in there struggling. And I was blessed enough to have people like my grandmother and my mom to show me that, you know what, it’s going to be OK. It’s going to be OK.

AMY GOODMAN: Leonard Peltier means so much to so many people around the world. Talk about what he means, not just to you as his daughter, but to you as an Indigenous woman.

MARQUETTA SHIELDS-PELTIER: Oh, man, my dad, I told him this before. He’s my hero. He’s the definition of what a warrior should be, you know, to be able to stand strong and still come out of that prison smiling, to be able to set an example. And, like, I look up to my dad, because I don’t know very many people that could go through the stuff he’s been through and still have a smile on his face. And it makes me proud to call him my dad. You know, that’s my dad.

AMY GOODMAN: Marquetta Shields-Peltier, the daughter of Leonard Peltier, speaking in [September 2025] at Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where Leonard has been living since being released from prison.

And that does it for today’s show. To see all of Democracy Now!’s coverage of Leonard Peltier and our interview with him over the years behind bars, you can go to democracynow.org. Special thanks to Denis Moynihan, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff and Zazu, the newshound.Democracy Now! is produced with Mike Burke, Renée Feltz, Deena Guzder, Messiah Rhodes, Nermeen Shaikh, María Taracena, Nicole Salazar, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Tey-Marie Astudillo, John Hamilton, Robby Karran, Hany Massoud and Safwat Nazzal. Our executive director is Julie Crosby. Special thanks to Becca Staley, Jon Randolph, Paul Powell, Mike Di Filippo, Miguel Nogueira, Hugh Gran, Carl Marxer, David Prude, Dennis McCormick, Matt Ealy, Anna Özbek, Emily Andersen, Dante Torrieri and Buffy Saint Marie Hernandez. I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks so much for joining us.

author: Robert Faturechi
title: Pentagon Weighs $15 Billion Loan to Startup With Ties to Trump Jr.
content:
The startup plans to use AI and robotics to build factories producing munitions, drones and other military equipment.

The startup plans to use AI and robotics to build factories producing munitions, drones and other military equipment.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.

Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.

Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.

It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which Hadrian specializes in.

In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits and risks.)

At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder, Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-one problem that the Navy’s identified is we can’t find enough skilled workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” he told reporters. The factory will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.

The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”

Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion — more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook.

When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow. A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval vessels.” Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just $6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation.

Hadrian executives told Forbes in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but outside estimates put it at a few hundred.

This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa, Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January. The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years.

A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and funded by Congress, some former defense officials said.

The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense contractors and other private-sector businesses.

But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government.

When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial applications.”

The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on their capital investment.

David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its size.

A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to allow it to continue issuing new loans.

“OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said. “Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that exceed its mandate.”

In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has shown a personal interest in defense tech and has criticized cronyism in defense spending.

The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company.

Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time, Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president, ProPublica previously reported. After defense officials got the White House request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a matter of weeks.

The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played no role in the deal.

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Indigenous Sovereignty Is Under Attack Today in the Name of Permitting Reform
content:
A bill now moving through Congress would allow tech oligarchs to circumvent tribal opposition to their projects.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In March 1621, months before the meal Americans now call the first Thanksgiving, the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin sat down with the Plymouth colonists and negotiated a mutual-defense treaty. His people had every reason to keep their distance: An epidemic carried by European traders had totally emptied the village of Patuxet only a few years earlier. They came to the table anyway.

That’s what reciprocity asks of you: the understanding that relationships between people — and between nations — run on ongoing giving, receiving, and responsibility.

Four hundred and five years later, the federal government has left a long record of making that table optional through ignoring treaties with tribal nations. Now it is seeking to throw out the table altogether.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) now moving through Congress puts forth a series of changes that would fast-track federal approvals for projects like data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure. The bill would collapse Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act by narrowing what is considered an “undertaking” –– where federal funding was the prior baseline ––and shrinking the scope of an “adverse effect”; it places review deadlines on projects, and offers program alternatives to fast-track approvals; and sets a 150-day limit to court challenges. BAAJA would render public input limited and optional, narrow what is deemed historic property, and diminish requirements for federal agencies to consult with Native nations. Despite its innocuous framing as “permitting reform,” the bill would allow tech oligarchs to legally circumvent the communities and tribes that clearly oppose expensive and extractive projects on their land.

Treaties — the supreme law of the land, alongside the Constitution — require nation-to-nation relations for all projects impacting tribal nations. BAAJA virtually eliminates whatever parity remains in this relationship.

BAAJA’s own name claims the bill is about affordability, and many proponents say it will create jobs and advance clean energy infrastructure. But the oil industry-backed bill, with roughly a page per year since that first colonial meal, pushes aside the land, water, and people who gave the Pilgrims food. BAAJA is championed first and foremost by the GOP, but it’s become a bipartisan bill. Fifteen Democrats pushed it through the Senate the same week that Capitol Police arrested Indigenous activists protesting the bill like Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of Honor the Earth. Her organization advocates against the “green colonialism” this bill is attempting to legally codify.

The Native American Rights Fund (NARF), the largest legal advocacy organization for tribes in the U.S., issued a social media statement: “You may have recently heard from certain members of Congress that BAAJA would help clean energy without weakening environmental protections or Tribal rights,” it said. “NARF attorneys reviewed the bill and found a different story: fewer safeguards, less say for Tribal Nations and the public, and fewer ways to stop harmful projects.”

Meanwhile, media pundits like Jason Hayes, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation, promote the bill’s emphasis on expediting permitting, framing the bill as providing cost- and time-saving mechanisms, and suggesting their reversal would risk corporate resources. Ezra Klein, a self-described liberal commentator at The New York Times, backs the bill, but tramples tribes by omission, never saying “Native American,” “Indigenous,” or “tribes” as he lays out his public support.

Klein’s advocacy for permitting reform is unsurprising, considering that it is central to a bestselling book he co-wrote, Abundance. But it carries a colonial logic of unlimited extraction with a greenwashed veneer. “We need to build and invent more of what we need,” Klein says. But who is “We”? Here it’s a pronoun that excludes tribes, and refers abstractly to technology and infrastructure development without context or consequence for the builder and the alleged beneficiaries. Such framing of development is greenwashing: a marketing practice that presents a product, policy, or company as more environmentally friendly than it actually is.

This has been done before: In 2024, the SunZia power line, a massive wind energy project, crossed New Mexico and Arizona into California, and transversed the Tohono O’odham Nation by running over historical properties. The Nation sued the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), but the suit was thrown out in a Tucson court that said the Nation waited too long to file an injunction.

The cycle repeated in 2021 for the Thacker Pass lithium mine in Nevada, sold as essential for electric vehicle batteries. The Biden administration fueled the lithium rush further by funneling billions of public dollars into clean energy projects, including $2.26 billion for Thacker Pass. The BLM’s tribal consultation process was minimal: One email was sent to the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe while staff were on furlough during a government shutdown.

Some of the same politicians and pundits who are trying to make extraction look green also attempt to make Zionism look reasonable, and even lend that project, itself an instrument of American power, a progressive sheen. New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, who received a letter from the Karuk Tribe urging him to strip the bill’s historic preservation changes, voted to advance it without any sort of public comment on tribal consultation. Schumer is also known as one of the staunchest defenders of Israel in Congress. Meanwhile, BAAJA architect Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island has also said he is “ardently pro-Israel.”

Zionism itself treats Jews’ Levantine presence 2,500 years ago as a sound basis for Jewish supremacy in Palestine today, all while Native genocide — waged through violence, land theft, and cultural genocide for over 500 years, and which continues to this day — is framed, in its elision, as a foregone conclusion. Both Palestinian and Native perspectives are regularly silenced in mainstream media, which removes from them the option of changing the narratives surrounding their own erasure. Cable news shows fail to include Palestinians, even at the height of genocide. Meanwhile, I have not seen Klein host a Native guest on his popular eponymous podcast, referring only to tribalism in politics with non-Native guests and making passing historical mention of tribes’ land dispossession in conversation with them. The perceived entitlement to both Palestinian and Native land repeats a colonial logic compounded by the dialectical erasure perpetuated in tandem. The situation is a hat on a hat: Tribes are excluded from the conversation on the exclusion of tribes.

Some environmental organizations like the Center for Biological Diversity and others call tribal exclusion more broadly from climate activism a form of “greenwashing.” Tom BK Goldtooth (Diné and Dakota), executive director of the Indigenous Environmental Network, has in the past called carbon offsets and “nature-based solutions” greenwashing: “Corporations and governments must cut carbon emission at source, rather than use [nature-based solutions] for greenwashing.” Adding insult to injury, tribes are lumped together as a monolith in BAAJA.

The exclusion is all the more crucial because tribes are leading more reciprocal and sustainable solutions to climate change. Colusa Indian Energy comes to mind. Its approach has buy-in from over 50 tribes and involves small data centers that require a fraction of the water of those produced by tech oligarchs. “If you’re using combined heat and power with dry cooling, potentially you’re looking at less than 100,000 gallons of water a day,” Chief Operating Officer Ken Ahmann (Cachil DeHe Band of Wintun Indians) told The Architect’s Newspaper. In October, the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs endured a fire without recourse except for mutual aid offered by other tribes. In California, Yurok fire leader Elizabeth Azzuz proactively performs cultural burns that reduce risk of wildfires and promote biodiversity — a reciprocal modus operandi functioning opposite to the extractive projects promoted by BAAJA. Scientists say climate change is intensifying California’s now-annual wildfires; cultural burning reduces the fuel that feeds them.

As we await the House’s vote expected after Thanksgiving, by November 30, we have an opportunity to reflect on the fact that the Pilgrims violated the covenant that sanctified reciprocity with the Wampanoag and how that dynamic reverberates to this day. Attacks on Indigenous sovereignty are not a thing of the past. Today, they are being carried out in the name of clean energy modernization and permitting reform. Native leaders like Ahmann and Azzuz are building their own table, but bills like BAAJA threaten even the most optimistic and expansive strategies — and partnership — for land stewardship and climate change mitigation.

In Lakota, Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ means literally “we are all related.” In practice, it suggests that a person’s value lies in their daily acts of care for the whole community. Whether or not they realize it, BAAJA’s proponents have pitted Indigenous sovereignty against a clean energy future. We must reject the notion that trampling on the rights of some will ostensibly benefit us all.

author: Dalia Abu Ramadan
title: In Gaza, We Have No Feasts to Give Thanks For
content:
As Americans feast on Thanksgiving, we are still facing widespread malnutrition and acute hunger in Gaza.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

I grew up believing that food was readily available, that having access to it was something ordinary and something I could always count on. I never imagined that one day I would be deprived of it, or that I would find myself wishing for a single loaf of bread despite having the money to buy one. Yet I, my family, and my people were deprived of food for prolonged periods throughout Israel’s war on Gaza. Although the war has publicly been declared over, we continue to suffer its consequences — only now they unfold away from the headlines, behind the scenes.

I had always heard that we were a people living under siege, but I never imagined that human cruelty could reach such depths. I thought the worst cruelty could bring was the use of weapons. It never crossed my mind that hunger itself could be turned into a weapon against us; that food, one of the most basic necessities of life, could become a means of deprivation and suffering. How can human beings strip others of their right to food with so little regard for their humanity?

No human being has the right to decide that another human being or an animal should be starved! How can we advance technologically while regressing as human beings?

Although famine conditions in Gaza have eased since the ceasefire, the consequences of the war have not. Many of these consequences remain hidden from the world. As of October 15, around 90 percent of Gaza’s population still relied on humanitarian food assistance amid the collapse of livelihoods and widespread loss of purchasing power, leaving families struggling to secure even their most basic needs. For many, food aid is no longer supplementary support; it has become a lifeline. Yet that very lifeline is now under threat, at a time when most people in Gaza remain unable to meet their own food needs.

On October 19, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut its food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, meaning that approximately 500,000 people would lose access to essential assistance. These cuts were not the result of declining humanitarian needs, but of a shortfall in international funding.

Since the ceasefire was announced in October 2025, the WFP had been providing assistance to approximately 1.6 million people in Gaza every month through food parcels, wheat flour, bread, hot meals, nutritional support, school snacks, and cash assistance. By October 2026, however, the food program had reduced the number of people it supported to 1.1 million.

The World Food Programme announced that 500,000 people would lose access to essential assistance.

The WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, told Australia’s ABC News that traditional donors, including the United States and European countries, had reduced their contributions. He also pointed to multiple humanitarian crises competing for limited funding and what he described as “donor fatigue.” Skau stressed that the cuts were not due to an inability to bring food into Gaza or a decline in people’s needs, but rather to a lack of funding.

A single disruption, seemingly small in itself, can push an entire population closer to famine.

On October 20, 2026, flour became scarce across Gaza after the WFP could no longer fund the bakeries that had been supplying bread to the population. That day, my uncle went to the market to see what he could find to feed his family. He was stunned to discover that flour was nowhere to be found. Wherever it was available, it was being sold at exorbitant prices because of the shortage.

He called my father and said, “Can you imagine, Imad? There’s no flour, no chicken, no eggs, nothing. They told me flour has become incredibly expensive, and most of the other goods are spoiled.”

“There is nothing we can do. We are in the same position as everyone else,” my father replied. “We don’t know how much longer we will have to keep thinking about stockpiling flour and food in case of a sudden famine that could last for days. We simply don’t know what might happen, and we can no longer count on food remaining available.”

That was the hardest day we had faced in terms of food since the so-called ceasefire was declared. We felt a level of despair we had never experienced before. That single day was enough to bring back memories of the famine we endured during the war, along with the anguish of families whose loved ones were lost while trying to secure food for their families.

In February 2024, at least 112 Palestinians were killed and 760 others injured while waiting for food aid.

How could we ever forget what happened during the famine in February 2024, at the Nabulsi Roundabout? According to a statement by the UN Human Rights Office for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, at least 112 Palestinians were killed and 760 others injured while waiting for food aid. The statement reported that Israeli forces had opened fire, alongside incidents of crowd crush and people being trampled.

That day, my brother, my father, and my uncles had gone to collect aid. We waited for them until morning, convinced that we had lost them after hearing the horrifying reports of those killed and the tragic stories emerging from the scene.

On October 20, 2026, my friend Ghada sent me a message expressing her frustration with the reality we have been forced to live through:

I feel so frustrated. What kind of life are we living? How much longer will we have to struggle to secure flour and chase after things that should be readily available in the first place? I feel as though we have lost our future entirely, while all we can think about is flour and food.

The shortage did not last long; flour returned to the markets within two days. But one question continued to haunt us: If we cannot even feel secure about having food, what is left for us to live for?

Imagine the children growing up in Gaza today, many of whom can barely remember the taste of certain fruits after being deprived of them for more than two years. Imagine what this young generation is going through. A 10-year-old child is thinking about stockpiling food instead of concentrating on schoolwork, playing, or dreaming about the future. The fear of food disappearing has taken over his thoughts at an age when his mind should be occupied with the ordinary concerns of childhood, not with whether he will have something to eat tomorrow.

We see food as a blessing that God has bestowed upon all of us. Only those who have been deprived of it can truly understand its worth.

On November 14, 2026, I was at a shopping mall buying a few necessities when I saw that everything was available, despite the high prices. I could not hold back my tears. I thought of all those who had been killed while trying to obtain food. I thought of how my people had been forced to endure humiliation and risk their lives just to secure a single meal for their children and families.

I remember vividly the severe famine I experienced in northern Gaza in 2024, when we were receiving food aid dropped from planes operated by several different countries. Perhaps those countries believed they were providing us with a way to survive, but they failed to understand that, as we waited for those aid packages, we had no way of knowing where they would drift or where they would land. Hunger drove people to run after them, desperately trying to secure something to feed their families. But for some, the desperate attempt to reach that aid ended in drowning.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, at least 17 Palestinians were reported killed in two incidents directly linked to airdropped aid in March 2024. On March 8, five Palestinians were killed when humanitarian aid fell on them after its parachutes malfunctioned near the Al Fayrouz Towers in Gaza City. On March 25, 12 Palestinians drowned while trying to reach aid packages that had fallen into the sea off the coast of Beit Lahia.

In Gaza, we have been humiliated in every possible way just to obtain food. On November 26, Thanksgiving Day in the United States, families gather around dining tables to celebrate and spend time together. In Gaza, however, we are forced to endure humiliation and hardship just to find something to eat. We long for the simplest moments that should never have been taken for granted: sitting together as a family around one table. Many have lost members of their families, and some tables no longer include those who once gathered around them.

I do not want to draw a comparison. Everyone has the right to celebrate, and food is a right that belongs to everyone. I am writing about this day for one reason: to remind people that there are others who are suffering. While families gather around tables filled with food, families in Gaza are still struggling to obtain the most basic thing they need to stay alive.

content:

New polling demonstrates that millions of Americans are likely to change their Thanksgiving plans due to concerns about costs, as prices for many staple items have shot up over the past year.

title: Federal Judge Permanently Bars Trump From Penalizing Groups Working With the ICC
content:
The ruling is a win against Trump’s attacks on the International Criminal Court amid its probes into the Gaza genocide.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Monday, a federal judge permanently barred the Trump administration from penalizing individuals and organizations who submit evidence to the International Criminal Court (ICC), in a victory for organizations that have faced sanctions for their efforts to bring accountability for the genocide in Gaza.

Monday’s ruling by Judge Jesse M. Furman expanded and made permanent a previous court order, issued in October, that blocked the Trump administration from imposing civil or criminal liability on the organizations Democracy for the Arab World Now and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide.

The two groups had sued the Trump administration in July after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in February threatening fines and up to 20 years in prison for individuals or groups that share evidence with the ICC, UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese, or Palestinian human rights groups Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

This week’s court order extended protections to all Americans who provide evidence to or advocate before the ICC, stating that bringing evidence to the ICC is First Amendment-protected speech. The ruling also rejected the Trump administration’s claims that the U.S. must be protected from the ICC, declaring that the government has failed to establish why it is necessary to penalize every instance of evidence provision to the court.

The ruling is a victory against Trump’s long-standing effort to undermine and attack the ICC for its investigations into war crimes committed in Gaza, which culminated in institutional sanctions against the entire court last month. The Trump administration had already sanctioned 11 ICC judges and prosecutors, preventing them from traveling to the U.S., freezing their U.S.-based assets, and severely limiting their ability to undertake financial transactions.

Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and even former Secretary of State Antony Blinken have all decried the ICC for its attempts to investigate and issue arrest warrants for Israeli officials over the genocide in Gaza.

“This landmark ruling dismantles a core part of Trump’s ICC draconian sanctions regime,” said Omar Shakir, executive director at Democracy for the Arab World Now. “The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal.”

Joseph Pace, attorney for Democracy for the Arab World Now and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, spoke to the weight of the victory.

“Typically, courts can now only offer relief to the plaintiffs — no matter how many thousands of nonparties are being victimized by an unconstitutional policy,” he said. “This decision is a major victory, not just because it invalidates a key part of the ICC sanctions’ regime, but because it universally bars the Trump Administration from using the sanctions to penalize anyone, anywhere in the country, for exercising their First Amendment rights.”

As a result of the decision, rights groups and individuals will be able to work with Albanese and Palestinian rights groups once again.

While the ruling protects evidence submission and advocacy, it leaves intact previously-applied sanctions that have frozen ICC members’ assets, funds, and financial transactions, including on individuals like Albanese.

In a separate ruling on Monday, Furman ruled against three ICC judges who asked to be removed from Trump’s sanctions list and for their frozen assets to be unblocked. The judge denied a preliminary injunction in their favor, stating that “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.” Furman also gave weight to Trump’s use of an International Emergency Economic Powers Act when he declared a national emergency over the ICC’s actions.

Earlier this month, Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide traveled to The Hague along with activists and human rights lawyers to submit evidence to the ICC. The group called for the ICC to issue arrest warrants for Trump, Rubio, and other U.S. officials for their complicity in the genocide in Gaza. Democracy for the Arab World Now is scheduled to give its own press conference at The Hague in early December.
