author: Amy Goodman
title: National Book Award Winner Links Denial of US Visa to Palestine Advocacy
content:
Egyptian author and former political prisoner Abdelrahman ElGendy speaks about his new memoir, Huna.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.

“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”

We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.

“Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

We are currently awaiting an Egyptian court decision on whether the closing of Mada Masr, the independent newspaper in Egypt, will stand. We’ll go to Cairo when we hear.

But right now we’re going to turn to what happened in the last few weeks here in this country, in New York, where we are. Novelists, essayists, poets and other writers from around the world took to the stage at the 77th annual National Book Awards ceremony in New York City last week. The winner of this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction, Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, though, was notably absent from the event, after the Trump administration denied his U.S. visa application, blocking him from entering the United States.

ElGendy’s debut book is called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, and chronicles his more than six years of imprisonment in Egypt following his arrest at the age of 17, alongside his father, during the crackdown on protests after the military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2013. He and his father were in their car, and Abdelrahman was taking a picture.

This is the moment the prize for nonfiction was presented by panel chair Robert Warrior.

ROBERT WARRIOR: It’s my distinct honor to announce that this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction goes to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor, Helen Thomaides, then took the stage and read a statement written by ElGendy.

HELEN THOMAIDES: If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you. Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would one day end up in a book, that the guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist, that the slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how to render on the page the torture my body was enduring. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I’d imagine that book winning an award, and deliver fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, fleetingly unincarcerated. Today, that dream should have come full circle, but like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor Helen Thomaides reading Abdelrahman’s words after his memoir Huna won the National Book Award just last week. Ahead of the ceremony, Abdelrahman wrote a piece in The New Yorker magazine. It’s headlined “I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa.”

Abdelrahman ElGendy wrote much of the book while in the United States, where he came two years after he was released from prison in Egypt. He studied at the University of Pittsburgh, where he obtained an MFA in creative nonfiction. Then, in April 2025, following the Trump administration’s widespread targeting of pro-Palestine voices, including international students and academics, Abdelrahman ElGendy decided to flee the U.S., fearing he’d be next, that he’d be detained and possibly deported back to Egypt over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations. At the time, he wrote in The Nation magazine, quote, “I was a political prisoner in Egypt. I didn’t want to become one again in America,” unquote.

For more, we’re joined now by Abdelrahman ElGendy from Europe, where he lives now.

Abdelrahman, I just want to congratulate you on this remarkable book, which I’ve just finished. And I had the joy, flying back from Turkey, the U.N. climate summit, of listening to your book, the audio book, which you read in your own words. The magnificence, the power, the pain of this book cannot be underestimated. I want to thank you so much for sharing your life with us, Abdelrahman ElGendy. Thank you for joining us.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Thank you. Thank you so much, Amy. Thanks for having me and for these kind words. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: So, we are awaiting word right now about whether Egypt will be forced to reopen Mada Masr, a place where you actually, I think, published your first words. You wrote throughout your six years in prison. But talk about — well, first, start with the title, and talk about what it meant to win the National Book Award in the United States, the place you wanted to stay, to be in exile, to be protected, but could not reenter for the award ceremony.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. Thank you. I mean, of course, it was a gutting thing to not be able to, you know, attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising. You know, we all know how this U.S. administration is now trying to keep everyone who criticizes policies out, especially when it comes, you know, to our region, especially when it’s around Palestine. You know, and if you’re a citizen of another country that doesn’t, you know, need a visa, they don’t want you. They just detain you at the point of entry at the airport. But if you do, like in my case, they just deny you, you know, at the embassy.

And I just — yeah, they love repeating the idea that the visa is, you know, a privilege and not a right. This is kind of the mantra that they keep, you know, repeating to everyone. But, yeah, this, I think, is just intentional distraction from the most important point here, which is that the visa process is being weaponized, and has been now for a while, as a form of transnational repression, which we’re very familiar with in Egypt, as well, because the Egyptian state also uses this form of transnational repression, you know, denying us certain paperwork and stuff like that to punish you for political speech and to keep certain bodies that you deem undesirable outside. So, same for the U.S. So, the visa denial itself being weaponized in that way is the issue, not the fact that the, yes, consul office can deny or approve, etc. So, I think this should be, yeah, the headline, really.

But it was also, like, very sad, I think, in a way that is very specific to my personal journey, you know, as a — this is not new to me. As a kid, you know, I worked my whole life to earn a scholarship to study engineering at this great school that my family couldn’t afford at the time. And then I was arrested on the eve of my first day as a freshman. This is — I speak about this in the book — before I get to live this dream. And then, when I was released in 2020, it happened straight into COVID in 2020. And I started, like, when the lockdown was being lifted, and I started slowly rebuilding community. Because of my writing with Mada Masr, actually, because I continued writing with Mada post-prison, word kind of circulated. Relatives who were well connected told me that my name is being kind of floated again for rearrest. And eventually, I was forced to flee Egypt because of that writing with Mada Masr. And since then, you know, I’ve never been able to share a room with Egyptian readers of my work, except accidentally in exile, you know, when we’re all, like, kind of shunned away from Egypt together. So I’ve had to do it from a distance.

And now, you know, this book, which I imagined writing from prison, which I wrote, you know, throughout my time in the U.S., and then, just as I was about to graduate from my MFA in the U.S., which this book was the graduation, the thesis for — right? — you know, I was forced again to temporarily leave for safety concerns of ICE targeting, as you mentioned, because of my political writing and pro-Palestine activism on campus. And so, I had to graduate from my MFA remotely, as well, witness that moment, you know, be celebrated remotely by people in the room that I was unable to be in. And I wanted to bring my family over to the U.S. to have that graduation ceremony, that prison denied us in Egypt, and we were deprived of that again.

I couldn’t do a U.S. book tour. And now the book, you know, has made it all the way into that room of the National Book Award. And, you know, to have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love who have witnessed this journey, it is gutting. But in a way, it is also just the story of my life. This is not new.

And still, I think I need to redirect all this back, you know, to Egyptian political prisoners, because as I said in my speech, a life that I’m living right now beyond prison, in which my dreams could even be crushed in this way, that was the dream back in prison. I dreamed of a day when I have these, like, unincarcerated people problems. But there are 60,000 political prisoners, you know, who don’t even have the luxury of such precarity, that at least opens into possibility, right? So, I think, yeah, I always want to redirect it to them. I am blessed, no matter what, like, everything that happened that was very sad and gutting and everything. But I always try to put that in relation to people back home behind bars in Egypt, my friends, Ayman and everyone else still behind bars. I’m still blessed to have these problems. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: Tell us why you named the book Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, I mean Huna, huna is the Arabic word for “here.” And it was inspired by a popular Arab protest song, “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which means “We Will Remain Here.” And I first heard that song, you know, up close on my third night in detention. We were in this, like, military camp in the middle of the desert, very excruciating physical conditions, where 68 of us were crammed into a tiny room, piled on top of one another. There were some people that were shot and wounded, so it was very heavy. My father was with me at the time. He was dying.

And then, out of nowhere, the guards finally allowed in the homemade food our families had brought to the gate. So, our families would come every day; they’d be sent back. But that day, they just brought in the food. And then, for the first time since the arrest, we had a taste of home.

And then something very magical happened. We just began to sing. The mood got lighter, and we began to sing. And one of the songs was “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which goes, “We will remain here until the pain subsides. We will remain here. The melody will sweeten.” And, you know, we sang together, and I started feeling those chills on my arms. You could feel that everyone in the room was entering this sort of visceral moment together.

And I found myself thinking, fascinated, that I didn’t want to remain here. Like, who wants — you know, none of us wants to remain here. We couldn’t wait to escape this room fast enough. My father was dying. We were being tortured. People were shot. So, what was this huna? What was this “here” that we were so touched by, that we were all actively choosing to inhabit together? What were we entering?

And I think I would say my book — if I would kind of put it in one line, I’d say it is a six-year pursuit of this huna, like the question of what it means to inhabit a space that is designed to erase you in body, in language, in your very sense of personhood, and still find ways to be. So, I try to trace, you know, that sense of nonphysical hereness and witness, that repeatedly saves me from being wholly conquered by prison.

And you also mentioned the becoming part, which is important to me, because I was arrested — I think sometimes that gets lost, the fact that I was arrested at 17 years old. So, to me, this is not just prison and revolution. It is also becoming, because I say this is a coming-of-age story. And so many people come to this political awakening that I had, you know, in high school age. They start getting politically agitated or involved. And to me, it happened that I went into prison in those formative years. So, my whole history of activism was two months — right? — after the Rabaa massacre until October 6, and then I was arrested. So, incarceration, in a way, was this school in which I was thinking about the world and my positionality inside it.

So, I was just politically activated before I went into prison, and I went into prison with all those agitated questions that were so unsettled for me. I was so angry. I carried so much rage at the military dictatorship, the police state. And I felt like I had a moral compass. But it was mostly motivated not by, you know, theory or intellectual thought or engaging with political theory. It was just rage at seeing certain injustices and wanting to intervene and be part of removing them or restoring justice. So, to me, that was — you know, I see people massacred, a military dictatorship. I think, “These things are wrong, and I don’t want to be on this side. I want to be on the other side that is against them.”

But in prison, I get into a more, I think, sophisticated approach. In prison, I think you have — you know, you have nothing more than time, and you sit down, and you just question everything. And I think prison forces you to confront so many not only political questions, but also very existential questions, you know, about what it means to be here, to be human, to be in relation to other humans, to your own father, to your friends, your mom, and what kinds of obligations does that carry.

So, every day, I was encountering new things that agitated me even more, and that were forcing me, you know, to think. You’re beaten. You’re tortured. You’re being beaten by those batons every day. You see your father hit. Everything around you radicalizes you and makes you think, you know, “I cannot afford to look away from these things. I don’t have the luxury of looking away from these questions,” because the batons are beating me every single day. I just cannot not think about them and my relationship to them and to other people fighting them, and whether I think of them, again, as allies or even political enemies. So, momentarily in prison, I have to align with factions that, you know, I don’t align with politically. It forces me to think about these questions. Like, in my cell, I don’t agree with you politically. I’m very aggravated by you. But we step up outside the cell, and the same police officers are beating us. So, what does that mean in terms of, you know, allyship, mobilization, working together? So, yeah, all those questions at 17, you wouldn’t be thinking about, I think. But I couldn’t afford not to, because my survival depended on grappling with them in prison.

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, this is also a story of a father and son, a mother and son, a brother, a cousin. Talk about how you were first detained with your dad. And it’s a relationship that carries throughout the book. I mean, you go from being a son to being your dad’s protector, to having to separate from your father. My goodness, I mean, you were arrested at the age of 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. One thing I always like to bring up about this is, one of my dear friends, when she read the manuscript of the book for the first time, before it was published, she told me, “Do you know what this book is?” And I told he, “What?” And she said, “This is a love letter to Baba.” And I found that very moving, because I do think this is one of — at least one of the things that this book is, because, you know, my father was apolitical. Like, he wasn’t even involved in politics. And I was a very hot-headed teenager. I really wanted to be on the streets. I was very — again, I was — I had this awakening, and I was attending protests very — you know, every single day, maybe three protests, you know, in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening. And they tolerated — my parents tolerated that for a while.

But then, on October 6, that was a particularly dangerous day. This is the Armed Forces Day. And protesters wanted to break into Tahrir Square. And because of its symbolic value, you know, revolutionary value, the police would get very brutal when people attempt to even approach Tahrir Square. Up until today, it’s a very heavily securitized area. And so, what happens, the arrangement is my mother forced my father to basically come chaperone me, you know, to this protest, to look out for me and make sure that I don’t get harmed or arrested, which, you know, doesn’t work out as planned, obviously.

So, we go there. I start shooting a video. I’m, like, speaking enthusiastically. I leave the car. He yells at me to come back, so I go back inside. I shoot from the window. And then I don’t notice there are two plainclothes officers standing right next to the window, who kind of, from my commentary, kind of deduce that I’m aligned with what’s happening. So, they, you know, pull the door open. They wrench me out. They start beating me, take my phone. And then my father comes, and he starts trying to wrench me away, you know, from their arms. And then they end up arresting him, as well. So, my father gets arrested just because, you know, I made him be in that space, which, of course, we can always argue that it’s a structural issue, it’s a state’s issue. But guilt, you know, doesn’t — it doesn’t work like that. And so, my — the whole six year begins from that kind of inciting incident and that guilt. It’s a very guilt-ridden story, you know, toward my father.

And we’ve always, my father and I, struggled, I think, to express affection to one another. There’s also commentary about Arab masculinity in the book a lot, and specifically father-son relationships. So, we struggled to do that, and I think we carried so much and so many unsaid things inside both of us. And through prison, it was very difficult to communicate, because you’re used to seeing your father as this protective figure, right? And then, in prison, you suddenly realize he is helpless, he cannot protect you. And in a way, he does his best to protect me in all those small ways in prison, of course, but in the bigger scheme of things, he cannot get me my freedom, right? And I cannot get him his freedom. And, you know, the state loves to weaponize love, the Egyptian state, any fascist state, really. So, in prison, they used that against us. They hurt my father to get to me. They hurt me to get to him, and so on. So it was a very difficult situation.

But what I also try to explore in the book is the avenues that opened up once my father and I were not only father and son in prison. I suddenly started seeing him in all those other kind of roles. He was also a prisoner in relation to the state, a prison cellmate or, you know, a prison mate to other prisoners, which was both difficult, but I think also opened up different avenues of communication between us, because sometimes, I don’t know, we’d have a fight in the cell, and we’d fight together with — like, against people and be aligned with one another, and I think, “Oh, my father and I are co-conspirators now.” There’s that first scene in the book where we do this. And through the night, my father, for the first time ever, he rests his hand, you know, on my back and leaves it there through the night. And I remember that being one of the first instances in my life where he touches me in that way.

So, when he read the book after, you know, it was published — I gave him the Arabic. I wrote it in Arabic. It’s coming out in Arabic, and he read the Arabic version. And again, he doesn’t — he was so struck, I think, by the intensity of the love, because I couldn’t express it to him verbally. So, he just said, “You know, I understand so many things much better now,” and then went on to, like, fact-check the entire book, because that’s his — you know, his language of love. So, eventually, I think this is just the sweetest, I think, closure that could have happened to this harrowing experience that we shared together. And if he was the only reader, you know, of this book, if this was the only thing to come out of it, that would have been enough for me.

AMY GOODMAN: And, of course, he gets out before you and then tries to get you out, and ultimately does, based on the fact that you were arrested at 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, and it is — I was wrongly tried — wrongfully tried as an adult instead of a minor. And this is — again, throughout the book, you come across the absurdity and arbitrariness, you know, of the Egyptian state. I was 17 at the time of arrest, two months shy of 18, right? So I had two months to turn 18. And then, the officer that arrested me breaks my ID, or both of our IDs, delivered us to the police station. And just so randomly, because of that, I get processed as an adult, and then I just keep getting processed as an adult throughout. In the prosecution, my lawyer ends up, you know, submitting appeal after appeal. None of them gets looked into, because we’re in Egypt. We get tried as this package deal, right? All of us together in a mass trial.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman, I want to continue this conversation after the show, but I want you to stay with us, because we’re going to go to Cairo right now.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: OK, yeah, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: This story doesn’t end, and I want you to be a part of it. We’re going to Cairo, Egypt, where an appeal was just heard in the case against Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr, for operating an unlicensed website, they’re saying, though she’s been operating it for years. Late last month, she was fined $50,000 or to shut down Mada Masr, following an expedited trial where her lawyers were denied time to prepare a defense, call witnesses or submit documentation. Lina Attalah is also facing charges for publishing so-called false news, that could lead to her imprisonment. We’re going right now outside the court to Hossam Bahgat, founder and director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, part of Mada Masr’s legal team, just outside the courthouse. And I want Abdelrahman to respond to what you report to us. Do we have a decision from the court whether Mada Masr can be reopened, Hossam?

HOSSAM BAHGAT: Thank you, Amy, for having me.

No, I mean, the defense team finished their oral pleadings and submitted the requests. The court has adjourned the session, and we should get a decision on this final appeal by the end of today. I mean, the good thing is that at least it looked more like a courtroom and more like a normal trial today compared to the absurdity that we saw in the first instance. Unfortunately, though, we don’t have any signs that there is an intent to look fairly at the situation, the position of Mada Masr. Today, the lawyers not only challenged the decision to convict Lina and shut down Mada Masr —

AMY GOODMAN: You’re breaking up.

HOSSAM BAHGAT: — and confiscate all its —

AMY GOODMAN: Hossam, you’re breaking up, but I want to tell people you can go to see our interview with Lina Attalah that I did with Anjali Kamat just as she was facing all of this, and also you can go to democracynow.org to see our visit to Mada Masr when we were in Egypt. I want to give Abdelrahman ElGendy the last word, though. You thank Lina Attalah and our former producer Sharif Abdel Kouddous for being able to find a way to get your words out of prison. Ultimately, you would smuggle them out. Is that right?

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yes, absolutely. I began writing in that way, smuggling my words out in prison. And I think you just — you know, once you, as a political prisoner, get a taste of that magic of being able to smuggle your language out to the world, and then receive the world’s language back in response, you just cannot stop. And Mada were the first place to, you know, offer my words a home, is how I thank them. And they feature in the book, as well, because Mada, you know, they sent me wanting to publish, you know, some of the things that I smuggled out, and ever since I had this relationship with them, I published six more pieces with Mada Masr from prison. And that was important to me.

I think that the project of the current Egyptian military dictatorship is — it’s a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before. It was possible, and therefore it is possible. And they don’t want it to be a thinkable or imaginable thing anymore.

And I think Mada Masr is a huge part of that. I cannot understand or speak about the campaign against Mada Masr, you know, divorced from the idea of this more bigger project of erasure of the Egyptian state, because Mada carries so much of the archive, you know, of our revolutionary history. It is the place that people like me, in prison and after prison, can go write in. It is the place where, you know, Alaa El-Fattah, who published “Graffiti for Two People” with Ahmed Douma. It is the place that speaks about prison letters and communication. And so, to erase it is to erase an archive. And also, it is to erase the more, I think, intimate and dangerous thing, is we go to Mada Masr to feel less alone, to remember, you know, that we were many, and therefore we are many still today. We have not been — you know, as Alaa says, we have not been fully defeated. And that, to me, is important. Maybe we’re not — maybe we are defeated in a way, but not wholly, not fully.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy, I want to thank you for being with us and for this incredible memoir. It’s called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. It has just won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and we’ll link to your New Yorker and Nation pieces. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman. This is Democracy Now!

author: Amir Khafagy
title: Airport Drivers Enter Third Year of Longest Ongoing Strike in US
content:
SkyHop Global workers have alleged backlash from management, which has so far refused to recognize the union since 2024.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

It’s 6 a.m. on a chilly October day, and outside the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Times Square, a few dozen workers already stand with picket signs in hand.

Gathered under the shadow of a giant inflatable rat known as Scabby, the workers are all striking drivers for SkyHop Global, an airport transportation company. With signs in hand, they wait to picket SkyHop vans driven by replacement workers who, throughout the day, pick up and drop off airline staff.

It’s a scene that has played out countless times since the workers first went out on strike right before Thanksgiving two years ago, on Nov. 24, 2024. Although a majority of the 60 workers, mostly immigrants, voted to join Teamsters Local 210 on May 10, 2024, they have fought an uphill battle to get management to the negotiating table.

Since they went on strike, workers have alleged retaliation, intimidation, and surveillance from management, which has so far refused to recognize the workers’ union. Many, struggling to pay their bills, have been forced to take second jobs like driving for Uber, while others have not found any jobs at all.

As the workers prepare to spend yet another Thanksgiving on the picket line — in what is now the nation’s longest ongoing strike — they hope their struggle is not forgotten.

“No, I won’t cross the picket line because this is for our benefit,” said Ana Solorzano, a 26-year-old SkyHop driver originally from Ecuador.

Edison Bonifas, a 57-year-old immigrant from Ecuador, says he has struggled to support his wife and four kids since he first walked off the job. Initially, he thought the strike would last only a few weeks. But as the strike enters its third year, making ends meet has become increasingly difficult. Although he’s tried getting another job, he hasn’t had any luck.

“The thing is, we’re waiting and waiting,” he told Documented at the rally on Oct. 21. “It’s basically hard right now because there are no jobs.”

What keeps him from crossing the picket line is his desire to secure health insurance, one of the key demands of the union. With a sick wife, it’s a demand that hits close to home.

“You know, you cannot live in New York City if you don’t have a medical,” he said.

SkyHop Global provides ground transportation for airline crew members between airports and hotels. Since the strike, several airlines have terminated contracts with SkyHop in the New York market; it currently only transports crew for Delta Air Lines.

Since its founding in 2014, the company has grown its operations to 33 airports across the country, including LaGuardia and JFK Airports. It now operates 200 passenger transport vans and employs 300 drivers, and is estimated to have generated over $70 million in revenue, according to court documents.

Instead of negotiating with the union to get drivers like Bonifas back to work, SkyHop has chosen to bust any efforts to unionize. On Aug. 31, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) General Counsel published an investigation that found SkyHop had violated the National Labor Relations Act when it “unlawfully tried to stop its employees from unionizing” and “violated the Act with complete disregard for its employees and their rights.”

According to the report, SkyHop management discharged at least 14 employees between 2024 and 2025 who were suspected of supporting the union effort. SkyHop also allegedly engaged in a widespread campaign of interrogations, surveillance, and retaliation.

The General Counsel report noted that one of the ways SkyHop surveilled workers was through the use of a fleet management technology called Samsara. Through cameras installed in each SkyHop van, Samsara generates safety scores for each driver on a 100-point scale. When there is a driver infraction, such as using a phone while driving or not wearing a seat belt, Samsara would alert management, which would then adjust a driver’s safety score and create a record for potential discipline. The General Counsel’s report found that SkyHop adjusted Samsara during the height of the 2024 union drive to target employees suspected of supporting the union, with certain minor infractions weighted more or less heavily to target specific workers.

“They just fire you for anything,” Amar Hemraj, a 32-year-old Guyanese driver, told Documented. “If you don’t wear that seatbelt, they can write you up for that.”

While driving for SkyHop before he went on strike, Hemraj says that he knew his every move was being recorded.

“It was an invasion of privacy, you know, like let’s say I’m on the phone with my wife, and we’re discussing something personal,” he said. “We weren’t feeling safe. We weren’t feeling job security.”

In addition to surveillance through Samsara, the General Counsel observed that the company would conduct “ride-alongs” where management would ride with drivers on the job to gauge their union stance. Managers allegedly kept a detailed spreadsheet that listed workers who were for or against the union. Detailed group text messages obtained by Documented via court documents show that SkyHop management coordinated to identify and interrogate pro-union employees.

Many of the group chat messages show the company’s co-founder and CEO, Kristine Scotto, directly asking managers if they thought certain workers were pro-union or not.

Neither Scotto nor SkyHop responded to Documented’s request for comment via phone and email.

The General Counsel’s report also found that those fired by SkyHop were disciplined disproportionately to their alleged infractions, and that discipline was related to their union activity.

One of the fired workers was Mamunur Rahid, a 47-year-old driver from Bangladesh. Despite having a driver score of 94 out of 100, Rahid was terminated in August 2025 after a minor fender bender. According to the NLRB General Counsel report, Rahid testified that prior to being fired, he was repeatedly asked to sign a petition opposing the union and that he would receive a $3 per hour raise if he signed. Although he did not join the strike, he was a supporter of the union and refused to sign the letter opposing the union.

“I only understood one thing that one of my neighbors told me that it is good to have a union job, and that’s why I did not want to separate from the Union,” he told the NLRB.

When he was fired, his manager allegedly told him he should “go join them,” meaning the striking workers. The General Counsel found that his firing was retaliation for not signing the documents.

Despite the findings of the General Counsel, the NLRB has not yet made a ruling. The NLRB could compel SkyHop to rehire Rahid or the other fired workers, or force the company to the negotiating table.

While the case works its way through the NLRB, for workers like Solorzano, the strike has already had a transformative effect on her life. Never having participated in anything political before, she knows how important solidarity is.

“I’m 26 years old, and I’m with people from different countries who are also part of this,” she said. “I’m friends with them, and I hear about their situation, and also I see my situation.”

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Trump Judicial Nominee at Center of GOP Drama Signed Off on Deadly Boat Strikes
content:
Nominated to be a federal judge, T. Elliot Gaiser signed off on deadly airstrikes experts call extrajudicial executions.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Media coverage of Republican infighting over judicial nominee T. Elliot Gaiser has focused on the strong words exchanged between Texas Senators John Cornyn and Ted Cruz. President Donald Trump nominated Gaiser to become a federal judge in Texas, but Cornyn blocked a crucial committee vote on November 18 to advance the pick forward.

“Everyone knows that I am a notorious cusser and screamer and that Ted is a fragile thing,” Cornyn said on November 21 in a social media post describing a previous heated exchange between the two lawmakers. Cornyn has argued that Gaiser is not from Texas and has little trial experience, while Cruz accuses Cornyn of handing an open judicial seat to Democrats.

However, what has received far less attention is Gaiser’s role in producing the legal opinion that greenlit the U.S. military’s deadly airstrikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean that the Trump administration has accused, without evidence, of smuggling drugs. The strikes have killed more than 200 people in what human rights groups say are effectively extrajudicial executions in blatant violation of U.S. and international law.

“We’re talking about legal opinions used to justify military strikes that have killed hundreds of people, alongside a broader pattern of putting the president’s personal interests ahead of the law,” said Michael Teter, co-founder of the Legal Accountability Center, in a statement.

Gaiser currently serves as assistant attorney general in the Justice Department, where he leads the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC). He is also Trump’s nominee for a lifetime federal judgeship in the Northern District of Texas. Cornyn used a procedural maneuver last week to block the Senate Judiciary Committee from advancing Gaiser’s nomination. However, Cornyn remains under pressure from Cruz and other conservatives to reverse course and allow a vote on Gaiser as Republicans race to confirm Trump nominees before a Democratic majority takes over in January.

Meanwhile, the Legal Accountability Center filed a bar complaint against Gaiser on November 18, calling for an investigation into his role in providing legal cover for the deadly airstrikes on civilian boats in international waters. The complaint also cites a series of opinions released by the OLC that allegedly prioritize Trump’s personal interests over federal law, including a controversial opinion declaring that the Presidential Records Act, a key oversight law, is unconstitutional and does not apply to Trump.

“Government lawyers have a duty to tell the president when the law says ‘no,’ not simply find ways to justify whatever he wants to do,” Teter said, adding that the allegations are “extraordinarily serious.”

At the center of the complaint is a secret legal opinion written under Gaiser’s leadership to provide legal justification for the Trump administration’s airstrikes on civilian boats suspected of smuggling drugs. Issued on September 5, 2025, the legal opinion followed an infamous September 2 attack in which two shipwrecked survivors of an initial U.S. airstrike were killed by a secondary (or “double tap”) strike while clinging to the wreckage in the water.

Rep. Jim Himes (D-Connecticut), who serves on the House Intelligence Committee and saw video of the strikes, pointed out that the second strike was impermissible by U.S. military manual standards. The bar complaint against Gaiser alleges he failed to exercise independent judgment and provided legal cover for unlawful killings.

While the legal opinion remains classified, court filings indicate the 49-page memo was signed by Gaiser, according to the bar complaint. Members of Congress who have seen the memo have publicly outlined its legal reasoning, which rests on a theory that the U.S. is engaged in a formal armed conflict with drug smugglers. The Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), a human rights group, calls this reasoning “badly flawed.”

The first Trump administration official to advocate on the record for military strikes on civilian vessels appears to be Emil Bove, Trump’s former personal attorney known for his extremism and loyalty to the president. In February 2025, Bove criticized traditional anti-drug smuggling efforts and declared the U.S. should “just sink the boats.” Trump then tapped Bove to sit on a federal appeals court, a controversial nomination narrowly approved by the Senate by a 50-49 vote in July 2025.

The boat strikes are a major escalation of the war on drugs and a twisted point of pride for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. At least 244 people have been killed in international waters by dozens of U.S. airstrikes since September 2025, according to the Drug Policy Alliance. The Trump administration claims the strikes target what it calls “narcoterrorists,” but family members and local officials have said that victims include fishers, human trafficking victims, and laborers.

More than a dozen fishers from Ecuador recently filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration after surviving an airstrike on their boat in the Pacific Ocean. The fishers say they have no connection to the drug trade, but U.S. drones sank their boat on March 17 and left two of them with serious burns, according to The Guardian.

The Office of Legal Counsel’s legal opinion reportedly claims the boat strikes target drugs for destruction, not people, and any casualties are treated as enemy combatants or collateral damage, The Guardian has reported. The targets are identified using a secret list of 24 drug cartels that the Trump administration unilaterally designated as international “terrorist” groups to justify military operations against them, according to WOLA.

“The boat strikes are a deadly evolution of the drug war, following a pattern of expanding government power at the expense of individual rights and democratic safeguards,” said Theshia Naidoo, a policy director at Drug Policy Alliance, in an interview.

Naidoo said the Trump administration claims the strikes are defending the nation from drugs smuggled into the U.S. to kill Americans, but in reality, the boats that are being blown up have little or nothing to do with the overdose crisis. Most fatal overdoses are caused by synthetic opioids, which are made in small labs in the U.S. and Mexico, not transported from South America in boats. In fact, experts worry Trump’s drug war policies will intensify the overdose crisis over time.

“The drugs that are typically transported in the Caribbean Sea or the Pacific Ocean — it’s usually cocaine, and it may be destined to other [countries], not the U.S.,” Naidoo said. “The driver of the overdose crisis in the U.S. is really fentanyl and synthetic opioids, so the boat strikes really have nothing to do with addressing the overdose crisis.”

Naidoo said the boat strikes have not achieved the stated goal of reducing the availability of illicit drugs in the United States. The Trump administration’s own law enforcement agencies acknowledge that traffickers have simply found ways to avoid the strikes.

“The result is a drug policy agenda that invests in violence instead of the health-based solutions that save lives and strengthen communities,” Naidoo said.

Naidoo said the Trump administration has slashed funding for health care and public health initiatives that are credited with helping to reduce overdose deaths by 27 percent in 2024, including a $333 million cut in federal funding for harm reduction programs that connect users with the overdose reversal drug naloxone as well as addiction treatment. Naidoo said the Trump administration treats drugs as a national security threat rather than a public health issue, and the “trade-offs are stark.”

“At home, federal funding for addiction treatment, overdose prevention, mental health services, and programs that support people in crisis have been slashed, including $1 trillion for Medicaid over 10 years, which is the largest payer of addiction and mental health treatment in the U.S.,” Naidoo said. “Abroad, the administration has spent billions in military funding for weapons and war.”

Naidoo said Trump’s war on drugs is also a war on democracy, an argument the Drug Policy Alliance lays out in a detailed new report. Originally declared by President Richard Nixon in the 1970s to criminalize the antiwar and Black liberation movements, the war on drugs has for decades justified the militarization of police and expansion of government power at the expense of individual rights and democratic safeguards. The boat strikes are a dangerous escalation of this trend.

“In the latest escalation of the drug war, the administration has treated suspicion of drugs as a matter of war — not drug enforcement, going above the law and circumventing due process,” Naidoo wrote in an email. “Instead of investigation, arrest, and prosecution, the people on these boats faced lawless execution.”

The boat strikes are not Trump’s only drug war escalation on Gaiser’s watch. The Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion on December 23, 2025, stating Trump “likely could conclude” that a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro would not constitute “war in the constitutional sense,” according to the Legal Accountability Center’s bar complaint. The White House cited the opinion to attack Venezuela without approval from Congress.

About 80 people were killed when the U.S. invaded Venezuela on January 3 and kidnapped Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Maduro now faces drug trafficking charges in the U.S., to which he has pleaded not guilty. International experts at the United Nations condemned the operation as a blatant and dangerous violation of international law.

While Cornyn has blocked Trump from installing Gaiser as a federal judge in Texas for now, the senator remains under pressure from Cruz and other Republicans to let the Senate Judiciary Committee advance Gaiser’s nomination before the GOP’s lame duck session ends in December.

“Perhaps [Gaiser] was interested in a judicial appointment and recognizes that he is never going to get one through a Senate controlled by the Democratic Party, and this was the last one that was available,” Teter said.

However, Cornyn is facing retirement from the Senate and has shown a willingness to buck the president after Trump endorsed his primary challenger, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, earlier this year. Paxton defeated Cornyn with Trump’s endorsement but went on to lose by a wide margin to Democrat James Talarico in a race that stunned Republicans nationwide.

author: Brett Wilkins
title: New Pentagon Strategy Embraces Potential Use of “Tactical” Nuclear Weapons
content:
Senators Edward Markey and Jeff Merkley have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “to drop these plans immediately.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A pair of Democratic senators on Tuesday urged US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to abandon the Pentagon’s renewed embrace of so-called “tactical” or battlefield nuclear weapons under President Donald Trump, warning that the development and potential use of lower-yield fissile armaments makes nuclear war more likely.

Sens. Edward Markey (D-Mass.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) sent a letter to Hegseth condemning the Trump administration’s reported push to widen options for so-called “limited” nuclear warfare, arguing that the strategy threatens to undermine decades of efforts to prevent the use of such weapons after the US unilaterally waged history’s only nuclear war over 80 years ago.

“More nuclear weapons, particularly lower-yield weapons that leaders may perceive to be more ‘usable,’ will only increase the risk of a catastrophic nuclear war,” wrote the senators, who co-chair the Nuclear Weapons and Arms Control Working Group.

“Tactical nuclear weapons are the gateway drug to nuclear destruction, and we urge you to drop these plans immediately,” they added.

The letter comes amid reports that the Pentagon is revising US nuclear guidance to emphasize tactical weapons and limited nuclear options in conflicts, possibly including the increasingly protracted Iran War.

The push aligns with Hegseth’s doctrine of “maximum lethality,” which — when paired with his embrace of autonomous warfare and stated disdain for “stupid rules of engagement” designed to minimize civilian harm — risks treating the mass slaughter of noncombatants as the unfortunate but acceptable price of battlefield success.

Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby has defended the mainstreaming of tactical nukes as necessary to provide the president with more options in any war against a nuclear-armed adversary.

“We want to be able to give the president and secretary credible, rational nuclear options,” Colby said at an August conference hosted by US Strategic Command.

While Trump’s own intelligence agencies have concluded that Iran does not have and is not trying to build nuclear weapons, in addition to the United States, China, France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, Russia, and the United Kingdom possess such arms.

Arms control advocates warn that the very idea of a limited nuclear war is dangerously misleading. A weapon’s smaller explosive yield does not guarantee that a nuclear-armed adversary will respond in a similarly restrained fashion, or that a catastrophic escalation could be avoided, as the 1983 “Proud Prophet” war game chillingly demonstrated.

Whitley Strieber and James Kunetka’s bestselling 1984 novel Warday recounts in an investigative journalistic style a “limited” nuclear exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union that lasts less than an hour, destroying just a handful of cities on each side. Yet tens of millions of people are killed in the United States alone on the day of the war and in the following years, and five years on, much of the world has been transformed almost beyond recognition.

Recalling that perilous era of hair-trigger tensions and nuclear near-misses, Markey and Merkley noted that during the Cold War, the US military maintained thousands of tactical nuclear weapons, including torpedoes, artillery shells, short-range missiles, and even portable atomic “backpack” devices designed for soldiers to carry behind enemy lines on suicide missions.

As the Cold War wound down, the US eventually abandoned much of that arsenal. In 1991, then-President George HW Bush announced plans to eliminate virtually all US tactical nuclear weapons, and the country’s stockpile of such weapons has since declined by more than 90%, according to the senators’ letter.

But the Trump administration has been moving in the opposite direction. Trump’s first term saw the deployment of the lower-yield W76-2 warhead on submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and the president is currently pursuing a new nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile and an accelerated weapons development initiative known as the Rapid Capabilities Program.

“If President Trump perceives the use of lower-yield weapons as more credible, their deployment increases the risk of nuclear war,” Markey and Merkley wrote.

A September analysis by the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy warned that expanding the role of tactical nuclear weapons risks normalizing their use in military conflicts and potentially triggering a renewed nuclear arms race.

The rise of lethal autonomous weapons systems, popularly called killer robots, has added an unprecedented level of risk — and urgency — to the equation.

Markey and Merkley urge Hegseth to abandon plans to expand the development and potential use of tactical nuclear weapons, while demanding answers about the Pentagon’s nuclear strategy, weapons programs, and whether it believes a limited nuclear exchange could avoid escalating into all-out thermonuclear Armageddon.

“Any use of nuclear weapons carries with it the high and inescapable risk of escalation into catastrophic nuclear war, which no one would win,” the senators wrote. “The clear firebreak against such a worldwide disaster is to draw a bright line between nuclear weapons and all other weapons. We must strive to keep that firebreak wide and strong.”

“Blurring the line by developing more tactical nuclear weapons is deeply unwise and increases nuclear risk,” they added. “We urge you to abandon these plans immediately.”

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: Affordability Worries Go Beyond Prices. Addressing Them Demands Systemic Change.
content:
We must increase workers’ resources and limit capitalists’ and elites’ political power, says economist Gerald Epstein.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

“Affordability” was the buzzword of the 2026 midterm elections, echoed often by Democrats as they scored a massive victory and captured both chambers of Congress. Indeed, the cost of living was the top issue on the mind of voters as they headed to the ballot box, according to polls. But the increasing economic pressure on working-class people is also inextricably linked in voters’ mind with corruption and the war on Iran. Now, as Democrats get ready to put forth new policies under their new majorities, it still isn’t exactly clear what a focus on “affordability” actually means.

As renowned progressive economist Gerald Epstein points out in the interview that follows, “affordability” is more than prices. The “affordability crisis” points to a plethora of economic and political ills facing the contemporary United States that need to be thoroughly addressed in order to make average citizens thrive. These include extreme wealth concentration, government corruption, corporate greed and unaccountability, an out-of-control health care system, unfair tax policy, and bloated military spending. Epstein argues that the policies to address these economic and social ills are already well-known, and only political will is needed to fix the broken system.

Epstein is professor of economics and co-director of the Political Economy Research Institute (PERI) at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the project called Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C. J. Polychroniou: The 2026 midterm elections have been interpreted as a referendum on President Donald Trump as voters worried about the state of the economy under his administration. In fact, “affordability” was the dominant issue in the election cycle as many people in the U.S. are struggling with the cost of housing, groceries, and health care, and worry about their financial prospects, all while the rich continue to get richer. Do you agree with this interpretation of the midterm elections? Moreover, what do we mean by “affordability” and how is it to be addressed?

Gerald Epstein: I do agree. The 2026 midterm elections could indeed be dubbed the “affordability” midterms. Poll after poll, both before and after the elections, identified the rise in the cost of living due to Trump’s Iranian adventure and romance with tariffs as the top concerns of voters. And close to the top was voters’ dissatisfaction with the corruption of Trump, his family, and his minions. In fact, corruption did not rise to the top of voters’ priorities until Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff effectively tied Trump’s corruption to American families’ affordability problems. And now that Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, they seem to be converging on a two-pronged strategy: promote legislation that will improve “affordability” and investigate the Trump administration’s corruption.

All of this raises several questions: What is meant by “affordability?” What are the policy tools available to the government at the federal but also state and local levels that could make life more affordable for Americans? And, finally, is this “affordability agenda” sufficient to address the multiple challenges facing U.S. workers?

There are many “affordability” agendas to choose from. The Congressional Progressive Caucus released a “New Affordability Agenda” in April. According to the caucus: “The New Affordability Agenda is a slate of creative new bills to help families get ahead by making things cheaper, putting money in pockets and getting big money out of politics.” The agenda includes policies such as making prescription drugs cheaper by making it easier to produce generic drugs; reducing grocery prices by reducing grocery chain monopolies; making housing more affordable by increasing rental assistance and assistance for down payments; levying windfall profits tax on oil to be returned to consumers; limiting AI’s use in dynamic pricing of products; setting a minimum of two weeks paid vacation for workers; raising federal overtime pay; and getting money out of politics by limiting super PACs.

Clearly, this is not a comprehensive agenda, but it illustrates the key approaches to enhancing affordability: Reduce the costs of good by limiting monopolies and increasing competition; subsidize important goods and services and/or have government provide those goods; tax and redistribute excess profits; and limit the political power of corporations that are trying to protect those profits.

I think it’s important to take note of the fact that this agenda on “affordability” is not confined to prices. It’s important because, as such, it distinguishes “affordability” from a set of policies designed to preserve the status quo and treats it instead as a comprehensive economy strategy to modify the way the U.S. economy works.

Yes, this agenda illustrates that “affordability” is not just about prices; it is also about workers’ incomes, public provision of important goods and services, and limiting the excessive political power of companies that are trying to keep things unaffordable.

However, other action plans go beyond “affordability” and focus more on the underlying power inequalities that have led over many decades to massive increases in income and wealth inequality — inequality that manifests, among other places, in the lack of affordability facing many American families.

The Economic Policy Institute has been especially focused on the wages and incomes side of the affordability trap. It argues that the primary cause of the inability of many families to afford a decent life is a large increase in income and wage inequality, with incomes and wages for the vast majority of Americans lagging far behind what they need to be to afford a decent life. Moreover, the institute argues that this large rise in income inequality has been driven by intentional policy changes that reduced workers’ bargaining power. The key to solving this affordability problem is to facilitate increases in workers’ bargaining power through increasing minimum wages, making it easier for workers to organize unions, and keeping the rate of unemployment low to enhance workers’ wages and power.

A related agenda that seeks to improve affordability through enhanced democratic rights and worker power is contained in the “Solidarity Agenda.” This eight-part action plan includes a focus on enhanced union power, green investment, increased taxation of the very wealthy, and enacting a foreign policy that is focused on solidarity with workers abroad in order to tame the power of multinational corporations.

There are many other agendas, including the Roosevelt Institute’s The Good Life Agenda, which goes well beyond affordability, and I am sure there will be more to come as we approach the 2028 elections.

At PERI, you launched and direct a project called Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America. Tell us how this project approaches “affordability” and some of the specific policies that it advocates for addressing the affordability crisis.

For our project, 40 analysts developed 30 bold economic policies to build a stronger, fairer, greener and more inclusive economy. This set includes a good number of policies that would enhance affordability for U.S. workers and families; but they also go beyond affordability and include an important focus on fairness, dealing with the climate emergency, increasing worker power, and enhancing democracy.

The Game Changers’ affordability agenda includes a detailed proposal for Medicare for All; other policies call for an end to profiteering in health care; creating a fully universal, federally funded child care program; enacting a universal basic income for children; making housing more affordable through national rent control; and providing single-payer national disaster insurance for all.

Housing plays a big role in the affordability crisis. We have a policy to make housing more available through a Social Housing Development Authority. We also explain how we would fund these policies by cutting military spending and raising taxes on the wealthy and corporations.

In addition, we propose policies that enhance well-being and worker power without incurring any increases in public expenditures. These include regulating harmful chemicals, phasing out fossil fuels, passing laws to regulate finance and avoid costly taxpayer bailouts, and increasing workers’ bargaining power by passing just cause protections so workers cannot be fired arbitrarily or in a discriminatory fashion.

These policies enhance affordability but also restore workers’ power, public accountability for corporations, and fairness in the tax system.

In short, as these policy agendas show, to really attack the problem of affordability, we must move well beyond policies to reduce specific prices, and increase the public and private resources that workers have to sustain their lives while limiting the political power of capitalists and elites to prevent workers, families, and communities from thriving.

Democrats will run the show on Capitol Hill come January 3, 2027, but past experience shows that we cannot rely on them to do what is right — especially not when establishment Democrats outnumber progressives. How do activists ramp up pressure on Democrats to do the right thing?

Of course, the first thing is to contact their congressional representative about the issues they feel passionately about. But, probably more effective would be to link up with the many activist groups that are already mobilized around the elections and are promoting parts of this progressive agenda. These include Swing Left, Our Revolution, the Sunrise Movement, and many others. People’s individual voices are powerful, but they are more powerful still when combined into an organized group.

author: William J. Ford
title: Abrego Garcia Self-Deports to Spain After 20-Month Battle With Trump Admin
content:
The Department of Homeland Security had tried to deport the Maryland resident to a third country for months.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.

The move ends 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents in March 2025 and erroneously deported to his native country.

Neither his attorneys nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday from States Newsroom.

But in a statement released shortly after midnight Wednesday morning, the immigration advocacy group We Are CASA said Abrego Garcia had “cleared his name of the Trump administration’s bogus charges against him and walked out of the United States a free man.”

The statement said Abrego Garcia was accompanied on a commercial flight by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney and a We Are CASA representative. It said they were met at the airport by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who removed the ankle monitoring bracelet Abrego Garcia has had to wear since courts ordered him released from detention and returned home to Beltsville.

Abrego Garcia said in the statement that “justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom. I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight,” his statement said. “I feel good. I feel confident. I believe everything will be okay because God is with us.”

Abrego Garcia’s deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.

Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.

It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S. and said he was “relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution.”

“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

Neither Van Hollen nor We Are CASA specified Abrego Garcia’s destination, but news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.

The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Uganda, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.

A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there. But it did not prevent the government from trying to send him to a third country — an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.

Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.

“Mr. Abrego Garcia had been asking permission to leave the country since August 2025,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of his attorneys, in the We Are CASA statement. “The Trump Administration held him and refused to allow him to depart, first in an ICE detention center for five months and then on electronic monitoring in Maryland for almost a year, all the while insisting on deporting him to a series of African countries. That retaliatory deportation campaign has now come to an end.”

Abrego Garcia was eventually returned from El Salvador in June 2025, but was immediately arrested and charged by ICE with human smuggling in Tennessee. Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding in Tennessee, when Abrego was driving an SUV carrying a number of Latino men.

Abrego Garcia was let go with a warning after the traffic stop and the case was closed. But federal officials reopened it two years later and charged Abrego Garcia with human smuggling as soon as he was returned from El Salvador.

Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued the flimsy charges were mere pretext to punish their client after he beat the administration in court. A federal judge in Tennessee agreed in May and tossed the case out as a vindictive prosecution and an abuse of government power.

It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen’s statement said.

Ama Frimpong, We Are CASA’s chief of legal services and another of Abrego Garcia’s attoenrys, called it “a victory that Kilmar gets to choose what comes next.”

“He is choosing where and how to lead his life. He is beginning this new chapter with the safety, freedom, and dignity he fought to reclaim,” Frimpong said in the statement. “That victory belongs first to Kilmar; to Jennifer, whose voice carried their family’s fight across the country; and to their family, who endured more than any family should.

title: AI Data Centers Linked to Hundreds of Premature Deaths Across US, Study Finds
content:

A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) finds that the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) has had substantial negative health and air quality impacts — not just in the areas where most of these centers are being built, but also in regions far away from them.

As a result, hundreds of people across the U.S. are dying annually, the study suggests, with researchers finding that pollution from electricity demands of data centers resulted in around 650 premature deaths in 2023 alone. author: Chris Walker
title: Despite Environmental Worries, Army Blasts Off 68 Barrels of Lead Azide in Iowa
content:
Some scientists urged residents to collect soil from before the blast, to compare with samples after the detonation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The United States Army has detonated 68 barrels of lead azide in southeastern Iowa, disregarding concerns of residents and environmental groups about the potential harms of such an explosion.

The blast occurred around 9 am Central Time. Video from local news outlets showed several plumes of smoke from the detonation, and journalists covering the event said they felt a shockwave afterward.

The Army gave little notice about the planned detonation to local residents, announcing earlier this month that it would occur on November 20. After outcry over the announcement, the Army said it would delay the blast. A lawsuit against the Army from environmental groups further delayed the detonation until a panel of judges on the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals decided earlier this week to allow it to proceed.

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator Lee Zeldin claimed the mitigation efforts for the detonation on Wednesday “exceeded expectations.” President Donald Trump made the same claim in a Truth Social post shortly after the explosion took place. However, environmental experts say it will take more time to determine whether the mitigation efforts were entirely successful, as well as the extent to which hazardous materials were released into the environment.

NEW: The U.S. Army has carried out a controlled detonation at an ammunition plant in Iowa to prevent an uncontrolled explosion. pic.twitter.com/u1k715srLb

New York Times reporter Quinn Glabicki said he and other journalists covering the blast “saw smoke climbing several hundred feet into the air.”

“In the distance, what appeared to be debris flew into the sky,” he added.

The 68 barrels of lead azide amounted to 9,700 pounds of the hazardous bomb-making material. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the small town of Middletown, Iowa. Previous warnings about the planned explosion suggested the toxins could spread beyond a 100-mile radius.

Winds were moving southwest at the time of the detonation, likely pushing any material that reached the atmosphere further into Iowa or potentially into parts of Missouri.

Before the blast, the Army issued a warning, writing: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults, and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

The Army also told nearby residents that, after an “all-clear” was issued after the blast, they should “wet-wipe high-contact exterior surfaces such as patios, decks, window sills, and outdoor play equipment to safely capture and remove any settled dust.”

Lead cleanup is notoriously difficult and often requires intervention from certified professionals. There is no safe level of lead exposure.

Two hours after the detonation, the Army held an inter-agency press conference, describing the situation as a “successful operation,” with one federal official stating that the EPA determined there was a “zero-point-zero percent detection level of lead in the atmosphere.”

Beyond the federal government’s follow-ups, some scientists said they planned to do their own investigations into the aftereffects of the blast. Shannon Bartelt-Hunt, chair of the civil and environmental engineering department at the University of Nebraska, told CNN that she urged residents in the area to collect topsoil samples before the detonation took place.

“I know the Army is doing some testing, but at the same time, I don’t think the extent of the testing that probably needs to be done is something they have fully planned,” Bartelt-Hunt explained.

Trump administration officials have claimed there was no “viable alternative” for disposing of the lead azide, which was at risk of becoming highly unstable. Incoming Democratic federal lawmakers have expressed skepticism about such claims, saying they do not excuse the government’s lack of transparency.

“I remain concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army’s planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa), adding in a social media post before the detonation:

We need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again. The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army’s communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning.

Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D-Iowa) expressed similar sentiments. “Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” Sand said.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Poll: Most Dems Want Congress to Defund War Next Month, Even at Risk of Shutdown
content:
Top Republicans have signaled an openness to defunding the war, as Democrats like Hakeem Jeffries have demurred.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

New polling finds that the majority of Democrats want members of Congress to use next month’s government funding bill to withhold funds for the Iran war, a strategy embraced by progressives and figures like Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) to end the war as soon as possible.

According to University of Maryland polling conducted this past weekend, 51 percent of Democrats say that they support the use of the upcoming funding bill, with a deadline of December 11, to defund the war even if it risks a government shutdown or a presidential veto. By contrast, only 16 percent of Democrats said they oppose the idea — a -35 point margin — while 32 percent said they don’t know.

The idea is also narrowly favored when responses from all ideologies are considered, 31 percent support to 28 percent opposition, despite 48 percent of Republicans opposing the idea.

Earlier this month, a group of four senators — Van Hollen, Michael Bennet (D-Colorado), Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) — vowed in a joint statement to oppose any funding bill that would fund the war. Lawmakers in favor of the effort have made clear that their intention is to effectively dare President Donald Trump to shut down the government in order to fund his war.

“Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict — we must force him to end it,” the lawmakers said. “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war.”

The proposal is imminently achievable. The Washington Post reported this week that top Republicans have said that they are open to allowing the bill to be used to cut off funding for the war in exchange for keeping the government funded. The Post cited Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) as two Republicans who said they are open to the effort.

Thune said that he is “open to anything that keeps the government funded and makes sure that we’ve got our military and national security requirements and needs met.”

In other words, the Democratic base wants Congress to defund the war at the soonest possible opportunity; several Democrats in Congress are pushing for the proposal; and even Republican leaders may be on board.

Part of the reason for this broad-based support may be the vast unpopularity of the war, in which U.S.-Israeli strikes have killed roughly 3,500 people in Iran.

University of Maryland’s polling found that a staggering 80 percent of Democrats say that they want the war to end now “regardless of the terms,” meaning that they would be fine with accepting any of Iran’s and U.S.’s terms in exchange for the war’s end. A majority of all respondents felt the same, at 55 percent, compared to 21 percent who said they prefer the current course, and 18 percent saying they favor a military escalation.

Experts have said that defunding the war is one of the most effective ways to force President Donald Trump to end the military portion of the war, with options like war powers resolutions unable to force his hand.

Some of the people not in support of the proposal, however, are top Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) said last week that he opposes even the idea of barring funds from being used for the war, in favor of a war powers resolution that the Trump administration is likely to ignore. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), facing a challenge to his leadership from one of the top Senate champions of the proposal to defund the war, has been mum on the issue.

The top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, Rosa DeLauro (Connecticut), has suggested that she does not want to use the continuing resolution to shut down the war.

“I think that the American people would like to see us end the war. I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war,” she said last week, her comments undercut by polling finding otherwise.
