author: Amy Goodman
title: Huang’s Return to Nvidia Shows the Unsustainable Power of AI Over the Economy
content:
The scandal over Jensen Huang reflects efforts from establishment hawks to ramp up hostilities between the US and China.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back.

“The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the [S&P 500] this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute.

We also speak with organizer and researcher Tobita Chow, who says Huang’s “spy scandal” that led to his ouster is part of a larger effort by anti-China figures in the U.S. national security establishment to escalate tensions between the countries.

“The national security leadership in both parties in D.C. has been greatly frustrated with President Trump, who has over the past year pursued policies to maintain very warm relations with Xi Jinping,” says Chow, who notes that Secretary of State Marco Rubio is one of the “chief” frustrated China hawks in the administration.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of the chip giant Nvidia, after President Trump personally called into a company board meeting Sunday to push for Huang’s reinstatement. Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago, after news reports revealed he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly in communication with China’s top spy agency. The woman worked with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of buying advanced Nvidia chips, then diverting them to China in violation of U.S. export rules. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist.

During an interview on CNBC, Trump was questioned about his role reinstating Huang.

EAMON JAVERS: Mr. President, did you give the board of directors an assurance that Jensen Huang would not be prosecuted at all for any of these —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I didn’t use the word “prosecuted.”

EAMON JAVERS: — questions around export controls?

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: But I said — I said that we believe — and I put out a statement. I think you probably saw that.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: That we believe he’s fine, he’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough —

CARL QUINTANILLA: There was a —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: — assurance.

AMY GOODMAN: President Trump also admitted that falling stock prices played a role in his decision to push for Huang to be reinstated. After Huang resigned, Nvidia’s stock fell sharply, along with those of several other AI and technology companies with ties to Nvidia.

One major holder of Nvidia stock has been Cantor Fitzgerald. The Wall Street investment firm is run by the sons of Howard Lutnick, Cantor’s former CEO, who serves as President Trump’s commerce secretary. Cantor Fitzgerald held shares in Nvidia worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The New York Times reports Lutnick pushed to weaken chip export rules that overlapped with his family’s business.

The Financial Times reports President Trump personally made up to $15 million on Monday alone, after Nvidia’s stock soared 30% following Huang’s return.

On Monday, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded to the Nvidia news and its impact on working people.

MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI: I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage. And yet, for many days, that had a massive impact. And what we’re also talking about here, speaking about Mr. Huang, we’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumored to be around $81 billion. That would be the cost of providing universal childcare for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year.

And a lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is that we can have democracy, we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few, we cannot have both. And when you look at our stock market and you look at how disproportionately dependent it is on artificial intelligence-related stocks, it cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how — how much this technology is now dominant, not just in terms of the discourse that we are having around it on a day-to-day basis, but also the strength of the United States economy.

AMY GOODMAN: To talk more about Nvidia and the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang, we’re joined by two guests. In Chicago, we’re joined by Tobita Chow, an organizer there. His most recent article for The Nation is headlined “Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives.” Aya Ibrahim is with us here in New York. She’s a senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute. She previously served as a senior adviser on the secretary of state’s policy planning staff, the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy and on the National Economic Council. She also served as senior economic adviser to Massachusetts Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! I want to get your response to the resignation, and then the reinstatement at the behest of President Trump, of Jensen Huang, and also the comments of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Aya.

AYA IBRAHIM: Thank you for having me, Amy.

You know, I think that the mayor’s comments really get at the heart of this issue, which is who is in control of our economy, who is critical to our national security, and who gets to decide the trajectory of both. For so long, we have had discussions that centered on the value of the free hand of the market, and now we have an economy where it seems to be the singular hand of President Trump. The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the S&P this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable. And that the president would feel the need to step in, and do so in a way that undermines serious concerns around national security, is a problem.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Aya, what about these concerns around national security? The Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday that there’s an investigation into Alice Huang, one of the women with which Jensen Huang had a relationship with, and her firm Megaspeed, that that’s ongoing. But it’s still unclear that Alice Huang is an alleged spy for the Chinese government. Your thoughts about this?

AYA IBRAHIM: Well, whatever the conclusion or finding as to the exact nature of the relationship, I think, is ultimately irrelevant, to the extent that regardless of the nature of the relationship, the result was that Jensen Huang was sidestepping and circumventing export controls. Right? These are violations of the law. So, the relationship itself is beside the point.

The bigger issue here is that we have one man, one firm, that many people, including those in our government, now believe are indispensable both to our economic growth and financial stability and to national security. And there’s an emerging discourse of “separate the artist from the art,” but usually the artist doesn’t have an impact on my retirement. So, this is a very unique set of circumstances, but it’s also the result of decades of technology and national security exceptionalism that allows the rise for firms to have such singular power and influence.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, I’d like to bring Tobita Chow into the conversation. Your initial thoughts on the breaking news that Jensen was reinstated? And I also — I’m wondering if you could talk some, because most of Nvidia’s chips — I mean, sorry, all of Nvidia’s advanced chips are manufactured in Taiwan by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, TSMC, and the the irony here of most of these most advanced chips being manufactured just 80 miles away from the Chinese mainland.

TOBITA CHOW: Yeah. Thanks for having me.

I would also lift up Mayor Mamdani’s comments on this issue as a real model. The fundamental issue here is that a handful of these AI oligarchs have seized total control of the future of the U.S. economy, enormous power over the jobs and welfare and pensions, and so on, of all of us without our consent. And the real solution is that we need to build a new economy that is not dependent on this AI industry as its sole source of growth.

Another thing that I admire about Mayor Mamdani’s comments is that he steered the conversation away from the whole issue of the U.S.-China relationship and national security. My read of this scandal and news cycle is that it has been a strategy led by China hawks in the national security establishment to accomplish two goals. One is to build greater political support for chip restrictions against China, and to build greater political support particularly within the Trump administration, because Trump has been inclined to ease these chip restrictions against China, which hurts the Chinese AI industry — the restrictions hurt the Chinese AI industry. The other goal that the China hawks had was to get rid of Jensen Huang, who has been the chief proponent within Silicon Valley of continued engagement between the U.S. and Chinese tech industries and very successfully lobbied the Trump administration around this issue of chip restrictions against China. So, I think there — we need to understand the role that these China hawks within the national security establishment have played in driving this whole news cycle.

As far as the role of TSMC within the global chip industry goes, yeah, it is located in Taiwan. It is critical to the global chip industry. But I think, like, you know, there are recurring concerns about China’s claims to — claims to have sovereignty over Taiwan and their talk of reunification between Taiwan and the Chinese mainland. This creates fears of some sort of Chinese military action against Taiwan that would disrupt the global chip industry. There are real concerns there, but I think that fears of imminent military action around Taiwan tend to be overblown in a lot of discourse.

AMY GOODMAN: Toby Chow, you talked about the rift in the national security establishment. Give it names — for example, Marco Rubio, a true China hawk, who is secretary of state. I think The Wall Street Journal has a piece today calling on him to step down so he doesn’t become this face of a failed foreign policy. And then you have Vice President Vance, and these two, Vance and Rubio, perhaps vying for the presidency in 2028. Explain the positions they’re taking here.

TOBITA CHOW: Marco Rubio is maybe chief among the frustrated China hawks within the Trump administration. So, the national security leadership in both parties in D.C. has been greatly frustrated with President Trump, who has over the past year pursued policies to maintain very warm relations with Xi Jinping, who he seems to admire as a fellow strongman leader. And so, his approach has been seen as way too, you know, soft on China by basically the entire national security establishment, and this includes a number of frustrated national security leaders within Trump’s own administration, Marco Rubio being chief among them. And yes, there are reports that Marco Rubio played a key role in leaking a report that drove this whole scandal around Jensen Huang.

JD Vance has taken a very different position. According to reports, he was instrumental in working with venture capitalists and other of Jensen Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley to pressure Trump to support the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia, and which led to a very successful meeting where Donald Trump met with the board of Nvidia and got them to reinstate Jensen Huang.

There are splits within Silicon Valley on this key question of chip controls vis-à-vis China that are at play here. On the one hand, you have companies like Nvidia, which can profit off of the Chinese tech industry. You also have venture capitalists in Silicon Valley — and JD Vance was one of these venture capitalists — who are investing in companies that can make profitable use of cheaper Chinese AI models. So, this is a faction of Silicon Valley that supports Jensen Huang and his efforts to ease chip restrictions against China. This is opposed to a different faction of Silicon Valley, which includes the frontier AI labs of Anthropic and OpenAI. These companies do not have any opportunity to profit off of the Chinese tech industry. For them, the Chinese tech industry is only a severe competitive threat, and even an existential threat to their business models, and so they have consistently lobbied for stronger chip restrictions against China, which puts them in a natural alliance with the China Hawks. So, that’s the division that we’re seeing at play here, both within Silicon Valley and within D.C., and even within Trump’s own administration.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, I’m wondering also if you could talk, Tobita, about the — we hear a lot about the relationship between Chinese companies, especially these advanced companies, and the Chinese government. But what about the relationship of the major companies here in the United States to the U.S. government and the U.S. military?

TOBITA CHOW: Yeah, there is — among national security leaders and China watchers, sometimes you’ll see them talk in very concerned tones about this thing that is called military-civil fusion in China, which is this growing — this effort to increase the level of integration between civilian industries, particularly in the tech industry, and the Chinese military. I agree that’s a very dangerous trend.

But that trend is, I feel like, if anything, more advanced in the United States. We are seeing within Silicon Valley movement of greater convergence and integration into the national security state, moving into, you know, arms manufacturing, into Pentagon contracts. Many of these companies also see — increasingly see the national security establishment as allies in protecting them from rising populist anger at Silicon Valley, and also getting them favorable policies.

I mean, part of what we have seen in this Jensen Huang scandal is that it was good for Anthropic and OpenAI. It very coincidentally overlapped with Anthropic’s debut on the stock market. But Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia suggested that the U.S. government might indeed move to strengthen these chip restrictions against China, thereby undermining the Chinese AI industry, which is a boon for both Anthropic and OpenAI. So, this is a demonstration of what national security leaders can provide to actors in Silicon Valley.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to go back to Aya Ibrahim. Apple still manufactures most of its iPhones in China. Tesla designs and sells electric vehicles plus energy storage systems in China. Google’s Android operating system runs on nearly 80% of smartphones in China. Can you talk about the significance of the focus on Nvidia shipping AI chips to China? Who benefits from Jensen’s ousting from the company? And ultimately, do you simply think he was too big to fail?

AYA IBRAHIM: So, no, nobody is too big to fail or too big to fire, and no one should be, again, this indispensable, whether to our economy or national security.

The question of companies that are operating in China, I mean, they’re — not all technologies are created the same. So, this is fundamentally a question about cutting-edge technology, advanced chips, that are necessary for defense and intelligence and national security purposes, and many view them as critical to our ability to maintain those systems. That is different than, you know, legacy chips that go into other products, like EVs.

I think that the focus on export controls misses a bigger issue. By all means, if there are loopholes, close the loopholes. But closing the loopholes is not an exhaustive solution, and it also does not get at the structural and systemic issues that allowed for the situation to come together in the first place. Right? Closing the loopholes in export control are not going to address the opaque financing that’s underpinning this ecosystem and its buildout. It’s not going to address the deep imbalances in our economy and financial markets, where one company’s IPO means that 5,000 people have more wealth than the bottom third of Americans. It is not going to address the lack of competition, such that we only have one company and we’re sitting here for weeks trying to figure out, well, how do we make sure that this company operates in a way that is consistent with national interest, ignoring the fact that at the end of the day, a company has commercial interests, and those are not always one and the same as national interest.

AMY GOODMAN: So, there is a huge change, the blue wave, with the incoming Congress. Both will be controlled by the Democrats. President Trump has made very clear that he doesn’t want AI regulated. What do you think should be the approach of this new wave?

AYA IBRAHIM: I think that AI and data centers specifically were an 80-20 issue for voters, and it really has scrambled our politics. So, it’s a cross-cutting and, frankly, a bipartisan issue. And we saw many Republicans shift, including Governor Abbott in Texas, who imposed a temporary moratorium. That is the level of frustration and anger, and to the degree that, again, even folks who are nominally very hands-off regulation-wise felt the need to respond.

I think that voters have made very clear the two big issues in this election were cost of living and corruption, and both of those issues are embodied fairly well in this larger debate about the AI buildout and who bears the cost and pays the price, and then who benefits. And it’s very clear that a handful of folks are benefiting at the expense of many people. The American people want us to regulate these companies. They want to see accountability for leaders that have made it very clear that they’re indifferent to what is in the interest of anyone but themselves or their share price.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re going to leave it there, but, of course, we’re going to continue to cover this issue. Aya Ibrahim is senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute. And Tobita Chow, Toby Chow, organizer in Chicago, we’ll link to your recent piece in The Nation, “Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives.”

Coming up, masked, unidentified, plainclothes ICE agents detain a father and daughter on the jetway at Sea-Tac Airport in Seattle as they’re trying to board a plane to attend a family baptism. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Really Real” by Allison Russell and Ganessa James of Rainbow Coalition, performing in our Democracy Now! studio.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: 160 Climate Scientists Warn BAAJA Would Destroy US Chances of Reaching Net Zero
content:
The bill would effectively lock in current levels of fossil fuel infrastructure and usage forever, they warn.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A group of over 160 climate scientists is urging the House to block the major bipartisan permitting reform bill from passage, warning that its entrenchment of fossil fuel infrastructure could likely prevent the U.S. from ever reaching net zero emissions, which would be disastrous for the climate.

In a letter published Tuesday, the scientists express “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which passed the Senate on Friday, would drastically weaken key environmental laws like the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA), while granting fossil fuel companies powerful tools to ensure its influence never wanes.

“BAAJA’s extensive changes to existing laws would make it almost impossible for a court to enjoin an action based on a violation of NEPA or of the National Historic Preservation Act, in effect pulling the teeth from these very important laws,” the letter says.

“Furthermore, we are concerned that BAAJA’s creation of the new ‘Disparate Treatment’ standard for energy permitting will prevent the rapid and nearly total phase out of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the U.S. and global energy systems. Without this phase out, and the subsequent reduction of emissions to (net) zero, the world will be unable to halt global heating,” the scientists wrote.

The letter effort was led by top climate scientists, including Michael Mann, of the University of Pennsylvania; Michael Oppenheimer, at Princeton University; and Robert Brulle and J. Timmons Roberts of Brown University, who have done critical research on the fossil fuel industry’s work to block action on the climate crisis.

The letter effort was necessary because “of the speed with which this deeply problematic bill seems headed toward passage without the due diligence and scrutiny any such far-reaching bill demands,” Mann told Truthout, “pushed through in the proverbial dark of night of the Thanksgiving holiday lull of a lame duck congressional session, and backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors.”

The “disparate treatment” standard in the bill, the letter explains, empowers fossil fuel companies to file lawsuits to defang or overturn climate legislation. Under the standard, companies would be able to sue if they are being granted permits at a lower standard than in previous years, with the potential to reclaim up to 100 percent of projected construction costs plus damages and legal fees — footed by the American taxpayer.

At the same time, the bill would majorly hamstring federal agencies in their ability to revise or revoke rules and permits in the interest of public health or the climate, barring “immediate” harm.

Taken together, these provisions would prevent the U.S. from ever taking steps to meaningfully reduce its greenhouse gas emissions, they warn.

“As environmental law scholar David Bookbinder notes, this effectively insulates not only the construction but the operation at normal capacity of all existing fossil fuel infrastructure. Such a lock-in of extant fossil-fuel infrastructure would effectively prevent the U.S. from ever reaching (net) zero emissions,” the letter says.

The scientists also cite research finding that BAAJA would cause emissions to rise and contribute to air pollution-related mortality.

“[A]s written the bill would prevent the rapid and nearly total phase out of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the U.S. and global energy systems, which science says we must do if we’re going to halt global heating,” said Genevieve Guenther, founding director of End Climate Silence and organizer of the letter. The disparate treatment standard, Guenther said, “means that it effectively makes the current balance of energy sources permanent.”

“BAAJA is not progress. It is a step in the wrong direction, away from a (net) zero economy,” Guenther warned.

The climate concerns are the latest to be brought up against BAAJA, which opponents have warned would also help fast track data center construction and majorly sideline Tribal sovereignty. Critics have also noted several corruption concerns in relation to the bill, including former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s role in lobbying for the bill, and reports that a natural gas pipeline executive may have been involved in drafting the bill as the chief of staff for one of its key Senate backers.

Despite these concerns, 15 Democrats joined Republicans in voting for the bill’s passage in the Senate. This includes Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), one of the top backers of the bill despite typically being known as one of the Senate’s top climate champions.

“It’s the very sort of thing he’s spent his whole career fighting, and it just doesn’t compute,” letter leader Mann said.

Mann said that Democrats should instead take advantage of their majority in the new Congress to pass climate legislation, including legislation to regulate data centers that they could force President Donald Trump and Republicans to oppose, exposing an unpopular view to the public.

“I hope that there are enough Democratic House members out there still listening to facts and reason that the bill — at least in its current form — can be blocked,” he said.

author: Stephen Zunes
title: From Israel to Iran, Schumer’s Positions Contradict Those of Many Dem Voters
content:
Electing Schumer to lead now would be like having a Democratic leader supporting the Vietnam War in the early 1970s.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

For the first time since his ascension to the Democratic Senate leadership a decade ago, Chuck Schumer is facing a serious challenge for the top post by Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland). Once considered a rather cautious center-left figure, Van Hollen has emerged in recent years as one the Democrats’ more progressive voices, proving himself willing to challenge the party’s hawkish foreign policy orthodoxy, even regarding U.S. relations with Israel.

Schumer’s decidedly hawkish views are so far to the right of those of rank-and-file Democrats that his reappointment to majority leader would constitute a major betrayal of the Democratic voters who have made it possible for him to once again hold that powerful position after four years in the minority. Most observers believe that while Van Hollen has been gaining momentum, Schumer will likely receive his colleagues’ endorsement when they vote by secret ballot on December 1.

As even leading Republicans admit, the war on Iran was a major reason for the margin of Democratic victory. Schumer, however, has consistently been an Iran hawk. An NBC News exit poll showed that 74 percent of voters noted the war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote. When President Donald Trump launched the war at the end of February, rather than categorically condemning the illegal and predictably disastrous use of force, Schumer issued a rather ambivalent statement asking the administration to be clearer about “the objectives of these strikes and what comes next,” calling for Trump to follow constitutional procedures but stressing “Iran must never be allowed to attain a nuclear weapon.”

This past June, when a U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding gave some hope for de-escalation and an end to the conflict, Schumer attempted to mobilize opposition to the peace effort by referring to the agreement as “the art of surrender” and falsely claimed that it would require the United States to pay Iran $300 billion.

As the war has dragged on and public opposition has grown, his criticisms of the war have increased, but this has come after decades of publicly belittling diplomacy and encouraging a more militaristic outlook toward Iran.

As Barack Obama was negotiating with Iran on the nuclear question during his presidential administration, Schumer repeatedly tried to undermine Obama’s diplomatic approach, signing a 2013 letter from a handful of senators, including then-Senators Lindsey Graham and John McCain, insisting that “a credible military threat remains on the table and we underscore the imperative that the current sanctions be maintained aggressively.” He also supported a Republican-backed resolution introduced by the notorious warmonger Graham, insisting that, in the event of war between Israel and Iran, the United States should provide “diplomatic, military, and economic support to the Government of Israel” — even if Israel attacked Iran first.

When such efforts to sabotage the talks failed and a nuclear deal was signed in 2015, Schumer was one of only two Democratic senators to oppose it.

During Israel’s unprovoked bombing of Iran in June of last year, Schumer insisted that “Israel has a right to defend itself” and reiterated that “[t]he United States’ commitment to Israel’s security and defense must be ironclad.” Just over a week earlier, he criticized Trump for even engaging in negotiations with Iran. Schumer refused to sign on to a war powers resolution proposed by Sen. Tim Kaine which could have prevented the United States from joining the war, as it did the following week. Just prior to the 12-day war Israel launched on Iran, during which the U.S. bombed Iranian nuclear sites, Schumer goaded Trump by posting a video to social media accusing him of “folding on Iran” by attempting to negotiate a deal, bemoaning how “Trump always chickens out” regarding the use of military force.

While Schumer’s hawkishness on Iran has garnered attention as Senate Democrats consider how they can constrain the war, his militaristic outlook is not reserved for that country alone. In 2002, Schumer was also among the right-wing minority of congressional Democrats to vote to authorize the U.S. invasion of Iraq, falsely claiming that Iraq had somehow redeveloped its chemical, biological, and nuclear programs; had stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons; and had rebuilt long-range missiles. He rejected the broad consensus of Middle East scholars, State Department officials, and most U.S. allies that, in addition to being conducted on false pretenses, an invasion of Iraq would be illegal, unnecessary, and have disastrous consequences. Even after acknowledging that Iraq didn’t really have those weapons, he insisted on keeping U.S. forces in that oil-rich country in a bloody counterinsurgency war for much of the subsequent decade.

Additionally, Schumer has supported arms transfers to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and other dictatorships across the Middle East, rejecting human rights concerns. Back in 2006, he was one of only a dozen Democrats to vote against an amendment to protect civilians from unexploded cluster munitions.

Long before Trump began waging his campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), Schumer vocally opposed the body. He supported a 2002 bill, colloquially known as The Hague Invasion Act, that prohibits the United States from cooperating in any way with the ICC and its prosecution of individuals responsible for serious crimes against humanity, restricts U.S. foreign aid to countries that support the ICC, and authorizes the use of military force to free those from the United States or allied countries held by the ICC.

More than anything, though, it is around U.S. policy toward Israel that Schumer has made his reputation as a militarist with little regard for human rights and international law.

In the face of three-quarters of Democratic voters opposing additional military aid to Israel and with all but seven Democratic senators supporting Trump’s latest arms package, Schumer announced earlier this year: “All the aid that Israel needs, I will continue to fight for it. And we delivered more security assistance to Israel, our ally, under my leadership than ever, ever before. We will keep doing that, everybody.”

Schumer first came to national attention when, as a member of the House, he spoke at the 1988 Democratic National Convention in opposition to a resolution calling for “mutual recognition, territorial compromise and self-determination for the Israelis and Palestinians.” He referred to its supporters as “disgraceful,” said the resolution was an effort to “reward intransigence and terrorism,” and called it a duplicitous proposal that threatened Israel’s security.

While eventually coming out in support of a two-state solution, Schumer has insisted it can only come on Israeli terms and without pressuring the Israeli government, which opposes any kind of Palestinian state, to compromise.

In the face of polls showing 80 percent of Democrats have an unfavorable view of Israel, Schumer calls himself a “Shomer Yisrael,” a guardian of Israel, arguing, “My job is to keep the left pro-Israel.” He does not simply support Israel, however — he supports the Israeli right. While most Senate Democrats now align with the moderate pro-Israel group J Street, Schumer remains firmly committed to the positions of the right-wing American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). The organization has not only praised Benjamin Netanyahu and his genocidal war on Palestinians, but has endorsed scores of Republican insurrectionists for reelection, targeted liberal Democrats for defeat, and viciously attacked even fellow Zionists who do not fully back Israel’s right-wing policies. Schumer was the only Democratic senator to speak at AIPAC’s most recent Congressional Summit.

In early 2023, when Netanyahu was facing growing international criticism for the increased repression in the occupied territories as well as massive protests within Israel for his anti-democratic policies, including efforts to restrict the independence of the courts, Schumer flew to Israel to show his support for the far right Israeli leader, prompting the leading Israeli newspaper Haaretz to wonder “What’s Behind Chuck Schumer’s Strange Embrace of Netanyahu?”

And Schumer was one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of Israel’s war on Gaza and an opponent of a ceasefire — even as polls, even during an early phase of the war, showed nearly three-quarters of Democratic voters supported such a ceasefire and later polls found a majority of Democrats recognize Israel’s actions as genocide.

In 2024, just after the ICC chief prosecutor applied for arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his defense minister, Yoav Gallant, along with three Hamas leaders, Schumer issued a formal invitation for the soon-to-be indicted war criminal to address a joint session of Congress. This came in the face of calls by hundreds of prominent Israelis — including a former prime minister; a Nobel Prize winner; the former intelligence chief; and others representing Israeli science, technology, politics, defense, law, and culture — to cancel the invitation.

Despite enormous evidence of Israel’s war crimes under Netanyahu and Gallant, Schumer denounced the ICC for indicting the two Israeli leaders. Though only two of the 73 people indicted by the International Criminal Court have been Israeli, and the overwhelming majority are African, Chuck Schumer insists that the ICC has an “anti-Israel bias.” He has defended Trump’s executive order sanctioning those associated with the International Criminal Court for prosecuting members of an allied government for war crimes. Schumer has also attacked Amnesty International for its meticulously documented reports on Israeli violations of international humanitarian law as somehow “delegitimizing the existence of the State of Israel.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has been a longtime supporter of Israel’s colonization drive in the occupied West Bank, insisting in 2018 that the settlements were not an obstacle to peace. In January 2017, he cosponsored a resolution insisting that it was “anti-Israel” for the United Nations to oppose illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied territories and that the United Nations has no business addressing the Israeli occupation, effectively siding with then-President-elect Trump by criticizing Obama for not vetoing a very modest resolution supported by every other government on the UN Security Council. Schumer went on to strongly support Trump’s controversial decision for the United States to become the world’s only major country to move its embassy to Jerusalem and to designate the city, much of which is recognized as part of the occupied Palestinian territories, as only belonging to Israel.

In 2015, Schumer signed a letter to the European Union trade minister attacking the EU for insisting that products produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank not be labeled as “made in Israel,” insisting that the EU initiative was promoting a “de-facto boycott of Israel.” This was despite the fact that the EU decision was only in reference to the occupied territories and, much to the consternation of human rights activists, did not call for boycotting any products from the settlements, much less Israel itself.

Even worse, Schumer helped push through a trade bill that formally defined “Israel” as including the occupied territories. Lara Friedman of the liberal Zionist group Americans for Peace Now notes how such efforts are “not about defending Israel at all,” but rather about “shielding Israeli settlements from pressure” and “seeking to codify in U.S. law the view that there is no distinction between Israel and Israeli settlements in the occupied territories.”

Additionally, Schumer supported a bill effectively criminalizing support for boycotts against Israel or companies doing business in the country or its occupied territories. If it had passed, it would have made it a crime to support or even furnish information about a boycott directed at Israel or the Israeli occupation supported by any entity of the United Nations, the European Union, or other “international governmental organization.”

From the invasion to Iraq to the Gaza genocide, Schumer has aligned with right-wing Christian fundamentalists against Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and the mainline Protestant churches. It is hard to imagine Democrats accepting a leader who would side with such tendencies regarding reproductive freedom and LGBTQ rights. Yet, on issues of human rights, international law, and war and peace, there seems to be a willingness to tolerate leaders allied with the Christian right.

Indeed, Schumer, who is Jewish, has his own version of the Christian Zionist view of God as a cosmic real estate agent designating the Holy Land as exclusively for the Jews by insisting, in reference to the Palestinians, “Of course, we say it’s our land, the Torah says it, but they don’t believe in the Torah. So that’s the reason there is not peace.” In short, even putting aside the fact that Muslims, like Christians, do recognize the Torah as sacred scripture and that the Torah is not a real estate deed, it underscores that Schumer’s support for Israeli supremacy is rooted not in political expediency, but deeply held ideological beliefs.

Having someone so far to the right of the Democratic mainstream on the Middle East policy today would be the equivalent of having a Democratic leader supporting the Vietnam War in the early 1970s or U.S. intervention in Central America during the 1980s.

The outcome of the vote will be an indicator of the direction of the Democratic-controlled Senate for the coming years. It will say a lot about the current crop of Democrats in the Senate if they choose to rebuff a clear mandate from voters for change and stick with Schumer instead.

title: Gaza Health Officials Say Meningitis Outbreak Is Due to Infrastructure Attacks
content:
Israel has attacked health and water infrastructure while blocking aid that could help with treatment.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On the heels of a major international report that accused Israel of committing “environmental war crimes” in Gaza, including by exposing Palestinians to toxins and endangering the drinking water supply with its continued US-backed bombardment, the exclave’s health ministry on Tuesday issued an “epidemiological alert” warning health workers and communities of a “shocking” rise in meningitis infections.

The Gaza Health Ministry called on the World Health Organization and the United Nations Children’s Fund to send lab supplies and antibiotics, and establish isolation wards as Dr. Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for the agency, said 272 meningitis cases had been reported in October — eight times the usual monthly average.

Bacterial meningitis cases rose from about 10-20 per month to 108 last month, and another 100 have been recorded in November. Fifteen people have died of the illness this year, including five between August-October.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that 77% of cases were in babies under one year of age.

Lab tests suggested the cases were linked to enteroviruses, which can spread through the water supply.

The health ministry said the outbreak was the “inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain.”

A report released by Oxfam International Monday warned that, among other harms, the destruction of wastewater treatment plants in Gaza made it more likely that Palestinians could come into contact with water contaminated with pathogens.

The ministry warned that children are particularly at risk for meningitis infections, which cause inflammation of the membranes around the spinal cord and brain.

Officials said that in addition to making the outbreak more likely by destroying infrastructure across Gaza and pushing Palestinians into crowded makeshift shelters, Israel has also made it impossible for healthcare workers to stop the outbreak from spreading, by blocking “maintenance spare parts, sterilization materials, and fuel” from reaching Gaza.

Winter rains earlier this month caused catastrophic flooding that destroyed tens of thousands of tents — the only shelter for more than 1 million people after the vast majority of structures have been decimated by Israel’s bombardment over the past three years. Makeshift encampments have been inundated with rainwater mixed with sewage.

“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak,” the ministry said.

Bahaa al-Sous, the father of newborn twin girls, told The New Arab Tuesday that he had discovered his daughter Ilat was sick 10 days ago after the storm.

“I came back from work to our tent, and God inspired me to bend down and kiss my daughter’s forehead. I was shocked by the burning heat coming from her small body,” he said.

His daughter finished treatment at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, but al-Sous was taking her sister, Elin, to the hospital Tuesday after she became ill.

A woman named Iman also brought her six-year-old daughter to the hospital for treatment, but had to buy some medications from private pharmacies.

“The water we drink is not clean like it was before the war. Nothing has stayed the same; even the air we breathe has changed and been polluted by [Israel’s] bombing and destruction,” Iman told The New Arab.

OCHA’s report on conditions in the territory on November 18 said that 45% of households surveyed by the agency were living less than 10 meters from sewage and sludge following the flooding.

“The severe overcrowding in displacement camps and the absence of a healthy, preventive environment greatly increase the likelihood of transmission,” Dr. Iyad Abu Mu’ailaq, a pediatrician at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, told The New Arab. “The complications of meningitis are very serious. If the child does not receive the right treatment at the right time, it may leave permanent effects on their growth and future, such as loss of hearing or sight.”

Despite last year’s ceasefire deal requiring Israel to allow humanitarian aid to reach Palestinians, the country has continued to block tents, shelter materials, and other supplies from entering Gaza.

Ahmed Abu Rukba, a representative for al-Iyadat camp in central Gaza, told The New Arab that new tents are needed, as well as sand to raise the low-lying camp and prevent worse flooding — especially since more storms are expected.

“If we don’t get the sand and the tents,” said Abu Rukba, “we will definitely flood again, and the children’s tragedy will be repeated.”

title: Mamdani: Rumored Huang Divorce Deal Could Fund Year of Universal Child Care
content:
Research has found that universal child care plans would cost roughly $35 billion per year.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threw the Jensen Huang scandal into sharp perspective after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, pointing out that just half of the disgraced CEO’s estimated wealth could fund an entire year of universal child care for children across the U.S.

Huang’s reinstatement comes just days after he resigned from the company due to reports of his extramarital affairs, including with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

When asked about Huang’s rehiring by the Nvidia board — a decision attributed by the White House and Nvidia to an intervention by Donald Trump — Mamdani criticized the outsized influence of the Huang scandal and the AI industry in general on the U.S. economy.

“I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage. And yet, for many days, that had a massive impact,” Mamdani said.

“We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumored to be around $81 billion,” he went on. “That would be the cost of providing universal child care for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year.”

Indeed, if Huang and his wife were to get divorced, it could be one of the largest divorce settlements in history. As Forbes points out, documents have shown that most of Huang’s over 3.5 percent stake in Nvidia is held in trusts in which he and his wife are listed as co-trustees. They also live in California, which has laws specifying that assets acquired during their 40-year marriage must be divided evenly in the case of a divorce.

Huang’s net worth has fluctuated significantly in the past few weeks amid the scandal, as the Nvidia stock has fallen and risen. Before the scandal and his resignation earlier this month, Huang’s net worth was roughly $180 billion, according to Forbes, and as of Tuesday, it was down to $134 billion.

Trump said on Monday that Huang and his “very, very, very good wife” have “worked it out,” suggesting that they may not divorce, though it’s unclear what Trump was basing this assertion on. At the same time, Huang reportedly admitted to the board before his reinstatement that he had had even more affairs than the ones already revealed to the public.

“A lot of this just brings to mind what [Supreme Court] Justice [Louis] Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is: ‘We can have democracy. We can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. We cannot have both,’” said Mamdani.

Such wealth could, indeed, fund a significant proportion of proposed universal child care plans. University of Pennsylvania research found in 2022 that universal pre-K for 3- and 4-year-olds would cost $351 billion over the next 10 years, including $41 billion in initial costs to build the necessary facilities. This would average out to roughly $35 billion per year.

During his presidential campaign in 2020, Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vermont) campaign introduced a plan for free universal child care covering children from 0 to 4, which his campaign said would cost $1.5 trillion over the next decade, or roughly $150 billion a year.

Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul have taken steps toward implementing universal child care for children 3 and under in the state. A program to fund free child care for children under 2 for two years and expand free child care for 3-year-olds in the state unveiled in January has a price tag of $1.7 billion.

Meanwhile, Mamdani also raised the concern that the U.S. economy, and millions of Americans’ retirement plans, are so closely tied to the success of a handful of major tech companies.

“When you look at our stock market, and you look at how disproportionately dependent it is on artificial intelligence-related stocks, it cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how much this technology is now dominant — not just in terms of the discourse that we are having around it on a day-to-day basis, but also the strength of the United States economy,” Mamdani said.

The democratic socialist’s comments stand in stark contrast to the reactions to the news by the Trump administration and its right-wing allies. The right has been in spin mode as Trump is accused of ordering the extraordinary move for corrupt reasons, with Trump having disclosed a massive stake in the company. According to an estimate by the Financial Times, Trump personally made up to $15 million by urging Huang to be reinstated.

“You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks,” Trump said on Monday.

On Fox News, host Jesse Watters downplayed the allegations that Huang was having an affair with a woman with ties to Chinese intelligence.

“If [J. Robert] Oppenheimer, when he was working on the atomic bomb, was caught sleeping with a beautiful Japanese woman, and the Japanese woman was maybe passing secrets to the emperor, should [President Harry S.] Truman have fired him?” Watters opined on Monday. “Or let him learn his lesson, send him back to work, so he can build the bomb to win the war? Trump says Jensen’s too valuable to put on the open market.”

Oppenheimer was indeed put on trial by the federal government for supposed ties to communist groups, as politicians whipped up a Red Scare to criminalize left-wing Americans and political beliefs. Oppenheimer’s security clearance was taken away and he was shunned from government and scientific work, though that decision was posthumously reversed in 2022.

When Oppenheimer was conducting research on building an atomic bomb, the U.S. had also imprisoned over 100,000 Japanese people in the U.S., without any form of due process, over concerns of “dual loyalties” with the Axis power.

author: Jonathan Shorman
title: Trump’s DOJ Is Already Working to Undermine Congressional Oversight
content:
The Justice Department is sending threatening letters to lawmakers likely to investigate the Trump administration.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.”

The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution for conducting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his aides. Legal experts have widely dismissed the threats as empty because the U.S. Constitution affords lawmakers wide protections from prosecution for official actions taken in Congress.

But the letters — and that short phrase within them — offer a blueprint for how the White House will try to undermine the investigations themselves, in addition to discrediting the investigators. Democrats will take control of Congress with majorities in both the House and Senate in early January.

The Justice Department is signaling it will attack congressional subpoenas seeking documents and testimony from federal officials as driven by retribution and outside the bounds of traditional oversight. The government appears ready to argue such requests cross a line into illegality.

The DOJ letters allege Democrats intend to violate federal laws that prohibit individuals acting in an official capacity from violating the constitutional rights of others. In this case, those supposedly having their rights violated would be Trump’s associates.

“As you should know, whatever investigations you and your fellow Democrats have planned must have a legitimate legislative purpose,” U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the top Justice Department official in the Southern District of Texas, wrote on Nov. 19 to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat.

Reitz, a former Republican candidate for Texas attorney general, included similar language in letters to Rep. Robert Garcia and Sen. Adam Schiff of California, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. All are Democrats likely to play prominent roles in investigating the Trump administration after the party takes control of Congress in January.

Additionally, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, in a Nov. 9 letter to Garcia wrote that “abusive and capricious threats” were spreading among Democratic legislators. He warned that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” and expected lawmakers to investigate within settled constitutional limits.

The defiant posture comes as Trump braces for a final two years in office marked by aggressive oversight from House and Senate committees, as Democrats probe alleged corruption and mismanagement.

Many Democrats credit the blue tsunami that gave the party large majorities in both chambers to voters’ frustration with self-enrichment by Trump and other government officials.

In addition to the Justice Department letters, Trump on Nov. 20 signed an executive order that requires federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information. Contractors are also required to abide by any White House instructions to withhold communications that the Trump administration says are covered by executive privilege.

Democrats are now on a collision course with the Trump administration that could end up in the courts.

Raskin pressed forward with his oversight efforts despite Reitz’s letters. The ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Raskin sent letters on Nov. 20 to the DOJ, FBI, Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Bureau of Prisons — demanding that they preserve all records, including Signal chats, which can be set to auto-delete.

Slotkin responded to Reitz in a letter last week, calling congressional oversight an important constitutional responsibility. She called the DOJ official’s threats frivolous and a violation of his ethical duties as an attorney. The nonpartisan watchdog group Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint against Reitz with the State Bar of Texas.

“I’m not going to participate in some sham investigation,” Slotkin said in a video response to Reitz. “Every American has freedom of speech. In particular, senators have special privileges and special responsibilities given by the Constitution for oversight.”

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told States Newsroom that Trump is willing to work with anyone “to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.”

“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” Bis said in a statement.

The Justice Department didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The U.S. Supreme Court has previously ruled Congress has broad power to investigate the federal government.

Constitutional law experts interviewed by States Newsroom said that while lawmakers don’t have unlimited investigative power, their oversight authority is sweeping, rooted in the need for lawmakers to have information before legislating.

“Although they are not stated in the Constitution, there is a clear line of cases that say as long as investigations are related to possible legislation, then they can proceed,” said John Vile, a professor of political science at Middle Tennessee State University who has written books on constitutional law.

In 1957, the Supreme Court found that the U.S. House Un-American Activities Committee had exceeded the bounds of congressional power after labor organizer John Watkins was prosecuted for refusing to answer lawmakers’ questions about whether certain individuals were members of the Communist Party.

The court threw out Watkins’ conviction, finding his due process rights were violated.

Retiz cites the case, known as Watkins vs. United States, in his letters to Democrats as he warns lawmakers that their planned investigations could be unlawful. In the court’s 6-1 decision, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that investigations solely to punish or for the “personal aggrandizement” of the investigators weren’t permissible.

Unmentioned by Reitz is that earlier in the same paragraph, Warren wrote that Congress’s power to investigate is “broad” and encompasses looking into both how current law is being applied and possible future law.

“It includes surveys of defects in our social, economic or political system for the purpose of enabling the Congress to remedy them,” Warren wrote. “It comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste.”

As recently as 2020, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the sweeping scope of Congress’ investigatory powers.

In a 7-2 decision in a case called Trump vs. Mazars USA, the justices didn’t immediately allow a congressional subpoena for Trump’s personal financial records to proceed, but they repeated Watkins’ description of lawmakers’ sweeping oversight authority.

“The congressional power to obtain information is ‘broad’ and ‘indispensable,’” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in the majority opinion.

Whatever the courts may decide about future subpoenas, constitutional scholars in recent weeks have been virtually unanimous in arguing that the Constitution’s speech or debate clause will protect Democratic lawmakers from criminal cases for launching congressional investigations into the Trump administration.

The clause says of lawmakers that “for any Speech or Debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any other Place.” The provision has its roots in England, where members of Parliament used to fear prosecution for offending the crown.

Its protections have been on display as recently as October, when federal agents searched the D.C. residence of Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Democrat. Recently unsealed court documents show a federal judge asked prosecutors for additional information on the “potential Speech or Debate Clause implications” of the search before signing off on a warrant.

Steve Vladeck, a professor of federal courts at Georgetown University Law Center and a leading expert on the Supreme Court, wrote on Nov. 23 that an indictment alleging lawmakers had conspired to deprive individuals of their rights through a “weaponized” oversight process would mean proving the illegitimacy of the investigation’s subpoenas, hearings or committee votes.

“Every one of those is a legislative act, for which the members’ motives are off the table,” Vladeck wrote in his newsletter, One First. “When the oversight itself is the alleged crime, the Speech or Debate Clause is arguably at its zenith.”

Lawmakers also can’t be sued for their speech in Congress, a protection that they sometimes use to make remarks that might otherwise open them up to allegations of defamation.

Last year, Rep. Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, accused her ex-fiance and three other men of being sexual “predators” in an explosive speech on the House floor. A federal judge later dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought against Mace by one of the men.

The Trump administration has also so far failed in other efforts to target Democratic lawmakers over their communications.

Just over a year ago, several lawmakers with military or national security backgrounds, including Slotkin, posted a video telling members of the military and intelligence community that they should refuse illegal orders.

Trump called the video evidence of seditious behavior and as recently as this month asked whether the lawmakers would ever face prosecution.

The Department of Defense attempted to demote one of the lawmakers, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired U.S. Navy captain. A federal judge has temporarily blocked the demotion, but the Trump administration has appealed the decision.

But even without prosecutions, Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the libertarian Cato Institute, said the White House can still work to slow down investigations.

The letters and the recent executive order serve as “markers” that could deter cooperation with Congress, she indicated. Individuals pressed for information might weigh the pros and cons of quick and full compliance.

“The fact that if I were a member of Congress I would not be particularly worried about a successful criminal prosecution doesn’t mean the administration doesn’t have a lot of tools at its disposal,” Nixon said.

title: Wisconsin’s Former GOP Maps Would Have Blocked Democratic “Blue Wave” — Analysis
content:
Had a previously gerrymandered map been allowed to remain, Wisconsin voters’ preferences would have been ignored.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A new analysis of election data suggests that, had a Republican gerrymandered map in Wisconsin remained in place for this year’s midterm races, it would have blocked the state’s “blue wave” of Democratic victories — enabling the GOP to maintain control of the legislature despite most voters’ preferences.

The midterm elections in Wisconsin, like in many other states, resulted in a Democratic “trifecta,” with Democrat David Crowley winning the governor’s race and the party wresting control of both the Assembly and Senate. It’s the first time that Democrats have had a trifecta in that state since 2008.

The result of the statewide legislative races means that Democrats will have a 53-46 seat majority in the Assembly in January. That result mirrors Crowley’s statewide performance, as he defeated U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany (R) by 54 percent to 46 percent.

Those results wouldn’t have happened, however, were it not for a series of events that dismantled maps drawn by legislative Republicans over the past 15 years, which gave them a significant advantage over Democrats by making most districts noncompetitive.

Liberal victories in statewide Supreme Court races led to that court reexamining the maps drawn by Republicans. In 2023, the court ruled they were illegal gerrymanders, and ordered new maps to be submitted by interested parties, including by Gov. Tony Evers’s (D) office and the Republican-held legislature. But before those proposals could be examined by the court, Evers and the Republicans agreed on compromise maps for the Senate and Assembly, passing them into law in 2024.

Had the court ruled differently in 2023, and had those new maps never come to pass, “the will of the majority of Wisconsin voters would still not be reflected in their Legislature” in this year’s midterm elections, a joint analysis from the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School and Wisconsin-based Law Forward found.

That analysis, published on Monday, examined election data from this year’s midterms, but placed voters’ partisan preferences into models using the old maps’ borders. “Even if Democrats had performed at 2026 levels, the Republican Party would have held a 61-38 majority of 23 seats in the Assembly,” likely resulting in Republicans maintaining control of the state legislature, the analysis concluded.

The analysis suggested that researchers’ findings provided ample argument for reforming the redistricting process.

“Wisconsin’s experience from 2011-2026 demonstrates the need for fundamental and sweeping reform in Wisconsin, as well as nationally, to ban the partisan gerrymandering of state legislative districts to prevent such efforts in the future,” the analysis said.

Doug Poland, an attorney for Law Forward, reiterated the analysis’s points in an interview with Wisconsin Public Radio.

“Yes, there was a wave election [for Democrats], and it was big. But guess what? As big as it was, if we had had those heavily gerrymandered districts, it wouldn’t have been enough to overcome the gerrymander,” Poland said. “And that’s the lesson to draw from this.”

Amid mid-census redistricting that Republicans initiated last year in hopes of diminishing likely losses in this year’s midterms, a group of Democrats submitted legislation to reform the process.

Among other provisions, the Redistricting Reform Act of 2025 would have required states to establish commissions that represent, in equal fashion, the top two political parties that won previous state legislative races. The bill also called for a ban on any state redistricting commission drawing maps between U.S. Census cycles, unless a court found that their previous maps were crafted unlawfully.

Voters likely would have supported that bill’s aims, and could back a similar bill if Democrats introduce one next year. An Economist/YouGov poll in April asked respondents their views on partisan gerrymandering, questioning whether political parties in charge of state legislatures should be allowed to intentionally draw maps favoring themselves. According to the poll, only 7 percent of Americans said that should be permitted, while 71 percent said parties shouldn’t be allowed to have that map-drawing advantage.

A Change Research poll, conducted after Election Day earlier this month, found that 75 percent of voters oppose mid-decade gerrymandering, while only 14 percent say they are fine with the practice continuing.

title: Court Allows Army to Go Ahead With Detonation of Toxic Lead Explosives in Iowa
content:
The detonation will release a plume of lead dust that can settle into soil and continue to expose people to neurotoxins.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The U.S. Army intends to detonate nearly five tons of lead-based explosives in southeast Iowa on Wednesday.

The Army had planned to use an emergency provision to proceed despite a now-lifted court-ordered pause on the federal permit authorizing the operation.

Dozens of barrels of volatile lead azide, a material used to make bombs, are stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. After decades in storage, their explosive contents have reformed into irregularly shaped crystals that are highly sensitive to friction and shock. The Army argues that freezing temperatures will make the crystals even more unstable and the barrels must be disposed of before winter sets in.

“A permit is not even necessary for the Army to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material,” reads the Department of Justice brief filed with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit on Sunday.

Late Monday, the court lifted its administrative stay on the permit for the detonation and rejected a request from petitioners to block the detonation for a longer period. The petitioners are suing the Environmental Protection Agency over its approval of the permit.

Maps released by the Army for last Friday’s planned detonation, which was called off, show a lead dust cloud spreading across potentially hundreds of miles of Eastern Iowa, with projected concentrations of the neurotoxin exceeding federal benchmarks for levels in homes and childcare facilities. Lead exposure isn’t safe for anyone, but it’s particularly dangerous for children.

In a post on Truth Social Monday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he ordered the military not to proceed with the detonation until both the appeals court and Gov.-elect Rob Sand agree to it.

In his post, Trump also blamed the Obama administration for improper storage of the explosives and said that Sand, a Democrat who does not take office until Jan. 12, would be held responsible for any catastrophic explosion caused by further delays.

Current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, a Republican, has activated the State Emergency Operations Center in preparation for the detonation. “While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” Reynolds said in a statement published Sunday.

The Army initially intended to detonate the barrels last Friday. Residents of Middletown learned of the plans at a town hall a month earlier. But most Iowa residents, including state agencies and officials such as Reynolds, received just five days’ notice. Army maps detailing the extent of the lead dust cloud were also released just a few days beforehand.

The maps, along with the short notice and limited information about cleanup efforts following the release of the plume, have sparked widespread concern in Iowa and neighboring states.

Last Thursday, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter sued the EPA over the emergency permit it granted the Army for the detonation. That same day, the Army announced it would postpone the operation and the court granted the petitioners’ motion for an administrative stay. Responding to the court’s stay, the Army and the Justice Department insisted that the detonation could and must take place, regardless of the permit’s status.

In court filings this weekend, the Justice Department cited a provision in the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 that allows for emergency treatment or containment of military munitions and other explosive materials without a permit, if the materials present an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Since submitting its emergency permit request to the EPA in September, the Army has repeatedly asserted that controlled detonation is the safest option for the barrels’ disposal, though doing so would release a neurotoxin-containing dust cloud over surrounding communities. Lead particles in the air can settle into soil, exposing people — particularly children — long after its arrival.

All alternatives to detonation would require opening or moving the barrels, the Army wrote in correspondence with the EPA submitted as evidence to the court this weekend. The sensitivity of lead azide crystals to friction and shock meant that any manipulation presented “an acute risk of unintentional detonation.”

The choice is “between a planned detonation … and an unplanned explosion that could come at any moment, with no warning and safeguards,” the Justice Department legal brief reads. “The United States recognizes that the controlled detonation will release lead dust. But a controlled detonation is the only way to minimize the release.”

A scheduled detonation would at least allow the Army to plan for weather conditions, notify the public and track the spread of lead dust, the Justice Department writes.

In a video released this weekend, Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson advised against further delays. “Each day that the disposal is delayed is another day that could increase the risk of major catastrophe. It is also another day that the lives of our residents are put on hold,” he said.

There is no safe level of the lead exposure for children, the EPA advises. It is especially harmful to infants and children with rapidly growing brains and nervous systems.

The Army has not disclosed when on Wednesday the detonation will occur, nor released updated plume maps outlining the regions most likely to be affected by lead deposition.

The dust cloud’s path will likely differ significantly from the projections released early last week, with southwest winds on Wednesday replacing last Friday’s northern winds.

“It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist,” said Michael Schmidt, general counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council, in response to the Army’s plans to go through with the detonation. “The public deserves to know immediately which communities will be impacted and how residents can most effectively protect themselves and mitigate impacts on their health and homes.”

Correspondence with EPA officials indicate that the Army was aware of the unstable condition of the barrels in Iowa before it began considering treatment options in January.

Previous Army communications, including a post by acting Army Secretary Adam Telle on the social media platform X last week, reported that the degraded lead azide was discovered in March.

Under the EPA emergency permit, the Army must provide five days’ public notice and regularly updated plume maps in the days leading up to the detonation. But if the Army bypasses the permitting process, as it has indicated it intends to do, it remains unclear which, if any, of the provisions of the permit’s requirements it plans to follow.

The Army did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

This story was updated Nov. 23, 2026, with the appeals court decision to lift the administrative stay on the permit.
