author: Cody Bloomfield
title: New Indictments of Michigan Palestine Activists Are Troubling – and Flimsy
content:
Prosecutors’ use of conspiracy charges resembles the attacks on anti-ICE protesters and Stop Cop City activists.

Prosecutors’ use of conspiracy charges resembles the attacks on anti-ICE protesters and Stop Cop City activists.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), the president set his sights on uprooting left-wing movements for liberation. What is obvious in the 14 months since the issuance of NSPM-7 is that the Trump administration has thus far failed: People continue to resist ICE, protest police brutality, and hold fast to criticisms of the U.S. national project.

But where the Trump administration has seen its campaign of widescale disruption falter, prosecutors have reached for increasingly attenuated theories of criminal liability to ensnare expanding cross-sections of the movement. On October 30, U.S. Attorneys unsealed a superseding indictment adding four defendants to a prosecution of pro-Palestine activists over the vandalism of University of Michigan campus officials’ homes and businesses with pro-divestment messages.

While the original defendants stand accused of holding the spray paint cans, none of the new defendants are charged with participating directly in the vandalism. Instead, they are charged with playing support roles, including media coordination and logistics planning. By sprawling the indictment into charges against activists accused of no substantive crime — merely conspiracy — federal prosecutors appear to be attempting to instill the type of fear capable of corroding a movement.

The superseding indictment is notable for what it omits: allegations that the new defendants were direct participants in the vandalism. Two defendants are accused of editing a Cryptpad document with a public statement. Federal prosecutors charged another defendant because he discussed locations to meet to plan an action. Still another activist’s alleged participation in the conspiracy is limited to operating a publicly-accessible police scanner. Charging conspiracy allows prosecutors to impose collective liability: Any of the new defendants could be found guilty of conspiracy to transmit interstate threats without ever a need to prove that they personally engaged in any criminal act. (In addition to the conspiracy to transmit interstate threats charges, one defendant also picked up a destruction of property to prevent seizure charge for allegedly removing the target of a search warrant from Signal chats.)

In the opinion of National Lawyers Guild Executive Director Xavier de Janon, the prosecution bears the hallmarks of NSPM-7, adding to the ranks of pending protest cases that include prosecutions of ICE protesters in Minnesota and Stop Cop City activists in Atlanta. In the first NSPM-7 case to secure a conviction, eight Prairieland protesters were convicted at trial of providing material support for terrorism after one protester nonfatally shot a police officer during a noise demonstration at an ICE detention center.

“U.S. Attorney Gorgon said that these alleged threats and attempts to terrorize government officials, businesses, and the Jewish Federation are anti-American. This so-called anti-American ideology is all over the NSPM-7 counterterrorism memorandum, and the topic of the prosecution — a free Palestine — matches its priorities,” said de Janon.

It marks an unusual escalation for federal prosecutors to take an interest in a local protest case. Most of the thousands of people arrested during campus protests against the genocide in Palestine faced minor charges in state court, or no charges at all. One of the defendants added to the indictment, Henry Mackeen-Shapiro, initially faced a state-level felony charge for resisting a police officer and a misdemeanor charge for trespassing. Both charges were dismissed in 2025.

De Janon raised the possibility that the federal charges are retaliatory. Two of the 12 defendants, including one of the newly added defendants, sued University of Michigan officials, alleging that the university violated their First Amendment rights by firing them following their participation in pro-Palestine protests.

“It’s very suspicious that the indictment came after the lawsuit,” said de Janon, noting that the lawsuit survived motions to dismiss.

Another possibility is the connection to Unity of Fields, formerly known as Palestine Action US. The superseding indictment never alleges that one of the newly added defendants, Joseph Fisher, engaged in vandalism or participated in the decision to do so. Instead, Fisher’s alleged participation in the conspiracy is limited to sending two Signal messages and editing a statement on the action that included a section for an official statement from Palestine Action. During the height of protests, Palestine Action frequently posted footage and photos from direct actions across the country on social media. The first Signal message introduced a participant in the action to an unnamed individual associated with Unity of Fields/Palestine Action. The other Signal message asked group chat members whether they had seen that Unity of Fields was scuffling with another left-wing organization. (While Fisher was not charged over the text, the indictment lists the message as an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy.)

Multimillionaire Fergie Chambers is a founding member of Palestine Action US, an offshoot of Palestine Action UK. Chambers used some of his considerable wealth to provide bail money to Palestine activists, including fronting $50,000 to bail out three pro-Palestine activists accused of trespass, riot, and sabotage against Elbit Systems, an Israeli-owned weapons company. In July 2026, Chambers was arrested in Spain on the orders of the United States. He now faces extradition over two protest-related riot charges and allegations that he transferred $7.5 million that ultimately went to Hamas. (His team maintains that the money went to humanitarian causes.) During the period between the issuance of the first and second University of Michigan indictments, the Trump administration designated Palestine Action UK a Specially Designated Global Terrorist. The superseding indictment notes that the activists posted demands on Unsalted Counter-Info, an anarchist blog formerly hosted by Autistici/Inventati, another Trump administration-designated terrorist entity.

De Janon connected the dots. “The OFAC designations set the stage to make it seem that anyone in the U.S. who communicates or engages with any designated terrorist group, or even any group remotely similar, is somehow engaging with terrorism, right? Someone’s reference to a communique, a political pamphlet, or a zine is turned into an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy,” he said.

With the noose tightening around left-wing activists, the Trump administration set its sights on the pro-Palestine movement. As with the targeting of anti-ICE protesters in Minnesota, prosecutors again reached for a weapon with the potential to wreak collateral damage on the movement: conspiracy charges.

“Conspiracy is the prosecutor’s darling,” said de Janon. “It’s easy to allege and doesn’t take much to prove.” Without ever committing an illegal act themselves, protesters can land in legal hot water, so long as prosecutors can successfully argue that they agreed to undertake an illegal objective and advanced that objective in some way. But, because circumstantial evidence can be used to prove agreement, protesters’ First Amendment-protected speech and organizing can be admissible as evidence.

Steffen Seitz, Litigation Fellow at the Denver University Sturm College of Law and author of a law review article on the subject, explained why conspiracy law is particularly problematic for activists. He drew on the example of Zoe Rosenberg, an animal rights activist convicted of a felony conspiracy charge related to the liberation of chickens from a factory farm. “Prosecutors could have just charged trespass, where the relevant evidence would have been things like, ‘did she go onto the property without permission?’” Seitz said. “Instead, because they used conspiracy, any organizing that she did with other people became relevant. And so there were hours and hours at trial where the prosecution would show pictures of the most intense protest that a witness had engaged in, the most distasteful social media posts that witness had made.”

If the University of Michigan case goes to trial, any confrontational speech made in advocacy of a free Palestine might not be used to prove that someone held the can of spray paint. Instead, prosecutors may argue that speech against genocide demonstrates that activists agreed to commit an illegal act, in this case, to transmit interstate threats.

Here, the indictment speaks volumes. Untethered from any particular defendant or charge, the general allegations start not with the 2024-2025 conduct at issue, but with October 7, 2023, and the organizing that followed. Omitting mention of Israel’s campaign of genocide against Gaza, the indictment includes the information that Hamas “raped, mutilated, and burned men, women, and children.” The indictment characterizes subsequent campus protests as symptomatic of increased support for Hamas. Though all of the criminal charges relate to vandalism and interference with the execution of a search warrant, the indictment notes that “defendants and unindicted coconspirators” ran a social media campaign, held teach-ins, and posted divestment demands online — all perfectly legal tactics.

In an alternative drafting, the indictment’s story could have read: Students witnessed the genocide in Gaza. Working with classmates, they engaged in lawful advocacy. When the university refused to divest, they pursued direct action. Instead, the indictment insinuates that both lawful and unlawful protest tactics reflect an affinity for terrorism.

In addition to prosecutors’ decision to loop two defendants into the indictment over their alleged coordination with Unity of Fields, prosecuting U.S. Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon’s comment in the press release reveals how the government views the purpose of the charges. “These alleged attempts to terrorize our Jewish community and government officials are nothing new,” he said. “From Pharaoh to Hitler to Hamas, those who terrorize Jews have been the bad guys. As Americans, our job is to fight the bad guys.” Despite his comments, U.S. Attorney Gorgon charged activists with conspiracy to transmit interstate threats, rather than returning an indictment on hate crime or terrorism-related charges. The indictment finds refuge in insinuation and hazy allegations of conspiracy.

By expanding the indictment to include protesters accused only of coordinating publicity or accessing a public police scanner, prosecutors seek to send the message that anyone engaged in illegal activity is radioactive; that activists should be afraid to play a supporting role, no matter how minor, in direct action tactics.

“This ends up becoming this dragnet approach with really sweeping, unpredictable liability,” Seitz commented. “Suddenly, movements as a whole, including ones that are just obviously engaging in lawful activity, can be chilled. My sense is that might be exactly what the government is trying to do.”

“The goal of these prosecutions isn’t to get a conviction,” de Janon concurred. “If that was the goal, then the government would be putting together stronger cases.”

But, while prosecutors may aim to suppress a movement, there is no guarantee that they will succeed. In Georgia, prosecutors’ sweeping RICO conspiracy indictment of Stop Cop City protesters collapsed last winter. The indictment, which included a recitation of basic principles of anarchism and an allegation that signing ACAB was an act in furtherance of the racketeering conspiracy, received widespread ridicule. The movement thrived, in spite of retribution and in rebuke to it.

“Just like the Cop City RICO conspiracy and the Broadview 6, when legal challenges start being made, it doesn’t actually take much for things to fall apart,” said de Janon. “These very, very expansive cases are held by a very weak theory of conspiracy.”

Asked what he would like to communicate to protesters, de Janon argued, “If the goal is to prosecute a movement, to prosecute ideas, then the response should be to be bolder, to be more public, to be less afraid. If the government’s desire is to shut down debate about freedom in Palestine, then we should make absolutely clear that we’re going to be talking about this. The antidote to fascism is more activism.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: European Union Was Not a Climate Champion at COP31, Activists Say
content:
The EU may have balked at fossil fuels’ absence from the final text, but they obstructed progress on climate finance.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The United Nations climate summit in Turkey, known as COP31, collapsed on Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal. A number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. Many poorer countries also objected to the lack of financial commitments from richer nations to assist them in adapting to the climate crisis.

“This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help,” says Filipino climate activist Lidy Nacpil. “The principle is that [wealthy nations] have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions.”

“What we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities,” says Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA. “That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP, but it’s becoming increasingly untenable.”

We also speak with two other leading climate justice advocates who attended COP31, Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network International and Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy of the Marshall Islands.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, back in New York.

In Turkey, the United Nations climate summit collapsed Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal as the Earth warms. The European Union and a number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The effort to strip the text of references to coal, oil and gas was led by Saudi Arabia and joined by Russia. The United States did not participate in COP31.

This is Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands.

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: The Republic of the Marshall Islands objects to the adoption of the CMA text and cannot join consensus. We came to Antalya to honor our commitment to the Paris Agreement and to do what we promised our people back home. We face an inevitable overshoot of 1.5. We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people and on providing the finance to do this. We have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot: a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.

AMY GOODMAN: Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien outlined the European Union’s opposition to the final text.

DARRAGH O’BRIEN: At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short. We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach. We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel.

AMY GOODMAN: Over the weekend, climate justice activists rallied against the final text. On Friday, a Malaysian climate activist, Amalen Sathananthar, was detained after interrupting the closing plenary. He stood on a table holding a red noose around his neck and wearing a shirt that read, “You are killing the future.”

AMALEN SATHANANTHAR: You are killing the future! You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now? The climate crisis is killing! … There’s no money! Just kill me now! The Global South can’t wait! The Global South can’t wait for this! And yet you just keep doing nothing, nothing at all! Racists! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! … You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future!

AMY GOODMAN: We are joined now by three leading climate justice activists who just returned to their home countries after attending the U.N. climate summit. Brandon Wu is with us from Washington, D.C., director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA. In Manila, Lidy Nacpil is with us, the longtime Filipina climate activist and coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development. And from Cape Town, South Africa, we’re joined by Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International.

I want to begin with Tasneem, but first let’s play a short video from Turkey of Tasneem Essop trying to interact with Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations from Australia.

TASNEEM ESSOP: You have an opportunity to save this process. We need decisions that will protect the people of the South. There’s nothing in the text, and corporate interests will be the only ones that benefit. CCUS, carbon dioxide removals are dangerous, dangerous, opens the door for fossil fuels. Please read the letter.

TASNEEM ESSOP: The Global South demands the protection of its people.

AMY GOODMAN: “The Global South demands the protection of its people,” Tasneem Essop said, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, joining us from Cape Town, South Africa.

Tasneem, you must be extremely tired at this point. I just saw you in Antalya, Turkey, and now you’re back home in Cape Town, South Africa. Can you respond to the collapse of the talks, as you tried to question the president of the COP, the Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen?

TASNEEM ESSOP: Thanks, Amy. Yeah, a bit tired from the COP itself, but also, in a sense, very disappointed that it had to come to this.

I wouldn’t characterize the COP as having collapsed. I think it’s important for your viewers to understand that there were two processes, actually, at this COP. The one was the formal negotiation process, and that is where the negotiations on different tracks — on the just transition, on adaptation, on mitigation, on climate finance — was taking place. And then there was the cover decision.

The cover decision was a decision by the COP presidencies, in fact, driven by the COP president for negotiations, Australia, as a way of including political statements, if I can call it that. And it’s really that where there was no agreement reached. The others had — you know, they were largely procedural. They had passed through. There was one or two where there were objections, like the mitigation work program track. But certainly, it was the cover decision that caused the most controversy.

Presidencies do not need to have cover decisions. We were concerned about this cover decision from the start, when they announced this at the pre-COP. And so, we saw that, in fact, this cover decision distracted the entire negotiations. All of the political attention that was needed in the formal negotiations got taken out and into the cover decision negotiations and discussions. So, that is where things collapsed, if you might call it that. It’s disappointing that it had to come.

I think the biggest lesson here is cover decisions just do not work. We need to pay attention and focus on the mandated negotiations. And that is where developed countries, actually, the ones that, you know, had the theater around rejecting a cover decision — that’s where they actually gutted the negotiations. That’s where — and it’s hidden — where the problems arose. The finance for adaptation track didn’t move forward. They kept on resisting the delivery plan for a commitment they made on tripling finance for adaptation. The just transition track didn’t move, because they obstructed the creation of a just transition mechanism.

And so, if you go through all of the formal negotiation tracks, it was developed countries that actually blocked and obstructed, and then came to the cover decision and, you know, decided that they’re going to reject it, and pretended to be the champions, when, in fact, the real negotiations were happening elsewhere, and they actually obstructed this.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring Brandon Wu into the conversation, of ActionAid USA. He also just returned from the U.N. climate summit. If you can give your analysis of what took place? A lot of people are saying COP31 collapses as EU rejects texts for being weak on fossil fuels. But when we were at the U.N. climate summit, we were speaking to many, including a young European activist who was saying, in fact, to their shock, the European Union replaced President Trump, who had pulled the U.S. out, in pushing for fossil fuels at the U.N. climate summit. What happened?

BRANDON WU: So, I think this has become the headline. I mean, you read these headlines at the top of the show, right? The COP collapses, and it’s because — and the EU is rejecting the text because of lack of fossil fuels. And I do think that that is actually a dangerous and deeply misleading story, because, as Tasneem said, the EU, you know, try to style themselves as the climate champions: “This is not enough ambition. We need more movement on phasing out fossil fuels,” which, of course, we do. We need more movement on fossil — on phasing out fossil fuels. And it’s got to start in the Global North.

The EU are being quite hypocritical, actually. Their transition plans away from fossil fuels are not at all aligned with the 1.5 degrees Celsius climate target that they claim to be defending so much. And the way these negotiations are structured, the Global North has the responsibility to reduce its emissions first and fastest, and also the responsibility to provide money and support to the Global South, so that the transition can be enabled in those poorer countries.

And what we saw is that the developed countries, across the board, acted more like bullies than champions. They come in demanding more of the Global South, but in every negotiating room blocking any progress on the finance that is going to make that transition possible.

And one thing, like two weeks before the negotiations started, the EU climate commissioner actually said any new climate finance commitments were, quote, “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” He actually said that. This was two months after the floods in Nepal that killed 1,500 people, with five over 5,000 people still missing. “Dead in the water.” It was shockingly tasteless and also a shocking way to approach the negotiations. They said out loud two weeks before the negotiations that they were coming in with nothing to offer, with no room for compromise on the one thing that is the major priority for the Global South countries in these negotiations.

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about what this means. What does it mean for the COP, for the conference of the parties, COP31, the longest, the largest, to collapse? And while I think up to 100,000 people participated, would you also say it’s one of the largest gatherings of fossil fuel lobbyists in the world?

BRANDON WU: So, yes, there are a lot of fossil fuel lobbyists that come up into these spaces. There are a lot of lobbyists for data centers, for, you know, Big Tech, all these things. It’s not a clean space, right? And the reason we have so many intransigent governments is because there’s so many profit-seeking interests that have their ear.

The way forward — I mean, as Tasneem said, the actual negotiations did not fully collapse. There were decisions that moved forward some key things on just transition, which is, you know, making sure communities are supported as we change our economies to more sustainable ones, on finance, on adaptation. Those tracks are not dead. We didn’t get anything we wanted, but it was only the cover decision that was fully rejected.

And so we live to fight another day, but we’re going to face the same problem over and over again. This has been happening for decades, right? The way that these negotiations are structured is the Global North, as I said, has to lead, on cutting emissions, on providing finance. They have the legal obligation to do that. They have the money to do that. We see how the U.S. is throwing trillions of dollars a year for genocide and war. The money is there. They need to provide it to the Global South to make the transition happen, and then the Global South can reduce emissions, their dependence on fossil fuels. And what we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities. That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP, but it’s becoming increasingly untenable.

AMY GOODMAN: And, I mean, I think part of the problem, being at the COP for this past week, is the level of jargon that most people just don’t have access to — “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “climate finance.” These may sound obvious to you. The cover decision and the cover letter, explain exactly what you mean.

BRANDON WU: Look, at the end of the day, this is a question of fairness. There are basic principles of fairness, that everyone understands, that are just being blown out of the water in this process. The rich developed countries — the U.S., EU, Australia, Japan, Canada — these are the countries that spewed greenhouse gases into the atmosphere over the last 150, 200 years, and have built their economies on the backs of fossil fuels. These are the countries that created the mess, and these are the countries that have to clean it up.

“Climate finance” is just a fancy term for sending money to poorer countries so that they can make the transition, as well, so that they can help their communities survive in a world in which, you know, we’re breaching the 1.5-degree limit. That’s another piece of jargon, but what that means, of course, is that climate impacts are getting worse. We all know this. They’re getting worse. They’re going to get much worse, much faster, I think. And countries need the support to deal with that. These are countries that have had nothing to do with the problem, and it’s their people whose lives are at stake. They’re basic principles of fairness. I think everybody can understand that.

AMY GOODMAN: And the cover decision?

BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, I mean, the reason that that’s important is because the rich countries are using what happened with the cover decision as a way to deflect blame. So, they are pointing at —

AMY GOODMAN: And “cover decision” means?

BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, again, it was a political text, that came out of nowhere. The presidency of the COP wrote it, so Türkiye and Australia. It was not part of the formal negotiating tracks, where you have all the different country blocs talking about issues of substance that they’ve decided should formally be on the agenda for the negotiations. So, it’s a political text that was written by the presidency, and then they tried to, in a top-down way, get buy-in from all the countries so they could include all their little pet projects and all the pet projects of the countries that had their ear.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring Lidy Nacpil into this conversation. Lidy Nacpil is a Filipina climate activist, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, with the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice. Lidy, thanks so much for being with us. You’re joining us, I believe, from Manila. Can you respond to what has taken place? You know, for so many COPs, so many of these U.N. climate summits, in the midst of them, the Philippines is hit with tsunamis, with hurricanes. I think of how many times Yeb Saño, first as a chief climate negotiator for the Philippines, now, as he’s described, as a climate pilgrim, but then he would stand up and talk about how the Philippines was being ravaged by the climate crisis. What this means for the Philippines, and what you think needs to happen now, Lidy?

LIDY NACPIL: Well, first of all, our reaction to COP31 is also amidst the backdrop of the UNEP report saying that the breach of 1.5 degrees is imminent and unavoidable. So we thought that this would at least imbue a sense of urgency for this COP to deliver very concrete and actionable agreements that will actually mean progress in the real world and not just in text language. So, of course, we are so deeply disappointed and enraged that we have not made this progress, and, in fact, backtracked on a number of things. There are, of course, some important gains we have made in terms of securing at least some meager progress on certain things. Tasneem has mentioned, for instance, other negotiating tracks. But this is not what — the progress we needed at this point. We need much, much more.

And in terms of the climate finance that we’re discussing here, I’d like to really make it clear: This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help. And this is one of the worst things that happen at COPs. They make us feel like, OK, here we come again with our finance demands. But this is a matter of principle, as well as practicality. The principle is that they have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions, including that of providing climate finance as part of the reparations for all the harm that has been caused. And the practicality is that we cannot fully transition away from fossil fuels, which we want to do. We will be one of the first people to be — to want to do that, because the impacts on us are huge and horrifying. But this is not simply possible to succeed in completing that transition if that climate finance is not delivered.

And this is a fact that they continuously leave out in their stories. And when I say “they” here, it’s the Global North. The EU, for instance, we were very appalled that they were, as Brandon said, hypocritically saying they’re going to reject the cover decision because there’s no mention of fossil fuel transition, but they leave out the fact that this is not going to happen unless they deliver on their climate finance, which they have successfully obstructed in all the negotiation tracks, any discussion on finance.

So, this leaves the Global South in a situation where we realize it’s — we really need to fight harder and build our power, because no way are these countries going to, or these governments, are going to negotiate it on the basis — negotiate on the basis of good faith, of good intention for the whole of humanity.

And by the way, it is not just for our sake that we need to complete that transition in our countries for which we need the climate finance. It’s for the entire world’s sake. We’re not going to succeed in solving the climate problem with just actions in the Global North. We know that. We need to act in the Global South, but we need to do more than our fair share. And for that to happen, we definitely need that climate finance.

So, we’re not here to beg. We are here to insist on what is owed us and to insist on what success for the whole of humanity, for the whole of the planet, what success requires.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring in Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner. We’ve just spoken with three well-known activists who have attended so many of the climate summits, from the Philippines, from South Africa, from the United States. Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner is also an activist, but now the climate envoy, one of the delegates, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands. We just played a clip of you speaking. And I wanted to ask you: What was it like from the inside? And how does climate change affect the Marshall Islands, even where they are?

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yeah. Thank you, Amy. I’m so glad to be here, and I’m glad you were able to catch me, actually.

But I would just say that in the — it was incredibly long hours of negotiations. I mean, I didn’t sleep that whole night. I got there to swap out my minister at 7 p.m., and then I was there until we delivered our statement. And so, we were negotiating at 3:00 in the morning, at 1:00 in the morning, and then again at 5:00 in the morning. And it was long hours of discussions between ourselves, our allies within the Pacific Small Island Developing States, within the Alliance of Small Island Developing States, and, of course, other countries, too. And we were really trying to figure out how do we make our way forward and whether or not we needed to sign on to the cover decision or not sign on to the cover decision. So, it was not an easy decision at all.

But I think, ultimately, for us, this deal did not provide on fossil fuel transition that we needed. It did not have the ambition on finance, on adaptation finance. It did not have enough strong language on the ICJ. It did not recognize how incredibly monumental the ICJ was, especially for those of us in the Pacific. And then, of course, it did not have enough on any of the other components that were so important to us, on IPCC.

And so, I think, ultimately, we did decide that we needed to not sign on to the cover decision. It is the first time that Marshall Islands did that, and we did not come to that decision lightly. But I think that I stand by it, you know, and I think that it was the right call to make. I think that the two COP presidencies had an incredibly difficult task of, first of all, working together, but also working with multiple different countries and all the different priorities. But I think the biggest thing of all was that we could not sign on to a decision that had to do with CCUS, the carbon capture, utilization, storage. We did not want this COP to be a CCUS. And, of course, I think also —

AMY GOODMAN: Kathy, if you could explain what CCUS is, what these options are that are being talked about?

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yeah. So, I’m not a climate scientist, so I’ll just say that CCUS is actually a way to capture carbon that actually utilizes fossil fuels. So, it basically would have opened up the way for more fossil fuel usage. And ultimately, we as the Marshall Islands could not agree to a deal that would actually open the path for further fossil fuel usage and actually make the environment worse. So, that was part of the reason why we didn’t sign on.

But it was also because there was extremely weak language on adaptation finance. So, I think that’s really important, because I think what’s coming away is that a lot of countries are saying, “They walked away only because it did not have transition away from fossil fuels.” Yes, definitely, so important, and also it did not have enough on adaptation finance. Countries like mine need both. We cannot survive the climate crisis without the transition away from fossil fuels and without the needed adaptation finance for developing countries, that we’re duly owed.

You know, the Marshall Islands is only two meters above sea level. We are dealing with massive impacts from climate, from climate change, including the worst drought in El Niño, super El Niño that’s about to hit us. And then we’re looking at adaptation at such a large scale, changing the landscape of our islands, that would cost tens of billions of dollars just for two of our urban centers. And we did not cause this problem. So, of course, we are owed that finance. So, I think that’s really important to come away with, too, is that we were betrayed on two fronts: on the transition away from fossil fuels and on adaptation finance.

AMY GOODMAN: I just have to quickly ask: You are — there’s something oddly appropriate about you — I don’t think you’re in your closet. I think you’re in some kind of store. But there are pocket books everywhere, which suggest money. And maybe that’s the most appropriate way to understand what took place.

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yes, yeah. You caught me on my day off right after, and so I’m out actually doing a little bit of sightseeing in Antalya.

AMY GOODMAN: Amazing. I wanted to end back with Brandon Wu. You’ve returned to the United States. President Trump just had his trilateral summit, or, I should say, photograph, with President Xi of China and President Putin of Russia. And one of the deals in their so-called peace declaration was increasing the production of fossil fuels. If you can talk about what it means to come back to the historically largest emitter of carbon, of carbon pollutants in the world, after Trump just met with now the current largest producer of carbon pollutants in the world, China, and their resolution to increase oil, gas production?

BRANDON WU: Yeah, I want to say two things about that. Excuse me. First, the U.S. is actually the country with the largest oil and gas expansion plans of any country in the world. And so, if we want to point a finger at anybody, it should be our own country, you know, and, of course, in addition to being the largest historical polluter.

The second thing is that, you know, I think what this really shows is it actually comes back to the importance of a multilateral democratic process like the COPs. You know, we come away from these COPs every year saying, “Well, that was a disaster.” And then, of course, so we always ask ourselves, “What’s the point? Why are we still fighting in these places that are dominated by countries in the Global North that don’t want to do anything, that have fossil fuel lobbyists roaming the hallways? Like, why are we here? What are we accomplishing?” And I think that trilateral summit really shows us kind of what the alternative is. Right? It is a world that is dominated by autocrats, or wannabe autocrats, and strongmen, who have very little accountability. And that is what we’re up against, right? And the UNFCCC and the U.N. spaces, in general, provide an alternative to that, where everybody, at least in theory, formally has a voice, and we, as civil society, have a space to input and to protest and to advocate.

And we have to preserve that. It’s not delivering the results that we need so far, and we know why. It’s because of the intransigence of many countries, where, as Lidy said, we need to be building power. We need to be pushing these governments to do better. Certainly in the U.S., we need to be doing that. And hopefully, we’ll have that opportunity in the very near future. But, yeah, I think the alternative to these multilateral spaces are places where we have even less power, even less of a say, and have even less of an opportunity to hold leaders accountable.

AMY GOODMAN: Brandan Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA; Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands; Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, speaking to us from Cape Town, South Africa; Lidy Nacpil, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and development, speaking to us from the Philippines. We want to thank you all for being with us.

Coming up, as Democrats flip another House seat in North Carolina, we speak to Bishop William Barber. He’s calling for the Third Reconstruction. What does that mean? What is he calling on Democrats to do, who now have the largest majority in the House of Representatives in 30 years? Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Fenfo,” “Something to Say,” by the Malian singer Fatoumata Diawara, performing in our Democracy Now! studio in 2018.

title: Trump, With Tens of Millions Invested in Nvidia, Told Board to Reinstate Huang
content:
The reinstatement of the disgraced CEO has sent Nvidia’s stock roaring back, rising 30 percent.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

President Donald Trump personally intervened to get the disgraced Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday — in turn, sending the company’s stock and, potentially, Trump’s personal portfolio soaring.

The tech company’s board announced that Huang has been reinstated immediately after members made the decision at a meeting on Monday, less than 10 days after he resigned in disgrace. The board directly cited the U.S. government’s involvement in the decision, saying that the board “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

The reference to “senior levels” of the government appears to refer at least in part to Trump, who spent Monday morning boasting about his role in the decision.

In an interview with CNBC, Trump said he “convinced them” and “made the deal” for the board to reinstate Huang. He said that Huang, accused of having an affair with a woman with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence and with two of his subordinates at the company, “did nothing wrong.”

title: 99 Percent of Gaza Is Polluted With Toxins Due to Israel’s Genocide, Report Says
content:
Oxfam found extensive toxic contamination throughout the strip’s air, soil, groundwater, and surface water.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

US government officials and commentators from both sides of the political aisle have insisted for years that Israel’s assault on Gaza is targeted at Hamas fighters and have bristled at accusations that Israel, with U.S. backing, is intentionally attempting to ethnically cleanse the exclave of Palestinians and make it uninhabitable for the population.

But one advocate for Palestinian rights said Monday that the “environmental war crimes” described in a new report on how Gaza’s air, soil, and water have become toxic due to more than three years of relentless bombing — despite a ceasefire deal reached last year — are “also known as genocide.”

The report by Oxfam International and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) — titled “Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s Military Assault Has Turned Gaza Into a Toxic Wasteland, Threatening Human Survival”—finds that while Israel’s military onslaught has directly impacted about 78% of Gaza’s land area, a spatial analysis identified indicators of potential contamination from heavy metals, residue from explosives, asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins, and biological contaminants across almost the entirety of Gaza — more than 99% of the exclave.

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, executive director of Oxfam. “The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.”

PRESS RELEASE: More than 99 per cent of #Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israel's military assault READ HERE: https://t.co/nIx81uPiPV pic.twitter.com/1k8QkTzMzU

The organizations used satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis, and other open-source data — including the United Nations Environment Program’s estimate that Israel’s U.S.-backed assault had generated more than 61 million tons of debris across Gaza — to build a comprehensive picture of the exclave’s contamination.

The highest levels of potential contamination were identified in Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia, and the Salah al-Din Road, which correspond closely “with the areas subjected to the most sustained bombardment, ground military operations, infrastructure destruction, and debris accumulation.”

The destruction of buildings, wastewater treatment facilities, industrial and energy facilities, and waste-management systems “has released a complex mixture of contaminants,” reads the report, including explosive residue, perchlorates, asbestos fibers, crystalline silica, persistent organic pollutants, and pathogens — all of which can then move through the air, soil, groundwater, and surface water.

“The population is likely to have been exposed to contaminants through multiple and interconnected pathways,” the report continues.

Contamination described in the report include:

Fecal coliforms, which indicate disease-causing pathogens in water, detected at a rate nearly 10 times more than that reported in 2021, with the coliforms found in 19% of 79 groundwater wells sampled across Gaza;

40,000m³ of raw sewage being pouring into the Mediterranean Sea each day due to the fact that only 19% of sewage pumping stations remain functional and 30% of the wastewater network is operational;

Heightened risks of long-term soil contamination in Beit Hanoun, Wadi Gaza, and the Khan Younis area due to their clay-rich soils — potentially threatening the safety of food crops when agricultural production resumes;

High risks of air contamination in Gaza City, Jabalia, and the North Gaza Governorateas pollutants from the intensive bombardment are resuspended due to vehicle movement and debris clearance;

High risks of drinking-water contamination in North Gaza, Gaza City, and Deir al-Balah, where remaining operational wells and desalination overlap with highly vulnerable groundwater systems and areas of heavy bombardment; and

Growing risks to people’s long-term respiratory health due to dust and pollution caused by the destruction of buildings and the burning of waste.

“It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers,” said Behar. “In an area as small, oppressed, and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests, and the risk of disease growing. Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them. The associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks.”

The analysis of the widespread, toxic contamination “contributes to the body of evidence relevant to the prohibition of deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the physical destruction of a protected group under Article II(c) of the Genocide Convention,” reads the report. Top human rights groups and Holocaust scholars are among those who have argued that Israel’s bombardment of Gaza amounts to a genocide, and South Africa has a genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice.

Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam who was the lead author of the report, said that the widespread contamination is made even more difficult to address and mitigate because “unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas.”

“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm reduction measures,” said Samad. “Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring, and specialized remediation of affected areas from contaminants like explosive residues, organic pollutants, and heavy metals.”

Under international law, the report states, “the natural environment is not legally neutral… It is civilian in character and therefore protected.”

“International humanitarian law explicitly protects both objects indispensable to civilian survival and the natural environment,” the report continues. In Israel’s attacks on Gaza, “the resulting contamination of groundwater, soil, air, and coastal waters is environmental harm that is legally relevant under international humanitarian law.”

Oxfam called on Israel to allow a “full, independent, field-based Post-Conflict Environmental Assessment.”

“Rebuilding without addressing environmental risks could expose Palestinians to entirely preventable harm,” said Saeda Shaebat, the director of the Palestinian Environmental Quality Authority in Jerusalem.

New Oxfam and CEOBS analysis finds 99% of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination. Toxic residues from Israel’s military assault is threatening the air, soil and water that people rely on. Israel must allow independent testing and essential aid. Read:… pic.twitter.com/Q19N7WQhN1

Behar said that “Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water, and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation, and recovery actions are prioritized.”

author: Ali Harb
title: New Wave of Progressives Turns Support for Israel Into a Question of Democracy
content:
Palestinian American author Ahmed Moor is challenging John Fetterman, one of Israel’s staunch supporters in the Senate.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Senator John Fetterman, one of Israel’s most uncompromising advocates in Congress, is facing a primary challenge from a Palestinian American writer born in Gaza.

Ahmed Moor had little name recognition when he launched his campaign for the U.S. Senate seat in Pennsylvania on November 9. But in less than two weeks, he has generated growing enthusiasm and acquired thousands of donations from across all 50 states, according to his campaign.

Moor says his Senate bid is motivated by the genocide in Gaza, but he stresses that the U.S. support for Israel’s atrocities in Palestine is a byproduct of “corruption” and the capture of public policy by special interest groups — a problem that ails all aspects of the U.S. political system. “My campaign is not only viable. My campaign is the future,” Moor told Truthout.

“We’re running on anti-corruption,” Moor added. “We’ve seen that in America, people are highly, highly motivated by the idea of cleaning up our civics. We have the capacity for renewal in this country. That’s what my campaign is about.”

Moor’s candidacy for the 2028 Democratic Senate nomination in Pennsylvania follows a string of significant victories by pro-Palestine progressives this year, including the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota. Left-wing State Representative Chris Rabb was also elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in Moor’s hometown of Philadelphia.

As rejecting U.S. support for Israel transforms from a taboo to a widely accepted position in U.S. politics, more progressives seeking public office are centering the issue in their campaigns. And they are connecting Washington’s foreign policy to problems at home, including affordability, cruel immigration enforcement, and access to health care.

The U.S. war on Iran, which Donald Trump has launched jointly with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has made the link between domestic and foreign policy more potent, further strengthening the argument of pro-Palestine progressives. The war, which saw Tehran restrict passage through the Strait of Hormuz, has sent energy prices spiraling and fueled inflation in the U.S. economy.

Moor told Truthout that the U.S. public does not want to be implicated “in the mass murder of children.” (Israel has killed more than 20,000 children in Gaza, according to local health authorities.) The Senate candidate added that Americans also care about the issue because “certain policy items contribute to the corrosion of American democracy and the diminishment of our quality of life over time.”

“The whole idea that there’s a foreign policy and a domestic policy is a mischaracterization of how things work,” he told Truthout. “There’s one budget and a funded line item here means something else isn’t getting funded elsewhere. So, you take that understanding and apply it also to the fact that the corruption crisis and the cost-of-living crisis are one and the same.”

For Moor, the unlimited campaign spending by special interest groups, such us the pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC (American Israel Public Affairs Committee), to pressure policy outcomes that they prefer is at the root of the problem. Moor also invoked the war with Iran.

“We’ve gone and funded a war for Benjamin Netanyahu in Iran, which has driven up the price of diesel, which has caused cascading inflation throughout our economy, which is making everybody who lives here poorer, the people of Pennsylvania poorer,” he said.

Fetterman, who has received public praise from AIPAC, has been one of the most outspoken supporters of Israel on Capitol Hill, regularly appearing on Fox News to defend the country’s leaders and attack its critics on the left. He has also voted against bills to rein in Trump’s power to continue the war with Iran and threatened to leave the Democratic Party over Israel. These positions appear to have alienated many voters. A recent Quinnipiac University poll suggested that only 13 percent of Democrats have a favorable opinion of the Democratic senator.

Left-wing candidates who oppose U.S. aid and arms sales to Israel defeated several Democratic incumbents earlier this year. While advocacy for Palestinian rights was not the sole issue that progressive candidates have championed, it was a constant theme that left-wing challengers brought up in the 2026 election cycle. For example, now Congresswoman-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier wore a keffiyeh in the video announcing her primary challenge against incumbent Adriano Espaillat in New York last year and cited her activism against “what we all know is a genocide in Palestine.” In New Jersey, Congressman-elect Adam Hamawy spoke extensively during the campaign about the horrors he witnessed when he volunteered in Gaza’s hospitals as a doctor during the genocide.

The ink has barely dried on the results of the general elections, but progressive challengers like Moor are already starting to emerge against conservative Democrats in the 2028 vote. In western Michigan, Ivan Diaz, a former Kent County commissioner, has launched a primary challenge against Democratic Congresswoman Hillary Scholten, who is staunchly pro-Israel. Scholten voted in 2024 for a measure to ban the State Department from citing the Palestinian death toll documented by the Gaza Health Ministry. She has also refused to endorse El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate race, citing his April appearance with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

“I do not support war. I do not support war crimes. I do not support genocide,” Diaz told Truthout. “This is not about any one particular country. It’s just my morals, my position that I do not support war. With that being said, it is undeniable at this point — the experts around the world have concluded that what is happening in Palestine is genocide, it is apartheid, and we need to stop it.”

“There is a deep desire to send people to Washington, D.C., who are going to fight for us,” Diaz said. “This is not about me. It’s not about Hillary Scholten. It’s about this system of corruption, this system of politics that throws people crumbs and expects us to be grateful for them.”

As Diaz is seeking office in a district in once conservative-leaning western Michigan, Moor is challenging for a statewide race in Pennsylvania, where Trump won in 2016 and 2024. Progressive advocates say the viability of their politics is no longer confined to deeply Democratic districts — and they have El-Sayed’s victory in the swing state of Michigan to back that argument. El-Sayed won comfortably in Kent County, where most of Scholten’s district is based, both in the primaries in August and the general elections on November 3.

Nusaiba Mubarak, founder of the newly formed progressive advocacy group Out-Organize, said the U.S. political climate has been a “whirlwind,” between the increasing rise of oligarchs, growing embrace of authoritarianism, and erosion of democratic guardrails.

“Because of that, the rise of Democratic Socialists and support for Palestinian rights didn’t come out of nowhere,” Mubarak told Truthout. “In 2020, when I served as Bernie’s National Muslim and Arab American Organizer, I witnessed a base of thousands of new and mobilized volunteers across the country become disillusioned with the Democratic Party.”

Sanders was one of the first prominent presidential candidates to push back against unconditional aid to Israel. In 2016, he clashed with former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton over Washington’s “one-sided” approach to the conflict. He also called out Israel for killing and injuring thousands of civilians in Gaza during a 2014 offensive in what was seen at the time as a stunning show of dissent against the bipartisan consensus in support of Israel.

The Vermont senator’s 2016 position now seems to be the accepted norm within the Democratic Party, especially amid the ongoing atrocities in Gaza.

Mubarak said the victories of progressives in 2026 who didn’t back down on Palestinian rights show that it is possible to push to “make life affordable with better policies while not compromising on our shared values.”

“Now, we’re looking to new candidates, like Ahmed Moor, who share those ideals and will stand up to the establishment,” she said.

Moor held his first public campaign event at a restaurant in Philadelphia on November 17. The venue quickly filled up with early supporters, many of whom wore keffiyeh-patterned shirts, dresses, and scarves.

Alissa Wise, the founding director of Rabbis for Ceasefire and a friend of Moor’s, was the first to take the makeshift stage atop a flight of stairs in the jam-packed restaurant. The rabbi recalled learning about the killing of nearly a dozen of Moor’s family members in 2023, after she was arrested during a protest at the U.S. Capitol calling for an immediate end to the war on Gaza.

“Knowing that from that moment of one of the deepest heartaches and tragedies of our time, that Ahmed would be able to rise from that pain and that grief to step forward to try to ensure that all of us have a life of dignity is profound,” Wise told the crowd. She concluded with a saying from Jewish tradition that seemed to describe the steady rise of the Palestinian rights movement in the U.S. after being maligned and demonized for decades: “The discarded stone has now become the foundation.”

“This political moment that we are in — it is time that we see the flipping of the scales,” Wise said.

title: DNC Mandates 2028 Presidential Hopefuls Reject Dark Money for Debate Eligibility
content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders celebrated the decision and called for it to be expanded to all Democratic primaries.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) has announced that it is requiring 2028 presidential candidates to reject “dark money” spending in order to qualify for the primary debate stage, potentially taking a step toward reducing the impact of super PACs and billionaires on elections.

The committee said that it is planning to hold 12 debates over the course of the presidential primaries, with the first taking place in June and July of 2027, and the final one taking place in March 2028.

In order to qualify for these debates, the committee is requiring candidates to sign a pledge that bars campaigns from reaching out to super PACs or 501(c)(4) groups to solicit spending on their behalf. It also requires candidates to “denounce” such spending done to back them on television, radio, digital, billboard, or mail advertising if it was done without their knowledge.

Spending that is not by a 501(c)(4) special interest group or super PAC — which are two of the largest vehicles for outside spending — or spending on a “different form of media” is still allowed.

author: Darius Tahir
title: Health Tech Is Pushing Data-Collecting “Smart” Implants That Raise Cost of Care
content:
Doctors can charge for examining data collected by devices that have little evidence for benefiting patient health.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.

Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”

It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.

Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.

Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.

Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.

The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.

Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”

Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.

“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”

The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “the world’s first and only” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance.

However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes.

There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect.

Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries received that service, known as “remote patient monitoring,” according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General. Medicare, the federal program covering older Americans and some with disabilities, paid medical providers $536 million for remote monitoring, more than double what it paid three years earlier. A review by the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker found about 300,000 adults with employer-sponsored insurance received at least one remote monitoring claim in 2023.

Medicare has proposed pulling back on some reimbursements after the department’s inspector general warned remote monitoring poses fraud risks: About 43% of patients in 2024 didn’t receive the full suite of services defined by the program — which includes educating the patient about the device and monitoring data for changes in health. The watchdog also cautioned that companies sometimes cold-call patients to offer and sign them up for devices they may not need.

The internet-connected devices may also pose risks to privacy or expose patients to unexpected consequences. In 2018, ProPublica reported that insurers watched the performance of CPAP machines and, determining some patients weren’t using them, denied coverage for replacement supplies such as masks.

In the case of Zimmer, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services spokesperson Christopher Krepich emailed KFF Health News that “CMS payment does not mean the agency endorses a manufacturer’s marketing claims or guarantees that a technology improves outcomes for every patient.” He said the agency regularly evaluates its reimbursement policies.

Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data.

The smart knee is one of the flagship orthopedic products of Indiana-based Zimmer Biomet, which also manufactures non-connected knee joints. The company — which hired professional strongman, actor, and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger to pitch its products as its “chief movement officer” — sold some $3.3 billion in knee joints last year.

Up the California coast in Contra Costa County, Jodi Murphy filed a lawsuit against Zimmer, Canary Medical, and her doctor after receiving a Persona IQ knee implant and being registered to use Zimmer’s app. The lawsuit alleges the doctor and companies were at fault because they acted “without disclosing this device or obtaining Plaintiff’s specific informed consent for its use.”

The doctor and her practice denied all allegations. Zimmer’s attorneys have said the company “does not practice medicine and as a matter of law had no duty to obtain consent to the treatment provided by her physician.” A hearing is scheduled for February.

The doctor did not respond to requests for comment. Murphy and her lawyer declined to comment.

Russak’s lawsuit alleges his doctor told him he “had not disclosed the electronic nature, wireless transmission functions, or data-collection capabilities of the Persona IQ to prior patients in whom he had implanted the same device.” It goes on to cite that exchange as evidence that the companies “failed to adequately educate” the doctor.

“I don’t believe that Zimmer or Canary are training the doctors, and it’s an issue,” Russak told KFF Health News.

Zimmer’s website says the implant allows care teams to “monitor and personalize” a patient’s experience and improve a practice’s efficiency. Many patients prefer the remote option, the company’s literature says. Farther down the webpage, the company says the implant is “not intended to support clinical decision-making” and has “not been shown to provide any clinical benefit.” The company also mentions the potential financial rewards for surgeons who implant the device — including ongoing payments for remote monitoring.

Kevin Bozic, an orthopedic surgeon who is chair of surgery and perioperative care at the University of Texas-Austin, reviewed research on the Zimmer smart knee provided by Zimmer spokesperson Kirkpatrick at KFF Health News’ request. “None of them compare Persona IQ to a more conventional [knee] implant,” he wrote in an email.

Bozic said orthopedic surgeons he knows are “ambivalent” about Zimmer’s smart knee devices and many don’t use them. The implant is the “most generic part of the operation and really doesn’t have a big impact at all on the outcome.”

In theory, he said, the data collected by the device about the number of steps a patient takes and the joint’s range of motion makes for better care. If a patient becomes more sedentary, that could be a useful signal for clinicians, he said.

But, in practice, “it’s a nice-to-have, certainly not a need-to-have,” Bozic said, “certainly not something that I would want to add significant cost to the procedure for.”

Surgeons already check on patients and ask to be informed if their health changes, he said. “It’s overkill to have it in the knee.”

Smart-knee manufacturers have also profited from a different Medicare benefit — a “new technology add-on payment” — that effectively temporarily subsidizes the adoption of otherwise money-losing new devices, thereby encouraging innovation. (The extra payment for Persona IQ lapsed in fall 2024.)

The payment program has undergone several adjustments in recent years. Beginning in late 2020 — until the government adjusted the benefit this year — there was no requirement that new technology substantially improve on older devices or pills. That lack of a requirement, predictably, meant more qualifying therapies. A 2025 study found an average of four approved annually in the near decade before the 2020 change; in the next four fiscal years, the authors said, the average moved up to nearly 15 a year.

The subsidy has lasting benefits for the manufacturers, said Dhruva, the UCSF cardiologist, who studies digital technologies and reimbursement. Medicare’s reimbursements are based on the average costs of a procedure. Since the subsidy increases the cost of the procedure, it increases the average costs, too — thereby driving up the basis for future costs.

Indeed, Dhruva said, the problem of payments for unproven services is present in Medicare reimbursement for remote patient monitoring, too.

Dhruva said there is a dearth of evidence showing the value of remote monitoring generally and of smart knees in particular, though taxpayers have been subsidizing it. “In general, the field is in need of much more rigorous data.”

Then there are the privacy concerns — the implications of what happens when someone the patient doesn’t want to get the data does.

Overall, these devices are dealing with “quite a bit of data, and oftentimes the issue really crystallizes around patients’ not understanding the information collection, use, and disclosure,” said Kate Black, a health data privacy lawyer not involved with the Russak or Murphy cases.

Consent standards for devices such as a smart knee “should be quite high,” she said, because, unlike a wearable product, an implanted device stays in for years.

“Every step you take, they know every step you take,” Russak said.
