author: Aspen Ford
title: SpaceX Lab Workers Allegedly Dried Metal Part in Employee Breakroom Toaster Oven
content:
Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company is fighting Washington state over three health violations and a $6,000 fine.

Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company is fighting Washington state over three health violations and a $6,000 fine.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Elon Musk’s multitrillion-dollar company is fighting with Washington state over a $6,000 labor fine, fending off allegations of an unsafe workplace.

In November 2024, the Washington Department of Labor and Industries opened a chemical exposure investigation at the Redmond headquarters of Starlink, the division of SpaceX that makes satellites.

The state had received complaints stating the customer service department was connected to an engineering lab that didn’t have proper ventilations. Workers were experiencing eye irritation and headaches and dust was accumulating on their desks.

Unlike the lab workers, the customer service department didn’t wear protective equipment, according to a complaint. The two teams shared a breakroom.

The complaints weren’t news to SpaceX management. Customer service workers had filed dozens of internal complaints alleging chemical exposure symptoms that stemmed from an adjacent production lab. Management did not act until Labor and Industries opened its investigation, InvestigateWest reported.

The agency’s inspection took place in an unassuming office complex in Seattle-area suburbia. Tenants of the building included a pediatric clinic, a pediatric dentistry office, a “holistic” medical clinic, a mortgage lender and the Starlink customer service department, which adjoined two small Starlink labs.

After detecting a high level of lead on a work bench, the state issued SpaceX a violation and the $6,000 fine.

The department issued a second violation because SpaceX had not evaluated their employees’ potential exposure to chemicals. For that, there was no fine.

The third violation was unexpected.

In the middle of the investigation, a state compliance officer received multiple photos of a toaster oven. Cooking inside of it was a small piece of metal laying on top of aluminum foil. Workers feared anyone who used the toaster oven might have been exposed to harmful chemicals.

The officer issued a third violation for not keeping eating areas “safe and healthy.” No fine.

SpaceX is contesting all three violations. After Labor and Industries rejected the initial appeal, SpaceX appealed again.

The matter is now before a judge with the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, a quasi-judicial agency independent of Labor and Industries. Potential outcomes range from affirming the fine and the three violations to vacating them, with numerous variations in between.

On Nov. 18 and 19, during a trial-like hearing conducted over Zoom, SpaceX attorney Skylar Sherwood and Assistant Attorney General Diane Cornell examined witnesses familiar with the investigation. Judge Magda Baker presided.

Haley Laing, former SpaceX environmental health and safety manager who was subpoenaed for testimony, described the layout of the customer service department as a “very open space” with two labs conducting lead-based work adjoining one side.

The labs were former conference rooms. They had windows and the doors were not airtight. SpaceX did not post signage to caution workers that toxic substances were used inside, Laing said.

The state compliance officer, Richard Caldwell, was not permitted to photograph inside the labs; SpaceX had a contract with “DARPA,” the federal government’s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, he said during testimony. To some employees, the labs were known as ‘Starshield,’ a type of satellite made for national security, InvestigateWest reported.

The labs’ proximity to the customer support department was supposed to be temporary; the compliance officer said he was told they would be moved to another site in 2025. It’s not clear whether that happened.

One lab was about the size of a storage closet, “probably 80 to 100 square feet,” Laing said. The other, “probably 250 square feet.” Inside, lab technicians cured parts in industrial ovens and assembled hardware onto circuit boards.

In December 2023, a year before the state investigated and prior to Laing’s employment, SpaceX safety employees reported a lab in the customer service building did not have “proper ventilation” for lead soldering and that lab workers had to “keep the door open.” They recommended ordering a fume extractor.

It didn’t happen immediately. During testimony, Laing said SpaceX installed the fume extractor fix in late 2024 “in direct response to” the state’s inspection, after the compliance officer alerted her to ventilation concerns.

Melissa Kiss worked as a customer support representative at Starlink from 2023 to 2025. Appearing via Zoom and under questioning from Cornell, the state’s attorney, she recalled the moment she witnessed something odd inside the employee breakroom.

A small metal part — described as a ‘connector’ in inspection files — was cooking in a toaster oven shared by more than 200 workers in the building, according to InvestigateWest.

“So, when you were in the break room, when you observed this, there was someone from the lab?” Cornell asked.

“And in speaking with an employee from the lab, what’s your understanding of what’s in the (oven)?”

“It was my understanding that it was some part from the lab and they were drying the part and that they did this often.”

Laing, the SpaceX manager, sent an email to all employees in the building months after the breakroom incident. She said the lab technician was drying off water and that the temperature of the toaster oven wasn’t high enough to “off-gas” or “volatilize” parts of the connector, according to an email obtained in a public records request.

One lab worker told Caldwell, the compliance officer, that his team was under a mandate to “triple production.”

Sherwood, who is a partnering attorney with Fox Rothschild, one of the highest grossing law firms in the country, tried to underline Laing’s argument during the Wednesday hearing.

“You never saw or handled that part that was pictured in the toaster oven, correct?” Sherwood asked Caldwell.

“And you don’t know whether the part had contacted any solvent or chemical?”

“You can’t put work parts in the employee break room toaster oven at all.”

“That’s not my question, Mr. Caldwell.”

“Uh, because the material,” Caldwell said, stammering. “We don’t know what’s on – the material is made of, the part is made of, I don’t know —”

“Your honor,” Sherwood interrupted. “He’s going way off script.”

Testifying the next day, Laing, the former safety manager, said the lab worker used the toaster oven because the industrial oven in the lab was occupied.

SpaceX is relying on the state’s vague description of how free of lead surfaces should be to argue against the first violation.

Labor and Industries argues that the lead found on a work bench in the small soldering lab was 18 times greater than the allowable limit.

According to state rules, surfaces should be kept “as free as practicable of accumulations of lead.” There’s no hard number, no scientific unit of measurement.

Instead, Caldwell said in testimony, the state relies on “industry leading standards” from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

“When there’s a small regulatory gap like this, you are supposed to go to industrial standards, industry leading standards,” the compliance officer said.

He went on to explain that lead is especially harmful for children, but also for anyone.

“Lead attacks the brain, the central nervous system, the kidneys and the reproductive system,” Caldwell said.

“Were employees exposed to lead?” asked Cornell, the state attorney.

“And how many employees were exposed to lead based on your inspection?”

“Two directly in the lab, but depending on how that dust migrates, it could be the entire customer service area.”

“Does it matter if the exposure is direct or indirect?”

“No,” Caldwell said. “Because you haven’t controlled the dust, and again, we don’t know where that dust is migrating.”

Attorneys for the two sides have until January 15 to submit briefs. After that, the judge will decide whether SpaceX kept areas as free as practicable of lead, whether SpaceX conducted an employee exposure evaluation and whether SpaceX kept eating areas “safe and healthy.”

If SpaceX ends up paying the fine, the money will go into a Labor and Industries account that supports families whose loved ones died at work.

Judge Baker said the ruling would take time.

“It’s gonna be a complicated decision to write,” Baker said.

title: Experts Urge EPA to Tackle Public Health Crisis of Nitrates in Drinking Water
content:
A 2019 study estimated that up to 12,594 new cancer cases each year are attributable to nitrate in drinking water.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When the federal government set its limit on how much nitrate drinking water can safely contain, the primary concern was blue baby syndrome, a condition that deprives infants of oxygen. In the 51 years since then, research has associated exposure to the contaminant with cancer and other health problems, fueling calls for a stricter standard.

On Monday, a coalition of national and local advocacy organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Union of Concerned Scientists, Prairie Rivers Network, and 11 others filed a petition calling on the U.S Environmental Protection Agency to lower that threshold from 10 milligrams per liter to 1 mg/liter. In its petition, the coalition argued that “nitrates in drinking water are causing a public health crisis across the country.”

“One in three Americans — nearly 120 million people in this country — are currently being served water with dangerous levels of nitrate in it,” said Tyler Lobdell, a senior staff attorney at Food & Water Watch. That figure includes people served water with nitrate concentrations above 1 mg/L — one-tenth of the current federal standard.

Nitrate pollution, much of it linked to fertilizer and manure runoff and leaching from agriculture, is a particular concern in farming regions, where contaminated groundwater can disproportionately impact rural, low-income, Latino, and farmworker communities. Studies have linked exposure with colorectal cancer, thyroid disease, and fetal abnormalities. A 2019 study estimated that up to 12,594 new cancer cases each year are attributable to nitrate in drinking water.

“This change would reflect the best available, peer-reviewed science and would bring substantial health benefits to communities across the country,” according to the petition.

Climate change can exacerbate nitrate contamination as increasingly intense rainfall and flooding washes fertilizer and manure into waterways and groundwater. Drought can concentrate pollutants.

In a statement to Grist, the EPA wrote that it would review the petition but noted that it completed its review of drinking water regulations, including the nitrate standard, in July 2024.

“EPA conducted a robust evaluation of available studies and applicable data for nitrate to determine if any new information provided a basis to support a regulatory revision that would improve or strengthen public health protection,” the statement read. “Based on the agency’s review, EPA determined that the nitrate rule was not a candidate for revision at the time.”

As part of the petition, the organizations commissioned the consulting firm One Water Econ to analyze the costs and benefits of adopting the proposed standard, especially in states most affected by nitrate contamination.

The 43-page report found that slashing the threshold isn’t cheap. The report estimates that adopting the 1mg/L benchmark would cost $94.5 billion over 50 years, which would cover everything from upgrading water treatment plants, maintenance, and replacing equipment. Despite the steep price tag, the analysis found that returns would significantly outweigh the investment, the benefits totaling $364 billion.

“People are paying with their health right now,” Lobdell said. “Costs are accruing right now in the real world, in the form of people losing their loved ones and children being born with abnormalities.”

The states with the largest impacted populations tend to cluster in the West and Midwest and account for 62 percent of the affected population, according to the analysis. Agricultural powerhouses like California, Texas, and Arizona topped that list, with traditional farming states like Iowa not far behind.

In Iowa, approximately 42 percent of residents are exposed to nitrate levels above 1 mg/L, according to the analysis. This summer, Des Moines-area residents faced water restrictions for the second year in a row amid high nitrate levels. Illinois faces a similar problem. Between 2021 and 2023, more than 2 million people were served drinking water that tested above 1 mg/l, said Robert Hirschfeld, the director of water policy at Prairie Rivers Network.

The current 10 mg/L threshold dates to 1975 and was formally adopted in 1991, based largely on the risk of blue baby syndrome. Advocates argue that the standard does not account for subsequent research associating nitrate exposure with other health problems.

The EPA has twice tried to reassess the nitrate benchmark as part of its required periodic review of national drinking water standards. The Obama administration began that process in 2016, but the Trump administration paused it in 2019. The Biden administration restarted it in 2023, before the second Trump administration cut the effort short by eliminating the office responsible for the reviews.

“We’ve done the EPA’s work for it,” Lobdell said.

The petition asks the EPA to take two immediate steps: adopt an interim benchmark for nitrate while it considers the new limit, and enforce other federal protections like the Clean Water Act and rein in industrial agriculture, which Lobdell said has been given “free pass to pollute.”

For communities confronting nitrate contamination, the debate is ultimately about where regulators draw the line between what is legal and what is safe.

author: Kelly Hayes
title: Here’s How to Secure Your Phone Ahead of Holiday Travel
content:
These steps make it a lot harder for the state to target and repress our movements.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

With the holidays approaching, many of us will soon be navigating airport security. That’s stressful enough, especially given the technical breakdowns we’ve seen lately. For activists and organizers, air travel can bring additional concerns, including the possibility of federal agents attempting to search or confiscate our devices.

After hearing about a recent incident in which border agents demanded access to a friend’s phone, I thought this would be a good time to revisit the subject of device security for activists who are headed to the airport. From the basic precautions everyone should be taking to more extensive measures, like using a secondary phone, I talked through our options with Troy*, an organizer with the Activist Checklist project. Activist Checklist is a website that offers practical checklists and tools to help activists protect their devices, communications, and sensitive information during protests, travel, and other potentially risky situations.

*Troy is a pseudonym used for safety reasons.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Kelly Hayes: We’ve seen a number of disturbing stories about activists and journalists having their phones searched or confiscated at airports. Activist Checklist distinguishes between basic security precautions everyone should take and enhanced protections for people who may face greater risks. How should people assess their own level of risk, particularly when traveling, and determine what kinds of precautions are appropriate for their circumstances?

Troy: It’s definitely the case that not all digital security advice is applicable to everyone. If you’re a US citizen crossing a border or taking a flight, start by asking yourself two questions.

First, how likely am I to be targeted for a device search? Since Trump took office in 2025, we’ve seen an increase in politically motivated device seizures at the border, often targeting people with a public profile in pro-Palestine, anti-ICE, and direct action organizing.

Second, if the cops did break into my phone, how much danger would the data on it expose other people to? We encourage folks to go beyond an individual view of their digital security and focus more on the risk to their communities. The consequences might be relatively low, such as revealing who you organize with in a lower-risk setting. If, on the other hand, you’re doing something like immigrant mutual aid and your Signal chats have the addresses of the undocumented folks you deliver groceries to, that could put them at serious risk, and you should definitely take more precautions. That might include backing up and then wiping your phone, or only traveling with a secondary phone.

Our resources are geared toward US citizens, so if you’re a visa holder or green card holder, you may want to check out the Asian Law Caucus’s resource Know Your Rights at Airports: International and Domestic.

I think people should also think about who they’re communicating with, and whether those people are likely to be targeted by the government. I’ve sat in court and watched prosecutors twist seemingly harmless personal messages into evidence. So if you’re shooting the shit about politics with people doing the kind of work the government seems hyped to criminalize, it’s worth thinking about how much of that conversation history you’re carrying around on your phone. Turning on Signal’s disappearing messages option is a worthwhile precaution, but it’s also important to think about what you’ve already got stored.

Now, let’s talk about what people can do before they leave home. If someone has limited time to prepare for a trip, what are the most important steps they can take to secure their phone or laptop? What difference do things like stronger passcodes, disabling facial recognition, and powering down a device actually make?

Fully power off your phone anytime you’re in a situation where the cops might confiscate it. That includes TSA, customs, immigration, or even higher-risk protests or actions. In addition, make sure to update your phone to the latest operating system version and use a randomly generated passcode that is eight or more digits. As long as you do those three things — updates, a strong passcode, fully powered down — and your phone is still getting security updates, you will make it much harder for the cops to break into your phone and get your sensitive data. Phones usually get updates for five to seven years after they are made. Our travel and flight digital security checklist has step-by-step instructions for people preparing to travel.

When I give folks this advice, a lot of people ask, “Why does powering down your phone make a difference? Can’t the cops just turn it on?” The answer is that before you unlock your phone the first time after powering it up, all the data is encrypted. It’s scrambled and meaningless. After the phone is turned on and the passcode has been entered, encryption keys that help decrypt your data become available, making it much easier for police phone hacking tools to access information on your phone.

If your passcode is something super guessable, like 333333, they will still be able to get in fairly quickly, which is why we suggest a randomly generated passcode. If you have an out-of-date operating system, they can often exploit publicly known security bugs in older versions to break into your phone and bypass the passcode.

The same steps go for your laptop. Update the operating system, choose a strong password, and power it fully down, rather than just putting it to sleep, before passing through any checkpoint. The additional step for laptops is to make sure full-disk encryption is enabled.

Since you won’t have your devices powered on, you should also print a paper boarding pass at one of the kiosks in the airport or at home.

Disabling the face unlock feature is a bonus step. Since face unlock doesn’t work the first time you unlock your phone after powering it on, disabling face unlock becomes most helpful for situations where they snatch your phone before you have time to power it down.

I suggest practicing turning off your phone a couple of times right now. How long does it take to grab it and power it down if you suddenly see cops walking toward you? Do you know how to do it quickly?

If you’re a citizen, I also encourage everyone to opt out of facial recognition when passing through TSA, boarding your flight, or re-entering through customs.

I really appreciate the security update checker on your website that helps people check whether their phone is still getting security updates, and whether they have the latest update. It’s a simple thing that I don’t think we can emphasize enough. If an update’s been issued and you haven’t gotten it, your phone is compromised. So please, always update, folks.

I also want to mention that I personally keep biometric unlocking turned off on my phone at all times, because we can’t always anticipate when our phones might be searched or confiscated, and we might not have an opportunity to power them down. Courts have also sometimes treated compelled biometric unlocking differently from compelling someone to enter a passcode, so that’s another consideration.

With holiday travel approaching, I think it’s important to distinguish between domestic and international flights. What kinds of digital security risks might people encounter when flying domestically, compared with crossing an international border, and how should those differences affect our preparations?

The border-search exception, which allows federal agents to search your devices without a warrant, applies in connection with international border crossings, so when you are either exiting or entering the country. Re-entering the US tends to be the highest risk situation, but you should take precautions whether you are leaving or re-entering.

If you are a US citizen traveling domestically, the risk of having your device seized is lower. That said, law enforcement can still seize your devices or detain you under certain circumstances, including when they have a warrant.

I always suggest that folks treat domestic flights as a chance to practice the skills of keeping your devices off. Even if it is a lower-risk encounter, we should all be in the habit of treating any interaction with the cops, including border cops, as a time to protect our data and devices.

Someone I know recently had their phone taken by customs officials, who demanded that they unlock it and said that if they refused, the government would confiscate the device and copy its contents. What is your take on that situation, and how should we respond or prepare for that possibility?

The cops definitely have tools that can help them break into a phone. As I mentioned above, keeping your phone powered down, updated to the latest operating system, and protected by a strong random passcode of eight or more digits significantly reduces their chances of getting in.

Travelers have fewer rights when crossing the US border. If you’re entering the US, border agents can confiscate your phone or laptop without a warrant. It’s important to know your rights and risks. If you are a US citizen, you can refuse to power on your device, unlock it, or give them your passcode. That said, if you are a citizen and you don’t unlock your phone, border agents may be more likely to confiscate it, and you may not get it back for weeks or months. If you are visiting the US, refusing to unlock your device may result in you being denied entry to the country.

Each person has to make their own assessment. Is it more important to me to protect the data on my phone, and the data of the people I organize with, even if it means I’m without this phone for weeks? If you can’t be without your phone, consider traveling with a secondary phone.

Also, since we should all be reminding each other all the time: don’t talk to the cops, including border cops. When they target activists at the border, they often ask who you organize with, what Signal groups you’re in, and so on. Beyond confirming your identity and citizenship, the best way to protect yourself and your community is to remain silent. If you have questions, get advice from a movement lawyer, such as the National Lawyers Guild (NLG) or the Civil Liberties Defense Center (CLDC).

What does preparing a secondary phone involve? What should and shouldn’t be on it?

Preparing a secondary device usually requires a few hours of work, but it does a lot to help protect the data of the people you organize with. These phones are sometimes called “burner phones,” but a true burner involves a lot more work and is designed for a higher degree of anonymity. Our goal with a secondary device is just having something with minimal data on it if it is confiscated or hacked.

To set up a secondary phone, you can use any old phone you can get access to. You can buy a pre-paid SIM card, activate it, and add the phone numbers you’ll need after you land.

It is very important to not install any apps or sign into any accounts that contain sensitive data (Signal, Google, Proton, CryptPad, Apple, your password manager, etc.) Those will sync to the new device and defeat the point of having it. If you need to sign into these apps or accounts after you cross the border or complete your domestic flight, you can, but the best case is to do as little as possible.

The steps for setting up a secondary laptop are similar: find someone with an old laptop they aren’t using that can lend it to you, factory reset it, and don’t sign in to any accounts or install any apps on it before you cross the border.

If you can’t manage to get a secondary phone set up in time for your travel, you can also back up your phone — ideally to your computer, not the cloud — do a full factory reset, and then not re-install any of your apps or restore any of your data until after you finish the border crossing. This is still fairly strong protection against your data being exposed as long as you don’t sign into any accounts or apps that have data you’re trying to protect.

Bringing a secondary device gives you the option to actually consent to unlocking your device at the border if they ask you to, because you will have nothing sensitive to show them, and it might mean you spend less time being harassed in an interview with them. If you want to go further, you can fill the phone with some pictures and apps (games, etc.) that help you look more like a normie, so your phone doesn’t look like it was just factory reset.

I know we’re covering some ground here that won’t be relevant for everyone. But I think it’s relevant for a lot more folks than it used to be. And whatever your risk level might be, whether you need basic precautions or more thorough ones, we want to give ourselves room to make these decisions before we wind up in tense situations. You don’t want to have to think through how sensitive the contents of your phone might be while a federal agent is standing there threatening to take it away. And if they confiscate your phone, you don’t want to be scrambling to figure out how to contact people or get around. Thinking all of this through ahead of time allows us to take decision-making out of the crisis zone. With a little preparation, we can just stick to the plan, whatever it is, and get where we need to go safely.

Your travel guide also emphasizes the importance of making a plan in case someone is detained or becomes unreachable. What should that kind of preparation involve? And if someone’s device is searched or confiscated, what steps can they take afterward to protect themselves and other people in their networks?

If you’re concerned about being detained, even just for extended questioning, make a travel safety plan with two to three emergency contacts. Let them know your flight number, when you plan to contact them after you land, and how long they should wait without hearing from you before they contact legal support. US citizens are usually detained for only a few hours. Green card holders and visitors have on occasion been detained for weeks or months.

If your device is confiscated and your organizing work includes sensitive data that could put others at risk, make sure to notify those folks. Remotely deleting data from your phone could be construed as destruction of evidence and result in additional charges, so talk to a movement lawyer (NLG, CLDC) for advice first. If you get your device back, in most cases it is best to assume that it is no longer trustworthy and replace it.

One thing I appreciate about Activist Checklist is your emphasis on making digital security something people do together. You encourage people to host “security parties” where friends and organizers work through these precautions collectively. What does that look like in practice, and how could people use this approach to help their communities prepare for holiday travel?

We make a point to encourage folks to organize security parties because we’ve seen how folks have a much easier time following through when they have some peer support and accountability.

A security party can be small and low-effort: a few buddies, a couple of hours set aside, some snacks, some music. You simply pull up one of the checklists and start working your way through it, often with each person moving at their own pace. You can do it online, but in person is usually more energizing. No one needs to be a digital security “expert” to host one, because the checklist does most of the work — though it can help to have someone a bit more tech-savvy who can help you find the right setting if you’re stuck.

You can host a security party with any group of politically-aligned folks, but it can be especially useful to do it with folks you’re already in an organizing formation with. Some groups carve out a few minutes at each regular meeting to do a couple of checklist items at a time. Other folks dedicate a whole meeting to digital security.

I always remind folks that the tone you set when talking about digital security matters. Talking about digital security can quickly become so overwhelming that everyone freezes or feels defeated. It’s important to remind folks that there’s actually a lot we can do to protect ourselves and our communities. Many of these steps are fairly accessible, and they make it a lot harder for the state to target and repress our movements.

author: Jessica Corbett
title: Trump Order Aims to Restrict What Federal Contractors Can Tell Congress
content:
The move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to obstruct Democrats’ planned probes.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

With Democratic leaders promising “accountability” when the party takes over the US Senate and House of Representatives in January, Republican President Donald Trump late Friday signed an executive order directing federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress and withhold anything his administration deems confidential.

Any contractor or subcontractor that fails to comply could face “potential termination or cancellation of contracts,” the order says.

The White House claimed that “Trump is ensuring that Americans’ confidential information and national and homeland security work is protected, and that the executive branch is able to serve the American people efficiently and economically.”

Major news: President Trump has signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to notify and coordinate with the executive branch on congressional oversight asks. Democrats have vowed to make defense contractors a major target next year. https://t.co/MMeFhNJWDy

However, his move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to limit Democrats’ planned probes into not only the federal government and its contractors but also Trump and businesses that may have benefited from his return to power.

Acknowledging the anticipated Democrat-led investigations, the White House fact sheet says that “certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on these executive prerogatives by seeking confidential executive branch information from executive agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the federal government.”

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of of the watchdog group Public Citizen, stressed in a Saturday statement that “contractors are paid with Americans’ tax money and must be the best for the job, full stop.”

“However, throughout the Trump administration we’ve seen widespread abuse of the contracting process, with lucrative contracts doled out to political allies, inexperienced startups, and flatly unqualified bidders, for everything from major ICE operations to Trump’s vanity projects,” she noted, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “No-bid and emergency awards have become the norm, circumventing rules designed to prevent corrupt contracting.”

“The new Congress rightfully has its sites set on this obvious cronyism for investigation and oversight,” she continued. “The American people have a right to know how their money is being spent, that it is going to capable contractors, and that is not be used to reward allies and punish perceived enemies.”

Gilbert added that the new order, “dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption. It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people.”

Friday’s order follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Scharf said certain Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has raised questions about the administration’s attempts to limit congressional oversight.“

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Executive privilege allows presidents to protect certain confidential communications, but courts can ⁠intervene in disputes over Congress’ authority to obtain information.

Earlier this week Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, sent document preservation letters to a dozen current and former Trump administration officials, and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), likely the next House Judiciary Committee chair, sent similar notices to federal law enforcement agencies.

“Voters gave congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people,” Garcia wrote in his letters, referring to the blue tsunami in the midterm elections earlier this month. “We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform.”

Raskin — who managed Trump’s historic second impeachment after his supporters stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 — said on social media Friday: “We will confront White House corruption and lawlessness with the full powers of Congress, the ‘predominant’ branch of government (Madison), the representatives of the people. Preserve all your records, Mr. President.”

Trump has been widely condemned as “the most openly corrupt president in American history” and, during just his first year back in the White House, pocketed at least $2.2 billion — over half of it from his family’s cryptocurrency grift. Companies affiliated with the president’s two eldest sons are have also scored key federal contracts during his second term.

In addition to Trump’s sons, Elon Musk — a former member of the administration, leading Republican donor, and the world’s richest person — could also be a key target of Democratic probes, as he leads multiple tech companies. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, sent a Friday letter to Musk about SpaceX’s role in the Starshield service disruptions in Ukraine last month.

Noting that inquiry on Musk’s social media platform X on Saturday, Jonathan Cohn, political director of the group Progressive Mass, said that “contracts with Musk are a national security risk and should be treated as such.”

author: Thomas Kennedy
title: Immigrants in US and Palestinians Face Mirroring Systems of Oppression
content:
In Florida, the movements for Palestine liberation and immigrant justice can create strength in solidarity.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The treatment of immigrants in the United States has long been brutal and cruel.

Since the 1980s, propelled by false narratives of migrant criminality associated with the Mariel boatlift, migration management has shifted sharply towards confinement and control, while portraying people crossing borders as uniquely dangerous. Immigration detention has expanded dramatically since the Mariel boatlift episode. By the early 2020s, most individuals held in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were detained in privately operated facilities with a for-profit motive. At that time, corporate revenues from immigration detention center contracts had reached historic highs and kept climbing.

Florida’s inhumane concentration camp, dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz,” in which over 6,700 immigrants were detained, is a perfect example of this carceral approach to migration. The conditions at this detention center were deplorable. The Department of Homeland Security itself reported that 32 detainees were packed into cages that were literally situated under flimsy tents, which had a maximum capacity of just 11 people. Detained individuals had to deal with overflowing toilets, which led to raw sewage and fecal matter seeping across the floor and sleeping areas. Showers were infrequent and limited by authorities to three days a week in bug-infested bathrooms. Detainees were offered food contaminated with insects.

In Alligator Alcatraz, which has since shut down, and other detention centers throughout South Florida, detainees were and are denied proper medical care in addition to living in poor, inhuman conditions. Sendra, a Cuban American immigrant, is a diabetic and was sent to Krome detention center. According to his wife, news reports, and court filings, Sendra suffered pancreatitis while in detention because he was not given the medical treatment he needed and required hospitalization.

Ending up in one of these dystopian detention centers is not a distant possibility; because of increased ICE raids, an immigrant who has been residing in Florida for decades can be arrested and sucked into this awful incarceration system simply by stepping outside. Additionally, a multitude of Florida localities and state entities have signed on to 287(g) agreements. These agreements allow local and state police officers to perform federal immigration enforcement functions, essentially transforming those police departments into appendages of ICE. Florida is among the leaders in the nation in immigration enforcement, with more than 25,000 arrests in the last year. Most arrests arise from racial profiling and routine traffic stops, such as having a vehicle with a broken taillight. Once individuals are arrested, there is a severe lack of due process. Detention facilities have blocked detained immigrants from accessing legal documents, having confidential phone calls, and receiving visits from their attorneys.

Meanwhile, those who advocate for immigrant rights in this bleak moment have faced immense backlash. We have seen in Minnesota how U.S. citizens demanding justice for immigrants have been surveilled, attacked by ICE agents, and in some cases, even killed. This suppression against immigration advocates exists in Florida too. At Florida International University, seven students who silently and peacefully protested the university’s police collaboration with ICE were disciplined by the university and ordered to submit a two-minute video reflecting on their behavior. The students sued the university on the basis of free speech and won.

The incarceration of immigrants and repression of immigrant advocates in Florida in some ways mirrors what Palestinian Americans, advocates for Palestine in the United States, and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are experiencing.

In the West Bank, Palestinian American Sama Safi, who has ties to Tampa, Florida, is currently detained in Damon Prison in Israel, a prison that solely holds female prisoners and is notorious for human rights abuses. For example, Israeli occupation authorities at Damon prison have confiscated detainees’ hijabs and forced them to wear only gray sports suits without head coverings. Women who refused to remove their hijabs were reportedly beaten, with these beatings often filmed. During winter, Israel occupation authorities at Damon prison regularly raid detainees’ rooms, handcuff and blindfold them, and force them to kneel with their heads lowered outside in the cold for several hours while police dogs and stun grenades are used against them.

Just like Alligator Alcatraz and Krome Detention Center, Damon prison has documented cases of overcrowding and unsanitary conditions. In some cases, more than a dozen women are made to share rooms with only four beds, with many women sleeping on the floor. Toilets are inside the cells, creating constant health problems. Dozens of detainees share one bar of soap, and there is an insufficient amount of sanitary pads for people on their periods. And just like Sendra, the Cuban American who was detained at Alligator Alcatraz, Sama suffers from medical conditions that are not being treated while she is detained. Safi suffers from a debilitating auto-inflammatory disease that requires regular medication and monitoring that her family reports she is not receiving.

Surveillance systems utilized along the U.S.-Mexico border are first tested in Palestine, and deportation infrastructure is weaponized against immigrants and Palestine advocates in the U.S.

We noted the increasing number of ICE raids in Florida, and the lack of due process that exists for immigrants once they are detained. In Palestine, there are increased raids occurring in the West Bank. The United Nations noted that settler-violence in Palestine hit an all-time high in 2026, and has increased every year since 2023. Just as in the United States, where even the smallest traffic violations can be used as a pretext to stop and detain an immigrant, Palestinians in the West Bank are often stopped by Israeli security forces who find ridiculous reasons to stop and detain them. For example, holding a Palestinian flag is enough grounds to detain a Palestinian, an injustice that is even more insulting when grounded in the context that Palestinians are indigenous to the land on which they currently live under a settler-colonial military occupation — land that they are fighting to stay on.

In total, an estimated 7,000 Palestinians are in prison. Once detained, they don’t have access to due process, just like the majority of detained immigrants in the United States. Detained Palestinians are often denied access to lawyers. Israeli courts can use secret evidence to detain a Palestinian accused of a crime, and the detained individual and their lawyer cannot see the evidence. Approximately 99 percent of detained Palestinians processed through Israeli military courts are convicted of a crime. Several Palestinian Americans have suffered from this system of unjust incarceration as well, including 17-year-old Floridian Mohammed Ibrahim, who was held for nine months in two different prisons (Ofer prison and Megiddo prison) from February-November 2025. During those nine months, Mohammed was given minimal regular nutrition, lost over 25 pounds, and developed scabies. A family representative who has acted as a spokesperson for Mohammed personally told us that a fellow prisoner, who was 17 years old and a close friend of Mohammed’s, died in his cell from scabies, in Mohammed’s arms.

Like the silencing and persecution of immigration justice advocates in the United States, U.S. advocates who stand up for Palestine face harsh repression. Hundreds of students have been disciplined or have even had their degrees revoked for advocating for Palestine and against genocide on campus. Immigrants in the United States who stand up for Palestine have suffered extreme consequences for their advocacy, and this repression shows how related these two fights can be.

Take Rümeysa Öztürk, a doctoral student at Tufts University, who wrote an op-ed criticizing her school’s response to the Gaza genocide. Shortly after the op-ed was published, ICE officials arrested her, her visa was revoked by the State Department, and she was detained in Louisiana for six weeks. Or take Salah Sarsour, the president of the largest mosque in Wisconsin, and a lawful permanent resident of the United States. Salah was arrested by ICE agents due to his advocacy for Palestine, and the federal government is now seeking to unfairly deport him to intimidate others.

These injustices don’t just happen in a vacuum. They happen because people in power make them — or at the very least, let them — happen. And it is often the same exact people in power who fuel both immigration-related and Palestine-related injustices. Take Florida’s Palm Beach County, for example. The county has signed a 287(g) agreement, and has invested a whopping $1 billion in Israel Bonds, which directly finance the genocide in Gaza and the occupation of Palestine. The injustices perpetrated by Israeli forces would not happen without the United States providing billions of dollars of funding and weapons to assist the occupation of Palestine, and Palm Beach County itself is culpable in this as the largest municipal investor in Israel Bonds in the world. Likewise, Palm Beach County has the highest rate of ICE arrests in Florida (and remember that Florida has among the highest rate of ICE arrests in the country). The logic of both cruelties is the same: profit and political clout for a few, at the expense of Black, Arab, and Brown communities’ lives, homes, and dignity.

Our struggles are interconnected. We can, and must, work toward our freedom together.

While these problems are interconnected, their solutions are often as well; we suffer indignities caused by the same offices and same politicians, and we have the same types of policies to dismantle. The movements for justice in Palestine and justice for immigrants will only benefit by seeing our struggles as interconnected, and as advocates we must move to bridge this gap. Our opposition sees no difference between the two movements: There are training exchanges between ICE and Israeli military forces, surveillance systems utilized along the U.S.-Mexico border are first tested in Palestine, and deportation infrastructure is weaponized against immigrants and Palestine advocates in the U.S.

Immigration advocates in the U.S. must explicitly adopt anti-Zionist principles in their work and be bold in centering Palestine and working with Palestinian organizations. Advocates for Palestine must mobilize their base to assist the immigrant rights movement in tangible ways, such as working to pass the DIGNITY Act or participating in court accompaniment programs for immigration court.

Our struggles are interconnected. We can, and must, work toward our freedom together.

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Trump Administration Is Hiking Immigration Bond Costs to Keep Migrants Locked Up
content:
Bond prices in many jurisdictions have doubled under the Trump administration, and bond funds are struggling to keep up.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

When Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 after campaigning on mass deportation, his administration got to work expanding immigration detention and reshaping the nation’s immigration courts to make it more difficult for jailed migrants to seek release. Almost two years later, data show just how successful those policies have been.

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office. The Trump administration has foreclosed most avenues through which jailed migrants have historically sought release. For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped. It rose to about 60 percent in the first year of Trump 2.0, up from about 53 percent in the last year of Biden’s tenure. The denial rate has continued to rise this year.

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased. Those amounts have even doubled from 2024 to the first months of 2026 in some of the federal circuit court jurisdictions with the most immigration bond cases, according to data compiled and analyzed by Bklg.org.

“This is a linchpin in the administration’s deportation strategy,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the Immigrants’ Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), told Truthout. “The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases, their claims to legal status, to remaining in the country, and to acquiesce to a deportation because they can’t stand being locked up for so long.”

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office.

Even for those who do not agree to so-called self-deportation, outcomes tend to be worse for those who fight their immigration cases while detained. Those who are released are more likely to have their immigration cases resolved with permission to remain in the U.S. than with deportation orders. Once freed, a person tends to have more resources and more time to participate in their case, gather evidence, and access other needed support. “It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout. Especially, he added, “when ICE moves people all over the place, and so it’s not the case that you’ll be detained often in your community or near your family [and] your lawyer. Instead, ICE is routinely shipping people to far-flung locations.”

Fisayo Okare, digital communications manager at Envision Freedom Fund, told Truthout that migrant community members with whom her organization works regularly face these pressures. “Families are thinking of whether it’s worth it or not to even remain in the country or just choosing to voluntarily deport,” she said. The nonprofit Envision Freedom Fund is the largest immigration bond fund in the nation; it helps cover bonds for individuals jailed in New York or New Jersey and those who will return home to the area on release. Since the fund launched in 2018, it has provided over $15 million in bond support to help secure the release of over 1,600 people from immigration jails.

An October report from Envision Freedom Fund shows how the increase in the number of migrants jailed and struggling to access release is affecting communities in New York and New Jersey. The volume of requests for support that the bond fund receives has risen so much that it projects it will cover nine times as many bonds in 2026 as in 2024, if it can raise the funds needed to meet demand through the end of the calendar year.

“The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases.”

The average bond amounts submitted to the fund for support have also risen from $6,200 in 2024 to $14,200 in 2026. Half of the requests the fund has received this year have involved bonds exceeding $10,000, and it has seen bonds set as high as $85,000 since Trump returned to the White House. The fund has also tracked tens of thousands of individuals who have been booked in to detention facilities in New York and New Jersey and then transferred to more than 100 other detention facilities across 25 states.

“The fact is that we’re forced to bond so many more people out now because the sheer volume of the system — everything is increasing,” Ben McCoubrey, Envision Freedom Fund’s data and advocacy manager, told Truthout.

It has never been easy for those in ICE jails to access bond, a process that entails securing a bond hearing in immigration court, finding a lawyer to present the case, then convincing the immigration judge to grant a bond, and ultimately finding someone outside with U.S. citizenship or a green card and the funds needed to post the bond. But the obstacles to accessing bond are now greater than ever before thanks to what Tan characterized to Truthout as the Trump administration’s “takeover of the immigration courts.”

Since Trump returned to office, he has signed executive orders to expand detention and restrict release. Based on those directives, ICE’s lawyers have made legal arguments and issued guidance meant to subject as many immigrants as possible to mandatory detention and limit their access to bond. Those directives have become standard practice following administration-friendly decisions from the Board of Immigration Appeals, which governs the immigration courts and judges from within the Department of Justice.

The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges. Many of these new judges come from the ranks of former military lawyers, ICE lawyers, and prosecutors with little or no experience or training in immigration law.

“They’ve fired immigration judges that they think, in their view, are too friendly to immigrants and replaced them with so-called deportation judges [and] for the judges who remain, who didn’t get fired, we know that the administration is exerting pressure on them to deny relief, and to really crack down, and serve as foot soldiers in a mass deportation campaign,” Tan told Truthout. “They’ve taken an immigration court system that is supposed to be neutral and fair and made it into an arm of the immigration enforcement system.”

The ACLU has litigated the Trump administration’s mandatory detention scheme in every circuit court where it could be heard, a total of 11 of the nation’s 13. Only two circuits have concurred with the administration’s interpretation of the law. Nine have rejected it, opening the door for more individuals to access bond hearings in the 40 states covered by those circuits. The Supreme Court will hear the issue in a case arising from the Second Circuit, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, next year; Tan told Truthout a decision is expected by the end of June. The outcome will affect access to bond hearings for those in ICE jails nationwide.

While the legal fight continues, the humanitarian crisis created by the Trump administration’s policy changes is deepening. Envision Freedom Fund’s recent report helps put a human face on the issue. “We paint a picture of what’s happening in the context of detention and deportation, how things are growing, and go beyond what we see when it’s just [the number of] people getting released on bonds,” McCoubrey told Truthout about the report’s aims.

The report includes stories of immigrants who have suffered medical neglect and other traumas in ICE jails and are navigating the lasting effects after being bonded out with Envision Freedom Fund’s support.

One man for whom the fund helped cover a $50,000 bond to secure his release in July 2026 shared that he “felt unmeasurably happy when [he] got released from the jail.” He had been jailed for over two months, and after release, said, “I believed that now everything will be okay. Because when I was in there, I was stressing a lot. I didn’t know what would happen because nowadays it’s really tough.” Just two weeks after the man’s release, his asylum case was granted — ending a more than four-year wait that began in 2022.

For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

More recently, Okare told Truthout that Envision Freedom Fund secured release for a man in his mid-thirties who had been transferred from Delaney Hall in New Jersey to an ICE jail in Georgia. The fund then coordinated with partners to arrange transportation to bring him home in time to be with his wife and witness the birth of his child. “His wife was actually in the hospital when we got the bond request, and he got out right in time,” she said.

Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide. For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

As the Trump administration continues pulling these communities apart, Okare told Truthout that organizations like hers will keep fighting to make them whole again: “[We’re] not just paying their bond but ensuring that they get out and make it back to their community.”

author: Jessica Holdman
title: South Carolinians Resist Proposed Dominion Energy/NextEra Mega-Merger
content:
The merger would create the world’s largest regulated utility across four states.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

About 30 South Carolinians spoke in opposition to the $67 billion merger of Florida-based NextEra Energy and Virginia-headquartered Dominion Energy during a public hearing Tuesday in Columbia.

The hearing was one of three held by state utility regulators across the Lowcountry and Midlands as they weigh whether to approve the takeover that would create the world’s largest regulated utility. One more set of meetings are scheduled for Dec. 8, from 9 a.m. to noon and 5-9 p.m., both virtual and in person at the Public Service Commission in Columbia.

A final decision is expected by Jan. 29 under a schedule accepted by the commission in August.

If approved, the newly combined company would serve a total of 10 million customers across four of the nation’s fastest-growing states — Florida, North Carolina, Virginia and South Carolina, where Dominion has 820,000 customers.

Opponents of the merger, who protested outside ahead of the hearing, called NextEra’s promise of $2.25 billion worth of monthly bill credits — $10 per every 1,000 kilowatt hours used, lasting two years — “a joke.”

By comparison, the companies offered Virginia four years of credits and $100 million in bill assistance and energy efficiency programs for low-income, disabled and elderly customers. Virginia’s governor is pushing for $29 monthly credits and a six-year rate freeze.

But for many who spoke, even that would not be enough to change their minds.

“No amount of credits or benefits that they promise us makes this a good deal,” said Anjani Moro, a member of the South Carolina Tenant Union and co-founder of the grassroots Stop NextEra SC Coalition. “A mega monopoly, the world’s largest utility company, will not have our interests at heart.”

Even under Dominion, Moro said she’s struggled.

Dominion expanded to South Carolina in 2019 after SCANA, parent company of South Carolina Electric & Gas, abandoned its joint effort with state-owned utility Santee Cooper to expand the V.C. Summer nuclear plant.

SCANA spiraled toward bankruptcy and Dominion Energy bought what was the only Fortune 500 company based in South Carolina.

“Ever since then the points of contact for people have diminished,” Moro said. “I know people that used to be able to pay in person can’t pay in person. And the rates have continued to go up.”

In May, regulators approved Dominion Energy South Carolina for a nearly 8% rate hike — the company’s second increase in two years.

Moro was among those who testified in opposition to the increase, which took effect in July.

“My electric bill was almost $200 when I testified,” Moro told the commissioners Tuesday. “Now it’s almost $400.”

“I’m a mother of a small child,” she added. “I live in a 1,000-square-foot house. When I testified in May, I told y’all that I had to withhold paying health insurance to make sure I could keep up with my rent and my electric bills.”

Then, days after her May testimony, Dominion and NextEra announced their merger intentions.

“Their shareholders get $360 million,” Moro said. “We get $10 a month for two years.”

Others who spoke also shared their monthly Dominion bill amounts: more than $300 in a high energy usage month, $450 when temperatures drop, $387 for natural gas near Florence.

They went on to cite numbers from California-based Energy and Policy Institute, showing NextEra’s Florida Power & Light as having some of the highest profit margins in the country.

The numbers, which come from Federal Energy Regulatory Commission filings, put Florida Power & Light’s net income at $5 million in 2025.

The institute estimates 27% of customers’ monthly bills go to pay for that — the highest of the 79 utility companies analyzed nationwide.

Dominion Energy South Carolina ranked 41st, with 15% of customers’ bills going to company profits.

“They (NextEra) are a company that comes and just tries to acquire other utilities, and their goal is to make as much money as possible,” Moro said.

NextEra has sought for years to expand by acquiring other utilities, though with little success.

Deals to purchase Hawaiian Electric, Texas-based Oncor and Duke Energy all fell through, as did NextEra’s bid to buy South Carolina’s state-owned utility Santee Cooper in the wake of the failed V.C. Summer nuclear expansion.

Beyond profits, 2024 U.S. Energy Information Agency Data showed Florida Power & Light ranked No. 2 in the country for shutting off customers’ power when they couldn’t or didn’t pay their bills, according to the Energy and Policy Institute.

“The next year they asked for the largest rate increase in the history of the United States,” Moro said. “They got it.”

The opponents told South Carolina’s Public Service Commission they don’t trust the commissioners to keep NextEra’s rates in check.

“Why would we believe that it would be any different in South Carolina?” said Annie Mahaffey, a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation in Columbia. “Oversight by a Public Service Commission that continues to favor greedy corporations provides no peace of mind.”

The single mother went on to say she works three jobs to make ends meet, finding it difficult to pay Dominion’s current rates.

“I didn’t turn my heat on this fall until the freeze over this past weekend,” Mahaffey said. “And even now, the thermostat is set at 62 degrees. I wake up in the night and hear the heat running and I’m so filled with anxiety at the thought of the bill that’s accruing, that most nights I can’t go back to sleep.”

Commissioner Swain Whitfield asked Mahaffey whether she had sought any help under Dominion Energy’s efficiency programs to reduce her energy usage. She said she had but Dominion told her she did not qualify because she’s a renter. Her landlord would have to apply.

Beyond South Carolina, the merger still needs approval from federal regulators, as well as state regulators in Virginia and North Carolina.

NextEra, which has a market value of about $194 billion, is proposing a stock swap — just over four-fifths of a share (0.814) of its stock for each outstanding share of Dominion — so NextEra shareholders would own about 75% of the combined company.

Dominion will maintain its Virginia headquarters, as well as its South Carolina offices.

In an October meeting with state legislators on the Public Utilities Review Committee, NextEra executives even batted around the idea of reinstating the name South Carolina Electric & Gas.

That move that would likely stir up bad memories for customers who continue to pay for SCANA’s share of $9 billion in debt from the failed nuclear expansion.

author: Mitchell Plitnick
title: Following ICJ Ruling on Myanmar Genocide, Is Israel Next?
content:
The reasons the International Court of Justice gives for its ruling all echo Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice announced its landmark ruling in the case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya people.

For the first time in the ICJ’s history, it found a state directly guilty of genocide.

It is hard to overstate the significance of this case. Supporters of Palestine are immediately, and correctly, going to draw parallels to South Africa’s case against Israel. But the ruling also has deeper, more global implications.

“Genocide” is a highly contested term. Defenders of Israel’s actions in Gaza often say that it is a legal term, and they’re not wrong. But it is not only a legal term; it has colloquial meanings as well.

The term was coined relatively recently, in 1944 by Raphael Lemkin. He was spurred to create the word in his book, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe by the Holocaust of World War II but did not intend for that horror to stand as the definition of the term. In fact, he noted himself that he would apply it to the Ottoman Empire’s atrocities against the Armenian people three decades prior.

The argument that genocide is a purely legal term is dangerous. With no court to rule, would that exclude the obvious genocide of the Indigenous Peoples of the Western Hemisphere? Perhaps more to the point, would the fact that no state has, before today, been found guilty of genocide by the ICJ mean that it has not happened since the agreement on the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide of 1948?

That would certainly be disputed in the cases of Rwanda, Darfur, Cambodia, Bosnia, the Yazidis in Iraq and Syria, and a depressing number of other cases, just in the past seventy-eight years.

These facts are important to note because the argument that the ICJ has not declared genocide in Gaza does not mean there is no genocide in Gaza. That will remain so even if the ICJ does not hold Israel responsible for the crime of genocide in Gaza.

But it is obvious that the outcome of South Africa’s case against Israel carries monumental weight, and the case against Myanmar holds many parallels.

The Rohingya lived under a brutal junta in Myanmar which severely restricted their rights. Myanmar claims that their actions against the Rohingya community were a response to Rohingya violence. Myanmar, like Israel, argued that the refugee crisis and the sizable number of civilian deaths were part of security operations.

Yet it was never certain what the ICJ ruling would turn out to be, and as much as the case has many similarities to Gaza, the ruling does not by any means guarantee that the case of Gaza will be decided in the same way. But it does offer a strong ray of hope in that direction.

Only two accusations of genocide had ever come before the ICJ prior to this one. One was a cross-accusation between Serbia and Croatia which the Court summarily dismissed. The other was the Srebrenica massacre of 1993, where Bosnia and Herzegovina accused Serbia and Montenegro of genocide.

In that case (which, it should be noted, took fourteen years between when it was filed and when it was decided), the ICJ decided that genocide had been committed, but that the states were not responsible for the genocide. The ICJ ruled only that Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide.

That was worrisome because the case clarified that conviction for genocide has an extremely high bar. The ICJ ruled that, to prove genocidal intent, the circumstances must lead to only one conclusion: that genocide was the goal of the state’s actions. If any other motive is possible, then intent cannot be legally established.

Proving intent is already difficult, since genocidal states do not generally announce, as the Nazis did, that they intended to wipe entire groups of people out of a specific place. Saying that such proof requires that no other conclusion is even possible was seen by many as a bar so high that no state could ever be held responsible for genocide.

The ruling against Myanmar shows that, although the bar is high, it can be reached. That is an enormous development for those who hope to see Israel held accountable for genocide.

Specifically, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar was guilty of both the commission of genocide and the failure to prevent it, which are two different crimes. That’s important because it covers both acts that were directly ordered by the Myanmar military or government as well as any acts that might have been perpetrated by Myanmar’s forces or others acting without direct or implied orders.

The Court also found that Myanmar had violated its order to preserve evidence related to the case. This will strengthen this precedent in the case of Israel and, should it ever come to trial, the case against Russia brought by Ukraine.

Interestingly, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar was not guilty of public incitement to genocide. That will likely be different for Israel, regardless of how the other verdicts land, given the unusually large volume of genocidal statements that Israeli officials made, especially in the earliest days of the genocide.

This part is complicated. Individuals held responsible for genocide are expected to be tried by their home countries first and foremost, but if that fails, international courts, such as the ICC, or tribunals are the alternative, according to the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

The Convention does not prescribe penalties for states. The Court can order reparations, but there are no specific guidelines or requirements for the Court to impose penalties on states.

In the Myanmar case, the Court ordered Myanmar to cease genocidal activities; prosecute any individuals responsible for the crime of genocide; assure the Rohingya that this won’t happen again; provide for the safe return of refugees who wish to return and ensure they are reunited with their families; and “to compensate the Rohingya group and its members for the damage caused,” the parameters of which the Court said it would determine in a subsequent document.

The Court also expects states that are party to the Convention to take their own actions, and this could be significant.

The European Union, unlike the United States and Israel, considers international law important. Although they have repeatedly shown a willingness to ignore it in Israel’s case, the EU’s procedures acknowledge the law and the international legal system. There is only so far they can bend these procedures.

In the case of Myanmar, the EU already had strong sanctions in place, since it was obvious, on a colloquial level, that the state had committed genocide or, at the very least, abhorrent crimes against the Rohingya.

But Israel is obviously treated differently.

Nonetheless, the politics of international law matters in Europe in a way it does not in the United States, let alone in Israel. EU agreements and the laws of many EU states mandate adherence to international law, creating a tension in Europe that, in a legal and political sense, doesn’t exist in the U.S.

In the case of Gaza, this is compounded by the fact that a case is pending before the ICJ against Germany. Nicaragua accuses Germany of breaching the Convention Against Genocide by supplying Israel with arms and by withdrawing funding for UNRWA. Germany has claimed the case is inadmissible and that Nicaragua lacks standing to bring it, and that decision is pending. It will not be decided for years, in all likelihood, even if it is not dismissed.

But Germany is concerned because, as Israel’s main benefactor aside from the United States, it faces disturbing historical echoes when it is accused of genocide, and its support for Israel has become increasingly controversial domestically, especially among rising parties on the left.

More significantly, a recent petition in Europe to suspend the EU-Israel Trade Agreement over Israel’s human rights violations reached one million verified EU signatures, which means the European Commission must consider the call.

No one seriously expects the EC to submit to the petition’s demand, but it is a big weight on the scale of moving EU policy toward Israel. A finding by the ICJ of genocide will give such a citizens’ demand a lot more weight.

Broader international sanctions would need to be mandated by the UN Security Council. For the foreseeable future, that is a dead end. The shift in American politics with the incoming Congress might change American policy in years to come, but for now, real punishment for Israel is still going to face a U.S. veto at the UNSC.

The ICJ decision is a monumental moment for international law. It crucially demonstrates that a finding of genocide is not beyond the ICJ. Indeed, it strengthens the argument that the crime of genocide, being understood as the worst possible crime, should need to meet a high bar for conviction.

The substance of the ruling was that the evidence proved the intent to commit genocide. The ruling states: “The Court considers that, in the present case, the scale and nature of Myanmar’s actions and the methods it employed went well beyond what would be required to punish the population and are instead characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group. Features of such intent include the large numbers of persons killed, injured or displaced and the widespread brutal attacks on women and children… In the Court’s view, the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State.”

The reasons the ICJ gives for its ruling all echo Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Giving even more hope for some justice, the Myanmar government was not so brazen or foolish as Israel as to state explicitly that it intended to carry out genocidal acts. Israel openly stated that it was cutting off food, water, medicine, electricity, and anything else it could cut to the entire population of Gaza and repeatedly ordered that besieged population to relocate from one destroyed area to another, on trips that were often hazardous.

The outcome of this ruling, in terms of its implications for the South Africa case in Gaza, could not have been better.

And as a demonstration that Israel and the United States have not yet succeeded in killing the entire concept of international law? That will be determined by whether this is a principle that holds in all cases, not just ones that the West approves of; and by whether the response of the international community suits the verdict, in Myanmar and in Palestine.

title: Texas Drops Lawsuits Against Out-of-State Abortion Providers
content:
”These cases were baseless from the start and designed to intimidate doctors nationwide,” said one abortion advocate.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton on Friday dropped two lawsuits that were filed against out-of-state doctors for sending abortion medication to Texas — a practice his successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed not to upkeep.

In January and February, Paxton sued two doctors in California and nurse practitioner Debra Lynch in Delaware for mailing abortion pills to Texas residents and operating services that help do so. But on Friday, Paxton filed notices of nonsuit in both cases, part of a wave of withdrawals his office has filed as he prepares to leave office in January.

It is illegal for Texas doctors to mail abortion medication within the state — but Paxton has also sued doctors in other states who prescribe the medication. Other states’ “shield laws,” which protect physicians who send abortion medications, have complicated Paxton’s efforts to seek damages against the doctors.
