author: Susan Kang
title: Young Leftists and K-Pop Stans Won Brazil for Lula — Now They’re Staying Engaged
content:
In Brazil’s election, Lula didn’t organize the youth. The youth organized Lula.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

There has been much ink spilled since October about the role of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s informal social media supporters, called “Lula’s Army,” in mobilizing for his victory in the second round of presidential votes. Following the first-round victory of Lula’s right-wing rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, on October 4, 2026, some political commentators declared Lula a lame duck, comparing him to President Joe Biden. But Lula defied expectations, pulling off a stunning and historic second-round victory, in a higher-turnout second-round vote that consolidated support for the now fourth-term incumbent.

Multiple media sources have credited Lula’s comeback to André Janones, the “general” of Lula’s Army, the WhatsApp community of more than 10 million that successfully used social media to share and boost support for the left-wing leader. Some commentators have considered how the digital army model could be replicated (with efforts beginning in Argentina, Venezuela, Colombia, and EU countries) in upcoming elections. But less attention in English-language media has been paid to the role of regular grassroots organizers in Brazil, many of whom were engaging in politics for the first time, and how they might continue to engage in their newly activated mobilization infrastructure.

Young Brazilian grassroots organizers, many of them first-time political activists not affiliated with any political party, were more than just loyal soldiers in the WhatsApp-driven campaign for Lula. They did not wait for official directives but instead began mass mobilizations on October 5 in Rio and other cities. Organizers began to mobilize support in their networks: students, K-pop and pop music fandoms, artists, and a generation of young leftists took to the streets and to group chats. When Lula marched down São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista on October 11, 2026, with an estimated 1 million supporters, he benefited from the self-organization of his newly activated support base. This event, called the March for Democracy, was organized by student groups, LGBTQ groups, and fan networks. The event was compared to the 1983 Diretas Já — the mass mobilization that demanded an end to the military dictatorship.

Notably, the grassroots mobilizing moved away from the official campaign’s core legacy message. Rather than provide voters a clear sense of what a fourth term Lula presidency might bring, Lula’s official campaign during the first round relied heavily on his laurels and the accomplishments of his three previous terms, such as the successful Bolsa Família, a direct cash transfer program that lifted millions of families out of poverty. During the election’s first round, Lula did not have a strong social media presence aside from some highly produced official videos, and famously did not have a cell phone. The official campaign did not promote social media posts or many mass public events, and Lula at times drew criticism for talking too much about artificial intelligence and defending Brazil’s rare minerals from Trump’s colonial designs, rather than centering people’s everyday concerns. Furthermore, any criticisms of the official campaign were reportedly not well received.

Recognizing the threat to democracy, independent youth organizers mobilized support for Lula in all kinds of places: at kitchen tables, on family group chats, and on neighbors’ doorsteps. Maria Clara de Oliveira, a 25-year-old photographer in São Paulo, told Truthout, “I flipped a lot of votes, mostly women’s.”

Her biggest success was changing the minds of her girlfriend’s aunts: older evangelical women with conservative views who had skipped the first round altogether. “Talking to those aunts made a big difference,” she said. With voters like them, “what worked was being frank, talking, and understanding that person’s reality.” She borrowed a line that circulated widely among organizers in those weeks: “Fight with all your strength, but never lose your tenderness.”

Others worked their own networks, one contact at a time. Lorrana Freitas, 27, had never organized anything before. She waited three days to get into Janones’s channel, then followed its instructions: hashtags to push up on X, far right content to ignore. She also brought her downstairs neighbor to a protest.

“She wouldn’t have gone if I hadn’t invited her, because she had no one to go with,” Freitas told Truthout. The strategy, as she saw it, “wasn’t necessarily each person flipping a vote, but each person who joined bringing one more person.”

Nicole Montilla, 18, got her voter ID this year and spent the campaign handing out stickers. To friends who had stayed home or spoiled their ballots, she explained to Truthout that “the best way to end the Bolsonaro-versus-Lula polarization was to vote 13 [Lula’s ballot line].”

Lucas Souza, 20, a student in São Paulo, handed out flyers and worked on his cousins. His father had voted for right-wing governor Ronaldo Caiado in the first round and planned to back Bolsonaro in the second round. Souza explained to Truthout “I talked his ear off so much that he said they were all bad and didn’t vote at all,” Souza said. “I don’t know if that counts as flipping a vote, but I think I took a vote away from Flávio.”

The organizing did not just add bodies to the streets. It changed the campaign. When Janones — who remained a strong ally to Lula despite no longer being an active member of the Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), of which Lula is a member — launched Lula’s Army on October 5, he did it, according to Metrópoles, without asking the campaign’s permission.

A friend of Souza’s turned his large K-pop fan page into a political operation, and Souza told us that the K-pop fanbase “practically became a member of the campaign.”

“That’s when I realized this wasn’t coming from Lula’s campaign,” Souza said. “It was something more, I don’t know, spontaneous. The campaign itself didn’t really get it and didn’t really know what to do.”

He told Truthout he had no contact with anyone from the PT “until the bigger protests started happening.” Two days after the first round, young PT lawmakers publicly demanded that Lula stop selling his biography and start offering a future.

Within weeks, the campaign was borrowing the movement’s playbook. Lula and his vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, began posting selfie-style videos. When a court shut Janones’s channel down on October 11, the electoral court changed its rules and the channel came back. For Freitas, the new tone made politics feel within reach. “Even for me, and I was already on the left, I feel much closer, more active and more included in political life than I did before,” Freitas told Truthout.

Montilla’s advice to the government is blunt: “Keep using social media, because that’s where young people are, not broadcast TV or newspapers.” But Souza is clear about who moved first. He explained to Truthout: “We were the ones who mobilized, we were the ones who took to the streets,” he said. “If we had waited for the government, I don’t know what would have happened.”

Going forward, Lula will face challenges from local government and both houses of the national legislature. Unlike in the U.S., where the midterms’ blue wave loosened the right’s hold on Congress, in Brazil, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won a plurality of seats.

Faced with this situation, the popular mobilization that propelled Lula’s reelection will need to continue to directly pressure Brazilian legislators to work with Lula to solve the issues that matter most to Brazilians: cost of living, inflation, jobs, inequality, corruption, public services, safety, and more.

Thankfully it appears that young people in Brazil are not done mobilizing in the aftermath of Lula’s historic victory.

Souza told Truthout that his chats have remained active and focused on politics, and the election of charismatic younger politicians has helped to keep younger voters engaged. He said:

Several of my friends said that: they felt their contribution helped, whether posting, talking to friends and family, or going to the streets. I think that’s usually missing. Politics feels very distant. But I felt closer to politicians I liked and already followed, even without knowing much about them. I think if we stay connected and feel part of it, that’s a good thing.

Freitas urged the PT and Lula government to continue engaging with young people as a necessary condition for Brazil’s democracy, telling Truthout: “If no one talks to young people, if we don’t talk to young people, if the left doesn’t take a stand with young people, someone else will, right? There are several books that say a vacuum is very fertile ground for fascism to take over. Fascism really does come in those moments of vacuum, maybe a lapse in power. It finds the fertilizer it needs to grow and put down roots.”

Montilla also credits the popularity of Guilherme Cortez — a progressive state deputy elected to national congress this year for the Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL) — for the continuation of youth and mass engagement, both in person and on social media. She believes that “continuing to talk about politics every day, keeping everyone informed about what’s happening in the world, in the presidential palace and in Congress” will help ensure that “people will also vote more consciously in the coming years.”

How can defenders of democracy and participants in the U.S. fight against right-wing encroachment take lessons from the success of Brazil’s grassroots victory?

The experiences of members of Lula’s Army are reminiscent of the mass youth mobilizations that fueled the successful election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose candidacy was once a long shot. Mamdani may have had underdog status, but his successful two rounds of the mayoral race relied on a strategy that grassroots communications practitioners call “surround sound organizing” in which potential voters/supporters see and hear messaging in all parts of their lives: receiving fliers and mailers, reading the news, seeing messaging on their social media networks, having in-person interactions with volunteer canvassers, and hearing about Mamdani informally through friends, family members, coworkers, and other community members.

Americans, especially those energized from the midterm elections, would do well to take a page from the mobilization of Brazilian leftists and remain committed to engaging in democracy as a long-term and regular activity, not just a responsibility around periodic elections. As Oliveira told Truthout “we always have to remind people, as real political education, that politics happens every day … To turn [the divisions in Brazilian society] into a collective struggle, you have to remind people that the political struggle is much bigger. Getting where we need to go takes a very long time.”

Democracy works best with the consistent mobilization and engagement of the people, and does not stop following electoral successes.

No matter who wins the contested House and Senate leadership fights, people in the U.S. should organize, mobilize, and demand more from the elected leadership and each other, to make our democracy work better for everyone.

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: The Worst Impacts of GOP Medicaid Cuts Haven’t Hit Yet. Dems Must Take Action.
content:
In the wake of the blue wave, Democrats can restore Medicaid and move toward passing Medicare for All.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Millions of people in the U.S. are currently in danger of losing their health care as a result of Donald Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which was passed in 2025 with Trump in the White House and Republican majorities in both the Senate and the House.

The new bill tilted the economy evermore in favor of the wealthy, rolling back hundreds of billions of dollars of taxes and clawing back a portion of the lost revenue through extreme cuts to social safety net programs.

The biggest loser in the bill was Medicaid, which was coming off of more than a decade of expansion under provisions of the Affordable Care Act that allowed states to broaden eligibility for the program. Onerous new workfare requirements — requiring able-bodied recipients to prove 80 hours a month of work or community service — paired with more frequent eligibility checks, were crafted specifically to drive down the numbers enrolled in the health care program. Estimates of the impact range widely, but there is general agreement that somewhere between just under 5 million and just over 10 million people stand to lose their health care as a result of this bill.

Add in the millions being driven off of Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans by Congress’s refusal to extend tax credits as well as by rising premium costs, and there’s a real chance that, in coming years, America will revert to pre-ACA-era numbers of uninsured.

During the 2026 enrollment period, as deductibles and premium costs soared, the number of Americans in ACA-subsidized insurance plans dropped by more than one-fifth compared to the previous year; and, for those who stayed enrolled, many opted for far less comprehensive “bronze” plans rather than the increasingly unaffordable “silver” options that had previously attracted the most enrollees.

Astoundingly, according to the Commonwealth Fund, as of late 2026 nearly half of American adults under the age of 65 either have no health insurance, have experienced health coverage gaps at some point in the previous year, or are currently significantly under-insured.

Somehow the GOP thought it could dodge the issue by crafting the cuts to health care in a way that meant the worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the 2026 elections. Given the pain that people in the U.S. were already feeling around health care, it was a strategy doomed to failure.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, polls suggested that the U.S. public was deeply worried about access to health care. Economic issues, including the high costs associated with health care, topped voters’ anxiety lists — with democracy and corruption issues coming in next. Kaiser Family Foundation data indicates that 6 in 10 voters were “very concerned” about the cost of health care; and by a 20-point spread those voters believed that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to address this challenge.

The Kaiser Family Foundation analysis suggests that in swing states where health care was of most concern to residents, by a two-to-one margin voters worried about health care costs voted Democrat over Republican. In states such as Maine and Michigan, where Democratic candidates won on platforms that included a promise to push for Medicare for All, large majorities of the electorate told the pollsters that they wanted the government to play a larger role in securing access to affordable medical coverage for residents. In newly blue Texas, where more than 5 million residents currently lack health coverage, Democratic lawmakers have been lining up to propose legislation to expand Medicaid access in the state — almost daring the Republican majority in the state senate to block them and to then try to justify that action to voters.

Three-quarters of people in the U.S. now live in states with Democratic governors, many of them also with both state legislative bodies blue, meaning that state-level health care reforms will likely complement congressional efforts to bring more people under health coverage umbrellas.

Come January, Democrats have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape the health care landscape in the United States — or, at the very least, to lay out a set of policy reforms that they would enact were they able to get beyond a Trump veto, or were they to win the White House in 2028.

Incoming congressional leaders, with backing from the party’s Cost-of-Living Healthcare Working Group, have already made it clear that they will seek to reverse the cuts to Medicaid and to restore the ACA tax credits. The working group has also been pushing for a commitment to expand Medicare as a move toward universal health care coverage.

Many proposals, including restoring Medicaid and ACA to their pre-2025 status, have been test-run during the current Congress. While they didn’t pass, bills such as representative Adam Gray’s Protecting Healthcare and Lowering Costs Act are ready to be dusted off and reintroduced now that Democrats have congressional majorities. The incoming majority has pledged to introduce legislation to roll back these cuts, as well as to protect access to vaccines, within the first 100 hours of the new Congress.

Beyond that, for the past few years Democrats have been developing a longer-term strategy to ratchet up pressure on the Trump administration to negotiate ways to expand Medicare eligibility, lower drug prices, and cap the percentage of household income that families spend on health care in any given year.

When the scale of the Republicans’ defeat became clear on election night, Trump announced that he was ready to become “Mr. Veto.” But it’s hard to see how the Republicans will stand united in blocking overwhelmingly popular health care reforms for the next two years. A window has opened up to create a better, more functional health care system. It will likely start with the Democrats reversing the Medicaid cuts; but that should be seen as the starting point, rather than the final goal, for a broader series of changes to how the country delivers health care to residents.

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Authors Sue LA Library Over Anti-Palestinian Discrimination After Talk Cancelled
content:
Even institutions meant to be dedicated to free speech and inclusion are censoring Palestinian writers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Two authors have filed a lawsuit against the City of Los Angeles, alleging that the Los Angeles Public Library engaged in anti-Palestinian discrimination and violated their free speech rights after the library’s leadership canceled an online event last December where the two were slated to speak to teens about their books, which feature Palestinian characters. This lawsuit against one of the largest public library systems in the nation comes at a time when anti-Palestinian racism and censorship are growing more entrenched across the country, now more than three years into the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.

“The stakes are really high, and it’s about so much more than the rights of the authors or even the rights of the readers,” Nora Lester Murad, one of the authors and plaintiffs in the case, told Truthout. “If kids and adults can’t be exposed to representation of Palestinians that’s diverse and nuanced and human and complex and multifaceted, [that erasure] converges with the anti-Palestinian and anti-Muslim narratives that are being used to justify genocide.”

Murad and Palestinian American author Jenan Matari filed the lawsuit in the Superior Court of Los Angeles in late September to demand accountability for the Los Angeles Public Library’s cancellation of their event and to draw attention to anti-Palestinian censorship in the arts.

Matari is the author of the picture book Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather. Murad was slated to discuss Ida in the Middle, her young adult novel about a 13-year-old Palestinian American girl. The two were scheduled to speak at an online event on December 6, 2025, as part of Read Palestine Week, a global weeklong program highlighting Palestinian authors and stories celebrated in late November and early December each year.

The Los Angeles Public Library’s teen council, a youth volunteer group, voted to host a Read Palestine Week event, and the library’s Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group invited Murad and Matari and acted as liaisons between the authors and library administration in the lead-up to the scheduled event, according to the legal complaint.

But just three days before the event was scheduled to take place, the group notified Murad and Matari that the library administration had canceled it. The notice provided no further explanation for the cancellation, according to the legal complaint.

Records obtained by Los Angeles Public Press in a public records request and cited in the legal complaint later revealed that a staff librarian had emailed library leadership in mid-November 2025, accusing Murad and Matari of having “strong terrorist ties and virulently antisemitic views.” The email said it was sent on behalf of a group of Jewish library staffers and referenced an article from the right-wing Washington Free Beacon and profiles of the authors on Canary Mission, a pro-Israel doxxing platform. It also accused the Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group of having “deeply antisemitic views” and showing “racist behavior to me and others in our Heritage group.”

“This attack was not from outside but from inside the library.”

Later in December 2025, City Librarian John Szabo sent an internal email to staff claiming Murad and Matari’s event had been canceled because the library “has a responsibility to remain nonpartisan and apolitical” and that doing so was “necessary to uphold the Library’s commitment to an inclusive environment free of hate, discrimination, and harassment,” according to a copy of that email obtained by The LA Reporter in a public records request.

Szabo did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment before deadline. A member of the library’s public relations team told Truthout that the library cannot comment on pending litigation.

Murad told Truthout the accusations and cancellation follow a familiar pattern in which criticism of Israel is conflated with antisemitism in order to silence Palestinian speakers like Matari, anti-Zionist Jewish speakers like Murad, or others who speak out to criticize Israel or in support of Palestinian liberation. But, she added, the Los Angeles Public Library case is also unique because the pressure to censor Palestine-related speech came not from outside pro-Israel pressure groups but from inside an institution mandated to oppose censorship.

“People assume that when an institution like a library caves into anti-Palestinian racism that the attack was from outside, and this attack was not from outside but from inside the library,” Murad told Truthout. “You have to address those things differently. One is you’re telling the library, ‘Please don’t cave into external pressure,’ and the other one is ‘Hey, Library, you are the censor.’”

Neither Murad nor Matari is unfamiliar with anti-Palestinian censorship. Murad has published about the silencing of Palestinian narratives in libraries and children’s books. Matari has had events canceled before: Two private bookshops had already canceled planned readings with her before the Los Angeles Public Library event, and she told The Guardianthat a New York library canceled a scheduled event with her after the Los Angeles news broke last year.

After the cancellation of Murad and Matari’s scheduled talk last December, more than 100 Los Angeles Public Library workers signed a letter condemning the move and emphasizing the library’s mission to oppose censorship. “Restrictions placed upon Palestinian voices are in direct opposition to the mission of the library,” the letter read. “It is the mission and the mandate of the Library to collect stories and protect them from censorship.”

The American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California and the National Coalition Against Censorship also called on the library to reschedule Murad and Matari’s talk in a joint letter in February 2026. That letter argued that the library “likely violated the First Amendment” when it canceled the event. It also criticized Szabo’s assertion that the library should remain “nonpartisan and apolitical,” calling it “absurd.” “If the library were to interpret its mission … to require it not to invite any author who has expressed strong political opinions, it would be hard pressed to find a single author to participate in its programming,” it read.

An Action Network campaign has since also resulted in more than 7,300 protest letters being sent to the Los Angeles Public Library from concerned patrons and community members. “The cancellation of an event that the youth of Los Angeles put the time and effort into putting on feels particularly antithetical to the mission of their library, both in their stated mission as well as the social function of the library as a space that fosters learning and exploring for youth,” Summer, a Los Angeles–based Palestinian artist and library patron who joined that campaign, told Truthout. “The library must be accountable to both the artists that they invited as well as the patrons who do not agree with that cancellation.”

“I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

Murad told Truthout that after such an outpouring of support failed to move library administrators, and after several unsuccessful attempts to engage them in conflict resolution talks, she and Matari felt they had little choice but to file a lawsuit. Their case alleges free speech violations, discrimination, and breach of contract, and seeks compensatory damages and an injunction that would require the library to reschedule the canceled event.

“When a library communicates through their actions that certain books and people are dangerous, so dangerous we can’t even let them come to the library and talk to us, it puts the weight of a public institution, so the government, behind a dangerous and racist message — it’s not just that our rights are being violated,” Murad told Truthout. “For Palestinians and for everyone’s right to learn from Palestinians and learn about Palestinians, we felt that we were doing a lawsuit for more than just us.”

Matari, in a press release announcing the lawsuit, said: “We need to hold public institutions accountable in order to protect free speech for all people, including the right to speak out for Palestinian freedom … I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

The city attorney’s office told Truthout it could not comment on pending litigation.

While it will take time before a resolution is reached in Murad and Matari’s case against the City of Los Angeles, Murad said she hopes the filing will send a message to other institutions that discrimination and silencing of Palestinian and other marginalized authors and narratives have consequences. “This isn’t just happening to us; Palestinians are being targeted by anti-Palestinian racism, and it’s affecting readers, and institutions have to be held accountable,” she said.

As Read Palestine Week approaches again, beginning November 29 this year, Summer told Truthout she hopes other arts institutions will reject the example set by the Los Angeles Public Library and that community members will advocate for those institutions to uplift Palestinian voices. “One of the ways people can support the blossoming of Palestinian art within public libraries is by requesting books and events by Palestinians,” she said. “All it takes is letting your desire to learn from them and read with them be known to your library branch.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: COP31 Declared a Failure as Declaration Text Excludes Mention of Fossil Fuels
content:
“I do not bear good news,” Panama’s environment minister said. “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.

“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.

“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from Turkey on the final scheduled day of the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.

Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: I do not bear good news. We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.

AMY GOODMAN: And this is Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s environment minister, speaking just before we went to air, flanked by representatives from Finland and Vanuatu, Belgium, Ivory Coast, France, Guatemala and other countries.

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: We have come together because we feel that the COP can still be saved if we focus on six key issues for our final declaration that clarifies for the world where we must go.

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.

Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly. We must transition away from fossil fuels in an orderly manner, if we are to confront climate change.

The third point for us, which is very important, is that fair contributions to climate finance must come from those with greatest responsibility. You pollute, you pay. It’s actually rather simple. You cause the problem, you must help to fix it. If you are the biggest emitter of CO2, if you are the biggest producers or consumers of petroleum, then you must contribute to solve this problem and these issues.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, in a packed room for the press, the Climate Action Network, which encompasses over 2,500 civil society groups worldwide, as speakers detailed the failures of the COP, there were activists in the room, journalists and many others representing this COP31. The activists on the stage called out the European Union and other developed nations for their obstruction. The room repeatedly broke out into chants of “shame.” The moderator of CAN called the draft text a “disgrace” and introduced speakers.

DANNI TAAFFE: Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International.

TASNEEM ESSOP: There is nothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. … This COP has had the highest number of lobbyists — fossil fuel lobbyists, AI lobbyists, CCUS lobbyists, CDR lobbyists. So, what we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to actually promote the interests of those culprits.

DANNI TAAFFE: Avantika Goswami from CSE India.

AVANTIKA GOSWAMI: The European Union have, in a way, taken on the mantle that the U.S. has left the vacuum of, the blocker that the U.S. was. Unfortunately, we expected them to be leaders, but they have disappointed us. … And these are the parties that posture the most in the media. They say they are committed to climate multilateralism, and they are concerned about 1.5°C and the breach of the Paris Agreement goals. … So, we want to let them know that we see them and the games they’ve played, and we will not stand for it.

DANNI TAAFFE: Anabella Rosemberg from CAN International.

ANABELLA ROSEMBERG: The COP is not dying. The COP is being killed, not because it’s bloated, not because it’s inefficient or useless. It’s being killed because it’s the last space where civil society, where developing countries can hold developed countries accountable. … We are now asked to accept more empty words. We say no. We will fight back. And we say thank you for nothing. … So, this is also an appeal for all of us, for all the movements, to keep working together and change the faces of who’s representing developed countries in this place.

DANNI TAAFFE: And Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa.

MOHAMED ADOW: I can tell you, without any doubt, that this has been the worst COP ever.

MOHAMED ADOW: Communities living in drought, floods and failed harvest were promised action. They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises. We’re effectively pushing poor, vulnerable countries into further debt to protect themselves from a crisis they did little to cause.

TASNEEM ESSOP: I want to just say two things. One, when you come into a COP and a commissioner of a very important regional bloc says, “We’re not coming with any finance. Finance is dead in the water,” think about that, “dead in the water.” For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal. So it’s a shameful way to come to a COP where we are going to be fighting for adaptation finance to protect people from being dead in the water.

Secondly, the pledges that they brought to this COP for adaptation finance, you would have seen totaled around $50 million, which we said in our ECO is half the cost of an F-35 Lightning fighter jet.

TASNEEM ESSOP: And we’re not even going to measure that $50 million in relation to the $3 trillion that rich nations are spending on wars, a genocide and conflicts across the world. Put that into perspective.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Tasneem Essop, the executive director of CAN, Climate Action Network International, and others speaking at a news conference earlier today. She is from South Africa.

For more, we’re joined by several leading environmental justice advocates.

Harjeet Singh is strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, a social justice organization, also global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.

Nafkote Dabi is the change policy lead for Oxfam International, where she works at the intersection of climate and inequality. She’s from Ethiopia, where the next COP, COP32, will be held, in Addis.

And Meena Raman is with us, head of programs at Third World Network and president of Friends of the Earth Malaysia.

We thank you all for being with us. We’re going to start with Harjeet. You, as well as Nafkote, were holding up a sign behind the speakers that said, ”ECO. End the Genocide,” with big letters, ”SHAME!” There was rage in this room. It was the most packed news conference I had seen, packed with activists. Talk about where we are at on this last scheduled day, though it’s clear it’s going to go further.

HARJEET SINGH: Well, it is a matter of shame, Amy. This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction. We have spent more time on talking about electrification, without any details whether it’s going to be green or is going to be accessible to people. We have removed the reference to —

AMY GOODMAN: Wait. Just to explain that, “electrification” is sort of the watchword here.

AMY GOODMAN: And the idea was renewable electrification.

AMY GOODMAN: But that seems to be — “renewable” — being dropped.

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. And otherwise, why are we talking about electrification in this space, if it is not green? That’s the question we should be asking. We do not see any reference to fossil fuel phaseout. Now, only the words are not enough, and I can explain that later, but that being dropped from the previous draft is just not acceptable. Adaptation finance, there was a clear agreement to scale it to $120 billion annually for developing countries.

AMY GOODMAN: No one knows what “adaptation finance” means.

HARJEET SINGH: OK. So, adaptation means helping communities prepare to deal with climate impacts. It’s about retrofitting their homes. It’s about building dikes. It’s about making sure that their agriculture is resilient and we are food-secure. And if you do not provide money — let’s take the example of Nepal. The reason they faced such a catastrophic disaster, because they were not prepared. When we see people in Ethiopia —

AMY GOODMAN: More than seven — what? About 7,000 people dead or missing?

HARJEET SINGH: Exactly. That’s the number.

AMY GOODMAN: Because of a glacier that melted?

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. So, it was a glacial lake outburst floods. And the numbers are important. They lost — the destruction was to the tune of $2.6 billion, and they will need now $5 billion for recovery and rehabilitation, which is 10% of their GDP. Imagine.

AMY GOODMAN: Why should the wealthy countries give it to them?

HARJEET SINGH: Because glaciers melted because of the burning of fossil fuels, and they did not provide money to Nepal for adaptation, and they are facing now loss and damage. So, Nepal, we should see it as a report card of the climate inaction that we have seen over the last 30 years. We did not phase out fossil fuels in time. That resulted in melting of glaciers. And we did not even have a plan or support to Nepal to deal with these climate impacts. And it shows that how we are failing to deal with climate impacts. And that’s why we say “shame.”

AMY GOODMAN: Meena Raman, you are head of programs at Third World Network, head of Friends of the Earth Malaysia. You have been to so many of these conferences. You, too, have expressed rage on each panel you are at. What do you want to see happen here?

MEENA RAMAN: Well, at this particular point in time, it’s relatively empty. The most important aspect of the COP is money, whether it’s for emission reductions, whether it’s for adaptation, whether it’s for loss and damage. The developing world came together, and they said, “We need money on the table of provision of finance.” What the developing countries demanded was actually to ensure that we talk about this. It was about talking about how the developed world is going to do that.

But all we came here as, you know, the EU commissioner was saying anything about finance is dead in the water. Now, that is horror, because we just came out of Nepal, as we know, and you say, “dead in the water.” People are literally dying due to the historical —

MEENA RAMAN: “Dead in the water.” That’s what Hoekstra said. It was — it was for us —

AMY GOODMAN: The EU negotiator.

MEENA RAMAN: The EU commissioner. The EU commissioner. So, even before this COP, he said it. So, when you go to the negotiating halls, what you saw was finance was dead in the water, nothing on finance. So there’s no point talking about having higher ambition in terms of emission reductions or developing countries having to do fossil fuel phaseout or having more targets on electrification. They’re not going to be able to do this, if what they say is the means to implement that is not available. So, this is where this COP always becomes a problem.

AMY GOODMAN: You are wearing a sign — you are wearing a sticker, Nafkote Dabi, on the back of your ID here that says “Make rich polluters pay.” You have said — you’ve talked about inequality. Oxfam International is known for their report, “Disaster Divide.” The richest 0.1%, or 8 million people, have more emissions than the bottom 3.5 billion people, and that their carbon emissions contribute to the increase of climate disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and food crises. Can you explain how you feel this can be remedied? And how close to a tipping point are we?

NAFKOTE DABI: So, at the heart of the negotiations right now lies money, because, ultimately, you know, to support communities to adapt to the climate crisis, they need finance. And what rich countries, especially the EU, is saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities. You know, just private jets alone, you can raise $45 billion a year. From the excess of profit of fossil fuel companies, you can raise $400 billion. So, this money is available, and you can support communities at home, whether in Europe or the U.S. And then you can commit to your international climate finance obligation and support communities in the Global South, especially, you know, in Africa, that are faced with droughts, floods, displacement and death.

AMY GOODMAN: You know, we just had a headline on a vote on war in the U.S. Senate, and the amount — the billions of dollars that are being spent on the war in Iran, which has also led the entire world to understand how dependent we are on fossil fuels.

NAFKOTE DABI: Exactly. You know, emissions from military is about 5%. This is something that we’re not talking about. There’s huge money, as you said, Amy, going towards militarization, when communities around the world are actually literally dying from escalating extreme weather events. For the first time, by the way, Amy, I’m feeling really desperate, because we’re being told next year is going to be the hottest year on record. It’s going to go up to 1.7. Right now as we’re speaking, communities around the world are faced with the worst El Niño on record, and there is no support. These are communities that have done the least to cause the climate crisis, but they’re being left alone to deal with this situation. So, it’s a very shameful COP.

AMY GOODMAN: Now, what are the NGOs going to do? We just have two minutes before we end with an 8-year-old child who spoke out. A few years ago, it was Greta Thunberg, when she was 15 years old. Now we’re going to Little Miss Environment Kenya, who is 8, who has something to teach her elders. But one last statement. Harjeet, where we go from here? Are the NGOs going to reject the text? And what does it matter? What role do you play?

HARJEET SINGH: So, we have already rejected the current text. And what we would like to see: the developing countries really standing up and reject this text. And we keep saying developing countries are here to represent their own citizens. They can’t accept a text which will not enable them to implement climate action back home because there is no money on the table. And that’s exactly the reason developing countries have now — need to be very loud and clear in saying this COP outcome is not going to help us, unless developed countries open their pockets. It’s all about money.

AMY GOODMAN: Meena, how can it be this is the largest COP, and you’re talking about it being the greatest failure? Pick up that mic.

MEENA RAMAN: Yeah. The problem is that when you have the developed world come here and say that they don’t have national budgets to put on the table, and they talk about leadership, I think it is really imperative that we work with our Global North to actually put the pressure on the developed countries. We can’t have COP after COP backsliding. We let alone scaling up our resources. The U.K. has cut its pledge to the Green Climate Fund. The Global Environment Facility, the worst replenishment ever. So, when they are backsliding, here we are asking for more top up.

AMY GOODMAN: And finally, Nafkote, if you can talk about next year? We’re going to Ethiopia for COP32. What is the point of these COPs?

NAFKOTE DABI: You know, Ethiopia is faced — is at the frontline of the climate crisis. Ethiopians know what it means to face drought. Ethiopians are the most resilient people. They have been through many droughts, droughts after droughts. Right now, as I said, we’re faced with El Niño. Next year, the Ethiopian COP presidency needs to deliver justice for communities at the frontline of the climate crisis.

AMY GOODMAN: We have to leave it there, Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International, Harjeet Singh of Fossil Food Treaty Initiative, Meena Raman of Third World Network.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Israel Uploaded 3.5M Photos of Palestinians to Amazon Facial Recognition Tech
content:
For years, Israel has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and restrict Palestinian movement.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A new report reveals that Israel uploaded 3.5 million photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s facial recognition platform shortly after it launched its genocide in Gaza — shining yet more light on the tech industry’s complicity in repression and human rights abuses around the world.

The report, written by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham and published in The Guardian this week, documents how the Israeli military uploaded the images to Amazon’s cloud soon after the start of Israel’s invasion and bombardment of Gaza in 2023. The military told Amazon that they uploaded the images specifically for the purpose of using Amazon’s Rekognition platform for facial recognition, according to documents leaked to the Guardian.

For years, the Israeli military has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and enact harsh restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement. Soldiers use a smartphone app called Blue Wolf, for example, to scan and catalog the faces of Palestinians passing through Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.

In Gaza, Israel has increased its use of facial recognition technology since the start of its 2023 assault. In early 2024, The New York Times called Israel’s facial recognition program in Gaza an “experimental effort” — acknowledging that the mass surveillance at times “wrongly flagged civilians as wanted Hamas militants.”

Davies and Abraham’s latest report builds on Abraham’s prior reporting for The Guardian and +972 Magazine, as well as the findings discussed in NAZA, a 2026 documentary co-directed by Abraham. The film highlights how Israel has used AI-based surveillance systems to facilitate Israel’s remote killings of thousands of civilians in Gaza since 2023.

The report also demonstrates how Israel has deepened its relationship with Amazon over the course of its genocide in Gaza. As noted by Who Profits, Israel awarded Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS) a large-scale tender in 2021, known as Project Nimbus, allowing Israel to transfer large quantities of data onto its services. Israel’s use of AWS has only expanded since then.

Last December, Mohammed Mhawish, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, wrote about how Israel has intensified its use of surveillance since the start of the genocide.

The Israeli military has used “artificial intelligence to generate kill lists, monitoring our social-media accounts, and storing in bulk the audio of our phone calls,” he wrote.

Israel used these technologies to target journalists specifically — both within their own homes and while they were reporting, Mhawish said. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, as well as other companies like Palantir Technologies, provide the infrastructure for the Israeli military to store Palestinians’ phone calls, analyze their communication, and decide who to target with a drone strike and when.

Last year, an investigative report by Abraham revealed the extensive use of Microsoft’s Azure platform by the Israeli military in order to surveil Palestinians’ phone calls before identifying targets for aerial bombardment. The revelations prompted tech workers to organize to force Microsoft to end Azure cloud storage and AI services in a partial withdrawal of contracts with Israel, though activists say that the company still retains contracts with the country.

Activists, including tech workers in No Tech for Apartheid, continue to organize against Google and Amazon’s Project Nimbus, and campaigns have grown internationally against Palantir.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: The Flatbush Building Collapse Is a Window Into Gentrification in Brooklyn
content:
Activists say the collapse was due to “a series of decisions that placed the profit model over the lives of the people.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On the afternoon of November 11, a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into an adjacent construction site. 1321 Flatbush Avenue — which hosted four apartment units and a store on its ground floor — collapsed within seconds, as did the wall of the neighboring building, exposing its interior.

The collapse killed eight people, all of them immigrants under the age of 32, two of them young children. Among those killed were people born in Guinea, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Colombia. Dozens more were injured and displaced.

The site of the collapse is one of negligence and oversight — the developer of the construction site is known for violating orders and failing to put in place safety precautions, and the adjacent building accumulated at least 98 housing code violations before its collapse. While the construction site had been approved for a three-story building, developers were seeking to build a nine-story building with 64 residential units.

But these violations are part of a larger story, local organizers say. The collapse comes as Flatbush, which is largely Black, with significant Haitian, Afro-Caribbean, and Latino communities, faces a gentrification and displacement crisis that has intensified over the past 15 years. And it’s not just Flatbush: Since 2010, nearly 70,000 Black people have been displaced from Brooklyn, historically a center for Black New Yorkers.

Gentrification — and the city’s decades of neglect of Black and immigrant neighborhoods — is at the heart of this tragedy, one organizer told Truthout.

“We, as Black and brown people, have been feeling the brunt of gentrification in our communities — it is permanent, involuntary displacement,” said Imani Henry of Equality for Flatbush, which has been organizing around issues like gentrification, police violence, and tenants’ rights in Brooklyn since 2013.

“We are constantly dealing with new luxury developments being built in our neighborhoods, and the complete and utter neglect” of buildings where Black and brown people live, with “the infrastructure crumbling and landlords doing nothing,” Henry said. “That’s our norm.”

He pointed to the collapse of a building in the Bronx in December 2023, which displaced 140 New Yorkers, most of them working class, Latino, Caribbean, and Black.

This latest building collapse reveals “the conditions that people in Flatbush have been living under for the last 15 years. We are dealing with slumlords,” as well as “landlords calling ICE” on their tenants, Henry said.

Yasmine Tiana, an activist from the Palaver Collective, which has been organizing in response to the collapse, told Truthout that the tragedy raises the question: “What is more important — the lives of people and families who live within these buildings and apartments, or developers, whose main goal is profit?”

“We can’t pretend this happened in a vacuum,” Tiana said. “It was a series of decisions that placed the profit model over the lives of the people, and now there’s eight people gone. The landlord knew about [the violations], but continued to neglect them.”

Angelina Landress, an organizer with the 75 Lenox Road Tenant Association, told Truthout that her building in Flatbush has hundreds of violations. Her union has been on rent strike for four months due to dangerous conditions and management’s neglect of the property.

Landress disputed the narrative that buildings are falling apart because they’re old, instead citing neglect and deregulation, often of previously rent-stabilized buildings.

Landlords buy up buildings in Flatbush and “don’t put any money into it, collect all the rent, make the conditions sub-par, and drive people out,” Landress said.

Among other problems, landlords are falsely stating they have fixed the problems in their buildings, she added. The tenants of 75 Lenox Road are organizing because they realize they “cannot let the system tell us that we have to follow the current process, because the current process will kill us, just like it killed our neighbors.”

When Truthout reached out to the management of 75 Lenox Road for comment, an office manager who went by Esther and declined to give her last name stated that the tenants association is “just 10 people looking to make trouble.”

“The allegations are totally untrue and false and have absolutely no merit,” she told Truthout over the phone. “Out of 80 apartments, if 10 of them decide to make trouble, because they’re thousands of dollars behind rent, they shouldn’t besmirch our name.”

Like Henry, Landress spoke about landlords’ use of ICE as an intimidation tactic against tenants. Just as some of the victims of the collapsed building stayed inside in the weeks before their deaths due to their fear of ICE, the residents of 75 Lenox, who are predominantly Caribbean immigrants, have also been affected by ICE raids in recent months.

“In October, our neighbor Roberto Lamour was taken by ICE around 6:30 in the morning,” Landress said. The three armed men said they were New York City Police Department (NYPD), and then “just grabbed him and took him,” bringing him to Delaney Hall in New Jersey before transferring him to an ICE jail in Mississippi. Later that month, the tenants union held a press conference demanding that their neighbor be brought home — and calling for the firing of NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch due to the NYPD’s collusion with ICE, Landress said.

Local activists have expressed frustration at inaction by the local government, both since the building collapse and as the issues of gentrification and neglect piled up over the years.

Henry said that “a lot of campaign promises” have been broken regarding protecting Black and brown people’s right to housing — in previous administrations, and now under the Mamdani administration. Despite repeatedly promising to expand public housing, for example, the current administration is carrying out demolitions of public housing in Manhattan.

“There’s a whole struggle around the Elliott-Chelsea Houses,” Henry told Truthout, referring to the fight against a redevelopment plan in Manhattan that involves demolishing over 2,000 public housing apartments and shifting to private management. The project has been backed and overseen by the Mamdani administration, and has sparked debate and pushback from residents and activists.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani “ran on a campaign of going after these landlords to the fullest extent, and that’s new, because typically, New York tends to support the money, the landlords, and the developers,” Landress told Truthout. “Since he’s been in office, we have seen a lot of promise of things, and all these task forces being created, but they don’t materialize as anything.” Landress gave the example of deed thefts and heat complaint investigations.

Landress put a measure of responsibility on New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) for the Flatbush building collapse, saying that it has a history of taking bribes from landlords and developers. “We knew that the response to this from the city, even from the Mamdani administration, would be to clean their hands of their own agency, and not hold the other parties accountable,” she said.

So the 75 Lenox Road Tenants Association created a coalition, joining with United Parkside Tenants, the Palaver Collective, Affordable For You, Tenant Union Flatbush, Flatbush Neighbors, and other community groups to organize a response.

“It was not acceptable for us that this would just be seen as another tragedy, and that’s it,” Landress said. “So we organized a three-day emergency mutual aid distribution table, right across the street from the site.”

Landress said that the coalition is in direct contact with families affected by the collapse, who say that the aid they have been given so far is insufficient.

“There’s been no transparency from the city as of yet in terms of the funds that have been collected by the Red Cross and when it’s going to be distributed,” said Tiana. “We [the coalition] have raised over $100,000, and in just a few days we’ve made a concrete plan to try to distribute this money as quickly as possible. And we don’t have a tenth of the mayor’s resources to be able to distribute these funds. But there’s been no concrete plan from the city about how the victims will be assisted.”

The coalition has also compiled a list of demands for the city, calling for the firing of the DOB commissioner; permanent housing for tenants within their local communities and for their rent to be covered for two years; the prosecution of the landlord responsible; all developers and construction companies involved to be held accountable; and a complete investigation into what occurred.

“There are empty, rent-stabilized apartments. There are empty, luxury high-rises,” Landress said. “You have the power to house these people, and pay their rent for two years while they rebuild their lives from a tragedy that was orchestrated out of greed and capitalism and the desire for gentrification.”

Tiana noted that among the donations the coalition received for the displaced families was “20 or 30 dollars” from Palestine.

“Somebody who is going through a genocide right now saw what was happening in Brooklyn, and felt they had to donate,” she said. “In moments like that, we realize that the struggle is not just isolated to New York. This is part of a global struggle against displacement, and a pattern of placing profit over the lives of people.”

author: Jake Johnson
title: 15 Democrats Join GOP to Pass Big Oil-Backed Permitting Bill in the Senate
content:
The bill would weaken environmental protections to fast-track approvals for data centers and fossil fuel projects.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Republican-controlled US Senate, with the support of more than a dozen Democrats, passed a hotly contested bill that would weaken the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and other key environmental laws to accelerate approval and development of energy projects, including climate-wrecking gas pipelines and data centers.

The final vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) was 62-33, with nearly every Republican and 15 Democrats supporting passage. The 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus who voted for the bill were Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Angus King (Maine), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (NY), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.), Mark Warner (Va.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI).

The legislation passed without ever facing a hearing in the Senate, a fact that Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) — an outspoken opponent of the bill — called “pretty damn outrageous and offensive.”

If passed by the House and signed into law by President Donald Trump — whose White House has backed the measure — BAAJA would limit the authority of federal courts to block energy projects due to violations of environmental protection laws. The measure would also exempt pipeline expansions from National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review, potentially bar future administrations from rolling back previously approved projects, and restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to block projects under the Clean Water Act.

The legislation was endorsed by the American Petroleum Institute, the largest fossil fuel industry lobbying organization in the US. The group applauded Thursday’s vote as “a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms” and praised the legislation’s lead sponsors, including Whitehouse and Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah).

Environmental organizations expressed support for some elements of the legislation, such as provisions that would speed up transmission and grid modernization. But the good provisions don’t outweigh the destructive ones, green groups said, arguing the bill’s benefits are heavily tilted toward fossil fuel projects — and would likely be further tilted in that direction by the Big Oil-friendly Trump administration.

“Senators who voted for this bill should be ashamed,” said Erich Pica, president of Friends of the Earth US. “Just weeks after Americans made clear they are tired of politicians putting corporate profits ahead of people, the Senate approved a giant giveaway to Big Tech and polluters. Calling this a bipartisan compromise doesn’t change what it is: a reckless attack on our clean air, clean water, wildlife, public lands, oceans, and communities.”

“It’s bad enough that Republicans wanted to gut our environmental laws,” Pica added. “It’s unconscionable that Democrats helped them do it.”

Some Democrats who supported advancing the bill in previous procedural votes switched their votes to no on final passage, including Sen. Andy Kim (NJ). In a statement posted to social media, Kim said he “voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage.”

“Unfortunately those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable,” said Kim.

BAAJA’s opponents called on the House, which will be narrowly controlled by Republicans until January, to reject the legislation.

“This bill identified the wrong problems and has therefore arrived at the wrong solutions,” said David Watkins, director of federal government relations for the Climate and Energy Programs at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “The Clean Water Act isn’t the problem — the fossil fuel industry and their enablers in the Trump administration are responsible for throttling renewable energy deployment across the United States.”

“The Senate’s bill is totally out of step with the message of the midterm elections. Policymakers must move on from the status quo driving high energy bills and record fossil fuel profits,” Watkins added. “The House should reject BAAJA and negotiate a better bill in the new Congress in January, one that protects our environment, includes meaningful input from communities burdened by fossil fuel pollution, and makes cheaper and cleaner renewable energy more accessible to everyone.”

author: Cami Koons
title: Army Postpones Detonation of Toxic Lead Azide in Iowa After Public Outcry
content:
Lead particles could spread 100 miles from the detonation site. The army says the detonation is now planned for Monday.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Environmental groups filed a lawsuit Thursday afternoon in an attempt to halt the planned detonation of degraded, lead-based explosive material at a munitions plant in southeast Iowa.

The lawsuit was filed hours before acting Secretary of the Army, Hon. Adam Telle announced the detonation would be postponed to Monday, Nov. 23, noting that “public safety is the Army’s top priority.” U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley said on social media the delay was to “further educate the public.”

Telle said in a post on social media that Monday was the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

Earthjustice, on behalf of Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, is suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its decision to grant an emergency permit to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to intentionally detonate 68 drums of deteriorated lead azide, an explosive that is unstable in its deteriorated state.

The detonation, which will occur inside concrete bunkers that are surrounded by sand barriers approximately two stories high according to news releases from the Army, will cause a plume of air “with some lead-containing particles.” Nearby areas have been warned to stay inside while the lead particles are expected to be airborne and to spray down outdoor materials after lead-containing dust has settled on the surfaces.

In the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. Appellate Court for the Eighth District, environmental groups ask the court to either rule on the motion before Friday at 10 a.m. or issue an administrative stay until the motion can be fully heard in court.

Iowa Environmental Council Executive Director Sarah Green said in a statement Thursday that it “could be the case that the U.S. Army has no other safe alternative to disposing of the toxic lead azide.”

“But our federal government needs to do better at communicating the potential health risks of lead contamination in our communities and providing more time to keep our communities and vulnerable groups safe, like children and pregnant women,” Green said.

Petitioners allege the emergency permit from EPA failed to: incorporate applicable environmental performance standards, require all permit conditions necessary to protect human health and the environment, consider less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead, and adequately notify the public of the plan.

“The Army’s planned detonation of 9,700 pounds of explosive lead material poses a significant risk of irreparable harm that cannot later be remedied,” the lawsuit said.

The Army and EPA have said the intentional detonation allows them to mitigate the “explosion risk” of the degraded lead azide which presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”

Essentially, they said the intentional detonation of the material allows for precautions and public awareness that would not be possible if the material exploded on its own.

Environmental groups said they “do not dispute the EPA and Army’s assertion that there is risk involved in leaving the lead azide at the IAAP untreated” but said the Army left the explosive “to degrade for roughly two decades until it decided that the only safe option became detonating them near populated areas.”

According to the proposed action report from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, the lead azide was submerged in a water/ethanol storage solution. Temperature fluctuations caused the material to “dissolve and recrystallize” into a form that is “acutely sensitive to shock, friction, static electricity, and heat.” The Army determined in March the material had degraded, and in April had a briefing with EPA, according to the emergency permit.

“That turned the Army’s storage management failure into a public health event for people in at least two states,” the lawsuit said. “This rushed final week is a symptom of that; the Army has been aware of the risk since at least March, yet it gave public notice of its plans a mere five days before intended detonation.”

The Army held an open house in Middletown in mid-October informing residents about the planned detonation, though the Friday schedule was not announced until Nov. 15, when the Army also provided air dispersion models that showed lead particles could be spread up to 100 miles from the detonation site, and dust deposition models that showed a potential spread of around 40 miles.

More recent maps, released by the Army Thursday showed the plume was expected to move more directly north, as opposed to northeast of the detonation site, and not stretch as far as the earlier model showed. The Army has said it will continue to release updated maps up until the detonation with information accurate to the latest atmospheric conditions.

The initial plume map showed air dispersion was intended to stretch across the Mississippi River and into New Boston, Illinois. The lawsuit alleges Illinois officials had not been notified of the detonation and potential risks.

On Thursday, the Illinois Department of Public Health issued public health guidance about the detonation. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services also posted safety tips and information Thursday about the detonation which it said it was “only very recently made aware of.”

Safety precautions include staying indoors, running air purifiers and turning off heating and cooling units while there is a potential for air dispersion, which the Army estimates will last about an hour. The Army, and state health departments have also said people in the affected areas should consider washing outdoor surfaces, like playground equipment, doors and cars to minimize the risk of consuming lead dust.

The lawsuit pushed back on this advice, noting that there is no safe level of lead exposure for children.

“The idea that widespread lead dust can simply be rinsed away with no harmful effect is absurd, counterfactual, and extremely harmful misinformation to share with the public,” the lawsuit said.

EPA and Army media contacts did not respond to a request for comment Thursday regarding the lawsuit.

Environmental groups allege EPA’s permit “largely ignored” the potential for the lead to spread to groundwater, surface water, soil and the atmosphere.

For example, the environmental groups point out, the EPA permit shows no conditions addressing the detonation’s potential for damage to domestic animals, wildlife, crops, vegetation and physical structures.

On Wednesday, the Iowa Department of Agriculture posted guidance for livestock producers near the detonation site, urging them to move livestock elsewhere or into a barn if possible and to move or cover feed and water supplies to “prevent possible contamination.”

While the EPA permit requires the Army to collect samples before, during and after the detonation at “all parks, public facilities, and private properties” they were given the right of entry, the lawsuit holds the testing requirements are not robust.

Researchers at the University of Iowa met with reporters Thursday afternoon and said they are conducting their own research. David Cwiertny, director of the Environmental Policy Research Program at UI, said researchers will be deploying air sensors, particle filters and collecting soil samples and surface wipes across the affected area.

“We’re doing all of this to add to the public record, not because we have any real doubt in the official monitoring that’s planned by the EPA or the Army,” Cwiertny said. “In an unprecedented event with so many unpredictable factors, we believe that having more independent data is always better for public transparency and for public health.”

The lawsuit urges the court to issue a stay and prevent the detonation because, it says, “once lead dust is dispersed, there is no undoing the harm.”

“What the Court must balance is the risks associated with the possibility of unplanned detonation while crucial additional time is given to take actions necessary to protect human health and the environment, against the very significant known harm of a massive lead dust plume,” the lawsuit read.
