author: Zane McNeill
title: The “Blue Tsunami” Can’t Leave Trans People Behind
content:
On this Trans Day of Remembrance, Democrats must recommit to rolling back the anti-trans assault of the past two years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Many are interpreting the “blue tsunami” that swept the nation earlier this month as a resounding rebuke of the MAGA movement’s fearmongering around transgender rights. But this Trans Day of Remembrance (TDOR), we owe it to ourselves and those we have lost to anti-trans violence to sit with the complicated, nuanced truth and not just comfort ourselves with a convenient, feel-good narrative.

It is true that many candidates who campaigned on explicitly anti-trans messaging and policies lost their elections, in spite of the hundreds of millions of dollars they spent on anti-trans ads. In fact, despite the deluge of anti-transgender messaging, many Democrats who refused to throw trans people under the bus, no matter what anti-trans rhetoric was thrown at them from their opponents, won their races across the country. Ten transgender people were elected into office — in Alabama, Georgia, Delaware, Montana, Florida, Washington, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Vermont voters approved a constitutional amendment adding explicit equal protection guarantees for sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression.

Polling suggests that voters have grown weary of the weaponization of trans issues by the far right, which they view as an attempt to distract them from the issues that matter most in their lives: inflation and the cost of living; jobs and the economy; and skyrocketing health care bills. Voters who were disenchanted with Donald Trump and the Republicans’ failure to deliver a better life for them mostly ignored the anti-trans messaging and voted blue.

But voting blue doesn’t automatically equate to being pro-trans. Some Democrats who did run on anti-trans policies still won their elections. Further, anti-trans ballot initiatives targeting transgender youth in schools passed in Washington, Arizona, Colorado, and Nebraska, and NBC exit polling showed that 52 percent of people in the U.S. feel that support for transgender rights has “gone too far.”

This sentiment persists despite the fact that at least 25 transgender people have died as a result of violence in the United States over the past year. The actual number of transgender people who have been murdered is certainly higher because the rampant misgendering and deadnaming in news reports and the lack of formal data collection makes accurate tracking and reporting difficult.

The United States has become increasingly untenable for trans people, who now must struggle greatly to survive, let alone thrive. More than half the country has banned medically necessary medication and surgical care for transgender youth and restricted their ability to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity. Across the country, 10 states prohibit people from correcting the gender marker on their birth certificates, eight states ban updates to gender markers on driver’s licenses, and nine states prohibit transgender people from using bathrooms and facilities that align with their gender identity in government-owned buildings and spaces, including K–12 schools and colleges.

Such policies have prompted 9 percent of trans people polled to relocate since 2024, fleeing states with anti-trans laws for supposedly safer havens like Washington and Colorado. But those states, too, have now passed similar anti-trans measures through ballot initiatives (though trans rights advocates have said they will fight to repeal them via legislation and litigation).

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has made attacks on transgender rights a central policy priority, making it increasingly difficult for trans youth to feel safe anywhere in the country. The Trump administration is especially fixated on undermining medical research and standards of care for transgender youth and has challenged states’ sovereign authority to regulate the practice of medicine within their borders. The Trump administration has also issued civil and grand jury subpoenas to hospitals in attempts to obtain transgender youths’ private medical records, targeted the medical associations responsible for researching and developing standards of care for transgender youth through civil investigative subpoenas and litigation, and stopped reimbursing states for Medicaid/CHIP coverage for trans medical care received by youth.

The administration has doubled down on false statements saying transgender people are violent, even in official memos, despite research finding that transgender people are more than four times more likely than cisgender people to be victims (not perpetrators) of violent crime. The Trump administration has also increasingly funded or commissioned misleading reports falsely framing being transgender or supporting transgender communities as indicators of political violence to justify using the nation’s national security apparatus to target and disenfranchise Democratic voters.

The administration has also weakened employment protections for transgender workers, restricted transgender people’s ability to obtain federal identification documents that reflect their gender identity, and disrupted hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding for research and services supporting transgender communities. These anti-trans policies restrict transgender people’s access to employment, health care, housing, and public services, thus increasing trans people’s risk of facing harassment, discrimination, and violence, and causing significant psychological harm.

Trans youth are especially vulnerable to internalizing anti-trans rhetoric. According to research by The Trevor Project, 94 percent of transgender and nonbinary youth reported that anti-LGBTQ+ policies, laws, and public debates caused them stress or anxiety. Additionally, research has found that transgender and nonbinary youth living in states that enacted anti-transgender laws reported up to a 72 percent increase in suicide attempts.

In light of this research, we cannot ignore the role and responsibility of anti-trans policies and state violence in the deaths of transgender people. Anti-trans policies appear to play an active part in normalizing violence against transgender people and contributing to death by suicide. As transgender journalist Erin Reed has written, “every trans suicide is a murder by those in power.” At least 20 transgender people have died from suicide over the past year.

Democratic attorneys general have challenged some of the Trump administration’s most egregious anti-trans policies in court and defended civil rights in their states. Bolstered by the “blue tsunami,” it is time for Democrats across the country to shift from defense to offense on trans rights.

Democrats now have the power to act, and they must use it to honor those who are no longer with us on this Trans Day of Remembrance. That means using state civil rights laws to hold accountable all the hospitals that preemptively discontinued care for transgender youth. It means transforming states like Texas, which has been among the most anti-trans states in the country, into places that protect trans youth by repealing anti-trans executive orders and withdrawing from anti-trans lawsuits. It means using the Democratic Party’s congressional power to hold the Trump administration and its political appointees across federal agencies accountable for their unlawful actions over the past two years.

It is up to us to hold the Democrats accountable for defending trans lives and undoing some of the tremendous violence wrought over the past few years, and ensuring that by the next Trans Day of Remembrance, the world is a safer place for trans people.

author: Z Waite
title: AI Is Monitoring and Scoring Fast-Food Workers’ Every Move
content:
One app measures how quickly workers walk to and from their cars. Another judges how warmly workers greet customers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see.

The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney said. As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.”

Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime®, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime®’s ability to track workers in real time down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores.

Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment.

Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior — how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom — into data that can score, rank, discipline and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring.

“They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools.

In February, Burger King announced that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders.

“It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez.

Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly.

Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added.

Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it, that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini.” “The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.”

Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations timestamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores.

Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.”

According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities.

Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias.

The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year.

Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it.

“If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.”

While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies — Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts” — a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility.

Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys and other chains.

Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts.

In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law.

Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.”

While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores and ranks all employees.

Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions. When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores.

Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.”

MashMore currently has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.”

Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on Sept. 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff.

Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty — but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.”

Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.” Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off.

When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing.

Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.”

author: Mike Ludwig
title: GOP Rams Through Trump FCC Nominee Opposed by Free Speech Groups
content:
Democrats boycotted the vote as Trump’s other lame duck nominees caused headaches for the Senate GOP.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As Democrats plan investigations into corruption and abuses of power, Republicans are working to shore up the president’s influence over the federal bureaucracy while they still can. But Senate Republicans are having mixed success as they attempt to speed through the federal nomination process for as many GOP-approved officials as they can.

Despite a boycott of the confirmation hearing by Democrats, Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted on November 18 to advance President Donald Trump’s nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to serve on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Thumann Severs is senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, and Democrats had called for an additional hearing to question her about internal records suggesting that she helped Carr pressure cable news outlets to change their content on Trump’s behalf.

“Today, Senator [Ted] Cruz greenlit a vote for an FCC nominee who not only provided false testimony to his committee, but did so to cover up her role in FCC Chairman Carr’s ongoing efforts to pressure and punish broadcasters that anger the president,” said Jessica J. González, co-CEO of the digital rights group Free Press, in a statement on Wednesday.

González pointed to internal FCC documents recently released to watchdogs under the Freedom of Information Act that show Thumann responding to emails about Trump and Carr’s jawboning of cable news outlets, including pressuring ABC to temporarily pull comedian Jimmy Kimmel off of late-night TV last year. Jawboning is the use of informal public pressure and veiled threats by government officials to cajole or coerce private actors, and the Senate Commerce Committee has advanced bipartisan legislation to rein it in.

Thumann is one of multiple Trump nominees that Republicans are attempting to ram through the confirmation process before Democrats regain majorities in Congress next year. Other high-profile Trump nominees failed to gain traction in the GOP-controlled Senate on Wednesday, including Jim O’Neill, a venture capitalist who is not a scientist but was nominated to run the National Science Foundation, despite vocal opposition from actual scientists.

Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) abruptly blocked a vote on O’Neill, citing a nasty shakeup over childhood vaccines at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, where Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. installed O’Neill as acting director after firing public health expert Susan Monarez. Monarez later testified that she was pushed out after resisting Kennedy’s efforts to fire career scientists and change public vaccine recommendations to align with anti-vax ideology.

The U.S. faces a severe measles outbreak and has officially lost its measles elimination status due in part to lower childhood vaccination rates. Senator Cassidy has said he now regrets casting a deciding vote last year to confirm Kennedy, a longtime leader of the anti-vaccine movement who regularly spreads misinformation from his perch at the Department of Health and Human Services.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said as he blocked O’Neill’s confirmation.

Additionally, the White House dropped its nomination of physician and abortion opponent Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration commissioner. The move came as a disappointment to some Republicans, including Cassidy, who suggested on Wednesday that the nomination had enough GOP votes to pass. Reproductive health advocates feared Overton would undermine access to medication abortion, which she has baselessly asserted is “dangerous to women.” Overton also controversially played a role in the White House’s overhaul of the childhood vaccination schedule, and infamously stood behind Trump as he falsely stated that the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal.”

Unlike O’Neill and Overton, however, Thumann Severs’s nomination will advance to a full Senate vote, and free speech advocates are urging lawmakers to reject it. Chris Lewis, president and CEO of the non-partisan group Public Knowledge, said Thumann Severs’s testimony during a November 10 hearing failed to assure lawmakers that she would remain independent from Carr and protect free speech.

“When she was asked if she disagreed with chairman Carr on any issues, she didn’t come up with anything,” Lewis told Truthout. “I don’t think she has been clear about her views, and whether they are independent from the chairman’s, whose views we believe have violated the First Amendment.”

In a November 17 letter, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-New Mexico) asked Cruz to put the confirmation vote on hold because it appears that Thumann Severs “misled the committee and offered false testimony” during the previous confirmation hearing.

The FCC is an independent agency, but critics accuse Carr of abusing his authority to pressure media companies on behalf of Trump. Carr has repeatedly threatened cable companies with regulatory punishment such as canceling licenses for local TV stations over content that angers the president. Thumann Severs told the committee she had not worked with Carr on any of these “media-related issues” at the FCC.

However, Free Press said the documents uncovered by Democracy Forward and Wired magazine under the Freedom of Information Act show that Thumann Severs played a role as Carr’s senior counsel in coordinating the FCC’s response to recent media-related controversies, including the commission’s response to consumers after Carr pressured ABC News to temporarily suspend the “Jimmy Kimmel Show” in September 2025. Kimmel often jokes about Trump in his monologues, and the president has repeatedly called for the comedian to be taken off the air.

In August, ABC and parent company Walt Disney sued the FCC after the agency demanded it submit its broadcast licenses for review ahead of schedule. The review came amid highly politicized FCC investigations of ABC’s “The View,” as well as probes into diversity, equity, and inclusion practices at Disney. The FCC does not regulate broadcast content, but Trump is an avid consumer of TV and has complained about “The View” as well as multiple other news outlets. In 2023, Trump described Disney as a “Woke and Disgusting shadow of its former self” on social media.

“The lawsuit from ABC would not exist if they thought [Carr] was following the law,” Lewis said.

During the hearing, Cruz plugged the JAWBONE Act, which he introduced with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) and was approved by the committee on September 16. However, Cruz did not specifically mention Carr’s threats against ABC and other outlets.

The internal emails also reveal that Thumann Severs was involved in the FCC’s approval of the controversial merger that could unite Skydance, Paramount, and Warner Bros. under one company controlled by tech oligarch David Ellison. In July 2025, on the same day that Ellison met with Carr and other advisors, Thumann Severs was asked to review a draft of a letter that Skydance was submitting as part of the proceedings. Thumann Severs later responded with an edited version.

“To be clear, the draft letter that Ms. Thumann reviewed, and apparently partially redlined, was not a letter that the Commission intended to send to Skydance or Paramount. It was a letter that Skydance later submitted to the Commission as its own work, a commitment that helped persuade the Commission that the merger was in the public interest, and that was cited in the Commission’s ultimate order approving the transaction,” Senator Luján wrote.

“This means that the Chairman’s office was editing a regulated company’s commitments behind closed doors and then presenting them to the public as company’s own pledges.”

Democrats say Republicans are making a partisan play to stack the FCC and protect Trump and Carr under the incoming Democratic majority. The five-seat FCC currently has two Republicans, and one Democrat, Commissioner Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term officially expired in June, but Cruz and the Republican majority on the committee failed to include her renomination alongside Thumann. The FCC requires only three of the five commissioners to be present for critical votes.

Cruz criticized Democrats for refusing to show up to the hearing and vote on the FCC nomination, but Democrats pointed the finger right back, arguing the GOP is rushing a Republican nominee toward confirmation despite a rebuke from voters in the midterm elections. In a collective statement, the 13 Democrats on the committee blamed the White House for pushing Thumann Severs while ignoring the renomination of Commissioner Gomez. In the past, nominations were made in bipartisan pairs.

“We made clear to Chairman Cruz that we had concerns about the nominee for the Federal Communications Commission … until a Democratic nominee is put forward and asked that she be pulled from the markup,” the Democrats said. “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times.”

In a November 16 letter, Democrats quoted Cruz making a similar argument in 2014, when he wrote that controversial nominees “should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.”

Meanwhile, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) called Democratic members of the committee “sons of bitches” and said their boycott of the confirmation vote was a “total disgrace.” (Moreno has recently come under fire for ignoring the Constitution’s guarantee of religious freedom after he made racist remarks about Muslims and Michigan Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed.)

González said Democrats should know that voters back their case on this nomination, on preserving a free press, and on preventing presidential interference on the airwaves.

“Senator Cruz could have paused, investigated and asked more questions. Instead, he sent Thumann Severs to a Senate floor vote, even as thousands of Americans have called the Senate in the past 24 hours to oppose her confirmation,” González said.

“Voters across the political spectrum have indicated that they want corruption out of government. Every senator who voted to advance Thumann Severs today is showing they don’t actually care about free speech or government transparency.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: Latest COP31 Text Drops Fossil Fuel Phase-Out and Embraces “Magic Technologies”
content:
“Saudi Arabia and some petroleum states have really won big time here,” says German activist Luisa Neubauer.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As we continue our week of broadcasts from the global United Nations climate conference known as COP31, we get an update on the formal negotiations from German activist Luisa Neubauer. The latest draft text of the key climate commitments that countries are debating has dropped language about phasing out fossil fuels, but it does include an emphasis on carbon capture and storage — a largely unproven technology that critics say cannot be deployed at scale to curb emissions.

“We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables,” says Neubauer. “This is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh. We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: As we reach the final hours of climate negotiations at this global conference, negotiators have released a second draft text for the final outcome of this year’s COP. Global civil society activists have already criticized the text for stripping out hard-won language on accountability from Global North countries and legal anchors to protect the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said climate negotiations are, quote, “looking bleak.” She criticized the European Union’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra.

TERESA ANDERSON: Before coming to COP, actually, the EU’s climate chief, Hoekstra, said any chance of a deal on new climate finance is “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” The more I think about it, the more shocked I am that he used that term, in the aftermath of Nepal, as El Niño floods are happening. I’m shocked that he chose that metaphor. When the next catastrophic flood happens, those words will haunt him.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Democracy Now! also caught up with campaigners who’ve been closely following the negotiations here at COP31. This is Kirtana Chandrasekaran from Friends of the Earth International speaking alongside a protest for just solutions from wealthy countries in the Global North.

PROTESTERS: No false solutions! Real solutions now! Real solutions now! No false solutions! No false solutions!

KIRTANA CHANDRASEKARAN: I’m Kirtana Chandrasekaran with Friends of the Earth International. I was at the “divan” meeting last night, and the divan is supposed to be a roundtable for leaders, but there was no leadership in the room. And all we saw is the Global North countries abandoning their moral and legal commitments, country after country saying that “we are worried about breaching 1.5,” with no irony about how we’ve got here, which is 30 years of inaction on their part, and the solution for that being so-called clean electrification.

And what we can see happening now, under the guise of clean electrification, we are seeing many, many new gas plants to electrify data centers. We are seeing many, many new coal plants in the Global South, a massive push, and nuclear, as well. So, they say the words, but they’re not doing any of it. And so they talk about roadmaps, but what is in the roadmap? You know, they were supposed to mobilize $100 million. If you talk about clean electrification, it requires over $2 trillion of investment just for grids and electricity.

AMY GOODMAN: At another protest just this morning, a young activist from Nepal urged people to visit her country to experience what it’s like to live on the frontlines of a climate change-fueled catastrophe.

SNEHA RAI: I think everybody here knows about the 26th August, 2026, flood. … This is not a single disaster. I think this is the one disaster that you have reached to you on the further side of the world. But we have been facing this on yearly. Yearly, every year, we have been facing this. We don’t need hope anymore. We don’t need words anymore. We need actions right now. And Nepal is a mountainous country, you know, and we have been saying that we are resilient people. We are resilient, but there is a limit to resilient.

AMY GOODMAN: Just some of the voices here at the U.N. climate summit.

For more, we’re joined by Luisa Neubauer. She is a climate justice activist, lead organizer of Germany’s Fridays for Future movement. In 2021, she was the lead plaintiff in the landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws.

We welcome you to Democracy Now! here at the U.N. climate summit. Right now as we’re sitting here, the second draft of the — for the final report here has just come out. And I’m wondering if you can talk about the progress that has been made, and not made, what you’re most concerned about, Luisa.

LUISA NEUBAUER: Yes, of course. So, this is a conference where we try to solve our existential climate problems. And we do know, we are all aware, that the root cause of that very problem is oil, coal and gas. That’s the fossil fuels.

So, now we are faced with a new draft negotiation text where the mention of having to get away from the use and exploitation of oil, coal and gas is being stripped out. So, what are we talking about then? And then, what we do see in the text, which is included, is that Saudi Arabia and some petroleum states have really won big time here, because suddenly there’s inclusion of, I would say, magic technologies sucking CO2 out of the atmosphere, which is mentioned big times. We do know those technologies won’t deliver in scale. We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables.

So, we see, really, this is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: And also, I mean, you mentioned Saudi Arabia and all these petroleum-producing states. Talk about the IPCC report —

NERMEEN SHAIKH: — which has now been delayed. And what justification was given for its delay?

LUISA NEUBAUER: It is a real achievement that everything that is being discussed here in these halls is based on the best available science. That is something people have fought for. It’s a real achievement.

And now we’ve seen in recent months that some of the most powerful countries, including the U.S., have been very vocal about kind of boycotting the involvement in the climate science here in these halls. But that means the doors are wide open for all kinds of denial and relativation of what we are seeing here.

So, now in the new negotiation text, there is a better, I would say, agreement that we have to have the science in the room, which you can call a achievement. But for me, honestly, that’s a bare minimum. I mean, what are we talking about? If this is about discussing should we have climate science in the room or not, what are we even aiming at?

NERMEEN SHAIKH: And, you know, you are from Germany and were one of the lead organizers of the Fridays for Future in Germany. Could you tell us why Germany has changed? It was, as you’ve pointed out, also a climate pioneer.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: And now it seems to have altered its position, and also, in fact, the entire EU no longer stands where it once did.

LUISA NEUBAUER: Yeah. Many of us activists here from, say, EU countries, we are here to really put pressure on our own governments, which are some of the richest countries in the world, who’ve accumulated that very wealth to the cost of others around the globe. That is what we’re seeing, right? They are paying the costs. It is emissions coming from countries like Germany who cause, you know, partly, floods in Nepal. That’s a climate change physics here. So we need these countries to step up.

And for a long time, Germany, you know, we have a very vocal climate movement. We have a lot of civil society really taking the streets. So, for a long time, Germany was really moving ahead. Yet, in recent years, we’ve seen a backlash in Germany and other countries. And that is a problem, because we need countries to step up so others can follow. And if even those countries who have the chance to do so, who have technologies at hand, who have enough money to fund, you know, renewables, if they don’t take that lead, who are we expecting to do that? So, that’s why —

AMY GOODMAN: And who is most affected by that?

AMY GOODMAN: When they don’t take the lead.

LUISA NEUBAUER: Yes, that’s — who is going to fill that void? And right now we’re seeing that, you know, other countries are taking advantage of that. So, suddenly we see fossil fuel lobbyists having a great time.

AMY GOODMAN: Let me ask you about this latest news. EU countries, the European Parliament have agreed to delay by two years rules requiring oil, gas and coal importers to report methane emissions due to energy market disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran. So, they’re using —

AMY GOODMAN: — the war in Iran as an excuse to say they won’t be reporting their methane emissions. What’s the significance of this?

LUISA NEUBAUER: Yeah. So, it sounds very technical, but what we’re seeing, when we tackle the climate crisis, we have a transparency issue. So, everyone is making up their own rules. Everyone is reporting different numbers. And by the end of the day, you don’t know who is responsible for emissions, what do we need to tackle, where are emissions even coming from, and how do we get out of this climate crisis mechanism. So we need real reporting. Yet we find that countries, but also industries, are very good and basically ducking away from that responsibility. And that makes us, you know, blind, in a way, from our own problems.

We could be, you know, clear-eyed, steering towards a future that is powered by renewable, that is, you know, producing more justice and a real future, especially for young generation. And instead, we once again see that fossil fuel industries and fossil fuel nations are making the rules, and we all will pay the cost.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, one of the words that has been repeated very often here is “electrification,” AI and data centers, of course, but also the transportation sector. And apparently, the very largest, by volume, sources that require electricity is air conditioning. So, if you could talk about the significance? What does it mean to electrify —

NERMEEN SHAIKH: — places? Where does the energy for that come from? And also the fact — I mean, it is extraordinary. I read these figures that in the U.S. about 90% of households have access to air conditioning. In India, it’s less than 20%, and in Nigeria, it’s about 5%.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, if you could just, I mean, talk about that, air conditioning? Of course, places are getting hotter, including Europe.

AMY GOODMAN: And at the same time, you have 50,000 people dying this year of the heat.

LUISA NEUBAUER: That is a — that is a real worry. Just a state, you know, what we negotiate here, what we see people talking about, it feels like they’re living on a different planet. This is a planet they negotiate with that waits for us, until we have, you know, agreed on a nitty-gritty paragraph that nobody even understands. Yet the world out there, the world we live on, is a world where we still miss thousands of people from the latest flood in Nepal, and that’s just the latest flood; where thousands, tens of thousands of people died on a privileged continent like Europe because of the heat, and they weren’t protected; where right now our colleagues in Honduras are faced with the consequences of the El Niño phenomenon. That is the real world out there, and for that world, we need to provide solutions.

And number one, of course, we need to be fast with whatever we do, because right now we see that the solutions we try to put on the problems are eaten up by the problem. And aircon is a perfect example. It’s getting hotter, so people need more air conditioning. And at the same time, that air conditioning is causing the problem that we’re trying to tackle. We’re not going to get out of this devil’s wheel if we’re not getting faster and better in applying these solutions.

And this is why this conference is talking about, rightfully so, to electrify, so to make sure we get away from fossil fuels, from coal, oil and gas, and into electricity powered by renewables, by the sun and by the wind. That is really important.

Yet now we see, once again, at this conference that those who are taking the lead in the negotiations, seemingly so, say, “Well, what about we electrify, so we, you know, provide electricity, but, you know, maybe it comes through some fossil fuel gas or from nuclear?” That means we are doing some nice modernization projects, but for that, we don’t need a climate conference, that you can solve an industrial project anywhere.

AMY GOODMAN: And let me say that 50,000 number that I said people have died of heat was on Europe alone, and people are saying it’s millions who die of heat-related diseases. But I wanted to end in the last minute by asking you about your landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws. How old were you when you brought this?

LUISA NEUBAUER: I was in my mid-twenties. And this was an amazing, an amazing case for us. We’ve been organizing hundreds of thousands of people to take the streets in Germany alone, but, I mean, we were all over the world. And it really proved people power works and activism works. And I find we forget that these days, that it matters where we show up, how we show up, how often we show up, that it matters most that we show up in dark times, but it’s not all easy, easy-peasy, and it’s not all flowing.

And what we did, once we took the streets with so many people, and we still saw the German government not acting in time, we took the courts. The courts alone won’t solve the crisis we’re in, but they are crucial mechanisms, and we must make use of that. And then we go back to the streets, and we make sure we are everywhere. We’re showing up again and again and again. And right now we see some of the richest billionaire people on the planet, some of the most powerful countries wanting to put this dystopian future upon us. And I guess it’s a good time to choose our own future and stand up for what we believe in.

AMY GOODMAN: Luisa Neubauer, we want to thank you so much for being with us, climate justice activist, lead organizer of Germany’s Fridays for Future movement, in 2021 the lead plaintiff in the landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws.

Coming up, we speak to Indigenous activists, one from Alaska. We’ll talk about the climate crisis and the election of Mary Peltola, who just made history for being the first Alaskan Native elected to the U.S. Senate. And then we’ll turn to Russia, where an Indigenous activist was arrested right after returning from COP30, the U.N. climate summit in Brazil. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “The Fire of Antalya,” performed at the COP31 opening ceremony here in Antalya, Turkey.

author: S. Baum
title: Ohio Bill Threatens to Criminalize Drag and Gender Nonconformity, Opponents Warn
content:
Civil liberties and trans rights advocates say the bill has nothing to do with the purported aim of protecting children.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Ohio appears to be on the cusp of passing a drag ban. Transgender Ohioans and their allies are sounding the alarm.

“House Bill 249 seeks to limit drag performances to strip clubs and similar locations, making it a crime to perform in drag in other places where a minor may be present,” an ACLU of Ohio petition to stop the bill reads.

“This bill broadly targets anyone who performs exhibiting a gender identity different than the entertainer’s biological sex at birth. HB 249 also relies on notoriously vague legal standards used to determine whether content is considered obscene and/or ‘harmful to juveniles.’”

Dara Adkison, the executive director of TransOhio, told Erin in the Morning that if this bill becomes law, it would be “the most extreme criminalization of drag and perceived gender nonconformity in the country.”

In addition to traditional drag, HB 249 also specifically targets transgender and gender nonconforming performers. Those found to violate all or part of these measures could be tried for a misdemeanor or felony, which could carry jail time.

Although in theory, the bill applies only to “performances,” not everyday Ohioans, its ambiguity blurs the line between lawful and unlawful; the bill fails to even articulate what constitutes a “performance.”

“If I’m doing my grocery shopping down at Kroger, and I whistle to myself as I’m going down the aisle or hum to the music overhead, has that suddenly become a drag performance in the middle of the Kroger shopping center?” Arienne Childrey, a transgender woman and community activist, asked while being interviewed by Erin in the Morning. She said the bill isn’t about drag performance or protecting children as much as it is about criminalizing gender nonconformity.

Childrey has been following the progression of Ohio’s drag ban for a long while—since 2023, to be exact, when HB 249’s predecessor bill, HB 245, was proposed. That bill was sponsored by Rep. Angie King, Childrey’s own representative in the statehouse. When Childrey and others staged a protest, King responded by mocking demonstrators, arguing they were fighting for the “right to twerk and gyrate in front of your minor children.”

An Ohio drag ban was reintroduced in April of last year. It passed in the House in March 2026 and then stalled for months in the Senate. On Nov. 17, analysts at TransOhio noticed it was put on the legislative calendar for a hearing sometime during the week beginning on Monday, Nov. 23. An exact date and time has not yet been announced.

“What we have right now is vengeance politics playing out in Ohio,” Childrey said, referring to the aftermath of this midterm cycle’s blue wave.

“Their veto-proof supermajority evaporates after the new year,” she continued. “Come January, that disappears. So they know that they are ‘do or die’ this time around; otherwise, they have a two-year legislative cycle where they won’t be able to move something like this through if they were to try.”

The state’s Senate Judiciary Committee must now vote on whether to pass the “sub bill,” or substitution bill, which is an amended version of the text. It will then need to be heard before the full Senate and be reconciled with the House if there are further changes.

However, it is still dripping with the same anti-trans animus and ill intent as before, even if its GOP proponents try to brand it as some sort of middle-of-the-road compromise, activists warned.

For example, the sub bill removed the definitions of “biological sex” that it previously codified, but those were enshrined by HB 96 anyway; the newer version also added a section making it a felony if “the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to two or more violations of this section.”

“The vagueness is actually more dangerous now,” Adkison, of TransOhio, told Erin in the Morning. “The sub bill INCREASES the criminal penalties for an offense that previously didn’t exist. Under this bill, gender nonconformity (even among cis people) will be scrutinized, and those who don’t look ‘male’ or ‘female’ enough will face potential prison time.”

“This is so clearly a violation of the First Amendment freedom of expression,” Adkison added.

author: Katie Myers
title: Trump Admin Proposes Easing Protections for Coal Miners From Black Lung Disease
content:
Miners’ advocates said revisions to a Biden-era rule on silica exposure would weaken already insufficient protections.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Coal mining is dangerous and takes a toll on the body, but a miner working underground can earn enough to buy a house, drive a nice car, and send the kids to college. There was a time when John Robinson thought the trade-off was worth it. No longer. He was diagnosed with black lung disease at age 47, a consequence of inhaling toxic silica dust in the mines of Virginia.

“These companies will bait you in with this big money,” said Robinson, who is now 60 and vice president of the National Black Lung Association. “When you get down and out, well, guess what? You’re like an old wore-out tire on the car or something. They’ll throw you to the side ’cause you ain’t worth nothing.”

For more than 50 years, coal miners, their families, and advocates have pressed the federal government for stricter limits on silica exposure, stronger enforcement of rules meant to protect miners, and improved health benefits for those disabled by the disease. In 2024, the Biden administration set the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica at 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, matching the Occupational Safety and Health Administration threshold for workers in other industries. The rule was finalized in 2024, with coal companies required to comply beginning in April 2025.

That regulation was meant to update protections in coal mines and in what regulators call metal and nonmetal mines, which extract everything from copper and critical minerals to stone, sand, and gravel. All of them carry a risk of inhaling silica dust, whose fine particles can lodge deep in the lungs. But research over the past two decades has shown that Central Appalachian coal miners have experienced an acute increase in exposure and the most severe forms of lung disease associated with it, including progressive massive fibrosis.

Though the Biden-era revision wasn’t perfect, advocates like Robinson and his wife Vonda Robinson, who is president of the National Black Lung Association, were hopeful. It seemed as though decades of organizing for a stronger standard were finally coming to an end. But a federal appeals court put the rule on hold last year while it considered legal challenges filed by the mining industry. Now the Mine Safety and Health Administration wants to revise the rule.

Its proposal would retain the 50-microgram silica limit while changing several requirements governing how mines monitor exposure and protect workers. Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy analyst with Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center, said those revisions could substantially weaken the protections behind the stricter limit.

Black lung is the common name for coal worker’s pneumoconiosis, an incurable, progressive, and fatal respiratory disease caused by inhaling coal dust and fine silica particles, which can cause severe inflammation in the lungs. Over time, that irritant scars and stiffens lung tissue, making respiration increasingly difficult until many of those afflicted with it cannot breathe at all.

In the 1960s and 1970s, according to the National Institutes of Health, as many as 1 in 3 miners with more than 25 years of work experience were testing positive for black lung. The United Mine Workers of America agitated for stricter protections again the disease, and in 1969, Congress passed the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act, which required regular inspections. Disease rates plummeted to a historic low in the 2000s, only to begin climbing again. Rates of black lung are now at a 50-year high and still climbing. A study led by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, or NIOSH, found these increases across all age groups, including miners in their 20s and 30s, although rates remained highest among those who had spent decades underground. In routine health screenings by the agency during the past three years, more than 1 in 3 miners in Central Appalachia once again tested positive for the disease, making the epidemic into a U-shaped curve.

The new rule was published in the Federal Register on November 12 and will be open for public comment until January 11. Although the stricter limit of 50 micrograms remains, Muckian-Bates said the fine print matters: Other changes in the rule undermine that threshold and give mine operators greater control over how it is enforced.

“On the one hand, it looks on the surface like the administration is saying, ‘Yes, we agree that silica is the leading cause of the black lung right now,’” Muckian-Bates said. “However, they’ve provided these measures to effectively nullify that.” Among them is a 21 percent margin of error in testing, meaning companies would only be fined if a sample exceeded the 50 microgram limit by at least that amount. That effectively gives companies a 10 microgram increase in the amount workers can be exposed to, according to Muckian-Bates.

The 2024 rule enforced regular silica monitoring by requiring air sampling in each underground mine every six months. The proposal eliminates that schedule, instead requiring mine operators to assess when changing conditions could increase exposure and test “as frequently as necessary.” Mines could therefore go longer than six months without being sampled if operators determine additional testing isn’t needed, as long as they remain below the exposure limit.

The proposed rule also would also make medical exams voluntary for new metal and nonmetal miners; the 2024 rule made them mandatory. Advocates and health professionals say those initial exams establish a baseline that can later help determine whether lung disease developed from workplace exposure rather than an earlier condition or exposure. That is particularly important because the consequences of silica exposure may not become apparent for decades.

“What we have in the pipeline right now is not going to show up until like 20 years later,” Muckian-Bates said. “That just means we’re going to have a new crop of sick miners who we don’t know are getting sick, and they don’t know they’re getting sick, until it’s too late.”

The Mine Safety and Health Administration did not respond to questions. A spokesperson for the Department of Labor said in an email that anyone interested in offering feedback can do so within the 60-day window that opened on November 12, or during a virtual meeting on December 15.

“MSHA looks forward to reviewing all stakeholder comments before publishing a final rule to better protect the health of the Nation’s miners,” the email stated. The agency noted in the Federal Register that “this rule, if finalized, is expected to be a deregulatory action,” quoting President Donald Trump’s executive order titled “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.”

MSHA estimates the proposed rule will save the industry $28.7 million per year, mostly from changes in monitoring. Of that, coal companies would save $2.43 million.

With the 2024 rule on hold, miners remain subject to silica standards whose basic framework dates to the early 1970s and effectively allows exposures of roughly 100 micrograms per cubic meter of air. Virginia Tech mining expert Emily Sarver said a tighter limit is so overdue that she would rather see the proposal move forward than face years of further delay.

“I don’t think our current legacy rule is sufficiently protective,” Sarver said. Among other things, she considers the 2024 rule’s sampling scheme, involving many different labs rather than MSHA labs, chaotic, making enforcement difficult. “I think the new rule that was passed in 2024 on paper looks more protective, but I think there’s certain problems with it.”

As for John and Vonda Robinson, they plan to keep fighting for stronger protection of those who work the mines.

“If us older coal miners don’t get nothing out of this,” John Robinson said, “we can help the next batch of coal miners [that] is going to come up, that’s going to be extremely sick. This don’t go away. This is going to last for years and to [their] death.”

title: Musk Says He’s Not MAGA After Spending Nearly Half a Billion Backing Republicans
content:
After years of promoting Trump’s far right agenda, Musk claimed that he is actually “quite moderate.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

After years of promoting Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) agenda, Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he no longer considers himself part of the pro-Trump movement.

Speaking remotely at The New York Times DealBook Summit, Musk attempted to suggest that he had never harbored such viewpoints — despite his stint as the head of the Trump administration’s so-called “Department of Government Efficiency,” or DOGE.

“I’m not MAGA. … I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m — like, if it means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the multi-billionaire said.

Musk further claimed that he prefers “checks and balances” in government, and described himself as “quite moderate.”

Musk added that he felt “pretty foolish for how much money I spent in the midterms” in support of MAGA-aligned Republicans.

Elon Musk claims he’s “not MAGA” pic.twitter.com/3hZZQgSPaN

Musk’s rejection of MAGA on Wednesday is a stark departure from his attitude over the past two years. In fact, Musk embraced MAGA while campaigning for Trump in 2024, describing himself as “dark MAGA” while wearing a black version of the red hat often donned by the president.

Musk didn’t just make speeches in support of the movement — he jubilantly championed MAGA, jumping wildly on campaign stages in rockstar fashion, with then-candidate Donald Trump alongside him.

His “dark MAGA” persona continued into 2025, when he wore the black cap during appearances at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) and in Oval Office meetings while discussing his work with DOGE.

Musk’s comments come as he has been trying to distance himself from the Trump administration in recent months, even going so far as to say he got “carried away” with the major funding cuts to international programs that he implemented as head of DOGE. Those cuts, experts have noted, could lead to the deaths of 14 million people worldwide, including 4.5 million children, by 2030.

Despite those comments, Musk still spent almost half a billion dollars in support of MAGA-aligned Republicans during the midterms, including an anti-trans ad blitz across multiple states.

Musk may be attempting to distance himself from MAGA with hopes that doing so will prompt Democrats to back away from their promised investigations into his work at DOGE and his companies’ many lucrative contracts with the government — though some Democrats have already publicly told the billionaire that won’t happen.

Musk’s attempts to rebrand himself as anti-MAGA could also stem from his recognition that the movement has run its course. Indeed, recent polling indicates that most Americans are tired of MAGA.

A Quinnipiac University poll in September, for example, found that only 32 percent of Americans remain dedicated to the movement, with 65 percent rejecting it. That poll also found that candidates describing themselves as MAGA did so at their own peril, with 51 percent of voters saying the label made them less likely to vote for a candidate and only 18 percent saying it made them more likely to do so.

A post-midterm poll from Politico also found that nearly one in two MAGA supporters recognize that their movement is dwindling, with 45 percent of those identifying with MAGA agreeing with the idea that they were “losers” in the elections held earlier this month.

author: Kevin Foster
title: CA Legislators Passed a Bill Targeting ICE Contractors. Newsom Vetoed It.
content:
The California governor singlehandedly shut down a bill that could have punished companies for working with ICE.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

California Assembly Bill 2465 passed out of both the California Senate and Assembly with near unanimous Democratic support, setting the stage for a first-of-its-kind bill to punish companies for working with immigration enforcement agencies — then Gov. Gavin Newsom killed it.

AB 2465 would have prohibited businesses from receiving any state-provided grant, loan, or tax credit if they directly invest in, own, operate, or manage a private detention facility, or contract with the federal government for immigration enforcement purposes. It also would have established the “Due Process for All Fund,” transferring money from the general fund toward immigration-related services and programs based on the total taxes collected from businesses made ineligible for tax credits by the bill.

Governor Newsom vetoed the bill on September 30, the final day for him to do so. When asked for comment, Diana Crofts-Pelayo, Newsom’s chief deputy director of communications, pointed to his veto message.

“I agree with the author that more must be done to hold the Trump administration accountable for the indiscriminate raids that have rounded up American citizens, people with legal status, and hardworking parents,” Newsom wrote. “While I appreciate the author’s goal of ensuring that state dollars do not support these egregious federal actions, this bill’s requirements are unclear and expand beyond the stated intent.”

Newsom’s concerns with the bill revolve around impacts on businesses “providing legitimate goods and services to a range of agencies with responsibilities beyond the type of immigration enforcement that inspired this bill.”

The bill would affect major private-prison contractors like CoreCivic and The GEO Group, but it contains a carveout for health care providers that contract with detention facilities or immigration enforcement to ensure they are not punished for tending to injured or ill people in detention.

California Assemblymember Liz Ortega, the author of the bill, took issue with Newsom’s veto justification.

“It is not a legitimate business practice to provide services to an agency that guns down citizens in the streets and violates people’s civil rights,” Ortega wrote in a statement for Truthout. “I was disappointed that AB 2465 was not signed. I still don’t think our tax dollars should be going to companies that are illegally locking up parents and separating families.”

The bill gathered 25 institutional opponents versus 144 supporters, per tracking from CalMatters. Some of those opponents included CalBroadband, the California Chamber of Commerce, and a range of construction, electrical, and manufacturing associations.

Immigrant Defenders Law Center was one of the many supporters. Luis Guerra, the law center’s director of advocacy and external relations, indicated the organization was not pleased with Newsom’s veto.

“Governor Newsom’s decision to veto AB 2465 was a missed opportunity to draw a clear line between California’s values and the corporations profiting from the detention, deportation, and separation of immigrant families,” Guerra told Truthout. “Every day, our attorneys see the devastating consequences of a system designed to detain and deport people while denying them a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights. California should be investing in due process and protecting immigrant communities, not preserving financial benefits for corporations that profit from their suffering.”

At the time of Newsom’s veto, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had reported 24 deaths in custody in 2026. As of October 29, 2026, this number rose to 32, according to the National Immigration Project, their count including people confirmed dead within 30 days of release — ICE reportedly stopped counting these deaths in June, which immigrant rights groups opposed. This follows a record-high of 33 deaths in ICE custody in 2025, exhibiting a uniform pattern of medical neglect.

It’s unclear which specific businesses Newsom is concerned about — Crofts-Pelayo did not respond to a request for comment on this matter.

“It is not a legitimate business practice to provide services to an agency that guns down citizens in the streets and violates people’s civil rights…. I still don’t think our tax dollars should be going to companies that are illegally locking up parents and separating families.”

Immigrant prisons and camps require a number of third-party contractors for construction and to remain functional. For example, Trinity Food Services is contracted for food service operations in two of California’s largest immigrant prisons, the California City Detention Facility and the Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Immigrant prisoners frequently report issues with hunger and inadequate food. An investigation from El País in August 2026 offers firsthand accounts from immigrants, including one who reportedly lost 40 pounds in eight months in California’s Adelanto ICE Processing Center.

The man, going by Carlos, said he went hungry every day, had to eat inedible pasta, and spent around $400 per month in commissary on priced-up goods to stave off hunger — he had to use funds deposited by relatives and coworkers. Activists outside the Otay Mesa immigrant prison tell a similar story of rapidly burning through tens of thousands of dollars in donations for phone calls and commissary purchases.

A May 2026 report from the California Department of Justice contains consistent accounts from immigrant prisoners of meals delivered at irregular and problematic hours, undercooked and spoiled food, and insufficient portion sizes, with one individual saying they get “just enough to survive.”

TKC Holdings, Trinity’s parent company, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A CoreCivic spokesperson said they have concerns about the findings of the report, but pointed to the positive food inspection at Otay Mesa by the San Diego County health inspectors issued on August 10, 2026. The spokesperson neglected to mention that CoreCivic and the Department of Homeland Security prevented county supervisors and Sen. Alex Padilla from completing an inspection of the facility on February 20, 2026.

The county has said they don’t know what the conditions were in February. They were only allowed inside 16 weeks later on June 12, 2026, following a lawsuit from the county and a preliminary injunction in federal court. This inspection also produced concerns about shortfalls in health and safety, including failures to report active or suspected tuberculosis cases within the 24 hours required by state law. This problem has persisted, with the facility taking three weeks to report a case in August.

While Newsom has signed a range of bills intended to rein in immigration agents, AB 2465 sticks out as a missed opportunity for financial accountability and reparations for immigrant services.

“By vetoing AB 2465, Governor Newsom also rejected an opportunity to direct additional critical resources toward immigration legal services and programs at a time when access to legal representation can mean the difference between a family remaining together or being permanently separated,” Guerra told Truthout. “Immigrant families deserve more than political promises. They deserve leaders willing to put their safety, rights, and futures ahead of corporate profits.”

Newsom signed his veto at a troubling time. ICE raids have been ongoing across California, but just a week after Newsom’s order, an ICE surge began in Southern California in the leadup to the midterms.

With the 2026 election now over, conversations have already shifted to 2028, when Newsom is widely expected to make a presidential run. But his veto raises further questions about his willingness to go beyond fiery rhetoric and stand up for vulnerable people.

Deaths in ICE detention are on track for another record-high year under the second Trump administration. With Gavin Newsom on his way out of the governorship, there may be new opportunities to bring innovative legislation forward to help immigrant communities in California.

“Trump signaled his intent to double down on terror against immigrant communities when he promoted Stephen Miller — and we have every reason to believe that the ICE contractor grift will continue,” Assemblymember Ortega wrote in a statement for Truthout. “So we’re looking at all potential strategies to make sure that our own state government isn’t subsidizing it.”

author: Stephen Prager
title: ICJ Finds Myanmar Guilty of Committing Genocide Against Rohingya Muslims
content:
The International Court of Justice for the first time in its 80-year history has found a state responsible for genocide.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In a historic ruling, the International Court of Justice on Thursday found Myanmar’s government responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority during its brutal military campaign in 2017.

It is the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that it has found a state responsible for committing genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention, with the court ruling in a 9-6 vote that “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part” of the Rohingya population.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court found that during Myanmar’s military campaign that began in northern Rakhine State in August 2017, “security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers.”

NEWS: @CIJ_ICJ determines Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State.@antonioguterres calls the judgement a demonstration of international justice.https://t.co/1RCbI9g5hb pic.twitter.com/E51EwzIIDf

In the case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, the court found that the evidence supported UN investigators’ estimate that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, including women and children. It also showed soldiers committed widespread rape and sexual violence. The ICJ additionally found that Rohingya villages were systematically burned and destroyed while neighboring villages belonging to other ethnic groups were spared. In all, more than 700,000 Rohingya were forced to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

The court ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute, and punish suspects, and enact laws implementing the Genocide Convention to prevent future violations. It also ordered the country to facilitate the voluntary return of displaced Rohingya, help locate missing people, return or replace lost or damaged property, provide rehabilitation for victims, and ensure protection against discrimination. Myanmar must also compensate the Rohingya for harm done with an amount to be determined later, the ICJ said.

The ruling was celebrated by human rights advocates. Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard called it “a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families.”

Genocide. The international Court of Justice is fully convinced that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. Complex and well presented lines of arguments on genocidal intent. Many implications for jurisprudence and future trials. Well evidenced and well argued…

She said the ruling “must serve as a wake-up call to the international community” and “must not simply be ignored,” especially since those who committed the atrocities are still in positions of power.

“The man who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya, the former head of the armed forces, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, is now Myanmar’s president following engineered elections,” she said. “Governments should not welcome him on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar. Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar.”

Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said that in addition to being a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” it also “provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice.”

Nimer Sultany, a law professor at the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies, said the ruling had massive implications for the December 2023 genocide case brought before the ICJ against Israel over its military campaign in Gaza.

“The court’s application of the law to the facts in Myanmar makes it highly likely it will reach a similar conclusion in the case of Israel, given the scale of its crimes in Gaza,” he said, adding that the ruling “breathes new life into the Genocide Convention.”

Amid systematic attacks against international law led by the Trump administration, which has waged war on institutions such as the International Criminal Court (ICC), Antonio Guterres, the United Nations secretary-general, said the ruling against Myanmar “is a demonstration of international justice & a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.”

🚨The ICJ has found that Myanmar has committed #genocide against the #Rohingya in #Myanmar. This is the first time ever that the #ICJ has found a state responsible for genocide. Huge finding and tremendously significant to Rohingya victims. https://t.co/qk7ZaO8yW6

While the ICJ’s rulings are legally binding, it has no independent means of compelling Myanmar to comply.

University of Manitoba law professor and genocide scholar Kjell Anderson argued that while the ruling “will not immediately change the situation on the ground,” it may help to “mobilize attention and support for the Rohingya.”

“This should also help to create some moral clarity for states in the region — like Malaysia, Thailand, India, and China — that are cozying up to the Myanmar government, and, in some cases, sending Rohingya back into a tremendously dangerous situation.”

Anderson shared a message he received from a Rohingya friend living in the Kutupalong camp in Bangladesh.

“Today is a deeply emotional and historic day for the Rohingya,” they said. “After everything our people have endured, this moment gives us renewed hope for justice, dignity, and a better future and return to the homeland.”
