author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Judge Nominee Won’t Say If He Can Run for President a Third Time
content:
James Sullivan, who refused to say if Trump could run for president again, is currently a Texas Supreme Court justice.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Wednesday, a nominee to a federal judgeship struggled to recall and then refused to answer basic questions about the 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which stipulates that a person cannot run for a third presidential term if they’ve previously been elected president twice.

James P. Sullivan, who is presently a Texas state Supreme Court justice, lost his reelection bid earlier this month when the state saw a “blue wave” in the midterm elections. Days after his loss, President Donald Trump nominated Sullivan to become a federal judge within the state.

Although Sullivan’s time as a judge was limited — he was appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott (R-Texas) in early 2025 and served just under two years on Texas’s high court after a vacancy occurred — he has a strong legal background rooted in conservatism, having previously served as general counsel to the governor from 2018 to 2025. Sullivan is also a member of the far right Federalist Society.

During his nomination hearing in the Senate on Wednesday, Sullivan refused to answer queries regarding basic constitutional theory and recent history.

When Sen. Chris Coons (D-Delaware) asked him to explain the meaning of the 22nd Amendment, Sullivan appeared to struggle, at one point closing his eyes tightly, as if to focus. After several seconds, Coons gave him a hint: “No person shall be elected…” he began, prompting Sullivan to recall that the amendment bars people from running for a third presidential term.

Coons then asked Sullivan if Trump could run for a third term, citing numerous remarks by the president suggesting he might try to do so. Sullivan refused to answer the question.

“As a nominee for a federal district court, it would be a violation, I believe, of Canon 5 for me to opine on something like that,” Sullivan responded, citing American Bar Association (ABA) standards for nominees for judgeships. He then described the issue as something that “seems like it’s the sort of thing that is the subject of ongoing political debate.”

Coons disagreed, stating that it seems clear that the amendment — and Trump’s suggestions that he could run again — are contradictory.

“The question of whether someone can serve a third term as president of the United States, I think, is only unresolved in the mind of President Trump, who has repeatedly said that he’s thinking he might run for a third time,” Coons explained.

“I don’t believe it is the subject of political debate,” he added.

After the two continued a short back-and-forth on the matter, Coons reiterated his disbelief in Sullivan’s non-answer.

“The amendment is bracingly clear: ‘No person shall be elected to the office of the president more than twice,’” he said. “There is no debate about this, in my view.”

OMG — Trump judicial nominee James P Sullivan (a Texas Supreme Court justice!) reveals he doesn't know what the 22nd amendment says, but then after Chris Coons explains it to him, he refuses to say it'd be illegal for Trump to serve an illegal third term 🤦 pic.twitter.com/YwkDcVa70C

The ABA’s Canon 5 rule does contain a subsection prohibiting “a candidate for judicial office from making statements that commit the candidate regarding cases, controversies or issues likely to come before the court.” However, there is a caveat to that rule that Sullivan appeared to ignore: “As a corollary, a candidate should emphasize in any public statement the candidate’s duty to uphold the law regardless of his or her personal views.”

Had Sullivan responded to Coons’s question on the 22nd Amendment by correctly pointing out that the law forbids Trump from running again, he likely wouldn’t have been in violation of the standard he cited.

Later during the hearing, multiple nominees were asked by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) to recall the events of January 6, 2021, when a mob of loyalists to Trump sought to violently disrupt the proceedings of Congress following Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 presidential race.

Blumenthal sought to discern whether any of the nominees were “willing to say the Capitol was attacked” on that date. The nominees, including Sullivan, did not respond.

“Nobody? It’s a sad day,” Blumenthal said.

Sullivan’s non-answers may be moot points, at least when it comes to Trump’s future in politics. The president’s approval ratings are currently nearing record-low levels, making it unlikely that he will attempt to illegally run for a third term and risk facing an embarrassing defeat.

That said, Trump has repeatedly suggested he might run again, including during an interview on “Meet the Press” last year.

“I’m not joking” about running for a third term, he told host Kristen Welker, claiming “there are methods which you could do it.”

title: Trump Has Turned SEC Into “Subservient Lapdog” for Corporations, Watchdog Says
content:
There are at least a dozen high level officials in the agency with potential conflicts of interest, a new report finds.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

One of the U.S.’s top financial regulators has been reduced to nothing but a “subservient lapdog” for corporate interests under the Trump administration, a government watchdog warns in a new report identifying at least a dozen high level officials in the agency with ties to the very firms they’re tasked with overseeing.

Under Paul Atkins, a Donald Trump appointee, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is being run by a swath of officials who have formerly done work on behalf of major private equity firms, fossil fuel corporations, crypto companies, military contractors, and more — including figures who previously served as defense attorneys for firms when they were being investigated by the agency, finds the report released Wednesday by Public Citizen.

The SEC was created in response to the Great Depression as a safeguard against the types of corruption and conflicts of interest that led to the economic disaster. Under Atkins, the group warns, conflicts of interest appear to be a selling point for leadership appointments.

“Under Paul Atkins, the SEC has radically transformed from a muscular investor watchdog into a drooling, subservient lapdog that does nothing but serve the very corporate interests it’s supposed to be keeping in check,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate for Public Citizen, in a statement.

Among the questionable actions since Atkins was confirmed by the Senate last year has been the SEC’s dropping of several of its cases against Atkins’s former clients. Atkins also seemingly has conflicts of interest related to work with several firms and companies, including his past leadership for three crypto companies and ownership of crypto assets.

Numerous other senior SEC officials similarly have deep ties to companies they’re supposed to regulate. One senior adviser to the Crypto Task Force, for instance, was a crypto lobbyist for a prominent crypto nonprofit known as the Coin Center up until he was appointed in February 2025.

The SEC’s Division of Enforcement, which is supposed to enforce laws, has been filled with figures who have represented the other side, serving as defense attorneys for companies and firms investigated by the SEC, Public Citizen found.

This includes the director of the division, David Woodcock — a former in-house counsel for ExxonMobil and leader in major law firm Gibson Dunn, where he headed the firm’s Securities Enforcement Practice Group. There, he represented numerous major companies, like AT&T, ExxonMobil, SpaceX, UPS, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, and more.

As the report finds, Woodcock was twice named on the list of the “Enforcement Elite” by legal hub Securities Docket — a distinction described as “the kind of defensive specialists critical to have on speed-dial should the SEC’s Division of Enforcement come calling.”

The detailed report finds numerous other potential conflicts of interest across other parts of the agency, including the SEC’s Division of Corporate Finance, its public relations head, and the Office of General Counsel, the latter of which is led by a former managing director for BlackRock and general counsel for major firm Focus Financial Partners.

Even the inspector general — the figure who is supposed to lead internal investigations into wrongdoing inside the agency — has potential conflicts of interest, the report found. SEC Inspector General Kevin Muhlendorf was formerly a criminal defense attorney for those accused by the SEC of violating financial regulations and laws, and also faced accusations of conflict of interest when he became the acting inspector general for the D.C. metro operator, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA).

“There are cases where criminal defense attorneys have transitioned to the IG community, but it certainly merits a pause to consider how adequately and aggressively someone who once defended alleged criminals and is now in charge of the office tasked with identifying and pursuing individuals who may have violated the law will be in their newfound role as an inspector general,” the report said.

The report also notes that the extent of potential conflicts of interest within the agency is not known because Muhlendorf and another official each declined to disclose 22 former clients in forms, citing confidentiality requirements.

“Trump has surrounded himself with people like Atkins, who view government service and political power as a means to bestow favors on their friends and associates and amass ever greater personal wealth,” said Public Citizen co-president Lisa Gilbert. “And once again, the millions of Americans whose retirement funds and life savings depend on a fair securities marketplace are left out to dry.”

The report may fuel further scrutiny of the SEC. Lawmakers, most prominently Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), have previously called out the SEC for effectively abdicating its mission of enforcing the law, ushering in what Warren calls a “Golden Age of Fraud.”

Indeed, the agency’s latest report on its actions in fiscal year 2026 show that its enforcement actions are plummeting. In the past year, the SEC’s enforcement penalties fell to an 18-year low, decreasing by nearly 24 percent over the previous fiscal year.

content:
National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The 2026 midterms didn’t only swell the ranks of progressives and green economic populists in Congress — they also ushered in a stunning number of Native American leaders in down-ballot races across the country. Among the state legislative races involving Indigenous candidates that have been called so far, Native American candidates won 83 percent of the time, according to ICT.

Montana led the way: 12 of 13 Indigenous candidates there, all Democrats, won legislative seats, including Natalie Weeks-O’Neal (Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux) in House District 31 and Katie Fire Thunder (Oglala Lakota) in House District 59.

In Nevada, Brian Wadsworth, a former Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribal Council member, won a seat on the Washoe County Commission representing the county’s rural north, becoming the first tribal member from any of the county’s tribal nations to serve on it, Wadsworth told Truthout. Native Republicans won too, including Emily McIntire (Muscogee) in Oregon and Heather Ellison (Navajo) in New Mexico.

In Alaska, Mary Peltola defeated the incumbent to became the first Native person to represent the state in the U.S. Senate.

Many of these candidates spoke to voters’ concerns on the campaign trail about the affordability of groceries and health care. In Northern Nevada, voters also raised concerns about water, land, and unchecked growth. And the offices these candidates won are increasingly in locales where fights over land, water, and AI data centers get decided, as the federal government weakens its obligation to consult tribes. “We have about 120 proposed hyperscale data centers for Indian Country,” said Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of environmental advocacy group Honor the Earth.

Locally, “these fights are currently being fought and won,” Two Bulls told Truthout. A U.S. Senate permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, despite its name, focuses on narrowing environmental review processes and threatens tribal consultation on projects affecting tribal water, land, and cultural sites. “That’s pretty much going to gut any kind of protections or legs that tribes can stand on to push back against these corporations,” said Two Bulls. The bill passed a preliminary vote on November 9 but has yet to clear the next hurdle in the Senate.

National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level, especially in states with multiple Indigenous candidate victories. Montana’s wins were historic: “It’s not lost on us that we’re making history, being the largest American Indian caucus in the United States at the state level,” said Weeks-O’Neal, adding that the state’s main media has yet to cover this fact.

Two Bulls expressed hope that the Indigenous bloc will be able to exert real leverage, saying: “They can actually throw a lot of wrenches into the fast tracking that’s currently happening.”

Despite Two Bulls’ forward-looking ambitions for the new class of Native politicians, especially around AI, Weeks-O’Neal faces extant costs to her district: The Zortman mines, which extracted gold from the Little Rocky Mountains in the 1980s and ’90s, contaminated Montana’s water and still cost $3 million a year to treat. “The water is devastated. It is tainted in perpetuity. That means forever,” she said. “Whatever profit was made from the mine, I mean, I can’t imagine.” The site has been re-listed for $52.5 million with geologists estimating “that only 20% of the gold and silver [was] harvested, leaving plenty of reserves for investors or operators,” the listing states.

House District 31 includes much of the Fort Peck Reservation, whose median age is 30 and median household income is roughly $53,000, far below the national median of around $87,000. It’s no surprise then that voters’ primary concern is affordability, especially groceries. “They were struggling to even feed their families,” said Weeks-O’Neal. Trump’s administration has moved to slash the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which could cut off access for 6.3 million people nationally.

Meanwhile Katie Fire Thunder’s constituents in South Bozeman, which is one of the wealthiest areas in the state, are also worried about affordability: Rising property taxes, driven by soaring land values, are creating a crisis for retirees on fixed incomes who are being priced out of homes they’d expected to keep for life. “That tax burden is being shifted on to residential and property owners,” she said, joining the call alongside Weeks-O’Neal.

Rep. Thedis Crowe (Blackfeet), reelected in House District 15, which borders Canada and includes part of the Blackfeet Reservation, said protecting the water compacts negotiated by the Blackfeet Nation and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes is a top priority, because both are “headwaters tribes.” He said data center bills expected in the coming session will force lawmakers to weigh impacts on rural and tribal communities, and on water quality.

Weeks-O’Neal said too many of those decisions in Montana have been left to counties, which she said “is just way too much power given to county entities,” and that it was part of why she ran for the Montana House of Representatives.

In northern Nevada, that county power is exactly what Brian Wadsworth just won. Wadsworth lives in Nixon, on the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation, about an hour from Reno. Rush-hour traffic along I-80 by the area’s industrial center was once quite rare, he said. Now, “it’s literally a daily occurrence,” something “that we haven’t seen in our lifetimes.”

Wadsworth told Truthout that voters are fed up with unchecked growth and have been asking cities to examine the area’s economic growth and really grapple with infrastructure issues.

“We definitely have a lack of adequate roads here in Washoe County,” said Wadsworth. Growth has far outpaced infrastructure, and that issue drove all the commissioner candidates in his election. The county’s tech boom is blamed by water experts, residents, and the Pyramid Lake Paiute for negative impacts on public roads and the doubling of home costs from roughly $280,000 in 2015, to an estimated $550,000 in 2026, according to The Nevada Independent.

Wadsworth was also outraised by 5 to 1, drumming up only $27,000. When asked how he won despite being outraised, Wadsworth credits his win to showing up instead. He drove an hour to attend meetings in Gerlach. He also held events in communities where, he said, people told him they’d “never had someone… come out and talk to us.” That’s why, he said, he didn’t have to raise hundreds of thousands of dollars to run a campaign: “It doesn’t take a lot of resources to drive out to a community and talk to people… it takes a lot of time.”

“I think the communities are looking to someone that is going to really listen to the concerns and issues of the county, and not just be pro-development, you know, approving developments at no matter what cost,” he said.

Many of Washoe County’s development concerns hinge on water. “We’re at the terminus endpoint of the Truckee River,” he said, adding that “we’re always concerned about growth and development with the upstream users.”

Pyramid Lake sits downstream of the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center, where data centers are going up alongside Tesla and a Walmart distribution center. “We’re greatly concerned about not only water quantity issues but also water quality issues,” Wadsworth said.

Right now, Wadsworth said, data centers can be built “under the guise of a warehouse,” with no guardrails on water, energy, or land use. He said he would “vehemently oppose” any project that uses excessive water in a region that is “always going to be in a constant state of drought.” For Pyramid Lake, at the end of the Truckee River, that is not at all abstract.

“Jurisdiction lines don’t matter,” Wadsworth said. “You know, the water is going to flow where the water is going to flow.”

In Arizona, Clara Pratte (Diné) made a percussive win, taking a seat on the Arizona Corporation Commission (an independent state regulatory body established by the Arizona Constitution), alongside fellow Democrat Jonathon Hill. Pratte and Hill’s election disrupted the GOP’s stranglehold on what had previously been an all-Republican commission.

“It’s these offices, these down-ballot offices, like planning and zoning, public utilities commissions, corporation commission,” Pratte told Truthout, that “really do play a vital role in how all of those things actually happen or don’t happen.” Her primary priority, she said, is investigating whether ratepayers are subsidizing infrastructure for large energy users like data centers. “Right now, the commission has no credibility with the public,” she told Truthout.

Not every race went that way. “We should not mistake these victories for having closed the representation gap,” Chrissie Castro, executive director of the California Native Vote Project, said in a written statement, noting that there are “communities where Native candidates faced truly significant barriers.”

In Montana, Angeline Cheek (Hunkpapa and Oglala Lakota) lost her bid for the Public Service Commission, 65 to 35 percent. Had she won, Two Bulls said, “it would have been a huge deal,” because utility regulators “make so many decisions that impact everyday folks.”

Shannon Wingfield finished fourth in the June primary for California State Assembly to represent District 68, including conservative-haven Orange County. In a state and year when tech billionaires are pouring more money than ever before into California’s elections, Wingfield felt the paucity in her campaign pocketbook. “It 100 percent would have been money,” she said. The two Democrats, David Penaloza and Jessie Lopez, went on to wage the most expensive legislative contest in California this year, with $5.6 million in spending, according to CalMatters.

Wingfield, who is tribal secretary for the Juaneño Band of Mission Indians, Acjachemen Nation, ran and lost in the state with 109 tribes, the largest number of tribes of any state. She said nearby tribes waited until the general election to back anyone Native, perhaps worried about electability. Wingfield told Truthout that an internal poll of about 7,000 likely voters by her campaign found only 23 percent support for a first Native woman legislator.

At the county level, though, Native candidates in California had a much stronger night.

In a written statement provided to Truthout, Castro noted that Native candidates in California won races including Inyo and Lake County supervisor seats but warned against mistaking these victories “for having closed the representation gap.” And while big decisions about tribal lands and water are often made on the local level, she said, “local representation cannot replace the federal government’s legal and trust responsibilities to tribal nations.”

Two Bulls is generally skeptical about elected officials’ ability — whether at the federal, state, or local level — to deliver for Native communities. “I don’t have a lot of hope as it is,” she said. But she says she has higher expectations of the new Indigenous legislators, saying, “I definitely do hold them more accountable.”

What Two Bulls expects of the new class is simple: Protect “land, air, and water.”

Weeks-O’Neal, meanwhile, frames the stakes in larger terms. Tribal communities, she said, have been stewards of the land for generations, “way beyond just the two terms of an elected official like myself.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $19,000 in the next 24 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: J. David McSwane
title: Trump’s DOJ Is Hiring Inexperienced Attorneys to Fill Purged or Vacated Ranks
content:
“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” said a former federal prosecutor.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.

After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.”

It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.

Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.

Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show.

That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data. But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools.

“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”

To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys.

More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show.

ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”

The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.

Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported, the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience.

While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan.

“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.”

Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said.

“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”

While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”

As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment.

The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades.

Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows.

As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat.

Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. Even in border districts where immigration proceedings can dominate the caseload, prosecutions have risen dramatically. For instance, New Mexico and the Southern District of California saw 300% and 125% increases in immigration cases, respectively, the ProPublica analysis shows. In the Western District of Texas, where Bigley and at least two other recent graduates just became prosecutors, immigration cases have surged at least 36%.

The immigration caseload, including tens of thousands of unlawful-detention cases filed in civil court, has strained the department so severely that the DOJ has drafted hundreds of attorneys from other federal agencies and the military to keep up, former officials said.

Those cases coincided with violent deportation sweeps led by masked immigration agents, who killed U.S. citizens, and the nationwide protests that sprouted up in response. Many of the cases Trump’s DOJ brought against people protesting immigration authorities’ actions fell apart, a ProPublica analysis showed. The news organization also reported how the truthfulness of Trump’s prosecutors has come under question in courts across the country. The DOJ previously said its attorneys “represent the United States with integrity.”

Amid the unrest, ProPublica has tracked nearly 100,000 habeas corpus petitions filed by immigrants arguing that their detentions were unjust. In each case, an assistant U.S. attorney must defend the government’s position, a task that had some U.S. attorneys reassigning veteran lawyers — experts in financial crimes, civil rights and human trafficking — to immigration. In Washington state, an acting U.S. attorney said he’s so overbooked with unlawful-detention petitions, his office cannot handle every case.

In South Florida, where an exodus of veteran lawyers presaged a drop in fraud and financial crime cases, one former white-collar crimes prosecutor said he and his colleagues could not decline an immigration case without permission from U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who abruptly resigned this month. Before his resignation, Quiñones had led the “grand conspiracy” investigation targeting former officials Trump alleged were part of a “deep state” plot against him.

“Every case takes time, and you want to put in effort, and now you’re wasting your time on cases you don’t believe in or think are unjust,” said the former prosecutor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he hopes to return to the Justice Department after Trump leaves office. “It affects morale.”

In recent months, the DOJ has ramped up efforts to recruit lawyers to replace the lost expertise, government data and the department’s recruiting materials show.

While Justice Department personnel data is kept secret, assistant U.S. attorneys are paid on a unique pay scale set by the attorney general, a quirk that dates to the 1950s and distinguishes them from other civil servants. By tracking the number of people compensated this way, it is possible to obtain broad data on the numbers of assistant U.S. attorneys.

As of January 2025, the department employed about 6,200 assistant U.S. attorneys, the data shows. Then Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency took a hatchet to the Justice Department and other federal agencies. Led by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, DOGE offered employees financial packages to resign from the federal government by September 2025. About 1 in 10 of all assistant U.S. attorney departures were part of that offer, the data suggests.

The ranks shrank much faster than the department anticipated, former officials said, and it was unable to hire sufficient replacements. By the end of January 2026, the DOJ lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys and replaced only about 470 of those attorneys.

The DOJ began turning to novice attorneys to fill the empty desks.

In early 2026, a former White House official shared a post on X, the social media platform owned by Musk, that hinted at the DOJ’s growing desperation to find new hires.

“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” wrote Chad Mizelle, who had recently left his DOJ role as chief of staff to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Mizelle did not respond to a request for comment.

In March, the department hit its lowest numbers since 2014. A month later, the University of Miami hosted an event titled “Lunch & Learn: Entry Level Opportunities with The U.S. Attorney’s Office.” The invite, targeted toward third-year law students, promised a new pathway to become a criminal prosecutor in one of the country’s busiest districts.

“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida is now recruiting 3Ls for entry-level positions beginning immediately after graduation — an exciting expansion of opportunities for Miami Law students interested in federal prosecution,” the invitation said.

To lure new hires, the DOJ is offering signing bonuses. As of August, due in part to the hiring spree focused on greener attorneys, the department lifted its ranks to about 5,600, still a 10% drop from the end of the Biden administration.

U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee and the presumed chair once Democrats take charge, told ProPublica that the shift toward inexperience is showing in courtrooms across the country.

“They’ve sacked some of the finest lawyers in America, by tradition, and replaced them with a large group of inexperienced lawyers,” said Raskin, himself an attorney.

In his home state of Maryland, fraud cases fell 31% and drug cases nearly 16%, while immigration charges nearly doubled. “Those numbers are jaw-dropping,” he said.

Jim Fang was among the veteran prosecutors who left.

Fang’s road to becoming a criminal prosecutor was winding. After working in tech for about a decade, he switched careers, and in 2009 graduated from Georgetown Law. He worked in private practice, focusing on intellectual property law, but couldn’t shake a feeling that what he really wanted was “to take down bad guys.”

In April 2020, he got his dream job and was named a federal criminal prosecutor in the District of Nevada. He moved to Las Vegas and, aided by his 11 years handling complex areas of the law, took on tough white-collar crime cases.

After the election, Trump picked Sigal Chattah, a former Republican political candidate, to run the Nevada U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Through court records and sources, ProPublica confirmed that more than 30 staff have left under Chattah’s tenure. The Nevada district is so depleted that for months it didn’t have prosecutors in its Reno office, about 450 miles away. Las Vegas prosecutors were asked to fly there for court appearances, sources said. Chattah disputed the 30 figure but acknowledged that Las Vegas-based staff flew to Reno “to ensure that our federal and local partners had competent and aggressive prosecutors.”

The office dropped cases it had been building as Chattah pushed immigration and politically motivated prosecutions. To ease the caseload, Chattah ordered her civil defense unit, charged with fighting lawsuits demanding cash from taxpayers, to pay out all cases that could be settled for $250,000 or less, multiple sources said. “We were ordered to settle those cases even if they didn’t have merit,” one former assistant U.S. attorney said. “It was just throwing money at a problem.”

Chattah called the allegations that she issued such a directive “patently false” and pushed back on her former employees’ characterizations of her tenure.

“There were attorneys that failed to meet the expectations of competent workmanship with the Department of Justice, and chose to leave or retire, some were terminated,” she wrote. “Former AUSAs who failed to handle an expected case load were replaced with aggressive prosecutors who will keep our state safe.”

In September 2025, Fang took the DOGE offer and went back into private practice as a defense attorney. He suspects the department’s loss of financial crime experts like him will result in fewer successful prosecutions.

“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” Fang said.

Now facing off against his former colleagues, he’s mostly busy representing clients who’ve filed habeas petitions. He was recently surprised to learn that one of the new hires brought into his former office had just passed the bar. “They’re taking a gamble on them,” he said.

Fang says they may well end up being fine attorneys but added, “There’s no way I could have taken that job and done it well right out of law school.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $19,000 in the next 24 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Jesse Hagopian
title: Students Around the World Are Skipping Class to Enter Class Struggle
content:
High school students’ revolts are shaking governments and transforming struggles over education into struggles over society itself.

High school students’ revolts are shaking governments and transforming struggles over education into struggles over society itself.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

“They never listen to us. They never listen to high schoolers. And if we don’t fight, nobody is going to fight for us,” one French high school student emphatically told the BBC at a recent mass youth protest.

Her frustration reflects a familiar political reality: Politicians routinely dismiss young people’s grievances rather than confront the conditions driving their anger. In 2024, the French newspaper Le Monde described a recurring caricature of French youth as “lazy, resistant to authority and even selfish.” In the United States, Fox News host Jesse Watters dismissed complaints about rising costs from “kids” who, he claimed, had “never had real jobs.” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt agreed, declaring, “It’s laziness,” and accusing Gen Z of having grown up with “everything handed to them.”

Writing off young people as entitled and incapable of serious political thought is an old political reflex. Yet while those in power accuse young people of laziness and debate what is wrong with them, youth around the globe are hard at work challenging what is wrong with society and changing the world.

On November 20, students and young people in more than 25 European countries will join a coordinated International Youth and Student Strike under the banner “Fight for Our Future, Not Their Wars,” an action emerging from a much wider wave of youth revolt stretching from Mayotte to Morocco, Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and beyond. The strike call links education and housing to austerity, climate breakdown, and militarization.

These revolts led by high school students show how struggles over schools can become struggles over society — and over who has the power to shape it.

While the mass protests in Paris have drawn international attention, the high school revolt began weeks earlier in France’s overseas territories. Students and teachers started mobilizing on August 31 at Lycée de la Cité du Nord in Mayotte — an island off East Africa that remains under French rule despite decades of UN resolutions recognizing it as part of the independent nation of Comoros. Thérèse Lebeault, a 10th-grade student at Lycée Younoussa Bamana, described the conditions:

There are too many students in the classrooms … There aren’t enough toilets — there are three when we’re nearly 3,000 students. There are no fans in the classrooms, not enough nurses, not enough buses for transportation. There’s also a shortage of teachers, a shortage of classrooms — everything, really … nothing is right.

On September 7, students at Lycée Félix-Éboué in French Guiana presented 17 demands over deteriorating school conditions. As the revolt spread, students in Martinique, Guadeloupe, and Réunion — all former colonies that remain under French rule — joined the wave, exposing how struggles over education are intertwined with colonial inequality.

In metropolitan France, students were confronting many of the same problems. Mohammed, a 17-year-old student in the Paris suburb of Sevran, described classrooms where “there aren’t enough chairs or desks to go around, so some students have to stand up,” and said some students go “months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced.” Fadila, 17, at Lycée Paul Éluard in Saint-Denis, described “cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school,” broken toilets without running water and classrooms reaching 104°F in summer. “We can’t work in those conditions,” she said. In Strasbourg, 17-year-old Raphael described overcrowding, extreme heat, too few toilets, and water leaks: “The building is falling apart.”

These revolts led by high school students show how struggles over schools can become struggles over society — and over who has the power to shape it.

These were not isolated complaints. Across France, students were identifying common grievances and organizing collective demands. The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, France’s main high school student union, pointed to “lack of teachers and staff,” “dilapidated high school buildings,” “overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes,” and “stress caused by Parcoursup,” France’s university admissions system.

These problems were not distributed equally. Students in poorer communities reported greater difficulty getting absent teachers replaced. A fight over missing teachers and leaking ceilings exposed deeper inequalities — raising the question of who gets to decide the conditions of young people’s lives.

In barely two weeks, the uprising had spread across the country. By October 1, more than 1,000 high schools — nearly one in four nationwide — were affected by strikes or protests, including more than 200 blockades. Students piled trash bins, shopping carts, and metal barriers across school entrances; in some cities, barricades burned and clashes erupted with police.

On October 6, the protests spilled far beyond the schools: The Interior Ministry counted 266,000 demonstrators nationwide, while student organizers put the figure at 450,000.

As the uprising spread, the state responded with extraordinary force. Between September 28 and October 5, police made 6,059 arrests, with 5,060 people placed in police custody, 87 percent of them minors. A 15-year-old student in Lens had his hand torn off by a police grenade. A 16-year-old lost the use of one eye, and a 14-year-old suffered a double jaw fracture after being struck at close range by a police grenade launcher. By October 7, France’s police inspectorate had been assigned 18 investigations into allegations of police misconduct.

Teachers and parents mobilized not only in support of the students’ demands, but to protect them. Educators formed human barriers between students and police, marched alongside their pupils, and joined blockades. “I’m here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” Juliette Estiville, a high school Spanish teacher in Paris, told reporters. “The teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”

By October 1, more than 1,000 high schools — nearly one in four nationwide — were affected by strikes or protests, including more than 200 blockades.

Solidarity soon extended far beyond teachers and parents. High school students were marching alongside university students, workers, farmers, and climate activists. By November, a coalition of unions representing millions of workers across education, transportation, public services, and private industry had joined the mobilization.

What began as a fight over missing teachers and deteriorating classrooms has become a broader confrontation over austerity, inequality, and society’s priorities.

The students may not have been in class studying history, but they were learning something about power, repression, and solidarity — and making history of their own.

France is not alone. Across borders, students have begun recognizing their struggles in one another. In Rome, students occupying a high school opened their statement with “like in France.” In Greece, secondary-school students joined university students and teachers demanding better-funded public education, chanting, “From Greece to France, we are fighting for public and free education.”

In Chile, high school students have been central to mass protests against education cuts and austerity. In Germany, more than 45,000 students in over 100 cities, primarily high schoolers, walked out on September 25 against compulsory military service and militarization. In Spain, young people have also been central to mass protests over the housing crisis — including in Valencia where roughly 30,000 teachers, students, and family members marched after a two-week education strike demanding smaller classes, more staff, and better school infrastructure. In the United Kingdom, school students have connected their organizing to the French revolt and are preparing November 20 walkouts as part of the wider international strike. In Argentina, secondary students occupied schools in protest against President Javier Milei’s education cuts. In India, the Cockroach movement grew from university graduates and job seekers to include teenagers furious over exam leaks and a lack of government accountability. Seventeen-year-old Saurav Kushwaha traveled overnight from Madhya Pradesh to join its first major Delhi protest. “I followed them on Instagram for fun,” he told Al Jazeera. “But there is a chance that we can actually get the minister to resign.” Seven weeks later, on July 25, India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned following weeks of youth-led protests. High school students in the United States have likewise moved into struggles beyond the classroom. During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, hundreds of Twin Cities students walked out against ICE and federal immigration enforcement. At Roosevelt High School, Border Patrol agents entered school grounds, detained a staff member, and used chemical weapons on a crowd that included students. Days later, hundreds walked out. “We’re fighting for our neighbors who can’t be out here,” 17-year-old Genevieve Neerland said.

As in France, student resistance soon converged with organized labor. Minneapolis and St. Paul teachers joined other unions in backing a January 23 call for “no work, no school and no shopping,” helping produce an economic shutdown that echoed Minneapolis’s historic 1934 general strike. A week later, students walked out nationwide.

Across these movements, young people begin with what they encounter directly — a teacher shortage, a dilapidated school, a rigged examination, federal agents invading their campus — and begin asking larger questions about who receives resources, whose communities are targeted, and who gets to decide their future. They earn an advanced degree in social studies when repression teaches them that the state is not simply a neutral referee, but an apparatus of power organized to defend the existing social order and its hierarchies.

One slogan from Italian high school protests distilled that widening analysis: “Money for schools, not for war.” In France, the defense budget rose from roughly €32 billion in 2017 to €57 billion in 2026, an increase of 77 percent. In the United States, Congress appropriated roughly $839 billion for the Pentagon in fiscal year 2026.

Those priorities become especially stark in the context of the genocide in Gaza. France has continued authorizing military exports to Israel, while the United States provided Israel approximately $21.7 billion in military aid during the first two years after October 7, 2023, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project. By June 2024 alone, the United States had sent Israel at least 14,000 2,000-pound bombs, 6,500 500-pound bombs, and thousands of other munitions. By April 2026, UNICEF reported that nearly 98 percent of Gaza’s school buildings had been damaged, with around 81 percent struck directly during Israel’s military assault.

That helps explain why Palestinian flags and keffiyehs have appeared throughout youth demonstrations. Organizers of the November 20 International Youth and Student Strike explicitly link austerity to militarization and war. Their manifesto declares: “Our future will not be given to us.”

France has seen these contradictions erupt into rebellion before. In the months leading up to May 1968, French high school students organized Comités d’action lycéens, or High School Action Committees, challenging authoritarian school structures, educational selection, and the Vietnam War. During the May uprising, students occupied schools and organized discussions about exams, school governance, the Vietnam War, and workers’ struggles. May 1968 is often remembered as a revolt of university students and workers, but high school students helped push educational struggles toward larger questions about power and society.

That pattern extends around the world. High school students helped initiate South Korea’s 1960 April Revolution, which grew into a nationwide uprising that toppled U.S.-backed dictator Syngman Rhee on April 26, ending his 12-year authoritarian rule; Black secondary students in the Soweto uprising challenged apartheid education in 1976, sparking nationwide resistance that helped reinvigorate the anti-apartheid movement; and Chilean high school students occupied schools during the 2006 “Penguin Revolution,” forcing increased education funding and reforms to the market-driven school system inherited from Pinochet’s dictatorship. The United States has its own deep history of high school revolt. In 1951, 16-year-old Barbara Johns organized a walkout against segregated and dilapidated conditions at her Virginia high school; the resulting lawsuit became part of Brown v. Board of Education. Jon N. Hale, a historian of student movements, told me that Johns showed young people were prepared “not only to join but lead and inspire elders in the movement.”

During the 1960s, young people helped propel the Civil Rights, Chicano, and antiwar movements. Thousands joined Birmingham’s Children’s Crusade; about 15,000 Mexican American students participated in the 1968 East Los Angeles walkouts; and historian Aaron G. Fountain Jr. told me that the late 1960s and early 1970s saw “over a thousand Black or Latino student uprisings.” In Des Moines, 13-year-old Mary Beth Tinker’s Vietnam War protest produced the landmark Tinker decision protecting student speech. Looking back, Tinker told me, “It was so clear to us that it was all connected, the anti-war and peace movement, and the fight for civil rights.” But student movements have rarely developed entirely in isolation. In another interview, historian Jarvis Givens described teachers as “essential to the shaping of the political imaginations of the people we often hold up.” He pointed to Martin Luther King Jr.’s high school English teacher, Sarah Grace Bradley, who helped the 15-year-old King develop a Black history speech and accompanied him to an oratorical competition.

Teachers do not manufacture movements; students already know when their classroom is overcrowded, their teacher is missing, or their building is falling apart. But learning history can reveal that inequality is neither natural nor inevitable. When young people learn how injustice has been created, resisted, and transformed, they can see that the world they inherited was made by people — and can be remade by them.

That helps explain why battles over history have become so fierce. UCLA researchers found that nearly half of public high school principals reported attempts to limit teaching about race and racism during the 2021-2022 school year, while the American Library Association reported 4,235 unique titles challenged for censorship in 2025.

These fights are not only about which facts students encounter. They are also about what students can imagine. A student who learns about Barbara Johns, East LA, or Soweto learns something larger: People their age have changed history before.

That knowledge changes what seems possible.

Historian Aaron Fountain, author of High School Students Unite!, told me that high school students constitute an oppressed group and that “you cannot truly reform society unless you first reform the high schools.”

From confronting segregation and apartheid to overthrowing dictatorships, they have demonstrated that the struggle to transform schools can become a struggle to transform society itself. High school students may begin by protesting dress codes, demanding repairs to crumbling school buildings, or fighting for the right to protest at school at all. But these struggles and their collective victories can grow into larger movements against segregation and apartheid — and even bring down dictatorships.

Time and again, when high school students go into struggle, they draw much of society with them. Part of the reason lies in the contradictions built into education itself.

Capitalist societies need schools to produce workers who can read, calculate, communicate, and think. Yet teaching youth those skills can be a risky gambit. It is difficult to teach history without inviting students to identify with people who rebelled, or to teach how to analyze a text or an argument while guaranteeing they will never use their power of analysis to question the institutions around them.

James Baldwin captured the contradiction of schooling in his 1963 “Talk To Teachers” — that “as one begins to become conscious one begins to examine the society in which he is being educated.”

On November 20, students will skip class — and teach the rest of us how history gets made.

Another contradiction built into capitalist schooling is that schools often train students to understand success as an individual competition — for grades, test scores, college admission, and eventually jobs. Yet schools also bring many young people together every day, creating opportunities for students to recognize that what appears to be an individual problem is actually collective, opening the door to collaboration and solidarity. Teachers — beset by the same conditions of underfunding and austerity — have also often developed a political consciousness through their experience, aid young people in investigating those contradictions, supporting them when they organize, and helping them ask critical questions about society that can connect their immediate experiences to the larger structures shaping their lives. As one French teacher put it in an interview with BT during a mass protest, the revolt is “still about high schools and students and young people and French youth. But it’s also about, basically, capitalism.”

Struggle then becomes another kind of education. Rayyan Seriket of the Fédération Syndicale Étudiante told Democracy Now! that the protests grew beyond high school students because they raised “the whole question not only of our living conditions, but also of who we are governed by and what interests they have.”

Once students begin asking those questions, they rarely stay confined to the schoolhouse. Parents, teachers, and workers can recognize their own struggles in the students’ demands. That is why struggles over education so often become struggles over society itself.

And they become more powerful when they cross borders. One slogan from the French protests captured that horizon: “Capitalism exploits us / The far right divides us / Anger brings us together.”

That is why November 20 matters. The planned international student strike represents an opportunity to turn scattered struggles over education, inequality, and war into a coordinated movement that challenges the systems producing these crises.

On November 20, students will skip class — and teach the rest of us how history gets made.

title: Ecuadorian Fishermen Sue US Over Boat Strike, Alleged Subsequent Torture

The group had previously announced their intention to sue the administration, and formally filed their lawsuit on Monday.

While the U.S. has acknowledged several boat strikes on the South American coasts (ostensibly targeting so-called “narcoterrorists”), the administration has not claimed responsibility for this specific attack. All fishermen aboard the boat survived the strike, but many reported experiencing serious injuries. They faced additional injuries after the strike, both physical and legal, they said.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: 7 Members-Elect Vote Against Jeffries for Speaker, Citing Medicare for All, Gaza
content:
The members said that their “constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate” on progressive issues.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A group of seven Democratic House representatives-elect cited a voter mandate for action on Gaza and Medicare for All in their opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries after the caucus selected him for speaker-elect on Wednesday, marking a break from the leader even as the vast majority of other Democrats voted “yes.”

On Wednesday morning, Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Jeffries for speaker in the new Congress in January, in a 251 to 11 yes or no vote, with two absences. The vote was done in a closed-door meeting, with a secret ballot, though Jeffries did call for a recorded vote rather than a simple voice vote. If elected on the House floor in January, he will become the first Black person to ever be the speaker of the House.

Several members spoke in favor of Jeffries ahead of the vote, reports say, including Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández (D-New Mexico) and Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), and Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D-Wisconsin). He was also nominated by Representatives Derek Tran (D-California) and Mark Pocan (D-Wisconsin).

Current Democratic Whip Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) was elected as majority leader, the number two position in the caucus. Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-California) was elected as majority whip, and Rep. Ted Lieu (D-California) was chosen as caucus chairman, the third and fourth positions, respectively.

Among the dissenters to Jeffries were seven representatives-elect who said that they are still not assured that Jeffries and his leadership team would help them deliver on key progressive issues.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote in a joint statement released after the vote.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” they continued.

The statement was signed by Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-New York), Adam Hamawy (D-New Jersey), Frederick Haynes (D-Texas), Melat Kiros (D-Colorado), Donavan McKinney (D-Michigan), Chris Rabb (D-Pennsylvania), and Claire Valdez (D-New York). Haynes, who is replacing Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), said that he narrowly missed the vote after waking up with an illness, but intended to vote no.

Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-California) also released a statement explaining her “no” vote, citing a need for leaders to advocate for affordable housing, Medicare for All, the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and accountability for “the corrupt elite.”

“Since day one, I have been telling leadership that Angelenos have not been satisfied with the status quo and are demanding transformative change. I voted NO today, keeping my community and the trust they instilled in me in mind,” she wrote.

The statements stop short of a full rebuke of Jeffries and his leadership style, but acknowledge many of progressives’ criticisms of the centrist lawmaker, like his vehemently pro-Israel stances and soft hand toward ICE.

Other progressives voted “yes” on Jeffries, however, including figures like Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), according to Axios.

In a social media post after the vote, Omar did not acknowledge the ballot, but called for progressive priorities to be passed. She listed a set of policies that Democrats passed with their recent trifecta in Minnesota, including universal school meals, paid sick leave, and legal marijuana.

“That’s how you use a majority,” she said. “Now it’s Congress’s turn.”

title: Mary Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Race Despite Trump’s Efforts to Halt Count
content:

Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has been declared the winner of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, following weeks of ballot counting since Election Day, which President Donald Trump had sought to derail.

The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday night, determining that, with 99 percent of the ballots counted, Peltola had secured around 50.1 percent of the vote. title: Jeffries, Who’s Pledged to End Trump’s War on Iran, Says “No” on Defunding It
content:
Jeffries instead advocated for a war powers resolution that Trump would likely completely ignore.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Despite his numerous pledges to work “aggressively” to end the war on Iran, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) suggested this week that he opposes efforts to defund the war, as some progressives and moderate Democrats have called for.

A small but vocal group of Senate and House Democrats have said that they wish to move to end the Iran war immediately, starting with barring funding for war efforts in the government funding package due by December 11. This, experts have said, is one of the strongest tools that Democrats have at their disposal to end the war; in fact, they say, it may be the only way to force the lawless Trump administration to withdraw troops.

On Tuesday, Jeffries said he’s a “no” for that effort.

In an interview at The Atlantic Summit, Jeffries said that Democrats must “move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran right out of the gate” when they take the majority in January, dismissing by omission the chance to act before then, despite Democrats’ leverage to do so.

Jeffries criticized President Donald Trump’s conduct of the war, saying that there is “no plan” or “strategy” for the war, and that Democrats must “aggressively” pass a war powers resolution. That would “take the fight around ending the war to the Oval Office,” Jeffries said.

“What does ending the war mean? Not funding their operations in the Gulf?” asked interviewer Jeffrey Goldberg, editor-in-chief of The Atlantic.

“Well, no,” said Jeffries. “It means a cessation of hostilities…. So that’s what a war powers resolution is able to do, right?”

When asked what the strategy is if Trump vetoes the resolution, Jeffries simply said that his plan is to make it so that vetoing such a resolution — or a bill to reenter the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — would be embarrassing for Trump.

Jeffries, who House Democrats elected to lead the caucus as speaker in the new Congress on Wednesday, did not once acknowledge that Iran also has a major say in ending the war, despite Goldberg asking him about Iran’s role multiple times.

Indeed, for months, Iranian leaders have been consistently asking that the U.S. follow the memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran struck in June. That agreement, which Trump unilaterally broke, stipulated an end to the U.S.’s strikes, naval blockade, and sanctions, in exchange for Iran ending its retaliatory strikes, renewing its pledge to not develop nuclear weapons, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Jeffries also did not acknowledge that the Trump administration, which experts say has already broken numerous laws to wage this war, is likely to completely ignore any stipulations on the war placed by a war powers resolution.

The presumptive speaker-elect also suggested on Tuesday that he’ll help grant funding for the war through year’s end.

According to Punchbowl, Jeffries said that he’s in “active conversation” with congressional leaders “to arrive at either a government funding agreement in advance of Dec. 11 that meets the needs of the American people in terms of their health, their safety, their national security, and their economic well-being, or we have to move toward a continuing resolution of funding that would put us into some point next year with Democrats holding the gavels in both the House and the Senate.”

The statement suggests that he isn’t in favor of efforts by figures like Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) to use the December funding deadline to defund the war.

The remarks are an about-face from Jeffries. For months, he has pledged to work to end Trump’s Iran war. In a press conference last Thursday, he even acknowledged that Democrats are opposed to funding it.

“House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine, to Pete Hegseth’s war machine over in the Middle East,” he said.

At the same time, however, he is not endorsing any of the legislative efforts to actually force an end to the war, only advocating for efforts to will that outcome into existence through an abstract pressure campaign.

“Jeffries’ Iran position is Trump needs to ‘end the war’ but he absolutely cannot do so without Iran agreeing to humiliating terms, zero war reparations and no security guarantees,” said media analyst Adam Johnson on social media. “Top Dems continue to ostensibly demand an end to the war but are conspicuously vague on acceptable terms.”

author: Stephen Prager
title: Thousands of Palestinians Flee Israel’s New Assault Past Gaza’s “Yellow Line”
content:
Defense Minister Israel Katz called for “turning these areas into permanent parts of Israel’s security zones.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Thousands of Palestinians have been forced to flee for their lives after Israeli forces launched a new ground assault on central Gaza on Wednesday, advancing past the so-called “yellow line” despite last year’s ceasefire agreement.

Since the agreement was signed last October, Israel has gradually expanded its control over Gaza in violation of the deal’s terms and killed over 1,600 Palestinians in near-daily strikes. Its surprise attack on Wednesday, which saw tanks rolling into areas near the Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps beyond the ceasefire line, is its first ground incursion into this area since the agreement went into effect.

At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across central Gaza, according to medical officials. Meanwhile, Middle East Eye reported that at least two people were wounded by “indiscriminate fire” near the Nuseirat refugee camp as scores of residents fled the area.

🚨 BREAKING: Palestinian families are once again fleeing their displacement shelters in northern Nuseirat central Gaza Strip after the Israeli army threatened to launch a military operation in the area. Scenes reminiscent of the first days of the war are repeating themselves in… https://t.co/2YGuWXaVIK pic.twitter.com/SbpuYVCyBU

The Israeli army said it was targeting “terrorist infrastructure” in residential areas where many Palestinian families and displaced residents live. In a message posted on social media after the assault had already begun, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories told residents to “stay away from the area where our forces are operating” until further updates were given.

In a statement Wednesday, Gaza’s Ministry of Social Development warned that the assault posed a “direct threat to the lives of tens of thousands of displaced people, forcibly driving them toward new waves of displacement.” It added that the “continuation of military operations in the vicinity of populated areas and shelters” was “a grave violation of international humanitarian law and a direct threat to the social protection system.”

The Palestinian militant group Hamas decried the new assault as “a serious development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement,” adding that “forced evacuation orders and the displacement of thousands of residents from their areas under threat and bombardment constitute a new crime against civilians and a blatant violation of international humanitarian law.”

BREAKING | Israeli military announces new assault on central Gaza in continued violation of 'ceasefire' agreement The Israeli military announced an operation near Salah al-Din Street, northwest of Bureij refugee camp and northeast of Nuseirat refugee camp, around the so-called… pic.twitter.com/a7zAV14IRh

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz indicated on Wednesday that the military intended to maintain its territorial control in Gaza, saying that in the event of further escalation, it was prepared to “maneuver and seize additional territory, while evacuating residents and destroying terrorist infrastructure on the ground, turning these areas into permanent parts of Israel’s security zones in the north and south.”

Katz said this policy was supported by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in May directed the military to seize at least 70% of Gaza, up from the 53% it was supposed to control temporarily under the original ceasefire agreement.

Despite the ceasefire’s requirement that Israel eventually hand territorial control back to Palestinians, Netanyahu said in September that Israel was “not withdrawing” from the territory it controls. He said Israel controlled 60% of Gaza and that “there is still more to come.”

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for Israel to fully annex territory “at least as far as the yellow line in Gaza,” rather than merely maintain it as a military buffer zone. He has also advocated repopulating the exclave with Israeli settlers.

Wednesday’s assault followed several other attacks over the past week, including some on civilian areas, which killed at least 37 Palestinians. Those attacks included an attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis on November 12, which killed six people, including a surgeon.

On Tuesday, Israeli forces killed at least four Palestinians, including 6-year-old Eyas Ahmed al-Namnam, who was shot near his displaced family’s tent east of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza.

Another child, 11-year-old Mansour Khader Nabhan, died Wednesday at al-Shifa Hospital after being critically injured when an Israeli drone dropped an explosive on civilians in Bir al-Naaja, west of Jabalia, in northern Gaza.

Israel kills 11-year-old Palestinian student in drone attack on northern Gaza —— The Palestinian Ministry of Education has mourned 11-year-old Mansour Khader Nabhan, a fifth-grade student at Abu Ubaida ibn al-Jarrah School in the North Gaza Education Directorate, who died of… pic.twitter.com/cnYddN62o4

In a report to the United Nations Security Council, the Gaza Board of Peace, created by U.S. President Donald Trump, criticized Israel’s continued attacks and restrictions on critical aid needed for recovery from devastating floods and warned that Israel’s actions were causing the ceasefire to collapse.

“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the board said. “Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts.”

“A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy, and no enabling environment to rebuild.”

As the world commemorated three years since the start of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to official estimates, 100 humanitarian organizations warned last month that Israel’s continued attacks, restrictions on humanitarian aid, and advances deeper into Gaza had become normalized despite last year’s ceasefire agreement.

“A ceasefire is meaningless if children are still being killed and families are still unable to rebuild their lives,” said Inger Ashing, the CEO of Save the Children. “Since the ceasefire was announced, nearly one child has been killed every day.”

Sarah Sanbar, the acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch, said, “The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story.”

“There is nothing normal,” she added, “about living in a tent under bombardment, without enough food or drinking water for your family.”
