author: Amy Goodman
title: Climate Finance Pledges at COP31 Amount to Mere “Pennies,” Policy Expert Says
content:
“The fossil fuel lobbyists are rampant in the halls,” says Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

As Democracy Now! continues broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, we speak with Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, about climate finance — the notion that efforts to mitigate the climate crisis must be funded. “Climate finance is not an abstract thing. It’s what countries need to be able to transition away from fossil fuels,” says Cleetus. “And right now we have pennies in these funds.” She notes that at a pledging event for the Adaptation Fund, which supports climate finance for developing countries, a mere $50 million was pledged. “It’s shameful, absolutely unjust, what’s happening here. And richer countries are continuing to block progress.” This comes as scientists say the world is set to overshoot the target, set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, of limiting global heating to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

As the climate negotiations here in Antalya, Turkey, enter their last days, we’re joined now by Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Can you talk about what’s happened and what hasn’t happened, and particularly talk about — again, it’s a buzzword — but the 1.5 degrees Celsius overshoot, what exactly that means, and why you are so concerned, representing the Union of Concerned Scientists?

RACHEL CLEETUS: Amy, so, we came into this COP with some really sobering science that had been shared, which is that the world now inevitably is going to breach 1.5 C of global warming, that treasured guardrail that we had secured in the Paris Agreement. And it —

AMY GOODMAN: And 1.5 degrees Celsius is 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit.

AMY GOODMAN: And it’s hard for people to imagine. We’re talking about a degree. Why could that matter so much to the world?

RACHEL CLEETUS: Well, the crucial thing is to understand that this is a global average. And actually, in many places in the world, including in parts of the United States, it’s heating up much faster than that. And that small fraction, that’s causing massive ice sheets and glaciers to melt, like we saw the horrific tragedy in Nepal. It’s causing oceans to boil. We’re seeing these intensified hurricanes, extreme flooding, droughts, catastrophic wildfires, like we saw in the United States and around the world, and these extreme, deadly heat waves that have taken tens of thousands of lives just this year. That’s what that 1.5 C breaching means.

And we came into this COP with scientists saying, “This is where we are, but we still have a narrow window. We need to act. The choices we make now are crucial.” And we didn’t get here by accident. We got here because of burning fossil fuels. We got here because policymakers, including world leaders in halls like this, have just not acted with urgency. And the fossil fuel industry has been just blocking progress, spreading disinformation about science.

AMY GOODMAN: Why do they even get to be here?

RACHEL CLEETUS: That’s the extraordinary thing.

AMY GOODMAN: It’s like a conference on tobacco and cancer, and the cigarette industry is as much as half of the people represented.

RACHEL CLEETUS: It’s extraordinary. The fossil fuel lobbyists are rampant in the halls here, and their sole task here is just to block progress. And it’s not just them; it’s also petrostates like Saudi Arabia that’s in rooms right now blocking the best available IPCC science from being available for the next global stocktake of the Paris Agreement. So, fossil fuels, they’re the core cause of climate change, and they’re also — the fossil fuel lobbyists are the core obstructors of progress.

AMY GOODMAN: The biggest issue we’re hearing again and again is climate finance, meaning how do the countries least responsible for climate change deal, whether we’re talking about long-term adaptation or the crises countries face, like Nepal.

RACHEL CLEETUS: Yeah, what we’re seeing is such a collision of both the climate crisis, the inflation that’s been set off by this illegal war against Iran, the debt crisis that countries are spiraling and suffering from. And it’s rich major polluters that are most responsible for the emissions that are causing climate change. They made a commitment. They have an obligation. They have a responsibility to pay up that climate finance. This is not aid or charity. This is living up to their responsibility, which they’re still continuing to fall short of. The EU right now is trying to block any progress on climate finance. Even as it’s paying lip service and hypocritically saying it upholds climate science, it’s acting in direct opposition to what that science shows is necessary.

Climate finance is not an abstract thing. It’s what countries need to be able to transition away from fossil fuels, to adapt to these fearsome climate impacts that are unfolding, and the loss and damage, that scale of devastation and suffering that’s beyond even ordinary adaptation. And right now we have pennies in these funds. Yesterday, there was a pledging event for the Adaptation Fund: $50 million. It’s shameful, absolutely unjust, what’s happening here. And richer countries are continuing to block progress.

AMY GOODMAN: And what about the U.S. not being here? You talk about Saudi Arabia being here and blocking progress, but the U.S. isn’t here at all.

RACHEL CLEETUS: Yeah, the Trump administration has pulled out of the Paris Agreement, the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, that bedrock treaty. But you know what? It’s a good thing they’re not here. They would only cause disruption and destruction, as they have back home with clean energy.

What we did have was subnational climate leaders from states, from local jurisdictions. There was a congressional delegation here saying, “We’re still in.” There is another face to the United States. There are a lot of people who care deeply, because they understand that this is a shared challenge. No one country can solve it on its own. We’re seeing terrible impacts in the United States, too. And we see the opportunities for clean renewable energy to provide economic benefits.

AMY GOODMAN: I just want to say, nuclear weapons is supposedly on top of this historic trilateral meeting of President Xi of China, President Trump and Vladimir Putin of Russia. Also, just talking here about the increasing discussion about nuclear power as being a renewable alternative, your response?

RACHEL CLEETUS: Well, we know what’s cheap, what’s reliable, what’s quickly available out there, and that is renewable energy: solar-plus-storage, wind. This is what is picking up the pace around the world. Even now in these dark times, we’re seeing a huge surge. Meanwhile, nuclear is so expensive, very risky, has never lived up to the promise. So, if we’re serious about solving the climate challenge, this is about a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to thank you, Rachel Cleetus. Your final message, as we come out of this conference in the next few days, of what you feel needs to be done?

RACHEL CLEETUS: Well, I think negotiators here have to act in light of the science, the latest science. And they have to do it in an equitable way, because, as I mentioned, it’s rich polluting countries that have an obligation here.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, as you talk about rich polluting countries, we’re going to turn to Brandon Wu of ActionAid. Rachel Cleetus, I want to thank you so much for being with us, climate —

AMY GOODMAN: — program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Earlier today, Brandon Wu of ActionAid USA addressed a “Polluters Must Pay” protest. He starts off by talking about the Loss and Damage Fund, established years ago in order to assist countries to recover after climate disasters like Nepal earlier this year, with a mountain glacier collapsing and killing thousands.

BRANDON WU: Now, Nepal came with a request for the Loss and Damage Fund a few months ago, saying, “Hey, you might have heard there were some floods. We need support.” The fund said, “We express our solidarity for you.” And then the board had an extraordinary meeting, a Zoom meeting, where they decided to set aside $20 million. Peanuts!

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, Brandon Wu of ActionAid USA addressed this “Polluters Must Pay” protest.

author: Chris Walker
title: The IRS Has Launched at Least 4 Criminal Probes Into Left-Wing Groups
content:
The investigations by the IRS follow a directive given by President Donald Trump after the killing of Charlie Kirk.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A newly unearthed memo from within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) details how the agency has initiated at least four criminal probes into left-wing organizations, as part of a crackdown directed by President Donald Trump in an executive order last year.

The memo, obtained by The New York Times, doesn’t include which groups have been investigated, nor does it specify how long the inquiries have gone on or why they were launched. But it delivers a clear sign that the president’s order has been followed, and that questionable inquiries into progressive organizations have taken place.

The memo showcases how the IRS has been involved in such investigations, detailing how it has worked with the FBI in rapid-response events. It lays out how the two agencies have cooperated with each other in investigating demonstrations outside Delaney Hall, an immigration jail in Newark, New Jersey.

The memo shows that IRS officials reviewed the financial information of protesters outside the jail, including their Venmo records. The agency also reviewed a number of organizations that the administration believed were funding the demonstrations.

The memo indicated that facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases were used to help identify some of the demonstrators at Delaney Hall.

The directive that paved the way for the IRS to launch such investigations into left-wing groups was part of Trump’s so-called “domestic terror” memo, which he signed in September 2025. In that document, the administration described “antifa” as a terrorist organization, but provided ambiguous definitions for what qualified a person as a member of that movement.

For example, “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity,” as well as “extremism on migration, race, and gender,” were all identified as hallmark beliefs animating “antifa.” But definitions for those terms were not included in the document, left to the discretion of the agencies Trump was directing his order to.

The order also identified hostility “towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality” as beliefs animating “antifa” — but again, the directive failed to define those terms.

Trump’s executive order required the IRS to determine whether nonprofit groups were “directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism,” and in March 2026, the task force began working directly with the FBI to achieve those goals.

The memo from the IRS also complains about how the task force’s work has been limited due to organizational restraints, and recommends that the agency be given broader abilities to focus on its investigations.

At the time it was signed, shortly after the killing of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, critics derided Trump’s executive order for being issued without any legal basis, as federal statutes do not allow presidents to define what groups may be “domestic terrorists.”

“You can’t, by executive order, create new crimes,” explained Daniel Richman, professor at Columbia Law School and former federal prosecutor, responding to the directive.

The order only focused on left-wing movements, ignoring right-wing violence that has been widely documented in recent years.

“The President is invoking political violence, which we all condemn, as an excuse to target non-profits and activists with the false and stigmatizing label of ‘domestic terrorism.’ This is a shameful and dangerous move,” said Hina Shamsi, director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s (ACLU) National Security Project, following Trump’s signing of the order, adding that Trump “cannot rewrite the Constitution by memo.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: As Congress Debates Ending Iran War, Trump Sends a Third Aircraft Carrier
content:
CENTCOM announced on Tuesday that it had carried out more strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A third U.S. aircraft carrier with thousands of U.S. troops has arrived in the Middle East to support the Iran war, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Monday, adding to the U.S.’s arsenal in the area as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for escalating the war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the area on Sunday, joining two other aircraft carriers, each with roughly 5,000 soldiers and dozens of fighter jets aboard, and about 20 other warships.

The carrier’s arrival comes as the U.S. continues its war on Iran with a naval blockade of Iranian ports, a sanctions campaign, and strikes. Reuters reported that the U.S. carried out a new round of airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday. Iran began firing back on U.S. assets in the region in recent days after reports found earlier this month that the U.S. has been secretly attacking Qeshm for weeks, despite President Donald Trump saying at the time that “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

Since then, Trump has said that the war is “militarily effectively over” and that he’s aiming to maintain “the status quo.” The status quo does still include U.S. military activity, and analysts have warned that inaction by Congress to force a withdrawal is stretching the conflict into a forever war.

Further, the arrival of the new aircraft carrier, which left its base in San Diego in September, gives Trump access to a massive amount of military might in the region that he could use at any time.

Reuters reported on Sunday that Trump has been telling allies that he may hold off on attacks if the U.S. doesn’t face new attacks from Iran or Houthi, or Ansar Allah, militants in Yemen. In public comments, he has indeed preferred to say that the war is winding down or is over.

However, Reuters, citing current and former U.S. officials, also noted that “Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear ‌to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict.”

Trump has reportedly been calling around to regional allies, like Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip ​Erdogan, apparently telling bin Salman in October that he was planning to resume intense attacks after the midterm elections. Both allies apparently asked him not to intensify strikes again.

Though the temperamental commander-in-chief may conduct a devastating campaign in Iran any time, Democrats in Congress who have pledged to end the war are dragging their feet on actually doing so. Though some progressives and Democrats have said that they plan to try to force a defunding of the war through the next government spending package, which is due December 11, others have said that they don’t want to risk a shutdown in order to end the war that killed roughly 3,500 Iranians as of July.

At the same time, lengthy deployments for U.S. soldiers on the aircraft carriers in the Middle East are overstretching the Navy, as reports have found that sailors have faced extreme hardship while on board, including a lack of food and a spike in suicidal ideation and attempts.

However, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao downplayed these concerns during his Senate confirmation hearing on Tuesday. Cao said that sailors who reported losing weight while deployed were just picky, “like my kids.” He said that the reported eight suicide attempts from the USS Abraham Lincoln earlier this year were not suicide attempts, but “eight suicide mitigations.”

Cao also displayed a complete disregard for basic facts about the costs of the war. Cao said he doesn’t know what the U.S.’s naval blockade on Iranian ports is costing daily in another line of questioning, and that Pentagon inspectors have still yet to fully assess damage to naval bases in the Middle East that were struck by Iran earlier in the war.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: CNN, NYT Push Dubious Reports on Iran That Critics Liken to Iraq WMD Lies
content:
The reports seem to manufacture consent for Trump to escalate strikes on Iran and its water infrastructure.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Major corporate media outlets pushed multiple stories on Monday seemingly aimed at manufacturing consent for the U.S. to intensify strikes on Iran and target civilian infrastructure while doing so — reports that were likened by critics to the media’s pro-war propaganda blitz when the U.S. invaded Iraq in the early aughts.

The New York Times published a story that framed dams in Iran as a mysterious “riddle,” with the country having built the “puzzling” water infrastructure for no apparent reason. Dams are used for many reasons — agriculture, manufacturing, energy, flood management, recreation, and to provide populations with water — but the Times, with a heavy hand, suggested that Iran’s dams are used for military purposes.

“Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?” the Times quoted one Iranian German academic as saying, noting that the U.S. and Israel have carried out many airstrikes near dams during the war. The reporting echoed similar articles in Israeli publications.

The Times even noted Iran’s historic, decades-long water crisis, and observed that dams in Iran often serve civilian purposes; one U.S. strike in July hit a hay storage shed for wild sheep, an environmentalist told the Times. However, the report treats recent arrests of environmentalists in the country as another reason for suspicion, though environmentalists and climate activists are commonly criminalized across the world.

Media critics and opponents of the war expressed anger at the Times report online, saying that it was published to justify the U.S. carrying out strikes on Iran’s water infrastructure — which could lead to disastrous results for the already ailing civilian population.

“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality. Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles!” wrote Kaveh Madani, former Iranian environmental official and director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment, and Health. “This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure.”

Critics had similarly harsh words for CNN after it published a report on Monday evening with an even more provocative claim. CNN asserted, citing U.S. officials, that intelligence sources have supposedly found that Iran is developing plans to use a chemical weapon or radiological device — a “dirty bomb,” as CNN deems it — in Washington, D.C.

The outlet said it’s unclear whether or not Iran would follow through with the supposed plan. Still, it claimed that the Iranian government could use people already inside the U.S. to smuggle bomb materials into the capital, not just drumming up support for preemptive “defensive” strikes on Iran, but also potentially endangering people in the U.S. who the Trump administration may “suspect” are smuggling such weapons.

The Trump administration, accordingly, drummed up bloodthirsty sentiment in response to the report. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that it would “cause an all-out war” if Iran attacked D.C., suggesting that the U.S.-Israeli war that has killed roughly 3,500 people in Iran as of June, damaged thousands of civilian sites, and reportedly wiped out all of Iran’s senior leadership has not already amounted to “all-out war.”

President Donald Trump once again struck a genocidal tone when asked about the report on Tuesday, saying that, if Iran even threatens to attack D.C., “they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before.”

Jake Tapper, who has long been criticized for cheering U.S. and Israeli assaults, featured the report on his evening program.

The report was met with immediate skepticism from critics of the war, however. Critics likened it to the media coverage in the months and years leading up to the U.S.’s invasion of Iraq, when major news outlets breathlessly parroted lies about Saddam Hussein’s “weapons of mass destruction.” The parallels run deep: In December 2002, just months before the invasion, CNN even reported on an intelligence report that suggested that Iraq had a “dirty bomb.”

Middle East expert Trita Parsi posted a side-by-side comparison on social media of the coverage of the two wars. In the first clip, Bush administration Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice told CNN, in September 2002, that military action would be necessary because there would “always be uncertainty” that Hussein could get a nuclear weapon, and that “we don’t want the smoking gun to be a mushroom cloud.”

In the second, Tapper interviewed one of the reporters on Monday’s CNN report, also saying that Iran is undertaking a “planning effort” for a “dirty bomb” attack on D.C. The reporter, Katie Bo Lillis, said that “it’s not an indicator — at least right now — of an imminent attack.”

Parsi pointed out that the report makes no mention of the fact that it comes just days after Israel’s propaganda chief visited the U.S. to speak with Trump administration officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, to discuss the war, which Israeli officials have been pushing the U.S. to intensify.

Even the typically warhawkish Times had cast doubt on Iran’s supposed plans to use a chemical weapon against the U.S. and its allies earlier this month. On November 3, the Times published a report saying that such allegations originated from Israeli intelligence sources, noting that it was “met with alarm by some American officials and deep skepticism by others.” It also noted that Iran has denied having chemical weapons.

Indeed, Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, called the reports “rubbish” in a post on X, similarly likening them to the media’s coverage in the buildup to the Iraq War.

“In the past 72 hours, pro-Israel media have ‘reported’ that Iran is supposedly plotting to use chemical weapons in DC while building missile bases under dams,” Araghchi wrote. “Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it. Nobody is buying it.”

Even if the reports were true, Middle East analyst Sina Toossi said, such a plan would be well within the realm of typical planning amid a war — but such information should be treated with far more care.

“[A]t this particularly dangerous juncture in the war, leaking and presenting uncertain intelligence in such alarming terms is fueling unwarranted fear and even hysteria in Washington and beyond,” Toossi said. “I also worry about the possibility that this was a strategic leak intended to build public support for continuing or escalating the war with Iran.”

Apparently not satisfied with just one pro-war report, CNN — which was recently acquired by the vehemently pro-Israel Ellison family — also aired a feature by Fareed Zakaria, sensationally entitled “Iran and the Bomb.” Zakaria said the report examined why “Iran has pursued a nuclear weapon despite decades of sanctions, security threats, and now war,” despite mountains of evidence that Iran has done no such thing.

The warmongering comes as the U.S. has already been striking Iran for weeks, despite media reports that the war is in a quiet period. It also comes as Democrats are poised to take control of Congress in January, potentially pushing the U.S. one step closer to finally ending the war on Iran.

author: Mike Ludwig
title: ICE Cancels Deportation Flights for Afghan War Refugees But Continues to Jail Them
content:
Around 8,000 Afghans are at risk of being deported by the Trump administration back to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Attorneys for an Afghan physician and refugee going by the pseudonym Ahmad say he worked as a doctor in support of United States and NATO forces during the U.S.-led war on Afghanistan. Facing persecution from the Taliban after the U.S. withdrawal in 2021, Ahmad fled to join thousands of other Afghan allies who assisted the war effort and were offered asylum in the U.S. under the Biden administration.

“Mr. Ahmad was an ally to the United States against the Taliban and helped his family members escape to refugee camps outside the country,” said Katie Blankenship, a managing operator of the legal aid group Sanctuary of the South, in a statement. “When he fled Afghanistan, he faced grave danger in his journey to the United States.”

Now Blankenship says Ahmad faces the cruelty of the U.S. immigration system. Ahmad has been in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) since December 2024, when he claimed asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. Ahmad remains locked up inside the Adams County Correctional Center, a Mississippi prison run by CoreCivic that contracts with ICE, where Blankenship says he is becoming increasingly desperate to be released and receive treatment for pre-existing medical conditions, including a tumor in his neck.

“He’s so desperate to get out of Adams because his health is deteriorating so much,” Blankenship told Truthout in an interview. “I am worried for him physically, and I am worried for him mentally — he is deteriorating.”

Blankenship has reason to worry. Despite claims by ICE that immigration prisoners receive adequate health care, reports of medical neglect within ICE’s privately run jails and prison camps are widespread. A 2025 investigation by Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff uncovered dozens of credible reports of medical neglect, and detainees have staged hundreds of hunger strikes in protest of inhumane conditions at ICE facilities across the country amid President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

At least 60 people have died in ICE custody since Trump took office, including Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, an Afghan special forces veteran and father of six children. Paktiawal fought alongside U.S. troops but died in March shortly after being arrested by ICE agents near his home in Texas. Family members said they pleaded with officers to give Paktiawal his asthma inhaler.

In a November 11 joint statement, Sanctuary of the South, the Council on American Islamic Relations-Legal Defense Fund, the Mississippi American Civil Liberties Union, and the Atlanta chapter of Asian Americans Advancing Justice said that Ahmad should be welcomed to the U.S. and celebrated for resisting the Taliban. Instead, his condition is worsening behind bars.

“This is normal procedure for ICE, to keep people locked up for as long as possible,” Blankenship said, adding that ICE’s private contractors are paid for each detainee under their watch. “The longer they are locked up the more money they get.”

At least 60 people have died in ICE custody since Trump took office, including Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, an Afghan special forces veteran and father of six children.

Despite promises made by previous administrations to protect Afghans who helped the U.S. from Taliban retribution, the Trump administration dismantled the federal program for resettling Afghans who served as allies to the U.S. following the invasion of Afghanistan in 2002, in addition to revoking asylum protections known as Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Afghan refugees.

As a result, about 8,000 Afghans are at risk of deportation back to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, which could amount to a death sentence, according to human rights advocates. Additionally, more than 1,000 Afghans have been stranded at a former U.S. Army base-turned-refugee camp in Qatar since the Trump administration suspended the resettlement process last year.

The As Sayliyah refugee camp in Doha was scheduled to shut down on September 30, leaving the Afghans stranded there with few options but to return to Afghanistan. About 150 of them are family of U.S. servicemembers. On September 29, a bipartisan group of lawmakers sent Secretary of State Marco Rubio a letter requesting emergency relief for the war refugees, and the State Department agreed to push back the deadline for closing the camp by nine months.

The uncertainty and ever-shifting statements by Trump administration officials are taking a severe psychological toll on the refugees, and that may be intentional, according to Shawn VanDiver, executive director of AfghanEvac, a group of veterans advocating for Afghan war allies.

“It’s always meant to incite fear; it’s always meant to scare the shit out of somebody, and they never give resolution,” VanDiver told Truthout. “So, people just live with that fear. And that is some shit that can cause some real mental health issues.”

The most recent scare came in the fevered days ahead of the midterm elections, when reports surfaced of a deportation flight scheduled to transfer Afghan refugees to Pakistan on November 3, which was also Election Day. Advocates feared the asylum seekers, including women and children, would be quickly handed over to the Taliban. The Trump administration has deported thousands of people to countries other than their own, which immigrant rights advocates say is illegal in cases where refugees are put in danger.

Even the Taliban’s foreign ministry issued a statement expressing “serious concern” about the U.S. plan to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, which remains in a tense and protracted conflict with the Taliban government. U.S. veterans and lawmakers sprang into action, with Rep. Scott Peters (D-California) spearheading another emergency letter from members of Congress to Rubio demanding the deportation flight be canceled.

“We are extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people who sought safety in the U.S. to Afghanistan or Iran will result in their persecution, torture, or even death,” the lawmakers wrote, arguing that deporting them would be a “violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops.”

The November 3 deportation flight never took off. The initial flight was canceled after a judge issued a federal injunction temporarily blocking the deportations to Pakistan, and VanDiver said that advocates for the refugees later learned from court filings that another deportation flight that was scheduled to remove Afghan refugees on November 16 was also canceled.

While the Afghan refugees remain in ICE custody, VanDiver said the canceled flights were a victory for AfghanEvac and activist veterans who have lobbied lawmakers to protect their wartime allies. VanDiver said there was no announcement about the cancellation from the Trump administration, which likely failed to properly plan for the deportations with the Pakistani government.

“This administration is unwilling to admit when they are wrong and is always looking to hide their fuckups,” VanDiver said.

Rep. Jason Crow, a veteran Army Ranger and Democrat from Colorado, introduced a petition on November 9 to force a vote on legislation that would restore TPS protections for Afghans. So far, 114 lawmakers have signed the petition, all of them Democrats.

When Democrats take the majority in Congress next year, VanDiver said they must go further to reverse the policies that turned Afghan war allies and refugees into targets for mass deportation. He encouraged lawmakers to look at “chief of mission” approvals under the Special Immigrant Visa program, which were withdrawn by the State Department in order to make Afghan war allies and their families ineligible for asylum and targets for deportation.

While many Afghan allies and their families remain in ICE custody or stranded at Camp As Sayliyah, VanDiver said the sweeping victory for Democrats in the midterm elections is reason for hope.

“We are really hoping to see oversight on Camp As Sayliyah, the ‘chief of mission’ revocations, and on these deportations and detentions,” VanDiver said.

Blankenship fears relief will come not fast enough for Ahmad, who is desperate to be released from the prison in Mississippi and receive medical treatment. Despite risking Taliban retribution to help the U.S. in wartime and making a harrowing escape from Afghanistan, Ahmad’s application for asylum was denied and he now faces a removal order.

In 2024, before Trump took office, immigration judges granted about 88 percent of asylum petitions from Afghans. Between October 2025 and September 2026, that rate had fallen to less than 55 percent. The overall asylum denial rate reached 94 percent in June 2026, up from 60 percent at the end of 2024. Under policies guided by White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the Trump administration has transformed refugee assistance into a system of mass incarceration, family separation, trauma, displacement, and death.

Blankenship says Ahmad’s case went before an immigration judge in Louisiana who is notorious for denying the vast majority of asylum claims. He is now desperate and wishes to be deported in order to receive medical treatment — even to a third country if necessary. Ahmad is eligible for a visa in Italy on humanitarian grounds after previously passing through the country, but Blankenship said ICE is not responding to requests filed by his attorneys, including a petition for release on medical grounds.

“There are multiple avenues that he should be able to get out — habeas corpus, parole for medical reasons, a visa to Italy because we can get it done,” Blankenship said. “But they won’t hear any of it.”

title: Senators Seek Details of RFK’s Samoa Trip as US Loses Measles Elimination Status
content:
Two Democratic senators want to know if Kennedy lied under oath during his Senate confirmation hearings.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Two Democratic senators have sent a letter to Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization formerly led by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., seeking details about Kennedy’s trip to Samoa in 2019.

The letter was sent last week by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), a member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. In it, the lawmakers said they are planning an investigation into evidence that Kennedy “unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” including during his 2025 confirmation hearings.

During those hearings, Kennedy said that his trip to Samoa in 2019 — which was followed by a massive measles outbreak on the island — was unrelated to his pushing an anti-vaccine agenda, the senators wrote.

“I went there, nothing to do with vaccines,” Kennedy said during his confirmation, claiming he was instead visiting to introduce officials to a “state-of-the-art” medical information system.

“It appears this statement was false,” the senators wrote, citing reports that Kennedy had written to Samoa’s Prime Minister Tuila’epa Sa’ilele Malielegaoi in January 2019, proposing that his team “conduct [a] detailed health informatics assessment in Samoa of what happened with your MMR vaccines.”

The senators’ letter also highlighted how Kennedy’s visit to Samoa in May 2019 included meeting “with anti-vaccine activists.”

Following Kennedy’s visit, 83 people on the island died in a devastating measles outbreak, mostly children.

Kennedy’s travel to Samoa occurred while he was still in charge of Children’s Health Defense. The letter from the senators requests “all documents related to any travel to Samoa undertaken by Kennedy or other employees, officers, directors, or associates of Children’s Health Defense,” and “all documents related to meetings or communications between Samoan government officials and employees, officers, directors, or associates” of the organization.

The letter is nonbinding, meaning that Children’s Health Defense could refuse to follow through with the senators’ demands. However, when Congress reconvenes in January 2027, the Democratic senators could urge their committees to issue subpoenas to the organization, requiring them to abide by the requests.

“We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children,” the senators added. “We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties.”

The letter was published just days before it was announced that the U.S. was set to lose its measles elimination status, which the country had attained a quarter of a century ago. That announcement was officially made by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization (WHO)-affiliated regional body that makes such decisions, on Tuesday morning.

Since Donald Trump re-entered the White House, annual measles cases in the U.S. have risen more than 20-fold. Only 285 cases were identified in the country in 2024 — that number increased to 2,289 cases in 2025, and, as of this week, 5,739 cases have been identified in 2026, according to a tracker managed by Johns Hopkins University.

Kennedy has dismissed the alarming increase in infections over the past two years, downplaying the risks associated with measles and promoting false remedies for the illness to parents.

The loss of the U.S.’s measles elimination status “highlight[s] the importance of measles vaccination and rapid detection and reporting of suspected and confirmed measles cases,” the Johns Hopkins University tracker pointed out.

title: Report: Parents Deported Under Trump Have Been Denied Contact With Their Kids
content:
In some cases, mothers being detained or deported were denied information on the whereabouts of their infant children.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new report finds that parents deported since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term have been cut off from their children or denied the opportunity to make decisions about their children’s future.

The report, published by legal advocacy group Justice in Motion on Tuesday, shines a light on the Trump administration’s moves to weaken and dismantle policies that previously provided protections for immigrant families — all while rapidly expanding the U.S.’s detention and deportation apparatus.

Justice in Motion, which partners with legal advocates in North and Central America, conducted 122 interviews with parents deported from the U.S. to Honduras, Guatemala, and Mexico since January 2025. They found that parents were repeatedly denied opportunities to contact their children after their arrest, and did not have reliable information about their children’s whereabouts and wellbeing both throughout their detention and after their deportation.

In some cases, mothers were separated from their infant children, and were not told the whereabouts of their babies during their detention or after their deportation.

A Brookings study published in May 2026 estimated that over 205,000 children have experienced the detention or deportation of a parent since the start of Trump’s second term. But little attention has been given to what happens after their deportation.

Dora Isabel Melara, a human rights attorney who spoke with deported parents, said in the Justice in Motion report that “deportation does not simply mean removing a person from one country to another; it means fragmenting a family.”

“When speaking with parents who are returned to Honduras, what I consistently observe is an emotional burden marked by desperation, uncertainty, and anguish,” she said. “Many parents arrive without clear information about their children. In most cases, the separation occurred while the parents were on their way to work or had just dropped their children off at school, without a chance to say goodbye or explain the situation to them.”

“What is not always visible from the United States is the complexity that follows that separation: the barriers to reestablishing communication… and a lack of knowledge about the legal processes necessary for reunification or custody,” she continued. “These realities prolong the separation well beyond the moment of deportation.”

Justice in Motion works to connect parents to attorneys to provide long-term support and assist in their reunification efforts after their deportation.

“Each time a parent loses contact, or a parent is denied the opportunity to make a determination about where their child should be, whether it’s with them or with someone else, it feels like a fundamental violation of the most innate responsibilities that a parent holds towards their child,” Justice in Motion’s Keeli Sorensen told Truthout.

In 2018, Trump’s “Zero Tolerance” family separation policy mandated the criminal prosecution of adults crossing the U.S. border without documentation, separating some 5,000 children from their families. Massive public outcry and nationwide protests pushed Trump to sign an executive order ending family separations in June 2018 — but his zero-tolerance framework remained in place, the report notes.

When President Joe Biden took office in 2021, the administration rescinded the 2018 zero-tolerance policy, the report says, and enacted some safeguards for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to consider children and families’ rights to stay together, under a parental rights directive. This was followed by a 10-year high of deportations under Biden, exceeding peak numbers from Trump’s first presidency.

In his second term, Trump has rescinded the majority of the safeguards for deported parents to exercise their parental rights — while ramping up family separation, detention, and deportations across the country.

“I think what we’re seeing now is grossly alarming to us because it’s just so much more widespread, it’s pervasive throughout the country, and it’s affecting families who have been here for a very long time, people who grew up here as children who are now parents,” Sorensen told Truthout.

ICE’s mandate to rapidly deport migrants has emboldened the agency to disregard the best interests of children and families — in some cases, flying in the face of state legal systems. As the report explains, “even if a state judge has ruled that a child must remain with a parent for their safety, federal immigration authorities maintain sole discretion to detain and deport that parent.”

Under Trump, ICE still has one directive regarding parents and their children, Sorensen told Truthout. That directive contains three core requirements: “They have to ask every person they arrest if they are a parent, and if they are a primary caregiver, they have to note that in their records. If a child is present at the time, they have to make sure that the child has safe access to care.”

“And then the third is that if they are going to remove that parent, they have to give them the opportunity to decide what it is they want to do with the child — whether they want the child to come with them, or to stay in the U.S.”

But ICE regularly violates all three of these requirements, Sorensen said. She gave the example of Maria, who worked in Atlanta for seven years and was attending immigration court proceedings before being told that she would be detained and deported. Maria “wasn’t given any information about what would happen to her children, two of whom were U.S. citizens, and she was not able to decide whether they would remain,” Sorensen said.

“There are others who say, ‘I would like my child to come with me,’ and that’s ignored. Or, ‘I want my child to stay,’ and that’s ignored. Or, ‘I don’t want my child placed with my abusive ex-partner,’ and that is ignored. We’ve seen violations across the board,” Sorensen went on.

The Justice in Motion report comes in the wake of devastating cuts to immigration oversight offices under both the Biden and Trump administrations — with Trump’s cuts during his second term nearly dismantling the Department of Homeland Security’s immigration oversight bodies entirely. As a result, there has been little to no recourse for immigrants whose rights are violated while in federal custody.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Fossil Fuel Companies Are Undermining Democracy, Climate Activist Says
content:
A bloc of countries are working on a parallel process to COP to create a binding agreement on fossil fuel phaseout.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

What will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? We speak to Kumi Naidoo, the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, which aims to reach a binding agreement for a global transition away from fossil fuels. Currently backed by over 25 countries from the Global South, the intergovernmental process began earlier this year in Santa Marta, Colombia. Meanwhile, at the United Nations, “for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels [in the outcome document]. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol,” says Naidoo. We discuss the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s goals, how the oil and gas industry drives global conflict, and the Trump administration’s glaring absence from international action on climate change.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. There are just four days remaining for nearly 200 countries to come to some agreement on the next steps to tackle climate change.

On Monday, negotiators published a wide-ranging 18-page draft document that’s been characterized as a shopping list of language and issues to be debated ahead of a Friday deadline for a final agreement. This is the global policy lead for Oil Change International.

ROMAIN IOUALALEN: So, I think this is a text that was designed to basically please everyone, and they took, you know, the best, the most ambitious demands from each group and put it in there. Obviously, throughout this week, what we’re going to see is a game of massacre in the negotiations. We’re going to see a lot of these — a lot of these recommendations or this language going to be cut by parties that don’t agree with any of this. And so, as the president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, just said, the text that we’re going to end up with is going to look very different.

AMY GOODMAN: Agreements here at COP are made by consensus, meaning every country essentially has veto power over the final text. Rich countries and fossil fuel-producing countries have historically thwarted the most ambitious climate goals.

These negotiations, of course, are happening as the Iran war has also drawn global attention to the world’s dependence on fossil fuels. So, what will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? A bloc of nearly 30 countries from the Global South have started a parallel process that’s aiming for a binding agreement to transition away from fossil fuels — a fossil fuel treaty. The first official conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels was held in Santa Marta, Colombia, earlier this year. Nearly 60 countries attended. A follow-up conference is scheduled to take place next year in Tuvalu.

To talk more about what can be achieved at this U.N. climate summit and what makes the process that began in Santa Marta different, we’re joined here in Turkey by Kumi Naidoo, longtime climate justice activist from South Africa, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative.

It’s nice to have you back, to see you again, Kumi. Let’s talk about what’s happened so far at this climate summit. In a moment, we’re going to be talking to the former ambassador from Nepal. They just suffered a calamitous glacier melting that led to at least 7,000 people dead and missing. That’s just one example of thousands. What has to happen here? And what is happening?

KUMI NAIDOO: We need to get serious about addressing the root cause of climate change. Eighty-six percent of what’s driving the crisis is our addiction and dependency on oil, coal and gas, what we call fossil fuels. The difficulty we have is that for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol in the outcome document.

Now, there are important things that we are pushing here on to get clarity on what a just transition would look like, trying to get resources to go in the Loss and Damage Fund and so on. But what is patently clear right now is we need a parallel process, one that will lead us to a binding agreement. So, what we’ve achieved in April through the Santa Marta conference is a parallel process that’s linked to the COP, right? And that is one way we hope we can grow the number of countries that are serious about fossil fuel phaseout. The good thing is the momentum is there.

We are not seeing here, still, enough movement on finance. Because let’s be very clear: You cannot tell poor countries in the Global South, who are carrying a lot of debt to the Global North, that they must stop producing fossil fuels, when rich countries continue to expand their fossil fuel production. The important thing is, any new, fresh investment, knowing what we know, knowing that every region, just not Nepal — every region in the world this year has experienced loss of life, serious events and so on. So we don’t even need the science anymore to tell us that we are in a deep crisis. And so far, I have to say, we are not seeing the urgency here, either on providing finance or on addressing the need to start phasing out fossil fuels.

AMY GOODMAN: It’s the largest U.N. climate summit here, I mean, something like 90,000 people. What’s the percentage of fossil fuel lobbyists and fossil fuel representatives in different governments? But also, there are many, many people deeply committed to dealing with climate change. Explain how it all happens and the terms that are like another language to the rest of the world, when you say, I mean, even “climate justice,” what that means. But here, it’s “climate finance.” It’s words like “ambition.” What do these mean?

KUMI NAIDOO: OK, on ambition, the science has told us that we have to keep warming below 1.5 degrees. We are already pushing towards that. That means from the time that we started burning fossil fuels, we cannot have a collective temperature rise beyond that. So, ambition means we need to take the actions to keep us within that threshold.

In terms of finance, what we are saying is that if we are saying to poor countries, “Leave the oil in the ground. Leave the coal in the ground. Leave the gas underneath the ground,” then they are willing to do that. But they’re saying, “Well, you built your economies in the rich countries on the basis of exploiting all those resources. So, you help us now to actually finance the new energies transition.”

And let’s be very clear: Today, Donald Trump actually has become the accidental advocate for the phaseout of fossil fuels. The U.S.-Iran illegal, unjustified war — and let’s be very blunt: There was no nuclear weapons. His own national intelligence adviser said there wasn’t and resigned. This is a war which we in the Global South call the Epstein war. This was a distraction from other crises that he had. But what it’s done is that so many countries, rich and poor countries, have said we have to now move to actually start building renewable energies. And we’re seeing a scale-up, because, clearly, it doesn’t make sense for us to continue to do that.

The one important point is, we have to recognize that fossil fuels is not only bad for the climate. Fossil fuels has been the major driver of war and conflict. The Harvard study says 7 million people are dying yearly now from carbon pollution, so it’s a negative health impact. And as we’ve seen in the United States when Trump convened the CEOs of the fossil fuel companies before the elections, we are seeing that the fossil fuel companies everywhere around the world are actually undermining democracy.

So, basically, the fight to restrict the power of the fossil fuel industry and put them out of business as fast as possible — we’re not thinking it will be done overnight, but we have to do it on the fastest possible timeline, in a fair way, and in which we are able to support and fund those countries who are saying, “Don’t exploit it for short-term profit, for long-term disaster. And stop playing political poker with the future of our children and the future of our planet.”

AMY GOODMAN: Explain Santa Marta. What happened in Colombia? What is the fossil fuel treaty?

KUMI NAIDOO: So, firstly, the fossil fuel treaty does not exist. It’s a Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, right? You remember, Amy, in Copenhagen, what we were asking for: a FAB deal — not a fabulous deal, a “fair, ambitious and binding” deal.

KUMI NAIDOO: ’09, right? And the binding deal has never happened. And so, what we are saying is that unless we can move in the direction, like on nuclear weapons, where we moved to a Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty — not perfect. The rich countries still, you know, ignore it, as we know. If we don’t have something equivalent — so, in Santa Marta, we got about 57 countries coming together saying, “We are serious about phasing out fossil fuel,” because here, there isn’t a conversation about fossil fuel phaseout, even though it’s 86%. It’s ridiculous, right? And so, what Santa Marta has given us is a parallel and connected process to the COP where we are focusing on what would it take to actually do the phaseout on the fastest possible timeline.

AMY GOODMAN: The right-wing president of Colombia has pulled Colombia out of the Santa Marta treaty initiative, which was accomplished under former president —

AMY GOODMAN: — ironically, his name, Petro.

KUMI NAIDOO: Yeah. Listen, one country making a move is not going to be the end of the process. The important thing is, people forget, it’s not just the 57 countries that went to Santa Marta, though that gave momentum to the U.N. General Assembly having a vote a few weeks later, where the International Court of Justice advisory opinion said countries needed to phase out fossil fuels and governments had a moral and legal responsibility to attack. A hundred and forty-one countries voted to support that, and by the way, the 11 countries that voted against it included Iran and the U.S. They might be bombing the hell out of each other, but they’re united on fossil fuels.

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to go back to another issue. In May of 2024, Turkey announced a total trade embargo on Israel. In his opening speech, the Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan described the suffering of the Palestinian people as, quote, “not only genocide, but also ecocide,” and called for a shift from “empty dialogue to direct implementation,” unquote. But a new report has revealed that despite Turkey’s declared trade embargo on Israel, at least 77 shipments of crude oil from the Turkish port of Ceyhan were delivered to Ashkelon in Israel as of June of this year. We were just at the People’s Climate Summit today, which is also taking place in another part of Antalya. You’ve also spoken there. A group of Turkish and global civil society activists demanded a stop to Turkish oil transfers to Israel. I had a chance to speak on Sunday with Joseph Griso from Energy Embargo for Palestine. Their new report, “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.”

JOSEPH GRISO: My name is Joseph. I’m here as a representative of Energy Embargo for Palestine. And ourselves, along with the Palestinian Youth Movement and the Progressive International, have produced this landmark report, which really clearly details the role that Türkiye is playing, specifically the port of Ceyhan in the south of Turkey is playing, in secretly delivering crude oil to the state of Israel.

AMY GOODMAN: So, the report is called “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.”

AMY GOODMAN: Explain what you have found out.

JOSEPH GRISO: So, there is a key oil infrastructure pipeline, the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, the BTC pipeline, and that is responsible for over 40% of the crude oil that Israel receives. This is crude oil that is, of course, refined in Israel and converted into oil products that are capable of — that play a key, integral role in sustaining the the military operations that have been responsible for the genocide in Gaza.

AMY GOODMAN: And how did you get the information?

JOSEPH GRISO: So, in May 2024, Türkiye announced its trade embargo. But what we were seeing through our analysis of shipping data, as well as our analysis of satellite images, is that the oil trade, very specifically transfers of oil from Ceyhan to Ashkelon port in Israel, have continued. And our report clearly details 77 specific oil shipments that have continued since May 2024 up to June 2026 to show that this is a constant, this is a secret and systematic trade pattern that is continuing to uphold Israel’s ability to carry out the genocide. And so, we’re calling for the Turkish government to halt these oil supplies, this oil route. And we’re calling really specifically for them to look at the two Greek shipping companies which are responsible, along with BP and SOCAR, the owners of the pipeline, to stop this oil trade and to implement sanctions, as well as legal processes, to uphold their trade embargo.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that’s Joseph Griso from Energy Embargo for Palestine. Their new report, “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.” And before we end, Kumi Naidoo, since you are from South Africa and South Africa has brought Israel to the International Court of Justice around the issue of genocide and war crimes, your thoughts on what they’re talking about? And this also goes to the issue of fossil fuels fueling war and violence.

KUMI NAIDOO: I’d just like to remind people about what Nelson Mandela said. He told us, as South Africans, we will never be free until the Palestinian people are free. And that action that was brought at the International Court of Justice, which has said that probably there’s a genocide — but let’s be very clear: Amnesty, including the two main human rights organizations within Israel, have declared it a genocide. You know, most of the American people can see it’s genocide, and that, we understand, played a role in the midterm elections.

And to President Erdoğan, I would make an appeal to him: Please be consistent. You say the right things on Palestine, but to continue to fuel the genocide by giving them war takes away the legitimacy of what you are saying. But more so, we have to say to President Erdoğan, as well, that you must release the political prisoners, who are in the thousands in Turkish prisons. They include politicians. They include writers, journalists and so on. And it’s also important that we note that just as this happens, on the eve of it, the LGBTI community has been attacked on a massive basis here. And what we need to understand is the climate justice issue and social justice issues are absolutely connected.

And as a South African and somebody who fought for human rights, we feel that right now the United States, under President Trump, is not only undermining the climate agenda; they are setting back us on democracy. They’re setting back us on human rights. And actually, today, the United States, under Trump, has become, without any doubt, a net negative source in the world. And we hope that the American people, who are rising up through the midterms and so on, continue to stand in partnership.

The important thing, I would say, is, which you mentioned, three states in the U.S., their legislatures have passed formal resolutions endorsing the idea of a fossil fuel treaty: California, Hawaii and Maine. And in addition to that, about 40 United States cities, from Philadelphia to San Francisco to Pittsburgh, have all endorsed it. So, the people of the U.S. are saying they want to be part of the global effort to phase out fossil fuels, to get a binding agreement. And what we would say to the American people, your brothers and sisters around the world are ready to embrace you, and we do not see American people as what the Trump administration represents to the world today.

AMY GOODMAN: And we are going to talk about the U.S. in just one minute, but I wanted to extend our condolences on the death of Desmond D’Sa, the South African anti-pollution campaigner who died in a car accident.

KUMI NAIDOO: Desmond D’Sa was an inspiration to all of us. I was at his funeral and memorial service. And Bobby Peek, who you might also have known, here, who worked with him. It’s a devastation. But what’s so beautiful about his life is that he was a working-class person. He got the biggest Goldman Prize of Environment. He never changed. He lived a working-class life, lived close to the people. And what I saw in the U.S. midterm elections, I saw many Desmond D’Sas emerge. And I hope that the mainstream of the Democratic Party will allow those voices to actually become more prominent, because the world needs those kinds of voices in the leadership of the United States.

AMY GOODMAN: Let’s not forget Desmond D’Sa’s last name is spelled D-S-A. Kumi Naidoo, longtime human rights and climate justice activist from South Africa, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative.

Coming up, while the Trump administration has pulled out of the U.N. climate summit, a number of U.S. mayors and governors came here. Many more are pledging to address the climate crisis at the state and local level. California Governor Gavin Newsom was one who came here and said he’s 100% behind a fossil fuel phaseout. We’ll speak with journalist Mark Hertsgaard. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: Mirvari Dance Ensemble performing “Holiday Suite” during the Climate Week summit in September.

title: Texas Attorney General Drops Lawsuit Aiming to Ban Muslim Civil Rights Group
content:
The Council on American-Islamic Relations, which has been targeted by Gov. Greg Abbott, called the news “a huge relief.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that sought to ban the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group from operating in Texas, state court records show.

The lawsuit, filed in February, had asked a Collin County judge to declare the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization. It alleged that CAIR was working with the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Muslim group, to “usurp governmental power and establish dominion through Sharia law.” At the time, CAIR said it was being punished for its opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

The petition came after Gov. Greg Abbott slapped the same designation against the two groups and urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR amid a surge in Republican candidates running anti-Islam campaigns.

Paxton’s office filed a notice of nonsuit Monday, voiding the lawsuit nearly two weeks after a blue wave sunk Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and swept Abbott out of office. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will remove the “foreign terrorist organization” label against CAIR.

title: Largest Data Centers in US Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark, Study Finds
content:
The largest US data centers use almost 2 percent of US electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new study published this week suggests that the combined yearly output of carbon dioxide from the largest data centers in the U.S. rivals that of some countries.

The study, which appeared in the journal Nature Sustainability on Monday, finds that the largest data centers in the country release a combined total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year. That accounts for about 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. — an amount that is greater than the yearly electricity use of Los Angeles and New York City combined.

The study examined 403 facilities in total, finding that their combined carbon emissions were comparable to those of countries the size of Bolivia or Denmark.

Some states’ data centers had larger carbon outputs than others. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio account for half of emissions alone, while other states, such as Oregon, have much smaller carbon emissions, due to a larger portion of electricity being generated through means other than fossil fuels.

title: Democrats Face First Test Post-Midterms: Fund or Oppose Forever Wars?
content:
The Democrats should use their midterm momentum to stop writing a blank check for the Pentagon.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The historic Democratic Party midterm victories were fueled in large part by deep opposition to the war on Iran, according to polling. Every Democrat who won in a competitive congressional race, except for one, opposed the war, including 13 in the Senate and 48 in the House, according to post-election analysis by the Progressive Change Institute.

New members won’t take office until January 3, when control of both houses shifts to Democrats. But the first test of whether Democrats in Congress will heed voters’ mandate for the end of the war on Iran, and respond to widespread opposition to “forever wars” more broadly, could occur much sooner. Although Democrats remain in the minority until January, they still have powerful leverage to block excessive Pentagon funding and stop the war in Iran during the current lame-duck session.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is key. The bill authorizes $1.15 trillion in military spending — along with dangerous policies to move toward integration of U.S. and Israeli military technology development, to build a destabilizing new generation of nuclear weapons, and to accelerate deployment of AI in weaponry.

The Trump administration is requesting an additional $350 billion just for the Iran War, bringing the total spending to a breathtaking $1.5 trillion dollars.

But Congress could just say no. The message delivered by the midterm elections could finally flip the script on the conventional wisdom that Congress will grant any level of Pentagon funding in the name of national security. Democrats must use their midterm momentum to stop destabilizing policies and sky-high defense spending, and finally take a stand for spending that meets the needs of families and communities.

The 2027 NDAA was passed by the House in July. But in the Senate, 60 votes are required to allow a measure to come to the floor for a vote, and Senate Democrats were able to stop the bill from progressing. They can do that again, with or without Republican support, and the midterm election results make clear that is what voters want them to do.

Opposing the massive increase in military spending and the war in Iran should be an easy call — especially at a time when so many Americans are struggling to get the food, housing, medical care, and education they need. But giant defense corporations invest heavily in lobbying to influence defense policy, with nearly $164 million spent on lobbying in just the first three quarters of 2026, according to OpenSecrets. Defense expenditures are distributed nationwide, so members of Congress are often reluctant to reduce budgets that could impact their districts. Funding the Pentagon is also conflated with support for U.S. service members and considered a signal of patriotism. It is time to put that falsehood to rest.

Neither the NDAA nor the Pentagon appropriations bill is truly a must-pass measure. The two bills serve different purposes: the NDAA authorizes military programs and establishes defense policies, while the appropriations bill actually provides the money to fund them. If an appropriation bill doesn’t pass, Congress can keep the Pentagon operating through a continuing resolution. And the programs and policies included in the NDAA do not have to be bundled into one massive annual bill; Congress can address them through separate legislation.

If either bill stalls, the incoming Congress, with its new Democratic majorities, could write new versions after members take office in January 2027. They could use these bills to end the war in Iran, to halt destructive new nuclear weapons development, to stop military technology integration with Israel, and to force a reduction in Pentagon spending.

Congress could redirect our taxpayer dollars toward unmet needs of families and communities, beginning by reversing cuts to Medicaid funding scheduled to take effect in the new year.

Only Congress has the Constitutional power to determine federal government funding, and it should use that power. Here are seven things it could do instead of rubber-stamping the Pentagon’s requests:

End the deeply unpopular war in Iran. The Iran war was a “crucial” or a “major factor” for 74 percent of voters, according to an NBC exit poll. Sixty-five percent disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war in Iran, according to Pew Research Center. There are multiple efforts in the works to end this disastrous conflict. “Simply throwing more money at an out-of-control military operation is not strategy. It’s a recipe for a forever war,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) said in a July 14 statement. Congress should ensure that any legislation to fund the government through the end of the year restricts Trump from spending on the Iran war.

Say no to the massive increase in military spending. The Trump administration’s $1.15 trillion national defense spending request would consume 63 percent of all federal discretionary funding, up from around half in recent years. An additional $350 billion is being requested through budget reconciliation, which is immune from the filibuster. Together, this $1.5 trillion total would raise the Defense budget to the highest level of spending since World War II. Separately, the administration has asked for an additional $67 billion as a supplemental budget, of which approximately $42.3 billion is directly tied to the Iran War. Funding for Defense comes both from taxpayers (and 65 percent of Americans polled in April oppose the increase to $1.5 trillion) and by going even more deeply into national debt, a financial hole that is now roughly the same size as the entire U.S. economy, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Congress could cut billions just by eliminating waste, fraud, and abuse — the Pentagon has not passed an audit in eight years. It could close foreign military bases and eliminate expensive and dangerous new weapons systems. The only areas where Congress should not skimp are pay and benefits for active-duty service members and veterans.

Reset our relationship with Israel. On November 3, President Trump announced an end to the annual $4 billion in direct military aid to Israel. But Section 1217 of the Senate version of the NDAA would establish a cooperative initiative with Israel to “expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation.” Since the beginning of the war on Gaza — which a UN commission has determined constitutes genocide — Americans have increasingly questioned the close relationship with the Israeli government. According to the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 56 percent of Americans say U.S. military aid to Israel should be either decreased (21 percent) or stopped altogether (35 percent), up considerably from 2012 when a combined 38 percent said the same. Congress should cut military support for Israel and reject the integration of U.S. and Israeli military technology development.

Work for nuclear safeguards, not new weapons systems. The NDAA authorizes nearly $42 billion for the Department of Energy, much of it for the National Nuclear Security Administration, which oversees U.S. nuclear weapons. Amendments to the NDAA or the appropriations bill could block the destabilizing new sea-launched nuclear cruise missile (SLCM-N) program and other new generation nuclear weapons. The New START treaty expired on February 5, 2026, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without a binding bilateral agreement limiting their strategic nuclear arsenals. Ninety-one percent of respondents to a YouGov poll want the U.S. to negotiate a new arms control agreement with Russia. In another YouGov poll, 68 percent expressed support for an international treaty in which the U.S. and other nations reduce and eventually eliminate nuclear weapons. Congress should require robust new arms-control talks aimed at reducing nuclear arsenals, not fuel a dangerous new nuclear arms race.

Prohibit using the U.S. military to threaten Canada and Greenland, or to seize the territory of other nations. Just a few years ago, it would have been unthinkable that we would threaten our closest neighbor, Canada, and a fellow member of NATO like Denmark. Doing so would violate the U.N. charter prohibiting the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. And the threat to Denmark could break NATO. Congress should make explicit that no U.S. military expenditures will be used to threaten these nations.

End extrajudicial killings of unidentified people aboard alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific. Congress must uphold international law and rein in the executive branch from using the military to conduct illegal assassinations.

Stop deployment of AI-controlled weapons. The NDAA includes some limits on AI-enabled autonomous weapon systems, but the Senate bill also directs the Pentagon to build systems for deploying agentic AI “at scale and speed.” Agentic AI refers to systems that can pursue goals and take actions with limited human direction, raising serious questions about human oversight of military operations. Three in four Americans agree that decisions to use lethal force require human judgment.

“We’re at a pivotal moment where Congress can either enshrine the Trump military budget and parts of the Trump military doctrine with it, making it harder to reverse,” said Lindsay Koshgarian, National Priorities Project program director at the Institute for Policy Studies, in an interview with the author. “Or Congress can chip away at a Pentagon budget that has been too high and too unaccountable for a long time, and turn those funds toward better uses.”

Rejecting the proposed increase and bringing national defense spending back to last year’s level — or better yet, cutting it further — would free up resources for the things voters across the nation are clamoring for — like restoring funding to Medicaid and SNAP, rebuilding our nation’s infrastructure, funding education, relieving student debt, building affordable housing, investing in science, stopping the heating of the planet, and so much more.

The midterm results have sent a message: Americans are tired of endless wars; a government that can find hundreds of billions for the Pentagon should instead fund people’s basic needs.

Yet the political opportunity is up for grabs. If Democrats rubber-stamp the $1.5 trillion in spending and the dangerous policies contained in the NDAA, they risk becoming the party of unaccountable military spending and forever wars, leaving Republicans free to claim the mantle of “America First” non-interventionism.

Both parties could instead compete to show which has one has the greater commitment to challenging the Pentagon’s unchecked power, stopping the carnage of war, and investing in what Americans actually need.

The first test will come within weeks. Voters led the way on November 3. Our elected leaders would do well to follow their lead.
