title: New Jersey Cops Are Using Opioid Settlement Funds For Drones, Cars, and Gym Gear
content:
A new bill would restrict police use of the funds, which are meant to cover addiction treatment and support services.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In Ocean County, a day’s work might mean Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a harm reductionist, helps someone struggling with drug addiction by getting them a ride to treatment, connecting them with a food pantry or housing assistance, or even traipsing into the woods to bring them a new tent.

Law enforcement agencies in Ocean County, though, have decided that helping people beat addiction means splurging on new police cars, canines, surveillance cameras, street signs, body armor, and more.

Police across New Jersey have commandeered millions of dollars that pharmaceutical companies have paid New Jersey, its 21 counties, and 241 of its largest municipalities since 2022 to settle lawsuits over the deadly opioid epidemic.

With the state set to receive over $1.1 billion in settlement funds through 2038, advocates now are demanding that lawmakers tighten oversight of spending to ensure it meets approved uses — addiction prevention, treatment, and support services for people in recovery.

“The police have been well-funded for very, very long, and they’re not recovery specialists,” said Burke Beaty, founder and CEO of Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center. “The money that they’re taking is not in the spirit of repairing all the harms caused by Big Pharma.”

A New Jersey Monitor analysis of municipalities’ spending reports and records on the watchdog site Opioid Audit shows that police spent opioid funds in all sorts of ways that don’t directly help people harmed by addiction.

Seventeen agencies spent more than $1.5 million on cars, lights, lettering, vehicle wraps, and related expenses. Eleven departments spent more than a half-million dollars on police canines, kennels, canine training, and veterinary care. Seven bought surveillance cameras and automated license plate reader systems.

At least 20 spent money on technology including drones, digital roadside billboards and radar systems, e-bikes, vape detectors for schools, police radios, mapping software and investigative databases, drug analyzers and breathalyzers, and defibrillators.

Scores more used settlement funds to pay for officer training, salaries and overtime, staff wellness programs, bicycles, gym equipment, subscription renewals, body armor, clothing, National Night Out costs, junior police academies, school assemblies, and associated promotional materials.

The departments typically characterized the spending as prevention, harm reduction, community engagement and education, and recovery support.

But officials often stretched the definition of those terms.

Wall Township explained spending more than $30,000 of opioid funds on treadmills, weights, and other gym equipment as an investment in the “mental health of first responders.” Garfield police cited public awareness as the chief goal of $5,450 they paid for a vehicle wrap and thousands more spent on a “Let’s Knock Out Opioid Use Together” festival that featured a live DJ, several inflatable bounce houses, food vendors, a pop-up party area, and a helicopter landing display.

While the settlement requires officials to invest in evidence-based strategies to reduce addiction and repair harms, some police spending seems to flout that rule. In Highland Park, police bought 10 anti-choking devices for $605 last year even though state health officials issued a cautionary statement about the devices and the federal Food and Drug Administration has warned that using them carries risks.

In many cases, police invested opioid funds in things that have historically been paid for out of their budgets, such as police salaries, vehicles, and safety gear. Watchdogs have long warned against using opioid money as “slush funds” or to plug budget gaps.

Much of such spending would be barred under new legislation Assemblywoman Maureen Rowan (D-Atlantic) introduced Monday.

Rowan’s bill would prohibit police and public officials from using opioid funds on any activities, equipment, or technology that normally would be paid out of municipal, county, or state budgets. It also would forbid spending the funds on police training and salaries not specifically tied to addiction remediation, drug takeback programs, and anything related to surveillance, crime detection, search and seizure, evidence gathering, and criminal processing.

It lists specific policing items as disallowed, including drones, traffic enforcement signage, drug simulation goggles, high-dose naloxone, and agency marketing and promotional items. And it would set a 5% cap on how much opioid funds an agency could spend on administrative expenses.

John Donnadio, who heads the New Jersey Association of Counties, welcomes the clarity.

His group and the New Jersey State League of Municipalities have pushed state officials to provide more guidance on acceptable spending, even though quite a bit already exists, including approved uses listed in the national settlement itself, a memorandum of agreement former Attorney General Andrew Bruck issued in 2022, a law New Jersey lawmakers passed in 2023, a lengthy strategic plan a state advisory panel put out last year, and guidance from harm reduction groups.

“Maybe if they were more specific, we would avoid this,” Donnadio said. “Like the state, or the Department of Human Services, the Attorney General’s Office, or whatever office said, ‘Alright, this is an inventory of what’s good: naloxone kits, transportation for individuals to treatment if they can’t afford it, reaching out to the homeless population.’ And ‘bouncy houses are bad things. Car wraps are bad things,’” he said. “I don’t know if that’s the answer, but I think that would be helpful. Then there’s no wiggle room. There’s no gray area.”

League officials didn’t respond to requests for comment. But Raymond Heck, a past president of the group and Millstone’s mayor, told lawmakers last month at a public hearing on opioid spending that many local governments want more detailed guidance.

Heck, a state correctional officer and member of the New Jersey Police Training Commission, denied any ill intent in past spending decisions.

“I don’t believe the municipalities, the counties, are doing wrong. The ones that are questionable? We just want to make it better. Give them direction,” Heck said.

Restrictions on police use of opioid funds are reasonable — and overdue, considering law enforcement historically has treated addiction as a crime instead of a public health crisis, harm reductionists say.

“Why would we be giving more money into that same system of criminalization?” said Eva Mancini of the New Jersey Organizing Project.

Katie Carter lost her mother to an overdose five years ago and struggled with addiction herself. She credited her recovery largely to help from harm reduction groups including Atlantic City’s Oasis. She now works with Mancini to help others still fighting for sobriety.

“In my own experience, the way people who use drugs are treated by police is not kind,” Carter said. “That’s personally why I think that they don’t deserve the money.”

title: 21 Dem Senators Join GOP to Move Forward Bill to Speed Up Data Center Permits
content:
The bill, which will change federal approval processes for fossil fuel projects, is backed by Big Oil and tech giants.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

US senators, including 21 members of the Democratic caucus, voted late Monday to end debate on permitting reform legislation that would weaken critical environmental safeguards to speed up the federal approval process for energy projects, including fossil fuel infrastructure and data centers.

One Democratic senator, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, opposed the cloture motion on Monday after previously voting to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation backed by the oil lobby, tech giants, and the climate-wrecking Trump White House, as well as major labor unions. Cortez Masto said after last week’s procedural vote that she would vote against advancing the bill to final passage if its changes to the National Historic Preservation Act were not removed.

The Senate Democratic caucus members who supported the cloture motion, which sets the stage for final passage, were: Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Andy Kim (NJ), Angus King (Maine), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (NY), Jeanne Shaheen (NH), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.), Mark Warner (Va.), Raphael Warnock (Ga.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI).

“The senators who voted to advance BAAJA just betrayed the voters who turned out en masse to demand that Congress rein in data center development, stop corruption, and bring down electricity costs,” said Elizabeth Bast, executive director of the advocacy group Oil Change International. “BAAJA would double down on Trump’s failed energy policies, which enrich Big Oil and his own stock portfolio at the expense of communities and our climate. Even analysis from the American Petroleum Institute, a major BAAJA backer, shows that the bill doesn’t stop energy prices from rising.”

“BAAJA would act as a kill switch for future climate action without offering any meaningful emissions reductions,” Bast warned. “At best, this bill leaves US emissions over 2.1 billion tons short in 2040 of even a modest climate goal. Big Oil and Big Tech have spent millions lobbying for this backroom deal, which has not had a single hearing, and are urging Congress to ram through the bill before the incoming Congress is sworn in.”

If, as expected, the Senate votes for final passage of BAAJA, the bill would move to the narrowly GOP-controlled House, where it has drawn significant opposition from Democratic lawmakers, including the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC). Environmental groups and other opponents have urged lawmakers in both chambers to press pause on the bill until Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“BAAJA includes important policies for which the CPC has advocated, including stronger federal authority to approve much-needed transmission lines to accelerate the clean energy transition,” the caucus said in a statement last week. “However, it also contains provisions that would undermine Tribal sovereignty and roll back key environmental laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. As a result, the public would lose key tools used to protect the environment and hold the administration accountable against ICE detention centers, Trump vanity projects, and more.”

The Senate’s cloture vote came days after around 100 environmental and energy law scholars warned in a letter to the chamber’s Democratic leadership that BAAJA “would inflict permanent, sweeping damage on the nation’s core environmental laws (and on the people and environment they are designed to protect).”

“Whatever modest emissions reductions its transmission reforms may deliver cannot justify the rollback that comes with them,” the letter reads. “And the threat posed by this lame-duck initiative provides a template and momentum for rollbacks far beyond environmental protections — potentially undercutting enforcement of public health protections, civil rights, public education, consumer finance, and more.”

title: Reports Say Trump Lied About Ending Aid to Israel, Funding Will Be Maintained
content:
Israeli outlets report that officials are, in fact, working to renew the funding for another five or 10 years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump’s claim on Election Day earlier this month that the U.S. was ending its annual funding to Israel at the end of 2026 was a lie, Israeli outlets have revealed, catching Trump in a last-ditch effort to boost Republicans that was seemingly nothing more than a PR stunt.

According to reporting by Israeli outlets Times of Israel and Ynet, several Israeli and U.S. officials say that there is no such deal in place between the countries. In fact, the current agreement being hashed out is for the U.S. and Israel to enter another memorandum of understanding (MOU) when the current one ends to continue sending Israel aid.

Details have yet to be worked out, but the general outline consists of a 5- or 10-year deal to phase out the U.S.’s annual $3.8 billion in annual aid sent to Israel. One version of this, according to Ynet, is for the U.S. to maintain current funding levels — with $3.3 billion of that funding allocated under the Foreign Military Financing program — for five years, after which it would be cut off.

title: Environmental Groups Warn Nitrate Pollution Is “Urgent Threat to Public Health”
content:
A petition sent to the EPA calls for tighter restrictions on a contaminant increasingly associated with many cancers.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Sixteen environmental and public health groups filed a legal petition with U.S. regulators on Monday seeking new restrictions on nitrate contamination — a type of water pollution the groups say is driving a “public health crisis across the country.”

The petition calls for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to slash the Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for nitrate in drinking water to 1 milligram per liter (mg/L), down from the current federal standard that allows for up to 10 mg/L. The groups are calling for the Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) to be set at 0 mg/L, which essentially would acknowledge that no amount of nitrate is considered safe for human health over lifetime exposure.

Such moves are warranted because scientific research shows that current levels of contamination pose “an urgent threat to public health,” including increasing the risk for certain cancers, the petition states.

The petitioners cite analysis showing that surface water levels of nitrate across the nation are increasing while nitrate monitoring is decreasing.

“One of the things we have sought to do here is to do the EPA’s job for it,” said Tyler Lobdell, an attorney with Food & Water Watch, one of the groups leading the petition effort. “One hundred and twenty million on people being serviced by public water systems are told the water is perfectly safe when the science says it is not.”

The petitioners include the Environmental Working Group, the Center for Biological Diversity, the Center for Food Safety, Food & Water Watch, Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, among others.

The petition blames not only the EPA but also federal, state, and local lawmakers and other public officials for failing to address nitrate pollution, which is linked to cancers and other health problems.

The groups cite excessive application of synthetic fertilizers, the “over-application” of animal waste from concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFO) onto farm fields, inadequately treated sewage and industrial discharges, and failed septic systems as culprits for the nitrate-laden water.

The legal petition for rule making requires a response by the EPA and could set in motion further legal actions, Lobdell noted.

When asked about the petition, the EPA said it would review it and said it is “committed to ensuring all Americans have access to clean drinking water.” However, the agency noted it completed its most recent review of drinking water regulations, including the regulations for nitrate, in July 2024, evaluating available studies and applicable data. And based on that information, there was no need for a revision of the MCL, the agency said. The agency said it will consider new studies for its next review.

The current standard of 10 mg/L for drinking water was initially set in the 1970s and finalized in 1991 at a level that was set to avoid causing methemoglobinemia, also known as blue baby syndrome. All public water systems are required to monitor for nitrate contamination to determine compliance with that MCL.

But research on nitrate health impacts has grown over the past 35 years and there is now a large and growing body of evidence that consuming even low levels of nitrate-contaminated water is associated with colon and rectal cancers, and ovarian cancer, bladder and kidney cancers, as well as other adverse health impacts such as neural tube defects and low birth weights in babies.

The petitioners said they identified 3,205 community water systems serving roughly 119.7 million people that recorded at least one nitrate sample at or above 1 mg/L between 2021 and 2023.

The petition comes as many U.S. states, including key farming states, wrestle with concerns about nitrates. Iowa, in particular, has drawn national scrutiny for its high levels of nitrate in prominent waterways and climbing rates of cancer.

Scientists point to farm operations as largely to blame for nitrate contamination, both because of the runoff of fertilizer applied to fields of corn and other crops, and the runoff of liquified manure generated by large livestock operations that is also often spread on farm fields. The runoff carries nitrates and phosphorus into surface and groundwaters, and ultimately into drinking water.

Iowa tops the list of U.S. states with the highest mean levels of nitrate in surface waters from January 2015 through August 2026, according to the petition, which cites analysis of water quality data from multiple national, state, and local monitoring systems. Iowa is followed by Minnesota, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana and Kansas.

People who get their drinking water from wells are at particular risk as nitrate is commonly found in groundwater.

“For decades EPA has given industrial agriculture a free pass to pollute, and now one in three Americans is drinking water with dangerous levels of nitrates, JP Rose, director of soil health at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a statement. “Tackling agricultural pollution at the source and improving treatment will help ensure all Americans have access to safe drinking water.”

One of the primary drivers of agricultural nitrate pollution is overapplication of fertilizer; synthetic nitrogen fertilizer is the largest nitrogen source in 41% of U.S. watersheds, the petition states.

Along with lowering the allowed levels of nitrate in drinking water, the EPA should take new steps to address the source of the nitrate pollution by implementing greater controls at the source point, the petition states. The petitioners point to cover cropping, wetlands protection and restoration, riparian buffers or field border strips, and crop diversification as practices that can help reduce nitrate pollution.

The petitioners noted that stricter regulations on nitrate pollution would also benefit ecosystems and fish and wildlife. Dozens of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are at risk due to the water pollution the petition notes.

The Iowa Environment Council (IEC), which has been pushing for stronger controls on nitrate contamination in that state, supports the call for strengthening the MCL, said IEC general counsel Michael Schmidt. But he noted a lowered MCL would not affect private wells, many of which exceed the 10 mg/L limit that applies to public water supplies. The state should take steps to help protect private well users in the near-term without waiting for EPA to act, he said.

Lowering the MCL for nitrate in drinking water could prove very costly for water utilities if the sources of the contamination are not significantly restricted. The current cost of nitrate treatment is “a substantial financial burden on water utilities,” according to recent research. Utilities spent up to 9% of their overall operating budgets just on nitrate treatment, according to a 2018 study by the Northeast-Midwest Institute.

The Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies did not respond to a request for comment on the petition. Neither did the the American Water Works Association.

The groups petitioning the EPA argue that their analysis demonstrates that an MCL of 1 mg/L is both “technically achievable and economically justified.”

They also say that the human health benefits of a lower MCL more than justify the costs of compliance. They say their analysis shows a nitrate MCL of 1 mg/L would “conservatively result in approximately $364.1 billion in present-value health benefits, compared with approximately $94.5 billion in compliance costs, yielding approximately $269.7 billion in net benefits over the 50-year analysis period.”

Nancy Stoner of the Environmental Law and Policy Center said in a press conference that the federal government should provide financial support to utilities to help them comply with a lowered standard.

“Americans should not suffer the adverse health outcomes resulting from drinking nitrate contaminated water because funds are not available to ensure safe drinking water, nor should communities be burdened with the full costs of reducing nitrate contamination driven by underregulated industrial agriculture,” the petition states.

author: Amy Goodman
title: COP31 Draft Shows Rich Nations May Offer Debt-Creating Loans for Climate Finance
content:
Asad Rehman says Global South countries need public finance to adapt to the impacts of climate change.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need.

“Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, ‘Our coffers are empty.’ But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Yes, this is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Turkey.

ASAD REHMAN: We are in the midst of a crisis, of a crisis of crisis. We could see that with the killer floods, droughts and famines impacting people everywhere. Our ecosystems are collapsing. We’re about to breach the critical 1.5-degree guardrail with devastating consequences.

AMY GOODMAN: That was longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He was outside on Saturday, marching with thousands of people in the rain, demanding climate action, joining us now inside the COP.

We welcome you back to Democracy Now!, Asad. Why don’t we start off by talking about what has been accomplished here? We’re midway through. Democracy Now! will be broadcasting throughout this week. The end is supposed to be on Friday. There was a draft release, a release of a draft document, today by the head of the COP. It’s here in Turkey, but it is being — you can explain this — officiated over by Australia. What was said, and what wasn’t, and what are the key issues, like electrification?

ASAD REHMAN: Sure. Always a pleasure to be here, Amy.

And so, the cover note is a political instrument. It’s not a negotiated text. And it’s generally written by the presidency of the COPs. We have a bit of a unique situation in that we have both Turkey and Australia currently in charge of these climate negotiations. So, Australia says it’s in charge of the negotiations, and Turkey in charge of the COP itself. So, the cover note is — I mean, it’s an interesting thing, because we’ve seen these cover notes now appear often at COPs. Many of them make grand announcements and then disappear into the dust. You may remember, I think back in Glasgow, at COP26, there were announcements about phasing out inefficient fossil fuels. There was announcements about increasing the ambition of emission reductions by 2030. None of those things came to pass. So, you have to take these cover notes also with a pinch of salt.

Now, in the cover note itself, there are so many different pieces, often very, very contradictory. But cut through all of the jargon, and there are three key things that are at play there. The first is electrification. This is a call by the Turkish presidency themselves that by 2035, 35% of our energy needs are met are electricity. Now, on paper, it sounds great, but lift the hood, and there are some real issues at it. First of all, when they talk about energy, they’re talking about clean energy, which includes nuclear. Secondly, this is not about energy access, so it’s not about the close to 700-800 million people who currently don’t have access to electricity. Often what they’re talking about is electricity for the richest countries to power gas — energy-guzzling data centers, electric vehicles, etc. Secondly, there is no commitment about actually the finance that is needed or the technology. So, it’s going to sound really, really great, but will it deliver to those people? Probably not.

The second thing that’s in here is a lot about what is being called the overshoot. Look, the lack of action by developed countries to do their fair share has now taken us to the brink of breaching the critical 1.5-degree guardrail. We’ve seen the consequences all around the world, of course, devastating fires, floods, famines. But now what these rich countries are saying is, “Well, let’s go beyond the 1.5. And what we’ll do is we’ll bank on risky and unproven technologies to suck carbon out of the atmosphere,” which will, of course, be a green light for massive land grabs, for massive ocean grabs. And secondly, what we’ll do is open the door to even more dangerous geoengineering possibilities, as well.

And the third big thing in there is, of course, about finance. Now, rich countries haven’t been meeting their promises. If you remember all the way back to Copenhagen, Hillary Clinton promised rich countries $100 billion in climate finance. Less than a third of that was ever provided in real grants. And since then, just in one year alone, poorer developing countries, often trapped in debt, have paid 225 times more in debt repayments than they’ve got in climate finance. And now what’s being offered to them again is more debt-creating loans, not public finance. And this is really critical, because whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses, which are totaling over a trillion right now, you need public finance. And the rich countries are saying, “Our coffers are empty.” But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires, who, of course, are not paying their fair share of tax, or the corporations.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to go to the Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who was just here at the COP31 last Thursday.

GRETA THUNBERG: We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights, and where basic necessities become luxury. And it is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying; it is being killed. And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it becomes our duty, everyone’s duty, but especially the more privileged you are, the bigger your responsibility to stand up, to be the adult in the room and to fight for the rights of our human rights and for everyone’s human rights.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that was Greta Thunberg on Thursday. And, of course, the context of all of this, the backdrop is the war in Iran and the amount of money that is being spent on it, the terrible casualties as a result, and the — what it makes the world aware of: The price we pay for fossil fuels was the shutting down of the Strait of Hormuz. Then you have President Trump, President Xi of China and Putin about to meet in the first-ever trilateral summit on Thursday. Your thoughts of what should be accomplished here and what they should be dealing with there?

ASAD REHMAN: Look, I think we all recognize that we’re not just dealing with a climate crisis and breaching the 1.5. Our ecosystem, the very things that humanity needs to survive, let alone thrive, are collapsing around us. But we’re also facing a growing crisis of inequality, economic inequality. Millions, if not billions, of people are struggling, not just now in the Global South, but increasingly in the Global North, as well. And that’s given rise to a rise of authoritarianism, of far-right and fascist politics, who are weaponizing inequality against change, who are saying, “Raise the walls and fences, pour more money into militarization to protect us,” rather than actually fighting to ensure that everybody can live with dignity.

So, what these governments are proposing and are on the table, actually, is far away from what we actually need. What we really need is governments to be doubling down and saying, “Actually, we can make sure that people have adequate and affordable homes, that are warm during the winter and cool during the summer. We can make sure that people have the right to food, to good incomes, to good jobs. And we can make sure we do that not just for our citizens in the Global North, but citizens in the Global South.” Instead, what we’re having is world leaders who are turning their backs on multilateralism, who are turning their backs on humanity as a whole, and are saying, “Well, actually, there is no future but a future of brutality and of war and of conflict.”

AMY GOODMAN: What do you think of the United States not being here, the historically largest carbon and gas emitter? And then you have the current largest polluter, China, has one of the largest delegations there, though not the president, Xi.

ASAD REHMAN: Look, this place is important, because the U.N. climate space is one of the very few places you have where every single country is represented and where the voices of people who are most impacted can actually try and hold our governments to account, because, otherwise, this will be held in shadowy backrooms, the richest countries by themselves. So it’s important. And, of course, it’s not — it’s key that the United States is here, but the United States has been here and has done its best to disrupt and dismantle the climate negotiations.

The real question is, is: What about the other rich developed countries, the United Kingdom, the European Union and others? Are they stepping up and doing their fair share? Are they showing?

ASAD REHMAN: Well, they’re not doing. I mean, I come from — I’m living in the United Kingdom. We’ve just greenlighted one fossil fuel expansion in Jackdaw. We have Rosebank, where the government is still hesitating. We’re about to expand airport expansions in Heathrow, and we’re giving a green light for more data centers. It’s sending the wrong signal to the rest of the world. It’s saying, “We are going to continue to pollute, but you don’t.” And what we need is finance and committed public finance. And what we’ve seen is these rich countries cutting their finance to the climate — to climate finance.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, we have to leave it there, but we are going to be here all week delving into these issues. Asad Rehman is the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

I want to really thank our team here in Turkey — some of us almost didn’t make it with the lockdown in the United States: Anjali Kamat, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Hany Massoud and Denis Moynihan. I also want to thank, in New York, Mike Burke and Deena Guzder and Messiah Rhodes and María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Robby Karran and Diego Ramos, as well as Laura Bustillos. I am Amy Goodman, here in Turkey for the U.N. summit.

title: Main Group Behind “No Kings” Overwhelmingly Endorses Van Hollen Over Schumer
content:
Indivisible said that 97% of its chapter leaders support the Maryland Democrat to be the next Senate majority leader.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Indivisible, one of the organizations behind the “No Kings” movement that brought millions of people into the streets to protest against President Donald Trump, is throwing its support behind Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s bid to be the next Senate majority leader.

In a Monday announcement, Indivisible said that 97% of its chapter leaders nationwide voted to endorse Van Hollen (D-Md.), who last week announced he was challenging current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) to lead Democrats in the upper congressional chamber next year.

Indivisible said Van Hollen won its endorsement because he shared three key priorities with the group: “Ending the war in Iran and the economic pain Americans are feeling at the pump; clawing back funding for ICE and Border Patrol while stopping devastating Medicaid cuts; and using every procedural tool available, including breaking the corrupt Senate filibuster on day one.”

The group also noted some of the high-profile fights Van Hollen has taken up with the Trump administration, such as his decision to meet with Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego after he was unlawfully deported to El Salvador in 2025.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump: “I Don’t Take Any Responsibility” for Ground Stop That Stranded 1.5M
content:
Trump said the repairs have been needed for 40 years, not noting he’s been president for six of those.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said that he doesn’t “take any responsibility” for the nationwide ground stop for air travel issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, instead saying that the crisis was former President Joe Biden’s fault.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump said in remarks to press on Monday, when asked if he feels responsible as president.

“I mean, the only responsibility should be — for 40 years they should have done this. This is a system that’s probably, on average, 50 years old,” he said, adding that he is now asking Congress for more funding. He did not acknowledge that he has served as president for nearly six years during that time.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also blamed “prior administrations” for the issues, without acknowledging that Trump was in charge of one of those prior administrations.

Instead, in a post on Truth Social on Sunday morning, the president blamed Biden. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” Trump wrote.

He echoed Duffy’s calls for Congress to allocate more money to the FAA in response to the ground stop. Democrats in Congress, however, pushed back on the Trump administration’s complaints.

“Let’s look at the facts. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration’s obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” said Representatives Rick Larsen (D-Washington) and André Carson (D-Indiana), ranking members of the House Committee on Transportation and Subcommittee on Aviation, respectively.

In a response to the Democrats, Duffy has said that the money allocated by Congress is already “all accounted for” and more is needed for a “new network,” which would require “new money to build new software.”

Duffy has said that the issue, which impacted 10,000 flights and stranded roughly 1.5 million travelers, was caused by an infrastructure upgrade that was being done in an unspecified “remote” facility by a contractor, L3Harris, which is also a major military contractor. The contractor was replacing copper wire with fiber optic cable, officials said. This caused a breakdown in communication systems that spiralled across the country, administration officials have claimed, without explaining how.

The union that represents public workers who typically do aviation infrastructure maintenance said that they were not involved in the upgrade, and said that the union has been sidelined in the process of reforming the nation’s air traffic control system.

The GAO warned in September that the speed of the upgrades currently being done under Duffy’s “Brand New Air Traffic Control System” plan is reckless and that the rapid replacement of old technologies would risk causing a major failure. Duffy has touted the FAA’s implementation of an AI-powered routing system, called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART), which the administration put into place nationwide just days before the nationwide ground stop.

Experts and members of Congress have indeed acknowledged the need for upgrades to the U.S.’s aviation infrastructure, which is, like many other parts of the U.S.’s infrastructure, in dire need of repairs. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave the aviation sector a D+ grade in its latest report on America’s infrastructure. The report said that bills like the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), signed into law by Biden in 2021, have provided some help, but that there is still a massive funding gap of roughly $114 billion over the next decade.

Critics have said that Trump has contributed to the state of aviation infrastructure. At the beginning of his second term, Trump ordered a pause on the disbursement of funding under the IIJA and Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, putting a pause on FAA funding, among other things, from the bills passed under Biden. It’s still unclear how much of that money in total was clawed back or withheld.

Further, the Trump administration has, in some ways, actively worked against aviation safety advancements. One of his first actions in his second term was to eliminate the Department of Homeland Security’s membership in the Aviation Security Advisory Committee. And, in February 2025, the Trump administration fired hundreds of FAA employees amid Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” slashes, contributing to shortages in air traffic control staff.

In his first term, Trump released a plan to privatize the air traffic control system. This was vehemently opposed by aviation experts, and the Government Accountability Organization (GAO) found in a report around that time that it would jeopardize safety, and Duffy has shifted away from that plan during Trump’s second term.

Trump was incensed and made an offhand racist remark when he was asked whether he should have focused more on aviation safety during his second term on Monday.

Trump to a Black reporter: "I know you don’t see dirt — but if you’d take a look at the White House, you’d never notice broken windows, obviously, from where you come from."

“Mr. President, what do you say to critics who say you were too focused on D.C. construction projects while our airline systems were crumbling, given the fact that Republicans have been in control?” a reporter asked.

“Well, if you take a look at the White House, it’s flawless,” he responded, before giving a spiel about his various construction projects. As the reporter tried to ask a follow up question, Trump interrupted, saying: “I have a responsibility — oh, you’re so pathetic. Listen, I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape.”

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: With Dems on the Rise, Organizers Ramp Up Push for Paid Family and Medical Leave
content:
Organizers say guaranteed national paid leave is possible — and a tax on corporations and the wealthy could pay for it.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The United States is one of the only nations in the world without a federally guaranteed paid family and medical leave policy. As U.S. workers continue to be caught between stagnant wages and rising costs, a single emergency such as an unexpected illness can put them into the untenable position of choosing between their physical health and their financial health.

In June 2025, Jasmine White of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, found herself in exactly such a situation when she became injured and unable to walk. The single mother of four had no safety net to sustain her catering business, Jazzy Good Eats & Catering. “I was forced to step away because my body wouldn’t allow me to keep going,” she said. “I didn’t have paid leave, disability coverage, or a safety net to fall back on.”

In the absence of federal action, a state-by-state movement for paid family and medical leave has spent years painstakingly pushing for policy changes — and has enjoyed growing success. According to Paid Leave for All, a nationwide coalition of organizations working on the issue, “fourteen states and the District of Columbia have passed laws to guarantee paid family and medical leave, while 18 states and D.C. along with several municipalities have paid sick time laws.”

With Pennsylvania not yet on that list of states, White was forced to take unpaid leave for four months while recuperating from her injury. “When I couldn’t work, the business couldn’t operate the way it needed to,” she said. The resulting financial precarity forced her to pivot her business model from a restaurant and catering operation toward exclusively catering, and she switched from employing full-time employees to hiring contract workers as needed.

“It feels like a never-ending cycle of working just to survive,” said White. “If you don’t work, you don’t eat. If you don’t work, you can’t pay your bills. If you don’t work, your children are affected. That reality keeps me in a constant state of work mode.”

Jennifer Driscoll of Coopersburg, Pennsylvania, experienced a similarly difficult situation when her daughter Lily was born seven weeks premature in 2007 and she needed to stay at home to care for her fragile newborn. “That decision came at a tremendous financial cost to our family,” said Driscoll. “We went into serious debt because of my extended time away from work.”

Driscoll and her husband started a nonprofit called Lily’s Hope Foundation in 2013. In her words, her goal was “to support families facing the unexpected challenges and financial hardships that come with having a premature baby or a child in the NICU.” While the organization has supported thousands of families across the U.S., Driscoll believes that “these families need more than care packages and emergency assistance.” They need state support.

According to Dawn Huckelbridge, founding director of Paid Leave for All, “the United States is one of the only countries in the entire world that doesn’t guarantee any kind of paid leave.” This includes vacation, sick leave, parental leave, or time off to care for an ailing family member.

In stark contrast to workers in the U.S., workers in Europe have a guaranteed right to four weeks of paid vacation, and varied but generous amounts of paid sick leave and parental leave depending on the country where they live.

It isn’t that Americans don’t want paid leave. A large majority of the public supports paid family and medical leave, regardless of political affiliation. “Literally any kind of demographic you could try to poll, a supermajority does support this issue,” said Huckelbridge.

It’s hard to believe that until relatively recently, working Americans didn’t even have the right to take unpaid leave for emergencies. The 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) allowed workers to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave per year without the risk of losing their job.

When the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020, advocates pushed lawmakers to expand on the FMLA with the passage of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, enabling eligible workers to access paid leave, and self-employed workers to get tax credits in very specific cases of COVID-19 infections. That law’s paid leave provisions lasted barely a year.

Then, under President Joe Biden and with the backing of Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York), advocates worked to include provisions for four weeks of paid leave in the 2021 Build Back Better bill. While the bill passed the House of Representatives, it failed in the Senate by one vote: Sen. Joe Manchin (D-West Virginia) refused to vote for the bill, effectively killing it.

The lack of guaranteed paid leave disproportionately impacts low-income women and people of color. Huckelbridge thinks that part of the reason why the U.S. has no federally guaranteed paid leave is that Congress has historically been white male-dominated. “There’s this bias of people who do less of the caregiving,” she said. “Issues that have disproportionately impacted women and people of color have often been sidelined; they’ve often been sort of cut and compromised because they haven’t been framed as fundamental and economic kitchen table issues, when in fact they are.”

In the wake of Manchin’s exit from politics, and historic Democratic Party congressional wins in the November 2026 midterm elections, Wendy Chun-Hoon, president and executive director of the Center for Law and Social Policy, is optimistic: “With the clear majority in both chambers of Congress, we expect Democrats to move swiftly to show voters ‘message received,’ and focus their first hours and days on advancing paid leave and child care for all,” she said.

Having come within a single vote of winning federally guaranteed paid leave in 2021, the Paid Leave for All coalition is now focused on passing a new bill introduced by Senator Gillibrand called the Family and Medical Insurance Leave (FAMILY) Act. Huckelbridge explained that if it were to pass, the bill would ensure paid leave for things like “serious health events, new babies, injuries, illness [in] your family.”

The question that routinely arises with such safety net proposals is how to pay for them and if businesses would suffer. According to Huckelbridge, “It would be administered by the federal government, it would be funded by the federal government, and it would in that way be very much a business support.”

The funding could come from general revenues or from a modest payroll tax. But, given that big corporations and wealthy individuals continue to be enriched from lower taxation, Huckelbridge suggested one simple funding source could come from “taking taxes from the wealthiest and big corporations to make them pay their fair share.”

When asked about the likelihood that President Donald Trump would veto every piece of Democratic Party-supported legislation landing on his desk, Chun-Hoon said, “If this White House chooses to continue to ignore families’ needs — if they veto paid leave — then Congress will have it ready for the next president to sign it in 2029.”

In the meantime, advocates in Pennsylvania, where there is no statewide paid leave, are continuing to push for legislation. Dan O’Brien, the family economic stability policy director at the Pennsylvania-based organization Children First, has been working on passing a state bill called the Family Care Act.

If passed, that act would establish an insurance fund to cover paid sick leave to recover from major surgery, as well as parental leave for the birth or adoption of a new child, and to care for children recovering from serious illness or for elderly parents needing critical care or rehabilitation.

That bill, which has passed the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, has bipartisan support in the Pennsylvania State Senate but, as of this writing, has not yet been introduced for a vote. O’Brien explained that “[state] senate leadership has decided to side with the big business lobbyists in Harrisburg who have been opposing our efforts.” He is confident that if it is brought to a vote in the state senate, it will pass.

Pennsylvania has traditionally been a politically “purple” state, swinging between support for Democrats and Republicans. O’Brien is hopeful that if Pennsylvania lawmakers pass the Family Care Act, it could be a “blueprint for conservative states and the federal government to do the same.”

Workers like White and Driscoll are among those for whom a paid leave guarantee would offer desperately needed relief. “Paid family and medical leave is about dignity, stability, and the ability to take care of ourselves and the people who depend on us,” said White. “We shouldn’t have to reach a breaking point before we’re allowed to rest.”

Driscoll concurred, saying, “No one should have to choose between being there for their family and being able to pay their bills.”

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: We’ve Reached the 31st Global Climate Summit and Have Yet to Phase Out Emissions
content:
COP31 is making clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency.

COP31 is making clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

With the 31st annual UN climate summit (COP31) currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, and deadly heat waves and catastrophic floods having been a hallmark of 2026, a year set to be the hottest on record, this is a propitious time to take stock of the progress made on climate change and the environment and reflect on the challenges of a world beyond fossil fuels.

No one anticipates any breakthroughs in negotiations at COP31, which concludes on Friday, November 20. Climate change is not even a major issue regularly getting the attention of global leadership, and global banks, including the largest U.S. banks, are dropping their climate commitments. If there was ever an international consensus in fighting climate change, it is surely gone, as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told COP31. Indeed, recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva scolded fellow leaders at the UN climate summit in Turkey by saying they are interested in “talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations.” It is thus not surprising that the leaders of major countries around the world (Germany, France, Italy, Canada, Japan, India, and China) skipped the event. U.S. President Donald Trump of course is also not attending since he (again) withdrew the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement.

Short-term political concerns have dominated past global climate summits, and it is no different this time around. COP31 has exposed yet again the deep divisions among developed and developing countries over adaptation funding and climate finance accountability. And Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez objected to calls for an end to the age of fossil fuels by telling the conference that “we reaffirm our sovereign right to strengthen our energy and oil industry as a driver of our national development.” Sadly enough, this is a view that is now openly shared by many leaders around the world, including Turkey, the host of this year’s climate summit which remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, especially coal-fired electricity generation. So while electrification has emerged as a major theme of this year’s summit, it seems more than likely that oil and gas could dominate for decades.

Moreover, like in all previous climate summits, the formal agenda of COP31 does not include an item on the relationship between militarism and climate action. No mention of the long-term environmental costs of war, militarism, and occupation — including the destruction of Gaza, which has unleashed massive greenhouse gas emissions — is expected to feature in COP31’s final text. In sum, COP31 will make clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency. Radical and legal activism are the best hopes for our future.

James K. Boyce is an author, naturalist, and a leading scholar of environmental economics and climate policy. In this interview, Boyce discusses the evolution of the political economy of the environment and of environmental movements, the opportunities and failures of global climate summits, and he highlights the links between climate change and inequality.

Boyce is professor emeritus of economics and senior fellow at the Political Economy Research Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. He is the author of many books, including Economics for People and the Planet: Inequality in the Era of Climate Change. He is also the recipient of major awards including the 2025 Common Wealth Prize, the 2024 Global Inequality Research Award, and the 2017 Leontief Prize for Advancing the Frontiers of Economic Thought.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C.J. Polychroniou: Climate change is the defining crisis of our time. We have also been in an environmental crisis since the late 1960s. Indeed, the first Earth Day took place in 1970 as a response to rising environmental concerns. Shortly thereafter, we also had the establishment of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), further evidence that the environment was becoming a top issue for voters. Now, you have devoted much of your career to investigating the dynamics of environmental degradation, including the link between inequality and the environment. Can you discuss a bit how the study of the political economy of the environment has evolved over the past 50 years?

James K. Boyce: Dirty air, polluted water, and depleted natural resources put environmental issues on the political map. As so often is the case, the economics profession was behind the curve. When I went to Oxford to study for my doctorate in 1980, the university did not offer a single course in environmental economics.

As the importance of environmental “externalities” — impacts of production and consumption that do not show up in market prices — became more evident, the new field of environmental economics developed with its focus on how to restore “efficiency,” in the cost-benefit analysis sense of maximizing net present value, once externalities are factored into the mix via “shadow prices.”

Initially, few economists connected the dots between environmental degradation and inequality. In part this reflected the times: The field emerged during the heyday of free-market fundamentalism, when most economists dismissed inequality as a non-issue. But two more things contributed to that neglect. One was the ideological axiom that the economic well-being of a society can be measured by summing the dollar value of output (adjusted, perhaps, for the imputed dollar value of environmental impacts) without considering how those dollars are distributed; that is, ignoring the elementary fact that a dollar is worth less to a billionaire than to a worker struggling to make ends meet. The second was ignoring the role of power — political power as well as purchasing power — in shaping how markets and governments alike function, including the role of power in shaping decisions on environmental policy.

Over time, this too has begun to change.

What about the evolution of the environmental movements? How has environmental activism evolved over the years, and what have been its main achievements so far?

There have always been diverse strands in environmental movements, within and across countries, so generalizations should be taken with a grain of salt. In the United States, I would say that in its early years the environmental movement saw the basic problem as one of protecting nature from people. “People” were seen as the problem. In practice, this often meant poor people who supposedly could not “afford” to care for the environment. This notion went hand-in-hand with the rampant Malthusianism of the time which portrayed population growth as the root of all ills.

Things began to change in the 1980s with the birth of the environmental justice (EJ) movement. Its initial focus was the disproportionate siting of hazardous waste facilities in communities composed primarily of Black people. Gradually, the movement widened its scope to disparities across a wide range of environmental impacts, along lines of class, ethnicity, and gender as well as race. Environmental justice reframed the environmental narrative not simply as protecting nature from people but protecting some people from environmental harms caused by the actions of other people.At the same time, the international women’s health movement effectively challenged the axiom that overpopulation is the main cause of poverty and environmental degradation.

In the U.S., race and ethnicity often are even stronger than income as predictors of exposure to environmental hazards.

A milestone was achieved in 1994 with the executive order issued by President Bill Clinton that directed federal agencies to address disproportionate environmental impacts on minorities and low-income people. The political fortunes of the environmental justice movement have risen and fallen over time — the Trump regime marks a nadir in this as in so many other respects — but environmental justice has made a lasting imprint on environmental activism.

Much has been achieved. Air quality and water quality have improved greatly, reducing illnesses and premature mortality from pollution. The Montreal Protocol, an international agreement that went into effect in 1989, protected the stratospheric ozone layer from depletion by chlorofluorocarbons. The decline of biodiversity has been arrested, though by no means halted. And a start has been made on the historic transition from fossil fuels to cleaner sources of energy. Much remains to be done, but it is important to recognize these achievements, if only to take heart from their evidence that we are on the right side of history.

Inequality is one of the biggest and most troubling issues of our time. What are the mechanisms by which economic inequality can lead to environmental degradation?

Economic inequality and the accompanying inequalities of power make it easier for those on top of the economic ladder to impose environmental costs on everyone else, and especially on those at or near the bottom.

This would be the case even in the ideal world of neoclassical economic orthodoxy, where maximizing the dollar value of net benefits is the touchstone for welfare optimization. Standard cost-benefit analysis is guided by the principle of “one dollar, one vote,” not “one person, one vote.” Under this formula, those people with more dollars have more votes. The cost of environmental harms is measured by willingness to pay to prevent them. If those who suffer the harms are poor — while those who reap the benefits from environmental degradation, via higher corporate profits and lower market prices, are relatively wealthy — then the so-called “efficient” level of environmental protection is weaker than would otherwise be the case.

The impact of inequality does not stop there, however. Political power often mirrors purchasing power. The result is to distort environmental policy-making even further by biasing decisions against those with less political voice. This helps to explain why in the U.S., race and ethnicity often are even stronger than income as predictors of exposure to environmental hazards.

It has been argued that climate change also increases economic inequalities. How so, and what can be done about that?

Like other kinds of environmental degradation, climate change tends to hit the poor harder than the rich. In part, this is because lower-income people have less ability to withstand environmental costs than do high-income people. If climate change led to a 10 percent decline in incomes that was equally distributed across the board, it would be a bother to the rich, a bigger deal for the middle class, and potentially fatal for some of the poorest people in the world. But it is also due to the fact that the costs of climate change are not, in fact, evenly distributed. Lower-income people often live in more vulnerable locations, and they are less able to afford house insurance, health insurance, air conditioning, and other means of escaping the worst effects of extreme weather events. This was vividly illustrated, for example, by the impacts of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans in 2005, a disaster that has been described as “environmental injustice in a fast-forward mode.”

In principle, climate adaptation investment should and could be preferentially channeled to those at most risk. All too often, however, scarce resources for this purpose flow to those with the most economic and political power.

What can be done about this? The first order of business is to move as quickly as possible to phase out the use of fossil fuels, doing so in a way that enhances the energy security for working people in the short run by increasing the money in their pockets, and in the long run by freeing them from periodic shortages and price gouging on the world markets for oil and gas. The second task is to make those most responsible for climate destabilization — the world’s biggest fossil fuel corporations — shoulder a fair share of the costs of disaster response and climate adaptation, and to ensure that funds for these purposes reach those in greatest need. Both of these things are possible, but only if working people exercise their democratic rights to call the shots rather than leaving environmental policy in the hands of oligarchs.

The COP31 summit is happening this month in Antalya, Turkey. How much impact do these global summits have?

The fact that we are now on the 31st summit and have yet to phase out emissions of greenhouse gases shows that their impact has been limited. But this is not to say that summits are useless. They raise the visibility of the issues across the world, and to some extent, they offer a forum for concerted action in reducing emissions and funding investments for climate adaptation and for compensation for losses and damages that have not been averted.

Local and national action to combat climate change does not have to wait for an international agreement.

Much more needs to be done. The fact that the U.S. administration today has chosen to obstruct progress rather than cooperate (let alone play a leading role in addressing climate change) only makes matters worse.

But it is crucial to recognize that local and national action to combat climate change does not have to wait for an international agreement. Curbing carbon emissions is often depicted as a textbook collective-action problem: Why should any country reduce emissions if others fail to do so? This was the argument invoked by President George W. Bush when he refused to ratify the 1997 Kyoto Protocol. This pretext for inaction rests on the misleading premise that the transition from fossil fuels to clean energy necessarily is a cost rather than a benefit to the country and its people.

In reality, proactive climate policies can bring enormous health benefits to the public thanks to cleaner air, for the simple reason that fossil fuels spew out multiple toxic pollutants along with carbon dioxide. Moreover, fossil-fuel phasedown policies can be designed to raise the purchasing power of working people through energy security cashbacks. These benefits of cleaner air and higher incomes accrue regardless of what other countries do. In addition, being a leader in the development of clean energy technologies will confer a strong competitive advantage to the country’s economy in coming decades. So national moves to cut emissions need not be held hostage to decisions by other countries.

Are you optimistic about humanity’s chances in curbing the climate crisis before it destroys civilization as we know it?

Well, “civilization as we know it” today has deep flaws in terms of obscene economic inequality and needless environmental degradation. To improve human well-being, we need to fix both.

Rephrasing the question in terms of curbing the climate crisis before it irreparably damages human well-being, I am optimistic that is possible. There is no scientific or technical reason it cannot be done; instead, there are political obstacles. These are formidable, but when it comes to politics, I take inspiration from Antonio Gramsci’s optimism of the will.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign.
