author: Ames Alexander
title: EPA Plane for Chemical Detection in Toxic Emergencies Can No Longer Do Its Job
content:
Former agency employees who worked on the airborne detection effort say the program has unraveled.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Okla., injured 74 people last November, the federal government’s chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” said Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

The program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists said two of those missions — the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana — were badly mismanaged.

At Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s Inspector General is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

Now — at a time when chemical emergencies are increasing — the plane can no longer do its job. In June, the EPA Inspector General found the plane’s systems can’t identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead the process takes about a week, far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA said the plane’s chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

But five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem.

The old sensors still work, they said. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

“I fear that the public is at risk,” said Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an important program, and they’ve allowed it to waste away to nothing.”

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology. The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over New Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, said the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he said.

The program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” said Thomas, who later went to work for a company that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas said.

During its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions — an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated — and more than 50 were treated at hospitals — when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a likely carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The U.S. Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021. The Trump administration, meanwhile, is proposing to roll back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

Former ASPECT program managers said they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators — who manage environmental emergencies — to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they said.

Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, said ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he said, the plane could save lives.

Instead, “It’s being shut down and not used.”

On Feb. 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion — and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil said, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7 — a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier — or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport — its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later said in an affidavit.

The National Transportation Safety Board later concluded the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors said threatened an explosion. Temperature readings showed the railcars were cooling.

An EPA Inspector General investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On Aug. 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, La.

Less than four miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek said, “It was just like it was raining oil.”

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek said he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he said, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek sued Smitty’s in September 2025. The lawsuit has been consolidated with an ongoing class-action case.

The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a one-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT — the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

The agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants — but at levels considered safe.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He said it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

Kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire. The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

In a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren’t flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

More than a year later, Polezcek said, the residue still coats much of his property. When his grandchildren play outside, he said, they come back inside with “little black feet.”

“That’s my biggest concern,” he told Floodlight. “What is it doing to them?”

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

“I really think it was a pitiful job,” he said. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’ ”

In June, the EPA Inspector General confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

Instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian company, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the new sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid-2027,” according to the EPA.

In contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the new equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the new sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent company of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”

The new sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects.

Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA or the firm where Thomas now works, said the new Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he said.

“To say, ‘We’re just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he said.

The old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas said. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a plan to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, Kroutil said.

He and his former colleagues said they have no confidence that the new sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offered a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”

title: Jeffries Accused of “Straight Up Lie” for Claiming AIPAC Is Ending Donations
content:
AIPAC isn’t “out of the political fundraising business,” as Jeffries claimed, but has rather shifted funding elsewhere.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Friday, a CNN pundit called out Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’s (D-New York) claim that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) is ending its campaign spending, calling the claim a “straight up lie.”

The remark comes as the House minority leader faces public scrutiny over his ties to the Israel lobby ahead of the new House Democratic leadership election this week.

In the CNN segment on Friday, panelists noted that Jeffries is facing pushback from the public despite his widespread support within the House Democratic caucus. The panel, hosted by Audie Cornish, questioned whether or not Jeffries can overcome his close ties to Israel to become more popular with the public, noting that he received nearly $50,000 from AIPAC in the 2025 to 2026 election cycle and $315,000 total from pro-Israel groups.

A clip of Jeffries speaking on talk show #RonaldMartinUnfiltered last Wednesday played before the group discussion. In that clip, Jeffries said: “AIPAC announced, like three weeks ago, that they were out of the political fundraising business — that they were going to shut down their PAC, which has the ability to give members of Congress $5,000 a year.”

“They were going to shut that down, they were going to stop making endorsements, and stop raising money,” Jeffries said.

Panelist Luke Thomas, a sports podcast host and political commentator, said that this claim is untrue and nothing more than a PR move.

“What he said in that interview was just a straight up lie,” Thomas said. AIPAC is “just rerouting it through pass-through organizations and the super PAC,” he said, referring to AIPAC’s United Democracy Project (UDP).

Facing an increasingly toxic public image, AIPAC announced in late October that it was no longer going to make direct PAC contributions or endorsements of candidates. However, the PAC is still planning to use its vast funding to influence elections, saying that they will still use individual donors to give to candidates. It will also still be directing funds to candidates using UDP, which means that it can launder its contributions behind the lesser-known group.

Jeffries has been caught trying to downplay AIPAC’s influence in the past. Though he’s repeated the claim several times, it’s extremely misleading to say that AIPAC can only give $5,000 per election cycle to candidates, since AIPAC routes tens of millions of dollars through other methods to candidates.

“They’re removing some of their public visibility in the way he’s describing, but this idea that they’re not involved in campaign donations in serious ways” is untrue, Thomas said.

Thomas brought up an incident last week in which 11 members of Jeffries’s caucus missed the critical vote to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in order to attend a meeting held by Elect Democratic Women (EDW), ultimately sinking the effort. EDW has been accused of being an AIPAC pass-through group, with its PAC having taken $1 million from UDP this spring. AIPAC has funneled donations through other groups this election cycle, many of them unknown because they haven’t been exposed by journalists.

“As a progressive, I was radicalized by the Iraq War. I was radicalized by Donald Trump. I have been absolutely radicalized by the failures of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. And I doubt that I’m the only person on the left who feels that way,” Thomas said.

Both Jeffries and Schumer, the Senate minority leader facing a challenge for his leadership position by Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), have been increasingly criticized for being backed by dark money groups that represent corporate and industry interests, rather than the good of the public.

According to an analysis by Sludge, Jeffries is the second-highest House Democratic recipient of corporate PAC fundraising this election cycle, with $1.32 million, from donors like the finance, military, and tech industries. He’s second only to House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (California), who’s gotten $1.42 million. Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (Massachusetts) is the fourth top recipient in the caucus, at $1.11 million.

content:

Dozens of incoming Democratic representatives-elect have signed on to an open letter demanding that leaders of their party within the House of Representatives support new rules that will prohibit stock trading by lawmakers.

The incoming lawmakers — fresh off their enormous victories in midterm election races across the United States earlier this month — noted that voters elected them to end “corrupt self-dealing” in Washington. Democrats can deliver on that promise “the day the new Congress is sworn in,” the letter-writers stated.

“We are calling on our Democratic leaders in the House to quickly adopt a rule barring members and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, derivatives, and other related securities, with limited exceptions such as a diversified mutual fund or an investment held in a qualified blind trust,” the letter said.

title: Even When Domestic Workers Have Labor Protections, Claiming Them Isn’t Easy
content:
For immigrant domestic workers, asserting their rights can lead to dangerous forms of retaliation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

For seven years, Teresa tended to another family’s children inside a Manhattan home. She now calls it the worst job of her life. They kept meticulous logbooks of the hours she put in, an unwitting manifestation of a household that tallied everything and answered for none of it.

Teresa first began working in Mexico when she was 13 years old, yet in all those years, no employer wore on her like this one. It was the family’s rule that she could not even speak to the other nannies at the playground. So through long afternoons she was mostly mute, laughing without a word and saving what she wanted to say for when she was out of sight. And beneath this stranglehold, the family wasn’t even paying her what she was owed.

Help arrived when a friend mentioned that the National Domestic Workers Alliance (NDWA) ran free training sessions for nannies. There, she learned a worker holds incontestable rights no matter their immigration status. And she realized the family’s ongoing pattern of underpayment was wage theft. Organizers told her she could fight back, but a claim lives or dies on proof through documentation of hours worked, cash receipts saved, and money exchanged as it passed from their hands to hers.

Then she remembered the logbooks.

“It occurred to me to grab the books without permission, knowing that they trusted me,” she said. “I took them home, took copies for the years I was there, 2017 until 2024. Then I returned the books to their place and didn’t touch anything else.”

“That’s been my most powerful weapon now to confront them,” she said.

Teresa, who is using a pseudonym for fear of retribution, moved to New York in 2003 and has made her living through housecleaning and childcare, which enabled her to put her own children through private school in the U.S. She knew the wealthy family whose logbooks she copied could destroy her, and she dreaded going to court, but she persevered with her claim “to show that it can be done.” Her former employer even agreed to an early settlement until the family’s lawyer went silent, forcing Teresa’s attorney to bring the case before a judge.

Teresa is one worker living through a pivotal moment for American domestic work, a national reckoning about whether existing protections translate into substantive security. Over the past 15 years in cities and states across the East Coast, nannies, house cleaners, and home care workers have secured once-impossible protections that promise minimum wage, written contracts, and safeguards against retaliation. But while these rights have been codified, exercising them safely is a fraught prospect for those whose livelihoods are jeopardized once they speak out.

Marrisa Senteno, director of NDWA’s New York chapter, has spent a decade building New York’s enforcement program, and recognizes that a statute does not guarantee instantaneous progress. “A law being passed isn’t a magic wand. You pass it, and things don’t just appear,” she said.

For immigrant workers, a household withholding wages can resort to more dangerous forms of retaliation, weaponizing their legal status to sidestep accountability. Nicole Kligerman, who founded the Pennsylvania chapter of NDWA in 2018, has witnessed a single reprisal hush an entire workforce. “That happens to one person, and everybody knows about it immediately,” she said. And when the city is sluggish in its investigation and a claim stalls, Kligerman added, “that’s a real chilling effect.”

When New York passed the country’s first Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights in 2010, the measure was billed as a national model for bringing labor law into the private home. The state’s domestic workforce — roughly 328,000 people in 2021, 63% of them immigrants and 92% women — gained overtime pay, a weekly day of rest, and protection from harassment. But six years later, Senteno could count the claims filed under the law on one hand, and she recalled state officials concluding, “Well, there must not be cases.”

Enforcement at the state labor department is complaint-driven, Senteno said, meaning an investigation typically begins only when a worker comes forward. Isolated inside their employers’ homes, domestic workers rarely have someone who can help them recognize a violation as it happens, and many have “zero knowledge” of how the process works to file a complaint, Senteno explained. Excluded from the National Labor Relations Act, domestic workers have no federally protected right to unionize, meaning there’s no shop steward to confide in or union meeting to air grievances.

So Senteno’s New York City chapter of NDWA set out to find the communal spaces where nannies and housekeepers already cross paths, settings where word of a missed overtime payment or a successful claim could pass from one worker to another. “Let’s change the definition of workplaces,” she suggested. “Those are the parks. Those are the libraries. Sometimes it’s a laundromat.” The chapter then trained domestic workers as enforcement fellows — using a curriculum Senteno likened to “law school 101” — and sent them out to do the talking, guided by the program’s mantra that “workers know each other the best.”

Leydis Muñoz is a member of NDWA’s NY-based enforcement program and a former fellow. She spent 18 years as a nanny and finds that workers rarely want to pursue a claim against a current employer because they fear losing steady work. Some employers retaliate online, posting photos beside warnings to other families and making allegations against specific workers. Muñoz now combs social media to reach those pictured. And for many, the Trump administration has sharpened a deeper fear tied to their immigration status. “If you don’t want to do it right now, it’s OK,” Muñoz tells them. “But now let’s prepare you … so when you are ready, you are ready to move.”

Even with this support, a worker filing a claim must still face the household they are accusing. Typically, a legal service provider reviews the worker’s case and sends the employer a demand letter laying out the violations they found. Once that letter arrives and the employer realizes someone is holding them accountable, Senteno said, their “shame and embarrassment turns immediately into anger,” which bears down on the worker through phone calls, texts, and threats until they are “paralyzed.”

Teresa’s employers tried stonewalling her well before she filed a complaint, when she returned after a brief job elsewhere and requested a written contract. “They told me, no, no contract. We know each other,” she recalled, and she let it slide. Once she took records to NDWA, the organization connected her with a lawyer, who found the family had recorded their own theft.

The challenges domestic workers face in labor disputes aren’t unique to New York.

In Washington, D.C., Mayor Muriel Bowser’s fiscal year 2027 spending plan proposed wiping out the attorney general’s grants to community groups, including NDWA’s DMV chapter, which serves the D.C. metro area. The suggested cut seems to be due to a drop in revenue. “That’s the only explanation that we really have,” said Alana Eichner, the DMV chapter co-director. “But everything about a budget is a choice.” By June, after a vigorous campaign by grantees, the D.C. Council’s Committee on the Judiciary and Public Safety restored the full $1.1 million to its budget recommendations.

The grants were seeded in 2018, when legal aid lawyers challenged a nanny’s firing over her pregnancy and discovered the District’s Human Rights Act shielded all employees from discrimination “except domestic servants.” Organizers spent four years fighting to purge the statute of language Eichner referred to as “archaic, racist, and sexist.” Finally, in 2022, the District passed a measure requiring employers to provide domestic workers with a written contract and establishing a program in the attorney general’s office to help enforce the new law.

But asserting that right can be a delicate maneuver, so DMV organizers rehearse with workers how to request a contract. Some workers assure organizers they asked, Eichner said. “And then we find out later, they actually did not do it.” The specter of backlash silences them, she explained, and all the more since the federal takeover of the city’s police in August 2025 and the surge in immigration enforcement that followed. Eichner recalled a worker who asked to be paid for all her hours, only to have her employers invoke her undocumented status and threaten to call Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) if she kept pushing.

Though New York pioneered the Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights that was replicated in DMV, Senteno said she now takes her cues from Philadelphia.

Kligerman’s chapter there retooled the city’s labor enforcement mechanism after Philadelphia’s 2020 Domestic Worker Bill of Rights proved too lax. At the time, workers took complaints to the city’s Office of Worker Protections, where an employer found to have stolen wages only had to repay them, with little in the way of fines or damages. Among those it failed was an undocumented Black Caribbean nanny in one of the city’s wealthiest, whitest neighborhoods. The nanny asked to negotiate a contract with her employer, and she was fired on the spot, then blacklisted through word of mouth and social media. The nanny waited months for word on her complaint, Kligerman recalled. “A law is nothing without its enforcement,” she said.

The worker-led overhaul arrived in 2025 with the POWER Act, which was passed unanimously and covers 750,000 Philadelphians. Sponsored by Councilmember Kendra Brooks, a former domestic worker herself, the law allows the city to open investigations without waiting for a complaint, pays damages directly to those harmed, strips repeat violators of business licenses and city contracts, and enters them into a public “Bad Actors” database.

From there, Brooks and Councilmember Rue Landau led the charge to address the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown directly, helping to pass the “ICE Out” package by a veto-proof majority. The package of seven bills restricts federal immigration enforcement in the city. Six of the bills went into effect July 7, though a lawsuit from the Trump administration halted one that banned the use of face coverings by ICE agents and law enforcement.

“There’s not a functional distinction between worker injustice and immigration injustice,” Kligerman said of the city’s efforts to limit immigration enforcement.

In the South, winning labor protections for low-wage workers remains painfully slow.

Jewel Gatling, who grew up in Portsmouth, Virginia, remembers her grandmother heading out to clean houses whenever a child fell sick, or the family needed extra income. Gatling now organizes for Care in Action, NDWA’s political affiliate in Virginia — a state that did not extend the minimum wage to domestic workers until 2020 and that still denies live-in workers any overtime protections.

A bill to address that gap, guaranteeing domestic workers time and a half for every hour beyond 40 a week, passed both chambers with bipartisan support in 2024 and 2025, but Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin vetoed it both times. His second rejection simply copied and pasted the explanation from his first. “Not a comma was different,” Gatling said.

This year, Gov. Abigail Spanberger finally signed Senate Bill 28 into law, though its protections won’t take effect until July 2028 — and only if the 2027 legislature reenacts it. To strip the bill of any fiscal impact and smooth its passage, advocates carved out home care workers paid through Medicaid, counting on a separate collective bargaining proposal to give them a path to overtime, though Spanberger vetoed that measure. The outcome especially stings for Gatling, whose organization knocked on doors to elect the officials who delivered it. “We value you for your endorsement,” she said. “We value you for pictures and photo ops. But we’re going to give you a pat on the head and ask you to still wait.”

“This is where the first enslaved landed,” Gatling said of Virginia. “If you lived on the property, they see you as property. A care provider is not a lawnmower. A care provider is not a washing machine. They are a person.” Immigrants face an added hazard, she noted, as some employers “will absolutely use immigration status to manipulate workers,” a tactic lawmakers banned in the same session. “It’s just now … you have an environment that condones it.”

Starting in 2023, workers who stood up to such employers could turn to the Department of Homeland Security’s Deferred Action for Labor Enforcement program, which granted more than 7,700 immigrants involved in labor investigations temporary deportation relief and work permits. However, last year the Trump administration scrapped the program without public notice.

Even if people have never hired a domestic worker, Eichner believes that caring about their labor rights is part of a well-functioning democracy. “If you have a society where people’s rights are regularly being violated, and laws are not being enforced, that undermines your whole society,” she said. “There are many, many laws that end up only existing on paper.”

In October, NDWA confirmed Teresa’s case had been resolved, though it did not share the terms. She kept a personal ledger of what the ordeal was worth. “Winning the case is important, but the most important part has been learning how to use my voice, being heard, and pursuing my justice,” she said. “Whatever comes from that verdict, the money isn’t the goal.”

Teresa said that word has spread among nannies in Brooklyn that families are bringing in childcare workers from countries such as Colombia, El Salvador, and Mexico on live-in contracts for a fraction of the standard rate. She said she met one earning just $5 an hour. “That’s robbery,” Teresa told the young woman, offering to introduce her to NDWA. But the worker declined, wary of burning a bridge with the only people she had in the country.

“I wish they would open their eyes,” Teresa said.

Prism Reports is an independent and nonprofit newsroom led by journalists of color. We report from the ground up and at the intersections of injustice.

author: Aneri Pattani
title: Local Governments Are Winning Opioid Settlements. How Do They Spend the Money?
content:
Governments spent about $3.7 billion in settlement funds last year, and it didn’t all go to preventing overdoses.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

State and local governments spent about $3.7 billion in opioid settlement funds last year. That’s more than the median annual income of 42,000 American families combined.

The money comes from companies that were sued for aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis.

Large amounts went to addiction treatment, recovery housing, and other initiatives that many public health researchers and families affected by the crisis agree fit the spirit of the settlements — to save lives and remediate the problem.

But other expenditures had tenuous ties to addiction, including:

$150,000 for street lighting in Camden, New Jersey.

$130,000 for Flock cameras in Carmel, Indiana.

At least $84,000 for city insurance, building utilities, vehicle repairs, and other standard city expenses in Mullens, West Virginia.

$36,200 for a pickleball court in Gilmer County, West Virginia.

KFF Health News uncovered these expenditures among about 17,500 examined through a yearlong investigation with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Shatterproof, a national nonprofit focused on addiction. The team filed public records requests, scoured government websites, and extracted expenditures, which were then sorted into categories such as treatment or prevention. The result is the most comprehensive national database documenting how opioid settlement money was used (or left unspent) in 2025.

The pot of settlement cash, which many addiction survivors and their advocates consider “blood money,” is expected to total about $60 billion over nearly two decades. It is split among state governments, counties, cities, and specially created opioid settlement councils in some places.

Although there are some spending guidelines within the settlement agreements, there is considerable flexibility, a vacuum of leadership and oversight, and significant gaps in how the public can track the dollars.

Much of the questionable spending — ranging from law enforcement gadgets to mundane municipal needs — happens at the county and city level, where local leaders often have no background in addiction policy and sometimes award the money to the first people who ask for it.

Nationwide, local decision-makers control nearly half the money, according to OpioidSettlementTracker.com, a site dedicated to following this cash. Proponents of local control say these officials know their communities best and are closest to the problem. But as dubious expenditures mount, some recovery advocates question if county and city officials are equipped to handle this once-in-a-generation opportunity.

“It shouldn’t be run by these politicians,” said Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a person in recovery and a New Jersey-based advocate who’s been following the opioid cash for years.

She said people directly affected by the crisis understand gaps in their local community care systems best and have the most insight into how funds can be used effectively. “This whole opioid settlement should be run by the people who’ve lost everything,” she said.

As executive director of the Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, Burke Beaty sees those people daily. A woman who lost her brother and father to addiction and later landed in the hospital herself. An 11-year-old boy, holding his grandfather’s hand at an overdose awareness event, as they mourned a family member.

“This is money from dead people and people left behind,” Burke Beaty said.

Of course, many local officials have lost friends and family to the crisis as well, and many care deeply about putting the money to good use.

Unlike state officials, who have access to health departments with specific expertise and staff whose entire job is writing policy, local decision-makers often work with bare-bones support. They may juggle other jobs alongside their official duties and can be bombarded by aggressive sales tactics from companies that view the settlements as a gold rush. They must determine how to make an impact with opioid settlement cash while facing the sober reality of needing to balance a government budget, keep public schools running, and ensure roads are maintained.

Burke Beaty acknowledges these challenges and offers to work with many local leaders in her area, often writing letters, showing up at public meetings, and creating reports with detailed feedback on how localities spent the money.

But when these efforts go ignored, she wonders if it’s because of a lack of resources or “a lack of willingness to do the right thing,” she said. “Did this come from a place of ignorance or an ‘I don’t care’ place?”

It can be tempting to suggest state governments should oversee all the cash, especially as some debatable spending patterns emerge at the local level.

In the Tobacco Master Settlement of 1998, cigarette companies paid hundreds of billions of dollars to states, typically without county or city involvement. Ultimately, much of the money went to plugging budget gaps, and, over 20 years, less than 3% of tobacco settlement and tax-related revenue was directed to anti-smoking programs.

“It is not likely that whatever model we pick is going to work flawlessly,” said Philip Rutherford, who leads substance use strategy at the National Council for Mental Wellbeing, a nonprofit representing community mental health and addiction treatment organizations.

Splitting the opioid money with local governments offers some advantages, he added. They spend less on administrative costs, can pivot more quickly as the drug landscape changes, and can test innovations.

It’s also not unusual for local officials to involve themselves in areas in which they lack personal expertise, said Annie Qing, who oversees health and human services work at the National Association of Counties.

“There are a lot of county commissioners that are making decisions on roads that may not be construction experts,” Qing said. Their role is to seek out subject matter experts, combine their knowledge with what they know their community needs, and identify investments “that make the most sense for their county.”

For support in allocating opioid settlement cash, they can turn to universities, county associations, and national public health and policy groups.

Still, it can be tricky to apply academic research and high-level principles to the messy, on-the-ground realities of settlement spending.

Take the case of automated external defibrillators, or AEDs. These portable electronic devices can save lives in the event of sudden cardiac arrest.

Last year, about 100 localities across 20 states committed $3.7 million in opioid funds to expenditures that included AEDs, cardiac monitors, and related accessories.

Many local leaders saw the purchases as saving lives from overdose, though the science doesn’t quite back them up.

Southfield, Michigan, purchased six Lifepak cardiac monitors and related supplies for about $350,000. Mayor Kenson Siver said overdose response has become increasingly complex, as people often use a mix of opioids and stimulants, and that paramedics need to be prepared for a range of situations.

Cardiac monitors go beyond traditional AEDs to measure how effectively someone is breathing, he said, which can help emergency responders determine if “interventions are working and identify deterioration or complications that require additional treatment.”

However, emergency medical responders say there’s a fundamental misunderstanding. AEDs and cardiac monitors are critical public health tools — but they are rarely used for opioid overdoses.

“I’m not saying that you never will, but the number is so low,” said Dalton Barrett, a paramedic in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, where he leads the post-overdose response team and oversees the county’s opioid settlement funds.

In opioid overdoses, people stop breathing. They typically need oxygen or naloxone, a medication that can reverse overdoses.

AEDs work only in cardiac emergencies and when the machine can detect a shockable heart rhythm — not common among overdose victims, Barrett said.

When jurisdictions buy AEDs with opioid dollars, they’re more likely plugging gaps in their general budget, which should be covering required ambulance equipment, he said. “I have a hard time identifying this as a particularly strong or targeted use of settlement funds.”

The only exception would be if a jurisdiction started a new ambulance team dedicated to overdose response and needed an AED to bring the vehicle to code, he said.

Generally, Barrett would prefer that opioid cash be spent hiring someone to follow up with people who have overdosed and connect them to treatment, housing, or other resources.

“People that suffer from addiction are looking for trust,” he said. “They’re not looking for fancy equipment.”

Some advocates are calling on states to rein in local governments’ spending from the settlements.

But no one is eager to take on that role. State officials don’t win friends by exerting control over local money. And, in some cases, they’re barred from doing so.

Jennifer Tourville is executive director of a University of Tennessee initiative that provides guidance to local governments on spending opioid cash. Her team’s work is funded by the state’s opioid abatement council.

“We aren’t permitted to tell counties what they can and cannot buy,” she said. “We try and provide guidance on the intent of the funds and what would be most impactful for their community.”

A few states have issued lists of items that opioid money cannot be used for, often called unallowable lists. They generally include law enforcement tools, such as body cameras and drones, as well as general emergency medical supplies, such as first aid kits and gloves.

But even those lists sometimes lack teeth.

For instance, Spencer County, Indiana, spent about $16,700 on eight new AEDs for its sheriff department — even though AEDs appeared on Indiana’s unallowable list, as they do on three other states’.

When asked if there’d be repercussions for the county, the Indiana Commission to Combat Substance Use Disorder said the unallowable list was simply guidance.

“Statute does not grant the state any enforcement authority related to how local entities spend opioid settlement funds,” said Shelby Thomas, a spokesperson for the commission.

Spencer County leaders did not respond to requests for comment.

A similar situation occurred in Iowa.

Van Buren County used $1,000 in opioid cash to help build a recreational site with pickleball, bocce, and tennis courts. In a report to the state, the county said this would provide a youth-focused activity and prevent misuse of opioids — an argument that has been used by many jurisdictions to justify a broad set of expenditures, ranging from funding an ice skating rink to hosting sock hops and concerts.

When asked how the county determined this was an appropriate priority, county auditor Lisa Plecker said, “The use of the funds was reported to the Iowa Attorney General’s office, as required, and our justification” for it “was not questioned.”

However, the Iowa attorney general’s office doesn’t evaluate reports.

The office “does not sign off on funds used by the counties,” said Jen Green, a spokesperson for Attorney General Brenna Bird. “The office serves as the collector and holder of the counties’ reports.”

Such examples have frustrated advocates nationwide, who feel they are the only watchdogs for this cash.

Localities view this as “really easy money,” said Burke Beaty of New Jersey. Even if their spending seems inappropriate to public health experts and families affected by addiction, “legally they can do it.”

She’s hopeful that a bill recently introduced in her state could change that. It would require the New Jersey Department of Human Services, which already collects county and city reports on opioid spending, to review those reports and force localities to pay back any misused funds.

Without such oversight, people who care about the opioid cash fear the nation is set to repeat the mistakes of the tobacco settlement — and foreshadow pitfalls for the social media settlements.

The Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health has taken a leading role in providing guidance to state and local governments on the use of opioid settlement funds. Faculty from the school collaborated with other experts in the field to create principles for using the money, which have been endorsed by over 60 organizations.

Shatterproof is a national nonprofit that addresses substance use disorder through distinct initiatives, including advocating for state and federal policies, ending addiction stigma, and educating communities about the treatment system.

Shatterproof is partnering with some states on projects funded by opioid settlements. KFF Health News, the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, and the Shatterproof team that worked on this report are not involved in those efforts.

author: Jamila Osman
title: Guantánamo Is a Linchpin at the Intersection of ICE and the “War on Terror”
content:
Guantánamo is no longer an anomaly — it has become a terrifying model for US detention at home and abroad.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Guantánamo Bay has repeatedly made headlines in recent months. In August, the Trump administration sent 12 Somali men to the remote prison, several of them from Minnesota, where the community has faced relentless harassment. Some of the men have since been deported to Somalia, while others remain in detention.

Dr. Maha Hilal, a scholar of institutionalized Islamophobia and the “war on terror,” told Truthout that the recent transfers have brought “renewed attention to Guantánamo and the prison as a site of carceral violence.” But, she added, “this isn’t the first time migrants have been held at Guantánamo. There’s a historical component.”

Guantánamo’s use for migrant detention predates its role in the war on terror. Following Haiti’s 1991 coup, the U.S. detained thousands of Haitian asylum seekers intercepted at sea. In the mid- to late-1990s, tens of thousands of people fleeing Cuba on makeshift rafts were also detained there. The offshore location allowed the government to circumvent its humanitarian and legal protections to asylum seekers.

The Guantánamo Migrant Operations Center, operated by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of State with support from private contractors, has continued to detain migrants intercepted at sea. During Donald Trump’s first term, DHS proposed housing migrant children at the base as a solution to overcrowded immigration jails on the U.S. mainland. At the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order directing the expansion of the Migrant Operations Center to hold up to 30,000 “high-priority criminal aliens.” For the first time, immigrants arrested within the United States were being transferred to Guantánamo for detention.

An August 2026 congressional oversight visit found that 852 immigrants had been flown to the facility since January 2025. Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois condemned the administration’s policy as “cruel, immoral, and an abuse of taxpayer funding.”

Although Guantánamo’s newest arrivals are being held under a different legal pretext than their predecessors, the instrumentalization of national security and racialized suspicion remains unchanged.

Two months after the September 11 attacks, President George W. Bush issued a military order authorizing the detention and military trial of certain noncitizens suspected of terrorism. The first 20 detainees arrived at Guantánamo Bay on January 11, 2002, as “unlawful enemy combatants,” a label that limited their ability to challenge their detention and placed them beyond the reach of habeas corpus protections. The Bush administration capitalized on the fear and national trauma that followed 9/11 to not only suspend the rule of law, but to create a geographic and legal space that existed entirely outside of it.

“Guantánamo’s significance is not in its size or scope, but in what it represents — the right to place people outside of the law.”

Since opening, Guantánamo has held approximately 780 Muslim men and boys, the youngest of whom, Omar Khadr, was just 15 years old at the time of his detention. The vast majority of the prison’s detainees have never been charged with a crime. Many were kidnapped and captured abroad, transferred from CIA black sites, or sold to U.S. forces by bounty hunters for sums ranging from $3,000 to $25,000.

In the context of the U.S. prison system where a staggering 2 million people are incarcerated, 780 men seems like a relatively small number, but as Hilal argues, “Guantánamo’s significance is not in its size or scope, but in what it represents — the right to place people outside of the law. In that sense, it’s a problem of great magnitude.”

Guantánamo Bay quickly became synonymous with human rights abuses during the Bush administration. The Department of Justice authorized the use of “enhanced interrogation techniques,” a euphemism that described practices like waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and prolonged isolation, despite longstanding prohibitions against torture under international law.

In 2006, a UN report found that the United States had violated its international human rights obligations, and called for Guantánamo’s closure and the trial or release of detainees. In December 2008, the Senate Armed Services Committee concluded an 18-month investigation into the abuse of detainees in military custody. The committee’s final report refuted the Bush administration’s claim that the abuse was the result of a “few bad apples.” Following the report’s release, Sen. Carl Levin released a statement: “How did it come about that American military personnel stripped detainees naked, put them in stress positions, used dogs to scare them, put leashes around their necks to humiliate them, hooded them, deprived them of sleep, and blasted music at them?”

The answer was damning: what had been allowed to happen at Guantánamo directly influenced the abusive treatment of prisoners in Iraq and Afghanistan. In February 2003, a U.S. military task force preparing for the invasion of Iraq adopted an interrogation policy previously developed in Afghanistan, changing little more than the letterhead. In July, an interrogation officer at Abu Ghraib submitted a nearly identical policy for approval. Just over a year later, photographs exposing the physical torture, psychological humiliation, and sexual abuse of detainees at Abu Ghraib sparked international outrage. But Abu Ghraib was not an aberration. The Department of Defense’s failure to hold senior officials accountable for their role in authorizing torture at Guantánamo had institutionalized a system of brutality and a culture of impunity.

Guantánamo was meant to be a temporary solution to what the Bush administration deemed an extraordinary threat. Instead, it became one of the most enduring legacies of the war on terror.

Barack Obama campaigned on closing the prison in 2008. Two days after taking office, he signed an executive order directing its closure within a year. The order was met with fierce opposition in Congress. By the end of his presidency, he reduced Guantánamo’s prison population from 242 to 41, but failed to deliver on his campaign promise.

The struggle to close Guantánamo has not been confined to courtrooms, campaign trails, and congressional hearings. It has been sustained by movements in Cuba, the U.S., and within the prison itself.

In 2018, Donald Trump revoked Obama’s order and reaffirmed the government’s authority to detain future “enemy combatants” at the facility. Joe Biden also campaigned on closing the prison. In 2021, seven former detainees who had been held without charge or trial made a personal appeal to the president: “Many of us were abducted from our homes, in front of our families … Some of us had children who were born in our absence and grew up without fathers … waiting in vain for news of our return.”

At the end of Biden’s presidency, he had only managed to secure the transfer of 11 Yemeni detainees to Oman, reducing the number of prisoners at Guantánamo to 15. These 15 men remain imprisoned: three have been approved for transfer, and three others have been dubbed “forever prisoners” — men who are allegedly too dangerous to be released but have not been brought to trial. Human rights groups criticized the Obama and Biden administrations, arguing that the failure to close the prison was not due to a lack of political power, but a lack of political will.

The struggle to close Guantánamo has not been confined to courtrooms, campaign trails, and congressional hearings. It has been sustained by movements in Cuba, the U.S., and within the prison itself. Those imprisoned there have routinely resisted their indefinite detention and the physical and psychological abuse that they endure.

Since its opening, hunger strikes have been a regular occurrence within the prison, happening on a large-scale and coordinated level. Tariq Ba Odah of Yemen undertook the longest hunger strike in Guantánamo’s history, lasting for eight years. In retaliation, he was force-fed twice a day, a practice condemned by medical professionals and human rights groups. Upon his release to Saudi Arabia in 2016, he weighed 75 pounds.

In Cuba, opposition to the prison is inseparable from the broader struggle for national sovereignty and an end to the U.S. occupation. Following the Spanish-American War, the Platt Amendment imposed conditions on Cuban independence, granting the United States the right to intervene in national affairs and lease naval bases on the island. Although the amendment was repealed in 1934, the lease on Guantánamo Bay remains in place despite the Cuban government’s demands for the territory’s return.

In February 2025, the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples condemned Trump’s plan to send immigrants to Guantánamo, calling it “a flagrant violation of human rights and an affront to human dignity.” Thousands of people also rallied in Guantánamo City to oppose both Trump’s plan and the U.S military presence on the island.

Onyesonwu Chatoyer, an organizer with the Venceremos Brigade and the National Network on Cuba, told Truthout that the impact of the U.S. military base on the residents of Guantánamo Province is often overlooked by those who don’t live on the island. The naval base has economic and environmental consequences for the communities who live there under a “high degree of surveillance.”

“The base blocks fishermen from accessing marine resources. It causes pollution. It’s a drain on the countryside,” Chatoyer said.

She invites people to visit the island so that they can see the truth for themselves: “The U.S. is constantly accusing Cuba of being a dictatorship, of persecuting its own people, and yet they are the ones torturing people and holding them indefinitely without charge on illegally occupied Cuban land.”

In Cuba, opposition to the prison is inseparable from the broader struggle for national sovereignty and an end to the U.S. occupation.

From the Mirador de Malones observation point, Chatoyer says visitors can see the “full scale of the occupation.” Through a telescope “cookie-cutter suburban houses” come into view and form a dystopian picture, replete with white picket fences, American flags, and the only McDonald’s on the island.

“It’s a scar on the land,” Chatoyer said.

For Chatoyer, the prison is emblematic of the new world order imposed across much of the Global South: “The places that are under the boot of U.S. imperialism are building massive mega-prisons, are massacring land defenders and poor working-class people, are building huge police forces, and are going all-in on AI for military technology.”

The stakes of the struggle to end the occupation and uphold national sovereignty are clear: “Guantánamo is the vision of the world that these people want,” she said.

Dr. Hilal has long warned that the government’s expansive and malleable definition of terrorism would eventually extend beyond its original targets. Guantánamo can no longer be seen as an anomaly, but as a model for U.S. detention at home and abroad.

“The construction of parts of Guantánamo was modeled after a supermax prison in the United States,” Hilal told Truthout. Federal communication management units (or CMUs) are restrictive prison units established in the post-9/11 counterterrorism era that isolate certain prisoners deemed “high-risk” and restrict their communications. CMUs are often referred to as “Little Gitmo” or “Guantánamo North” by those detained there and their advocates. While these units have disproportionately been used to hold Muslim prisoners, they have increasingly held people with “unpopular” political views, including environmental and animal rights activists.

As the boundaries between military and civilian systems of control grow increasingly porous, portraying entire populations as threats to national security has helped normalize state violence and shield it from accountability. A war without clear geographic limits or defined rules of engagement blurs the line between combatant and civilian, extending the battlefield into everyday life.

When Hilal first saw images of Venezuelan men being sent to Guantánamo, she was struck by their resemblance to photographs of Muslim detainees taken by the Department of Defense two decades earlier: “They look exactly the same. The same posture. The same forms of control,” she said.

The resemblance underscores Guantánamo’s enduring symbolic power and the ease with which its logic can be imposed on new targets. “The government can convince us that we are dealing with a different manifestation of the same threat. And that threat must be dealt with in the exact same way,” Hilal told Truthout.

Although several of the Somali men recently sent to Guantánamo had no criminal records, a DHS spokesperson described them as the “worst of the worst.” The phrase echoes former Vice President Dick Cheney’s description of the prison’s first detainees as “the worst of a very bad lot.” While previous presidents may have reduced the prison’s population, they did little to dismantle the legal and political architecture that sustained it. Arguably, their failure to take meaningful action to close Guantánamo facilitated the Trump administration’s ability to expand its use to detain immigrants. Across five administrations, Guantánamo’s legacy, and the narratives that fuel it, have only become more deeply entrenched.

Whether in the war on terror or Trump’s war on immigrants, what was sold to the American public as an exception has become the rule. The detention of immigrants at Guantánamo is the latest chapter in a familiar playbook. Dehumanize, detain, disappear. All that has changed is the enemy du jour.

author: Nour Abo Aisha
title: Desperate for Space, Some Gazans Now Live — and Even Give Birth — in a Cemetery
content:
“There is no space left for us in Gaza except this cemetery. We live beside the dead,” said one Palestinian.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

When I went to meet Rasha Swerki, I couldn’t find a place to sit except for the tombstones. So I stood during the whole interview.

Swerki, 41, lives with her two sisters in a tent set up on the edge of Sheikh Radwan Cemetery, west of Gaza City. She cooks on a hearth among the graves and spreads her laundry on a tightrope among the gravestones.

I asked Swerki why she chose to live in a cemetery. She said she didn’t choose to: “We lived in the Zeitoun area … of Gaza City. But because of social customs and traditions, our relatives refused to let us stay with them since my sisters and I were on our own without a man.” Then her brother told her that he had found a place near him for them to set up a tent and drove them to it. “I found myself getting out of the car and into the cemetery,” Swerki said.

Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, many Gazans have had nowhere to return. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 85 percent of the Gaza Strip is now under evacuation orders or inside military zones, including along the so-called “Yellow Line,” which bars Palestinians from returning to the rubble of their homes. As a result, hundreds of thousands of people are crammed into less than 15 percent of the territory. With no empty ground left to pitch a tent, the overcrowding has spread to the walls of Sheikh Radwan Cemetery, turning graves from a resting place for the dead into a last refuge for the living.

While there are no official exact figures on how many displaced people are currently sheltering inside Gaza’s cemeteries, many families have been forced into grave sites across the Strip, according to photos and my own observations. From Rafah and Deir al-Balah to Gaza City, living among the dead has become a repeating reality as every single square meter of livable space disappears under relentless displacement.

Swerki lives with her two sisters, Nariman, 60 years old, and Islam, 37 years old. She says they have been orphans since before the war, and no one supports them financially except her brother when his salary comes in every month. She describes their daily lives: “I cook among the graves, and everyone looks at me from the street. There is no privacy. We are afraid of rodents at night, and we have no light in the tent. There is no life, and there is not even money to support ourselves.”

Swerki pointed to her sister Nariman, who was sitting and eating among the graves. She said in a voice full of sadness, “As you can see, my sister sits among the graves all day. She gets up from the tent at 5:00 in the morning at sunrise and stays right there until sunset. It has taken a heavy psychological toll on her.”

During my time with Swerki and Nariman, I observed how Nariman barely spoke, offering only a one-word reply in response to my question about her welfare. The only full sentence she uttered in my presence was, “This is the grave of Abdullah Al-Mohandes” — a phrase she uttered while pointing at a nearby grave. Then she stopped talking completely.

“Before the war, we lived the best life,” Swerki said. She now fears what winter brings: “The tent is torn. We will flood, and the tent will fall on us without anyone caring about us. Life is very tragic.”

In a nearby tent, the story of Khader Abo Khader, 62, and his wife, Kamila, 59, is similar.

When their grandchildren and married daughters visit them, Kamila said they say to her, “We are afraid to sleep here. How do you live in the cemetery?”

Khader said, “There is no other place to go. I didn’t leave a shelter, school, or camp without going and asking for an empty place. They all refused.” He explained that in each of these places, the overcrowding was so severe that the tents were already pitched right up against each other.

“We and the dead are one and the same. Not even stray dogs would accept living like this.”

Khader once owned a three-story house, but it was destroyed in the 2023 war on Gaza. Now, he has been living in the cemetery for nearly a year, having already endured an entire winter amid the graves. Because of the sloped construction of the cemetery, rainwater flows from the graves and accumulates in the area where his tent is pitched. Moving the tent is not an option because others’ tents are already pitched in the rest of the available space.

“The ground here isn’t flat, so we were drowning,” he said. “Rainwater flooded over us, leaving us to literally swim through it.”

The struggle for survival extends far beyond the elements; recently, Khader awoke to the terrifying sound of a snake sliding inside his tent: “If I hadn’t woken up, which one of us would have been killed by its venom?”

For Khader, the boundaries separating the displaced from the dead have completely dissolved. “This is a miserable existence,” he said, looking across the crowded grave markers. “We and the dead are one and the same. Not even stray dogs would accept living like this.”

His wife, Kamila, describes the unbearable weight of survival: “Winter is terrifying, but summer is infinitely harder. I can’t handle the heat, the mosquitoes, and the rodents.”

She speaks of rodents gnawing through their meager bags of flour and lentils and of the grim reality of what she cooks each day: “I am still living through famine. I cook famine food because it’s all that’s available. I don’t have a single onion or a tomato.”

Reflecting on how life has completely collapsed, Kamila recalls when 10 shekels could sustain a person for a whole day in Gaza. Today, “even the 10 shekels have vanished from our lives.” When the suffocation of displacement peaks, she said, “I envy the dead. At least they died and found rest.”

When Basma Hammouda, 29, and her husband first arrived at the cemetery in October 2025, it looked nothing like it does today: “It was a mountain of rubble,” she said.

Her husband dug a massive pit and buried the debris just to level the ground enough to pitch their tent. “I had no other choice,” he said. “There is no space left for us in Gaza except this cemetery. We live beside the dead; they are the ones who went before us, and we are the ones to follow.”

Hammouda is in her final month of pregnancy, expecting to give birth very soon. “I don’t know how I’m going to protect my baby in this tent,” she said, anxiety etched across her face. “I haven’t been able to buy him any clothes to protect him from the cold, and we don’t have winter blankets.”

“There is no space left for us in Gaza except this cemetery. We live beside the dead; they are the ones who went before us, and we are the ones to follow.”

This will be her third child. One of her children is in kindergarten, her other child is almost 3 years old, and her husband is unemployed. Their toilet is nothing more than a crude plastic hole in the ground. Hammouda describes what she is enduring as severe prenatal depression. On the day of my visit, her sister brought her a kilogram of flour.

“I don’t want to complain, because complaining to anyone but Allah is a humiliation,” her husband said. “But these are the raw details of our lives.”

Animals walk freely into the tent because there is no door. Just the night before, he woke up to a stray dog standing right at the entrance. “Dogs have turned predatory after the war,” he said. “What would that dog have done if I hadn’t woken up?”

Staring blankly into the distance, Hammouda adds, “The cemetery constantly reminds me of my family. My entire family was killed in the war, except for me and my sisters. I just keep crying for the dead and praying for them. If my parents were still alive, they would have never let me live beside graves. But who is going to help me now that I’m an orphan?”

She mentions that her young son dreams of simply eating chicken and that they are waiting to sell their single cooking gas canister just to buy food. “Nobody feels our pain,” Hammouda said. “All I wish for, before I give birth, is for someone to at least buy me a proper tent.”

As I left the tents behind, I couldn’t shake the image of Nariman eating among the gravestones. I used to pass by this cemetery, feeling a quiet sorrow from afar for the tents scattered across it, but I never truly knew what lay within.

In Gaza, people used to say that the grave is one’s final home. But in Sheikh Radwan, the grave has become an immediate neighbor. People who lost their homes, their families, and their sense of safety have found themselves forced to live beside the dead, simply because the land of the living had no space left for them.

In Gaza, people used to say that the grave is one’s final home. But in Sheikh Radwan, the grave has become an immediate neighbor.

Hammouda’s third child will arrive in this world inside a tent surrounded by tombstones. All his mother asked of the world was for someone to buy her a proper tent before her delivery. How has the basic “right to a tent” become the absolute ceiling of human ambition in Gaza in the 21st century?

Don’t the living have the right to exist above ground with both body and soul, rather than being reduced to suffering bodies above the earth while their spirits already dwell among the graves? Who will relieve the people of Gaza from this ongoing tragedy?

The question remains open. But as long as the tents of the living stand pitched beside the dead, it is a question addressed to the entire world, not to Gaza alone.

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Ecuadorian Fishers Sue US Over Boat Bombing, Alleged Kidnapping and Torture
content:
The 16 fishers say they were held captive for weeks as part of the Trump administration’s boat bombing spree.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Sixteen Ecuadorian fishers are suing the US government over “catastrophic” harm resulting from a drone strike in the eastern Pacific Ocean earlier this year, and what they say was their subsequent abduction and torture, as part of the Trump administration’s boat-bombing spree supposedly targeting drug smugglers.

The Guardian reported Saturday that the lawsuit is set to be filed Monday in the US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania. The suit concerns a March 17 drone strike on the fishing vessel La Negra Francesca Duarte II, which the fishers said was returning from a two-week expedition when it was bombed approximately 385 nautical miles off Ecuador’s coast.

According to the filing, Ecuadorian authorities had inspected the vessel shortly before the attack and concluded it was carrying no drugs and that its crew had no affiliation with drug cartels.

However, two drones bombed the vessel, setting it ablaze and seriously burning two crew members. The fishers jumped into the water and escaped aboard smaller emergency boats before being intercepted by US military personnel, who allegedly restrained them with zip ties and covered their heads with plastic hoods.

The survivors say they were subsequently taken to a detention center in El Salvador, where they were held for several weeks before being returned to Ecuador. Their lawsuit seeks unspecified financial compensation for what it describes as a “manifestly unlawful” attack and the subsequent “kidnapping and torture.”

Other survivors of US boat strikes have also said they were abducted and tortured by American forces.

“There is no actual armed conflict that could justify the use of military force against the boats, nor was there one on March 17 when the attack took place,” the lawsuit states. “The US’ campaign of bombings against defenseless vessels and individuals violates long-standing and well-accepted international law.”

Dan Kovalik, the attorney filing the lawsuit, told The Guardian that the men “go out fishing, they don’t come home for a month, they’re … in a migrant detention center in El Salvador, and as we know those centers are not so nice.”

“So there’s a lot of trauma there,” he continued. “It was catastrophic for them. They are home now, but they are struggling financially, and the two guys who were hurt bad are still dealing with that.”

“They would also like the US to stop these boat strikes,” Kovalik added. “That’s another goal of all this, and I think the US public and the media have been, honestly, not outraged enough about these strikes.”

The suit is the latest legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s Operation Southern Spear, which the administration launched in September 2025, ostensibly to combat drug trafficking. But US officials have provided scant evidence to support claims that targeted vessels were engaged in narcotrafficking.

The Washington Office on Latin America, a human rights NGO, estimates that as many as 250 people have been killed in the campaign.

In January, relatives of two Trinidadian fishers killed by a US boat strike last year filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the Trump administration in a Massachusetts court. The men were among six people killed in an October 14, 2025 missile strike while traveling from Venezuela to Trinidad. Their families, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Center for Constitutional Rights (CCR), are seeking damages under the Death on the High Seas Act and the Alien Tort Statute.

The ACLU, CCR, and New York Civil Liberties Union also filed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit last December demanding the release of a secret Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel opinion purportedly providing the legal framework for the strikes.

Relatives of a Colombian man killed during Operation Southern Spear also lodged a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights last December, accusing US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — who earlier this week survived an attempt to impeach him, in part over the boat strikes — of ordering murder.

Meanwhile, The Washington Post reported in August that strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats near the Galápagos Islands earlier this year were carried out by the Central Intelligence Agency.

Eight crew members of one vessel, the Fiorella, also disappeared after an apparent attack in January and remain missing.

The Former Judge Advocates General Working Group, which includes former officials who served as legal advisers for the US military, said last year that Hegseth’s alleged order to “kill everybody” in one September 2025 boat strike — which resulted in a follow-up attack on two survivors — suggested that the defense secretary committed “war crimes, murder, or both.”

Kovalik said he looks forward to the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress holding Trump administration officials accountable for the strikes.

“Some of the Democrats that we met with are very interested in doing hearings on these boat strikes,” he said. “We hope this case will encourage the Democrats when they get sworn in in January to start some hearings. I think it will have that impact.”
