author: Taya Graham
title: Voters in Pennsylvania Sent a Message to Those in Power. Will They Be Heard?
content:
Progressives have been working to flip Pennsylvania’s deep-red districts for nearly a decade. It’s finally working.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In 2018, covering our first midterm election, we followed the ultimately unsuccessful campaign of an electoral upstart named Jess King.

King was a progressive candidate touting ideas like Medicare for All and a higher minimum wage in Pennsylvania’s deep-red 11th District. Her campaign seemed improbable at the time.

Her opponent, conservative Republican Lloyd Smucker, had won his previous race by roughly 10 points. In 2018, the district was gerrymandered to be even more Republican.

Despite the long odds, King made an argument we hadn’t heard before. Even though she was running as a Democrat, her pitch to voters was not exclusively partisan.

“I think what we see is that voters aren’t necessarily on the left-right spectrum as much as they are on a bottom-to-top spectrum,” King told us at a campaign event. “We need to talk more about two political parties that have sold out to special interests.”

Call it the inequality proposition or a power-to-the-people mantra, King made it clear that viewing politics through the prism of party was not only outdated, but destructive.

Ultimately, her pitch fell short. She lost to Smucker.

But the 2026 election may have proved that King was simply ahead of the curve. Alongside historic wins for Democrats, her message re-emerged with new potency among an electorate increasingly angry with the status quo, regardless of party.

“You hear people talking about this top-down message instead of this left-right message,” said Pennsylvania state Representative-elect Ce-Ce Gerlach. Gerlach won with the help of the Working Families Party and the progressive group Lehigh Valley Stands Up.

She said her message of economic populism trumped party politics.

“People are struggling. People don’t want to hear all this rhetoric about Republican, Democrat, socialist, progressive. No one wants to hear all that,” she told us.

This year, we spent two weeks in Pennsylvania’s Republican-held 7th District, which includes Gerlach’s seat. It covers much of the Lehigh Valley, including the cities of Allentown and Easton.

The voters we spoke to shared a similar perspective. Concentrated wealth, corruption, and even the Epstein files were top of mind. What we didn’t hear much about was Democrats or Republicans.

“60 million Americans live from paycheck to paycheck,” a voter named Thomas Fantini told us. “It’s a travesty that, in the greatest country in the world, we’re the only country that doesn’t have universal healthcare.”

His concerns were similar to many voters in the district: pragmatic demands for better policy, rarely couched in the language of partisanship.

Indeed, activists say the election was a referendum on a political system unable to solve serious problems.

“By no means do we think that this election was simply pro-Democratic or anti-Republican,” said Mary Collier, an organizer with Lehigh Valley Stands Up. “It was very much about affordability. How much people are paying for gas, how much they are struggling, and hoping for change.”

Collier points to several candidates her organization backed as proof: Rachel Cuevas, Meriam Sabih, and Jeff Warren all flipped Republican-held state House seats. All ran on a purposely progressive agenda.

“We have been sowing the seeds for a while,” Collier said.

Those seeds go back further than this cycle.

Lancaster Stands Up, a sister group, was central to King’s 2018 campaign. Since then, it and the other chapters of Pennsylvania Stands Up have turned their focus to local races.

This year, that work culminated in a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania. The party took control of the state Senate while holding the House and the governor’s mansion.

Collier says the priority now is making sure the newly empowered majority delivers, regardless of party affiliation.

“Otherwise, we’ll be back to square one.”

author: Amy Maxmen
title: The US Has Officially Lost Its Measles Elimination Status
content:
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized in the US due to preventable measles outbreaks.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States.

“It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate. States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren’t vaccinated before they’re a year old.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts. Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.

But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks. For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children’s immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.

After health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations “without reviewing the evidence.” She added that “we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years” and that, “if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return.”

Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, including Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. “The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading. That’s no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.

Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children’s hospital in Minnesota during the nation’s last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems. Two children at the hospital died of measles. “That changed my career forever,” she said.

Back then, she said, the federal government “saw the urgency.” Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC’s flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.

When data suggested that some children weren’t mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot. When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn’t been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.

Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated. “Elimination” allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can’t be protected by vaccines.

People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity. With at least 95% of people within communities immunized, outbreaks petered out and vulnerable people were protected.

It would be 14 years before a significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC’s Schuchat to testify on the situation. “Vaccination wasn’t a partisan issue,” she recalled. “This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?”

National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street’s Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.

In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak concentrated in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.

“Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable,” Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.

Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the “importance of on-time vaccination.”

And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC’s MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. “The MMWR is the voice of the CDC,” Schuchat said, “alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action.”

Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16. Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to “deaths every year.”

Congress didn’t call a hearing, and HHS didn’t send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn’t publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.

“A lot of this is the dog didn’t bark,” said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law-San Francisco. “Something that normally happens isn’t happening.”

Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. “There’s a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration,” one official said.

“Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved,” another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that covid vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.

“The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false,” Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News. She said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.

More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC’s journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced potentially lethal brain swelling due to the virus.

The MMWR still hasn’t published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC’s national measles update hasn’t appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.

CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.

“We have two CDCs now,” an official at the agency said. “One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website.”

The CDC’s measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.

Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year. It now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order “to prevent vaccine hesitancy.”

The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal,” and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism. Stephen Miller, now Trump’s White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors “pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences.” Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.

Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. “Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable,” Schuchat said.

When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven’t repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.

Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.

At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.

To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn’t on the horizon.

“Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire,” he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
content:
These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Eureka, a small city in Northern California, provided Roger “Chapreges” Jones an anchor in his Yurok culture. He took public K-12 Yurok language classes and Indian Ed covered school supplies. But when his parents divorced and he moved to Redding at 13, those resources vanished — and so did his appetite.

Chapreges got his first job at a Native American mental health clinic while grappling with an eating disorder hidden in plain sight. His new role at Two Feathers Native American Family Services became a kind of Trojan horse: He walked through the door looking for employment and found therapy waiting inside.

Founded in 1998 by a tribal consortium to strengthen Native family units in Humboldt County, Two Feathers has grown significantly since 2018, when its current executive director, Virgil Moorehead, joined. It went from having four staff members to having 32, including mental health clinicians, substance abuse counselors, and cultural coordinators.

Two Feathers serves a disproportionately large Native population across Northern California, where many Tribes and their citizens are either unrecognized federally or have been disenrolled. Critically, it serves Native families regardless of enrollment status — a stance that resists the disenrollment politics that plague underfunded tribes across Indian Country.

Chapreges is one of dozens of Native youth accessing Two Feathers services in a region where waitlists are long and federal funding cuts have gutted alternatives. A 2022 study from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health echoes mounting research on the importance of cultural connection to Native youth’s mental health.

Chapreges’s experience speaks to that truth. He had struggled to acclimate to Redding without other Native youth or regular cultural resources beyond the annual Stillwater Powwow. In his sophomore year, he and his father, overwhelmed by the isolation, returned to Eureka, where Chapreges completed high school.

The following year, he became a youth ambassador at Two Feathers, promoting their culturally tailored programming: stick games, flower dance, trips to the local powwow, and the Young Bucks and Spotted Does programs for youth ages 8 to 12.

Moorehead is also a licensed clinical psychologist and has helmed a new era for the organization, implementing circular Native philosophy by creating a continuum of school- and family-oriented treatment services for Native youth and their families. Two Feathers’ approach reflects a broader Indigenous understanding of mental health that recognizes the effects of historical trauma while at the same time accounting for the distinct experiences of different Native communities.

One such program, the Acorn Youth Wellness Program, works with youth individually to bolster their cultural identity. “But I think giving them hope, you know, sense of belonging,” said Moorehead, “Those are all things that are measured.”

Moorehead said the program tracks attendance, cultural identity, and hope for the future. “I always say that if you don’t have kids that come to the program, you don’t have a program. And so through the way we did Acorn, it engaged kids and had them show up in the sense of coming back and back and back.”

In 2020, the California State Assembly’s Select Committee on Native American Affairs conferred the honor of a plaque, letter, and on-site visit recognizing the organization’s work to improve and stabilize the lives of Native youth and families in Northern California. The program’s success has attracted interest from other Native Nations seeking to replicate the model. Moorehead said he’s in early conversations with one tribe planning to launch their own version next year, though he declined to name specific nations in preliminary stages.

Another member of the Two Feathers staff, Jayla, who asked to be identified by first name only to protect her privacy, joined the organization at age 15 after seeing an employment ad. A year into her time at Two Feathers, in 2025, President Donald Trump proposed consolidating behavioral health funding. Despite the fact that Trump’s proposal has only been partially implemented, Jayla still sees the impact of it firsthand: “After there were all the budget cuts, they got hit pretty hard with that … They were getting both federal and state funding, and I think a lot of what they’re getting now is just from California.”

Despite these cuts, Two Feathers’ budget has grown roughly twentyfold since Moorehead’s arrival, from about $594,000 in fiscal year 2018 to $11.7 million in fiscal year 2025, according to IRS filings, with grants and contributions making up nearly 95 percent of revenue. Two Feathers draws on all three levels of government. Its largest grant is a five-year, $7.2 million SAMHSA award for school-based youth mental health that runs through 2028. It bills Medi-Cal through a Humboldt County contract and holds state grants for youth opioid prevention.

Those filings run only through June 2025, before the full weight of federal cuts; Moorehead said the organization’s biggest challenge is escaping the cycle of one-, three-, and five-year awards. Two Feathers now bills for services, which Moorehead acknowledged has made it “a little bit more mainstream,” because billing requires diagnoses. But he rejects the idea that federal and state money forces programs to abandon their values.

“You think that you can receive federal and state funding and still not lose your values and your identity,” he said. “But I think that it takes leadership.”

Moorehead said long-term funding remains a central challenge for Two Feathers, which relies on grants while seeking more sustainable funding arrangements. “How do we create more sustainable funding?” he asked. “So that we can continue to build and get better, and not be stuck in just chasing after those grants, chasing after that funding.”

He compares the work to being a coyote, a trickster figure in many Native traditions, playing the game of federal funding and diagnostic billing without losing yourself to it. Whether these programs can truly keep doing that may depend far less on proving they work than on funders willing to commit for longer than a grant cycle.

In 2026, Moorehead and his program manager Amy Mathieson each received the James Irvine Foundation Leadership Award, which included a $350,000 grant conferred toward their organization to expand bespoke Native youth mental health programs, according to Moorehead. The award comes as Two Feathers continues to navigate funding challenges in the wake of Trump’s federal funding cuts.

Once at Two Feathers, Chapreges quickly realized what the organization could offer beyond employment. Under staff supervision, Chapreges’s manager suggested he seek support from the mental health clinicians on staff. Chapreges agreed.

“I feel a lot better. I have someone to actually talk to about how I’m feeling throughout the week compared to before, where I wouldn’t really tell anyone because I didn’t want to feel like a burden,” Chapreges told Truthout.

Outspoken about his support for the program, Chapreges encourages others even outside the scope of the Two Feathers program to seek mental health support. “I would recommend all Native youth to talk to someone, if it’s a federal one [Indian Health Service mental health program] or if it’s Two Feathers,” he said.

Jayla, Seminole, is also a youth ambassador and moved from South Carolina, where she was raised, to work at Two Feathers in McKinleyville, California, over five hours’ drive north of San Francisco. She supports the Young Bucks and Spotted Does program, among others.

“They try and use local teachings and elders and understand how trauma goes through generations of people and how it just lingers,” Jayla said. “It’s always kind of there through each generation. But how can we fix it? How can we help our generation so other generations in the future don’t have to struggle so hard?”

Culturally competent care is a central goal at Two Feathers, aiming to mitigate the many physical and mental health effects of colonization. “Last year we made little dresses that the girls were able to take home that they created and got to make their own designs,” said Jayla. “Every year, Two Feathers takes a group of kids to the Stillwater Powwow, and it’s a very intentional time where they’re able to see not only their own culture but other cultures as well.”

They also organize a trip to a conference co-produced by Two Feathers, the Wiyot Tribe, Blue Lake Rancheria, and Queer Humboldt for two-spirits — the inter-tribal term for the unique historical and contemporary social roles tied to LGBTQ Natives. Amplifying two-spirit youth voices has remained at the core of Two Feathers programming, despite widespread attacks on DEI under the Trump administration.

“I think that what success looks like in this program … it’s people being able to move on from the program eventually,” said Jayla. “And to be able to use the connections they made from Two Feathers to further along their own careers and their passions.”

This model — employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community — isn’t isolated to Humboldt County. In Oakland, the American Indian Child Resource Center (AICRC) bucks Western metrics that are often used to qualify health organizations for federal grant funding.

AICRC offers similar programming to Two Feathers: tobacco prevention, youth employment through gardening, after-school academics, and culture.

Three vehicles pick up roughly 20 Native youth from three to four schools in the afternoon for the 4-6:30pm program. Gardening offers a trifecta of camaraderie, modest pay, and education on living in good relations with the land — a striking tradition for Native youth who are the fourth generation to inherit Oakland as their homeland since the urban Indian relocation program started over 75 years ago.

“We have three plants that are interconnected and help one another,” said the California Native garden coordinator Joshua Hoyt. “[We’re] kind of juxtaposing that with modern Western agriculture, which is, you know, everything’s in rows and squares … using that as a way of thinking about how Native people see the world differently.”

Twenty-five-year AICRC veteran Mary Trimble Norris hesitated to give Truthout exact participant numbers for its after-school program, underscoring the organization’s refusal to define operations by metrics and instead emphasizing its intimate, student-focused approach.

“We’re not funded at that scale to generate the kind of metrics,” said Trimble Norris. AICRC operates on roughly $1.1 millon a year, nearly all of it grants: federal Indian Child Welfare Act dollars from the Bureau of Indian Affairs, state funding for its Indian Education center through the California Department of Education, and Bay Are foundations such as the East Bay Community Foundation. The budget has barely grown at all since 2011.

Manny Lieras, a youth services director who has worked at AICRC for 25 years, described the program’s intergenerational impact: “The institution’s size hasn’t shaped its intergenerational popularity,” he said. “One of two staff members whom I supervise is a former alum of the program when I ran it. On the other side of the coin are now several of the youth who are part of our program, that are offspring of alumni.”

In D.C., the Center for Native American Youth (CNAY), housed within the Aspen Institute supports leadership development among urban and reservation-based Native youth. For Jazmine Wildcat, a Northern Arapaho graduate of CNAY’s Champions For Change fellowship, the Center offered economic and social support after leaving Wyoming’s Wind River Reservation for college. After earning three bachelor’s degrees at the University of Wyoming, she moved to Washington, D.C., where she is pursuing a master’s in public health at George Washington University. “Being surrounded by like-minded individuals was really reassuring and was also just very empowering and motivational,” said Wildcat.

That support also had a lasting impact on how Wildcat thought about her own well-being. “I don’t think I’m going to be truly understood by anyone at these schools … as much as I have been understood by people at CNAY [and] my fellow youth and my peers because they’re all going through the same thing that I am,” said Wildcat. Her ability to see other Native youth incorporate traditional practices into their daily lives helped her find ways to stay grounded, she said. “I was able to see and observe what other people were doing that worked for them, and kind of take that and kind of see what works for myself.”

Katy Stewart, a CNAY staff member, says the organization has spent several years developing a rich Indigenous framework for its leadership curriculum, grounded by cultural and spiritual practices, elders, and activities such as medicine pouch-making and other in-person gatherings. Its core values include identity and culture, respect, relationships, responsibility, community, and humility.

“Sometimes a clinical model isn’t always inclusive of the Indigenous models and traditional ways of knowing that our youth really understand,” Stewart said. She argues that well-being cannot simply be reduced to individual outcomes but must also account for young people’s living relationships to their communities. CNAY’s Democracy is Indigenous Program is one unusual example, offering microgrants to youth ages 11 to 24 to develop community projects; staff help applicants write a budget and proposal, that is often their first. The program distributed $500,000 so far, Steward said. In Oakland, one recipient hosted a “beats and beading” event, where community members beaded together during a DJ set while talking about mental health. In Philadelphia, a 20-year-old graphic designer used her grant to design and place Missing and Murdered Indigenous People Awareness posters across the city’s bus and subway system for two months, an effort she estimates reached more than 600,000 riders.

Though CNAY is housed within the Aspen Institute, it actually raises its own money, Stewart said, including a 2025 grant from the Decolonizing Wealth Project’s new Youth Mental Health Fund. So far, she said, federal cuts haven’t touched its programs, but many of the young people it works with are finding urban Indian health centers and other behavioral health services hard to access. “Our goal is to figure out ways to sort of like supplement the support that youth would find in other places,” she said.

Taken together, these programs suggest that culturally grounded care can draw Native youth in and keep them coming back, but their growth has been uneven and precarious. Two Feathers’ budget has grown twentyfold since 2018, while AICRC operates on about the same shoestring budget it had in 2011. All three organizations depend heavily on grants that expire every few years, and the Trump administration’s cuts have shrunk the clinics and behavioral programs that young people would otherwise turn to. Their leaders say the biggest gaps lie in what short-term grants can’t buy: long-term, intensive support for the young people carrying the most trauma, continued care after youth age out of school-based services at 18, and staff rooted enough to stay in one place with these kids for years. Other Native nations have already approached Two Feathers about replicating its model, Moorehead said. Whether it spreads may depend less on proving that the model works than on finding financial backers who are willing to take the plunge beyond a grant cycle.

For Wildcat, healing has meant becoming more comfortable with herself and learning to share what she has learned with others finding their way. The connections she found through CNAY helped her feel understood in spaces where she often felt alone.

“There are plenty of people out there who understand and have gone through similar feelings and issues,” said Wildcat. “I just hope that they know they’re not alone, and … there’s resources out there.”

author: Blanca Missé
title: Residents in CA Agricultural Town Face Down ICE Facility and Amazon Data Center
content:
Residents and activists in the town of Gilroy are drawing links between Big Tech surveillance and immigration jails.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

South of San Jose, California, residents of the city of Gilroy are fighting a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility and an Amazon data center. Organizers with ICE Out of Gilroy, a coalition that launched in May of this year, have linked the two fights in a united struggle against detention and Big Tech surveillance. The coalitionincludes Community Agency for Resources, Advocacy, and Services (CARAS), a Gilroy-based immigrant-rights group; Services, Immigrant Rights & Education Network (SIREN), based in San Jose; and Bay Resistance, a Bay Area coalition for racial and economic justice which formed after Trump’s 2016 election and reactivated in 2025.

Gilroy’s farms and service economy depend on immigrant labor. The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure. The projects have distinct origins, but both raise the same question: Who gets to use Gilroy’s land, labor and infrastructure — and who gets to decide how?

On August 23, 2026, local residents joined the “Dump Big Tech” march opposing the ICE facility on Holsclaw Road, Amazon’s data center on Camino Arroyo, and the 54 automated license plate readers (ALPRs) owned by Flock throughout Gilroy. Mateo, an organizer with CARAS and the rapid-response network who asked to use a pseudonym due to concerns about potential repression, summed up why the coalition has linked the fights: “The data centers take our resources; the detention center takes our people.”

Kim Woo, a community organizer with SIREN, traced the connection in another direction: “Flock cameras lead us to the data center, and then to detention facilities.” Kim is concerned with how surveillance data moves across agencies to circumvent sanctuary policies. Records show out-of-state police searched the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) Flock data for ICE-related purposes. Separately, an SFPD audit found a regional fusion-center network routed 299 federal and out-of-state queries; none were marked immigration-related. Kim calls these indirect channels “side-door sharing.” Rebeca Armendáriz, chair of the ICE Out of Gilroy Coalition and now a council-member-elect, says Flock data are being used to identify local rapid-response activists and monitor journalists. She calls all these technologies part of “the authoritarian state machine.”

The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure.

A WIRED investigation found that, since 2023, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have spent at least $515 million on services from Palantir, Microsoft, Amazon and Google. Palantir supplies investigative and case-management software; the others provide cloud and computing services. ICE’s Palantir case-management system runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and the companies also have a technology partnership. The government contracts are separate: ICE committed $86.3 million to Palantir on April 30, 2026, for case-management modernization; on September 8, the Department of Homeland Security committed $18.3 million to AWS for cloud infrastructure supporting ICE. All together, these figures exceed $619 million today.

The proposed ICE facility in Gilroy would generate rent and construction payments for a private landlord, Elmwood Capital Group, which is based in Beverly Hills. On January 8, 2025, the Trump administration awarded Elmwood a 20-year lease for up to $26,551,532 in rent. A March 2026 amendment authorized up to $8.66 million in construction reimbursements, bringing potential federal payments to the Elmwood Capital Group subsidiary ECG6 to $35.2 million over 20 years, according to the court order. Rent begins when General Services Administration (GSA) accepts the completed site, under a 20-year lease with a 15-year firm term. This arrangement uses public money to prepare private property for detention and then lease it to the government for profit.

On May 14, residents and immigrant-rights advocates rallied with county officials, who pledged to fight the project and said they were coordinating with Attorney General Rob Bonta, which led organizers to hold a community briefing and a mass organizing call on May 22. In response, the state of California and Santa Clara County sued after federal agencies began construction without the environmental review required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Gilroy’s then at-large city council, which had no Latino members, declined to join the lawsuit.

The complaint alleges Elmwood described the project to county planners as “office and operations space,” without disclosing its holding rooms or the scale of construction. ICE’s court filing estimates about 10 detainees on a normal day; the state and county say plans show rooms for up to 150. A judge found the state and county likely to prevail on their NEPA claim and halted construction; the court later extended the pause.

The Gilroy lease is part of a national detention buildout. An internal ICE memo from February outlined to expand capacity to 92,600 beds across the U.S.

Seven ICE-contracted detention facilities have been active in California in 2025, according to the DOJ; the eighth, the Central Valley Annex, began holding detainees in April 2026. The California Department of Justice says, affirming what families and attorneys are saying, that facilities are remote and hard to reach.

The Beverly Hills capital group’s reach extends beyond Gilroy: The state and county’s complaint alleges the firm leased at least two properties to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in Montana and Texas. In Billings, Montana, Elmwood’s portfolio lists a 14,444-square-foot GSA property; city records identify an ICE facility at 1711 6th Ave. N. A 2022 remodel permit lists Noah Zeligman as the owner of the property and describes jail processing spaces and holding cells.

The contracts reach beyond detention operators to surveillance firms, deportation contractors and property owners, as part of a broader detention-industrial complex. In the first year of Trump’s second term, ICE obligated about $5.4 billion to 679 contractors; the top ten received roughly $3.8 billion, according to a joint POGO–IRW analysis. Those top recipients included Palantir (surveillance analytics), CoreCivic and GEO Group (private detention), and CSI Aviation (deportation flights). ICE paid $129.3 million for a warehouse formerly majority-owned by Goldman Sachs and $68.2 million for one sold by a Carlyle-linked entity, CoStar and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Those are sale prices, not the firms’ disclosed profits. WIRED found ICE and CBP had spent at least $515 million with Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Palantir since 2023. Some firms, executives or PACs donated to Trump-aligned campaigns or initiatives, and some lobbied on ICE-related issues. More than 50 members of Congress launched separate investigations into six contractors, brokers and property owners, Salon reported.

Armendáriz warned KTVU that construction of an ICE facility may push farmworkers to leave Gilroy: “Our community is going to live in fear because this is going to be so close.” Law enforcement pressure is already palpable at county jails: On October 28, federal agents pursued two men after they were released from Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas; one was tased. Observers reported seeing 10 to 12 agents at county jails daily the week before. Sheriff’s office figures show about 70 people detained near county jails since June 2025, local reporting found.

Farmworkers have the legal right to organize, but only about 10,000 of California’s 800,000-plus farmworkers arecovered by union contracts, a UC Davis review estimated in 2025. In a UC Merced survey of farmworkers in the state, 19 percent of respondents said an employer had withheld payment of wages; 43 percent said employers never provided the required heat-illness prevention plan. A national study found that spikes in immigration arrests cut noncitizen farmworkers’ weekly hours by as much as 23.1 percent that month. The threat of detention compounds workers’ risk of retaliation when they report wage theft or unsafe conditions.

Mateo said early marches in May drew mostly white allies from San Jose, Santa Cruz, and Salinas. In a small town, he said, residents feared detention, violence, or provocations that could lead to mass arrests. As more Latino residents saw other communities stand with them, they began joining — and calling for more people to join them in the streets.

The organizing efforts drew people from beyond Gilroy — from Stockton to Salinas and across the Bay Area. Organizers say about 800 people joined an emergency online call to action on May 22 after news broke that the ICE processing center was being built. Union members joined rapid-response work; Pacific Printing donated thousands of red-and-yellow campaign materials; SEIU 2015 and other health-care workers’ unions helped organize actions, while nurses brought material aid and joined protests. SEIU-USWW and the local labor council also supported the campaign.

More recently, on October 25, the coalition screened When ICE Melts, a documentary about Minneapolis resistance to Operation Metro Surge, in San Jose. The film follows unions, immigrant groups, and rapid-response networks as they defend their neighbors and build toward a mass strike. The film’s organizing argument has a local echo: Immigrant defense belongs inside labor organizing.

Amazon’s 56-acre data center at 8050 Camino Arroyo is a reported $2 billion project with two planned buildings. Its first phase requires a 49-megawatt connection to Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E). That is the first building’s peak demand; the full site could require 98 MW, with any effect on household bills depending on who pays for grid upgrades.On July 3, 2025, Gilroy’s Community Development Director approved it under existing industrial zoning, without a planning commission hearing or city council vote. The Council later adopted new public-notice and hearing requirements for future large projects; Amazon’s approval remains in force. Resident Georgine Scott-Codiga told KSBW, “What they have done is they shut the people down; the people have no voice.”

Gilroy’s approval findings say the project’s benefits outweighed its unavoidable environmental impacts, including converting prime farmland and increasing vehicle travel above California’s environmental review threshold, which increases pollution from employee commutes. The city described the parcel’s long period of underdevelopment as “detrimental to the economic development of the City as a whole” and cited its goal of attracting technology companies seeking less costly locations. The city projects $40 million in revenue over the first decade, about 70 percent from a 5 percent tax on electricity use, according to its revenue FAQ. The city’s tax revenue rises with the facility’s power consumption.

The project requires off-site PG&E transmission upgrades. Gilroy’s Community Development Director says Amazon will fund a dedicated substation, but the California Public Utilities Commission’s Public Advocates Office issued a statewide warning that ratepayers could bear transmission costs if projected demand falls short. The city says newer state protections may limit that risk, though it remains unclear whether they cover Gilroy’s approved project.

Kim Woo of SIREN says the centers will “drastically deplete our electricity and water resources.” The project’s Water Supply Assessment estimates up to 23 acre-feet of water a year — about 7.5 million gallons — for cooling, irrigation and domestic use. Once recycled-water service is connected, expected by 2030, potable use should fall to about 2 acre-feet annually. Amazon must pay for the recycled-water infrastructure, which the city says will also serve future customers.

Gilroy City Council’s jobs argument centers on construction: The city projects hundreds of temporary jobs under a project labor agreement that prioritizes local hiring and prevailing wages. Those jobs matter to workers, but they end when construction does. The approval report’s employment projections estimate up to 25 full-time employees initially and 50 after Phase II. At full buildout, up to 125 employees and contractors, including part-time workers, could be on site. The figure of up to 125 people on site includes part-time workers and contractors. Hundreds of workers may build the reported $2 billion project; only a few dozen are expected to run it.

That is the point. Data centers are a massive fixed-capital investment designed to produce more output with less workers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said generative AI and agents will mean fewer people doing some of today’s jobs, while his company announced two rounds of cuts affecting about 30,000 office-based corporate roles: 14,000 in October 2025 and 16,000 in January 2026, according to its October notice and January notice. A Fairwork investigation documents how AI and robotics intensify warehouse work, while algorithmic monitoring narrows workers’ control over their pace and tasks.

Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) research director Alex Hanna describes AI as “making our expertise an add-on, and making us more interchangeable.” Alongside replacing some jobs, these systems can speed up work, expand surveillance and make the workers who remain easier to replace. A Truthout investigation found that Amazon’s Atlas model draws on hundreds of data points — including worker feedback, injuries and proximity to union activity — to assess “labor risk” and anticipate organizing. Workers build and power this infrastructure while Amazon gains new tools to reorganize their work and contain resistance.

After the court injunction paused work at Holsclaw Road, Gilroy’s Council passed a 45-day moratorium on new detention facilities on October 5, then extended it through October 4, 2027. The ordinance covers detention and custodial-facility applications where city authority applies, but not Holsclaw Road, outside city limits. Mateo calls the injunction and moratorium partial victories. The coalition’s tactic, he says, is “to delay these projects while we build a broader opposition.”

“We need to fight these systems of mass surveillance now with a mass united front that brings immigrant defense together with the fight for civil liberties.”

On October 5, 2026, a community-backed proposal to bar immigration-enforcement staging on city property failed to advance. Kim had pressed for no-staging zones: “Our city property belongs to us, the community, not the ICE agenda coming here to harass and kidnap us.”

On October 19, the Council extended its moratorium on new data-center applications through September 3, 2027, but Amazon’s project remains exempt. The coalition is using the pause to press for the Holsclaw project’s cancellation, and a permanent data-center moratorium.

As a result of this grassroots movement, Gilroy’s political representation is changing. Before district elections, its at-large Council had no Latino members despite a population that is nearly 60 percent Latino, according to local reporting. After a lawyer’s December 2024 letter threatened a California Voting Rights Act lawsuit, amid Latino residents’ calls for greater representation, the Council voted in February 2025 to switch to district elections. The first were held in November 2026, when voters chose three Latinas—Diana Sanchez Bentz, Christina Tovar, and Rebeca Armendáriz—for the three seats on the ballot. Armendáriz, ICE Out of Gilroy’s chair, was among those elected and campaigned on protecting residents from ICE.

The struggle also crosses city lines. Kim sees the proposed Gilroy facility and the former Dublin federal prison as parts of one regional system, with Gilroy processing people and Dublin detaining them. Armendáriz wants the newly elected Congress to defund ICE, reverse its inhumane policies, and end qualified immunity for ICE agents. She is looking ahead to 2027: “It is a key year, and the community is ready for a general strike.”

For Betty, a San Jose teacher who asked to use a pseudonym due to fears of state repression, said that fight must unite immigrant defense with civil liberties. “We need to fight these systems of mass surveillance now with a mass united front that brings immigrant defense together with the fight for civil liberties,” said Betty, who is active with Workers’ Voice. “That means unions, immigrant rights groups and civil liberties organizations organizing together across the Bay Area, across California and nationally.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Fresh Off Electoral Defeat on Iran War, Trump Floats New Military Front in Cuba
content:
The Trump administration’s fuel blockade has already been likened to an act of war by critics.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said this week that he wants to “get Cuba done” before his term is over, casually saying that he is considering opening yet another military front in a country whose civilian population is already being killed and starved by his sweeping sanctions campaign.

When asked by conservative talk show host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday whether or not he would use military force in Cuba, Trump said he “would certainly consider” a military campaign on the small island nation.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah,” said Trump.

“We have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump went on. “Because Marco’s parents are from — Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba, as you probably know and he would love to do that. So we’re watching it very closely. It’s doing very poorly, it’s essentially a failed place, nation, whatever you want to call it, it’s failed. And we’re watching it. I would like to be able to do it.”

The suggestion to open a new military front comes despite voters delivering Trump and the Republicans a historic loss in last week’s midterm elections, due in large part to his failed war on Iran.

author: Chris Walker
title: Poll: Most US Voters Want a Popular Vote Model for Picking Future Presidents
content:
Democrats in several states have indicated support for the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

New polling demonstrates that a majority of registered voters in the United States support changing the method through which presidents are selected.

Currently, the Electoral College is the mechanism used to pick presidents. Each state receives electoral votes equal to its number of congressional representatives — the number of House districts in the state plus its two Senate seats. These electors are directed by their states to vote for a presidential candidate following an election.

For most states, their entire slate of electors is given to the presidential candidate who won the most votes in their state. To win the presidency, a candidate must receive a majority of the tallied Electoral College votes, which is currently 270.

Due to significant population differences among states that are not accurately reflected in the Electoral College, the model can sometimes choose a presidential winner who did not win the popular vote among voters nationwide. Indeed, there have been five elections in U.S. history — including two elections since 2000 — in which the popular vote winner did not end up becoming president.

The post-midterm Economist/YouGov poll, conducted November 9-11, asked respondents whether they favored keeping the Electoral College or preferred to replace it with a popular vote system. Among registered voters, 51 percent said they wanted presidents to be selected through a popular vote, while only 28 percent said they wanted to keep the current system in place. Another 21 percent said they were unsure.

According to the poll, one in five registered voters (22 percent) have either heard of the Electoral College but don’t know how it works, or have never heard of it at all. It’s possible that a large segment of this population of voters would also support a popular vote model if they learned more about the undemocratic way in which the Electoral College functions.

With the results of the midterms flipping several state governments to Democratic Party control, there now exists a real opportunity for lawmakers to implement a popular vote system.

Complete abolition of the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment. But advocates for a plan called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact say the rules of the Electoral College can actually be used to create a popular vote system.

Per the Constitution, each state determines for itself how its electors are chosen. If the compact was implemented, states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes would direct their electors to the candidate who won the majority of votes nationwide, rather than the candidate who won the majority of votes in their state.

The compact doesn’t kick in until states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes sign on. As it stands right now, just 48 electoral votes are needed for the compact to go into effect.

In this month’s midterm elections, Democrats won new trifecta governments (e.g., states in which Democrats have control of the state legislature and governor’s office) in Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, and Pennsylvania. Each of those states has yet to back the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — but if they do, they would represent more than enough of the remaining electoral votes needed to put it in place.

Lawmakers from those states have indicated that they are planning to pursue that route or are open to the idea of doing so.

Even if those states pass the compact, there’s one more hurdle: Article I Section 10 of the Constitution also requires Congress to approve most interstate compacts. That means the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress must pass a resolution to approve the idea — and that a filibuster by Republicans in the Senate could block it.

That is, unless Democrats change rules in that chamber to limit how and when a filibuster can occur, a matter that is presently dividing members of the party.

author: Lisa Sorg
title: Critics Slam Department of the Interior’s New Strategic Plan for Public Lands
content:
They say data center developers, mining firms, and energy companies could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. Department of the Interior could transfer swaths of public lands to state, local and tribal governments through sales or land swaps, according to the agency’s new strategic plan.

Critics are concerned that many states, cities and counties can’t afford to maintain the lands, and would sell them to private interests — the first step toward a wholesale privatization of lands that have belonged to Americans for more than 150 years.

“This is the biggest attack we’ve ever seen on public lands,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director for the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities.

The Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The agency manages more than 500 million acres of land in addition to 3.2 billion acres of offshore resources and 700 million acres of underground minerals. All told, the department manages 20 percent of the country’s lands, from national parks to wildlife refuges.

Data center developers, mining firms and energy companies — all favored industries of the Trump administration — could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts for their environmentally harmful operations, critics say.

The plan says Interior “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate” through the sales. That will allow the department to “focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” according to the plan, with some of the sales proceeds going back to “the purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes.”

The plan also says the agency will “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” Interior has already lost more than 17 percent of its workforce under the second Trump administration.

In the plan’s introduction, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that the agency will streamline environmental reviews and expedite leasing and permitting for energy companies. Nowhere in the plan does the agency mention wind or solar power. The first goal outlined in the plan is “Increase American Prosperity,” and the opening pages feature pictures of an oil rig and an offshore oil operation.

“Together, we can simplify processes and remove red tape that creates drudgery for our team members and impedes progress,” Burgum wrote. “We can bring forward new ideas and better ways of working. For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence.”

Burgum has made millions of dollars off investments in artificial intelligence, powered by data centers, ProPublica reported Nov. 6.

The plan doesn’t specifically identify data centers as potential customers to purchase federal property, but the White House previously asked Bureau of Land Management state offices to identify lands that would be appropriate for these uses.

Last June, BLM approved an AI data center on 81 acres of public land near Boulder City, Nevada. The builder had received federal approval in 2023 to construct a solar farm, but amended its application to include a data center.

A federal judge has halted the project because BLM did not conduct a new environmental analysis but rather used the previous one for the solar project, a likely violation of the National Environmental Policy Act.

Energy and mining interests have long sought — and received — access to the oil, gas and minerals beneath public lands via leases. The new Interior plan would allow BLM to sell or transfer those properties outright to agencies that could then resell them.

The plan runs from fiscal year 2026 to 2030. However, the Trump administration has already begun planning to offload some public lands in particular.

This September, the Forest Service, which is under the U.S. Department of Agriculture, issued a permit to Pitkin County in Colorado to manage a section of the White River National Forest that contains the Maroon Bells Scenic Area, the gateway to stunning burgundy peaks where hundreds of thousands of recreators visit annually. Critics see this move as a trial run for public land transfers.

In Alaska, the federal government is expected to soon open 28 million acres to new development and land ownership, according to the Juneau Independent.

Last March the Forest Service officially transferred a sacred indigenous site to Resolution Copper, a mining company.

BLM needs congressional approval to sell public parcels over 2,500 acres. However, federal law contains loopholes, Groetzinger said. The sales, for example, must serve the national interest, which can be broadly interpreted. The plan lays the foundation for that claim by repeatedly justifying future sales on national security grounds.

Not only does the Interior Department propose shrinking its current inventory of public lands, but the plan also forecloses the possibility of buying more. Instead of using the Land and Water Conservation Fund to purchase additional acreage, the agency says it will “shift its investment focus” to buying recreational and conservation easements on privately owned lands.

The Land and Water Conservation Fund protects thousands of parks, natural areas, historic sites and other projects nationwide from private development. “That’s an important function of the fund,” Groetzinger said. “For them to not use any of those funds to buy new land is just unprecedented.”

Jayson O’Neill is a spokesman for Save Our Parks and lives in Montana, where recreation and tourism driven by access to public lands and waters is critical for the local economy. “We need somebody that actually understands how important this is to the economic viability of our communities and also our way of life,” O’Neill said. “Instead they’re literally calling to give away federal public lands and public resources to industry.”

Inside Climate News reporter Jake Bolster contributed reporting.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide Calls on ICC to Arrest Trump, Rubio Over Gaza
content:
The alliance accused Trump and Rubio of aiding and abetting “genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A delegation of U.S. taxpayers and human rights attorneys has called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to issue arrest warrants for President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their role in the genocide in Gaza.

On Wednesday, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) delivered evidence against Trump and Rubio at the Hague, the headquarters of the ICC in the Netherlands, calling for their arrests for “aiding and abetting Israel in the commission of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

The organization announced its submission to the ICC at a press conference at the Hague on Wednesday.

Individuals and organizations working with the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide collected evidence for nearly a year, including sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness testimonies, and whistleblower accounts related to U.S. military, financial, and diplomatic support for Israel throughout the course of the three-year genocide in Gaza.

The submission to the Office of the Prosecutor includes testimony of medical professionals who treated victims of 2,000-pound bombs and victims of shootings at distribution sites of the U.S. and Israel-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation — and notes that the Trump administration lifted a hold on 2,000-pound bombs, with Trump personally confirming the release of these bombs in early 2025. Rubio, the document states, also “approved or facilitated major arms transfers” including “large quantities of 2,000-pound bomb bodies or penetrator warheads,” while “waiving or compressing congressional review.” In addition, Rubio “participated in, funded, or defended” activities of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, even after Médecins Sans Frontières, the UN, USAID, and other organizations warned that the foundation was involved in “mass casualties, hunger, and aid-site danger.”

Seth Donnelly, co-founder of TAAG, introduced Wednesday’s press conference, explaining that the organization had attempted to utilize the U.S. court system to stop the government’s participation in the genocide — but that the U.S. court system “has proven incapable again, and again, and again, from addressing this crime,” forcing them to turn to the ICC.

“It is not enough to wait for elections, or to vote them out,” Donnelly said, of U.S. government officials including Trump and Rubio. “Those responsible for grave crimes against humanity, including genocide, must be prosecuted — even if they are the most powerful officials in the world.”

Lawyers working with TAAG spoke at the press conference, explaining that the evidence submitted demonstrates that Trump and Rubio “knowingly supplied, released, expedited, and protected the transfer of weapons to Israel after repeated warnings that those weapons were being used to cause mass civilian deaths, destruction, starvation, displacement, and to create conditions that made life virtually impossible in Gaza.”

Trump and Rubio’s attempts to dismantle the ICC were also addressed at the press conference. The Trump administration has “withdrawn from international human rights mechanisms and sought to undermine institutions” that aim to hold the powerful to account, argued Palestinian American human rights lawyer and TAAG member Huwaida Arraf.

Francesca Albanese, human rights expert and UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, also spoke at the press conference, saying, “This administration’s attack on the ICC, on UNRWA, and the United Nations as a whole reveal an ambition to entrench global hegemony and extinguish the possibility of justice, not just in Palestine — everywhere.”

Albanese decried Trump’s celebration of the so-called ceasefire, during which the Israeli military has killed more than a thousand Palestinians in Gaza, and his creation of the “Board of Peace,” which, she says, “revives imperial ambitions and colonial tones while securing conditions for Palestine’s continued erasure and Israel’s impunity.”

“Let us be clear: the genocide of the Palestinian people would not have been possible without the unwavering support of the United States,” Albanese said.
