author: Amy Goodman
title: Nvidia Scandal Has Exposed “How Precarious the Governance of This AI Truly Is”
content:
Tech critic Paris Marx and Professor Ramesh Srinivasan discuss the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI industry.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.

Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.

We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips.

Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him.

Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia.

REPORTER: When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?

ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not.

I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department. I’ve read some of the stories, which, you know, are sourced or not sourced, and so I don’t have any — but, no, I don’t have — the answer to your question is, no, I don’t have any — I don’t have any concerns.

AMY GOODMAN: On Capitol Hill, Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for probes into Nvidia’s actions and the Trump administration’s policies regarding chip exports to China. Republican Senator Tim Scott, the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has requested Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify. Democratic lawmakers Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Neal of Massachusetts are investigating the Trump administration’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.

For more on Nvidia and questions about the concentration of power in the AI industry, we’re joined now by two guests. In Toronto, Canada, we’re joined by Paris Marx, a tech critic and host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. And in Germany, we’re joined by Ramesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA and host of the podcast Utopias.

Paris Marx and Ramesh Srinivasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Professor Srinivasan, let’s begin with you. What should we understand about what has just taken place? And talk about the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI bubble, to the whole AI industry.

RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. Thank you so much for having me, Amy.

AI is not magic. It comes from the planet, and the technologies that produce it often return to the planet as electronic waste. It’s powered by water, energy sources, labor and our data, and those come from us, from the planet itself. Right? So, what has occurred is this astonishing technology that reduces life to data and numbers, and reduces intelligence to pattern recognition, has been — has now been governed and run by just a few people on the planet, mainly men, and men that you’ve discussed, you know, commonly on Democracy Now!, who were there at the inauguration and so on.

So, now when we have soap opera sorts of moments, like Mr. Jensen Huang being connected to, you know, this Chinese — potential Chinese spy, various affairs and so on, you can see how precarious the governance of this AI truly is, because the administration has completely handed the keys to this incredibly powerful technology, that feeds off of all of us and the planet, to basically a few people, and they can do what they want — their vagaries, their mishaps, their corruption in certain cases, their gluttony. That is what is being accumulated more and more.

So, the story of AI is a story that’s tied to data centers — right? — which you cover all the time, which are, you know, computing and so on, much like server farms in the past. They’re tied to chips, and that’s very key to this story, the Nvidia chips, or superchips, that were originally used in the context of gaming and now were applied to artificial intelligence and large language models. But it also comes from all of our data, and then the screens and systems that determine and shape our lives.

So, this is a technology that is harvested, extracted from our planet and all of us to create potentially trillions of dollars of valuation, which might be a massive bubble — and we can talk about that — with returning almost next to nothing for the rest of us, other than anxiety, insecurity and deep concerns. The technology doesn’t have to go in that direction, but that’s the direction the Trump administration has taken it.

And I think it’s incredibly notable that it’s the China — it’s the China scare yet again, just like we saw with Huawei, just like we saw with COVID. It’s the China scare that’s forcing all of this action and this spectacle and this controversy, rather than the real conditions of AI, which are disenfranchising and robbing people of many aspects of their futures.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, if you could continue, talking about what is the role of Nvidia when it comes to, overall, fueling so much? And explain the issue of the ban on these — on these superchips, why they’re so significant, what kind of monopoly Nvidia has on this, and why you believe he is so close to President Trump, who didn’t want him to resign.

PARIS MARX: Absolutely. Great to join you this morning, Amy.

You know, Nvidia is key to this AI market. You know, it controls about 90% or so of the chips that go into, you know, all these data centers that are powering the AI boom that we have seen occurring now for the past few years, right? And as a result of that, Nvidia has become one of the most valued companies, and for a while has been, you know, the most valuable publicly traded company on the planet, which is just staggering to imagine, right? You know, it went from kind of just, you know, a regular old tech company, you know, not particularly notable — sure, it made some graphics cards for gamers — to being now one of the key companies that, as you say, you know, is so important for what so many other companies are doing.

And it’s not just the fact that it creates these chips — right? — these chips that are just essential to, you know, the generative AI workloads behind ChatGPT and the image generators and those sorts of things, but because Nvidia has made so much money for the past number of years, it has also become a major investor, plowing more than $120 billion into other AI companies across the economy, across the United States, around the world, which has meant that now there are all these companies that not just depend on Nvidia’s chips, but also depend on Nvidia’s financing. You know, I’m sure you’ve been talking on the show about the upcoming Anthropic IPO, you know, Anthropic looking to go public. It is expecting about $10 billion from Nvidia as part of its public offering. And so, Nvidia has been really key here.

And because of that, you know, because Nvidia was valued at something like more than $5 trillion until recently, it’s no surprise, then, that Jensen Huang has become very close with Donald Trump, right? It’s a very valuable company. It is a company that makes the technology that is very important to the broader AI boom that has been kind of lifting the U.S. economy and the U.S. stock market — right? — because of the investment, not just in all these AI products, but in all these data centers that, you know, have been being built across the country, as well. And so, Jensen Huang has become a major adviser to Donald Trump on AI policy and has certainly been pushing him to weaken the restrictions on, you know, basically, his ability to sell these chips to China.

And I think now in light of these revelations, there are questions as to whether, you know, that is kind of a firmly held belief that Jensen Huang had because there was obviously, you know, as someone who runs a major company, a big market opportunity in selling those chips to China, or whether there was influence on his thoughts, you know, from Alice Huang. And I think those are questions that we don’t have answered yet, but certainly is probably, you know, what some of these lawmakers are hoping to try to get more insight into by having Jensen Huang come speak to congresspeople.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, in your book, you quote one investor who describes Nvidia as “the central bank of AI.” And there are many descriptions of how Huang is really the conduit from the other tech billionaire bros to reaching President Trump and making the demands that they want.

PARIS MARX: Absolutely. You know, as I was mentioning, when we look at Nvidia, it is not just a company that is selling all these chips. It is a company that has gone to a lot of these other AI and data center companies and made sure that they had investment, sure, so that they could, you know, grow, expand their businesses, what have you, but also that they — so that they could then buy more Nvidia chips from Nvidia, right? So, it’s kind of like a circular financing scheme, where Nvidia gives it the money to operate, and then they buy the chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia makes more money in that way, right? So the money comes back to Nvidia all the time.

And then, of course, linked with that is it has also used that money to try to support companies that were in difficult situations. So, for example, a company called CoreWeave, that creates data centers to power AI and kind of sells that computing power to these AI companies, has been in trouble, on and off, for a number of years, and Nvidia has often been there to support that company when it has been in dire straits. And it’s not the only one like that.

And so, of course, you know, linked to that, Jensen Huang has developed this really close relationship with Donald Trump. You know, we saw this just the other day, just yesterday, after Jensen Huang resigned, and, you know, Donald Trump came out and said that he was talking to Jensen and, you know, that things are difficult, and, you know, basically, had this really kind of personal relationship to him, seems to be someone who he really trusts. And as a result of that, I’m sure that Donald Trump has been open when Jensen Huang has been discussing AI and tech policy with him.

And, of course, Jensen has been pushing to make sure that there is not regulation of AI products, in the way that your other guest has been talking about, you know, is really necessary, but then, on top of that, again, trying to weaken these restrictions on the ability to sell chips to China. And, of course, you know, the U.S. government’s concern and many lawmakers’ concern there is that by selling those chips, because they are some of the — because they are the most advanced chips that are out there, that if they get sold to China, you know, China will not just be able — Chinese companies will not just be able to use them to power their own AI products, but that there’s a concern that, you know, Chinese companies will be able to kind of reverse-engineer the technology and then have a big kind of leap in their — in their kind of chip-making capabilities, essentially.

AMY GOODMAN: In October of last year, Jensen Huang spoke to the media about whether China should have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

JENSEN HUANG: The China market is large, and it’s a vibrant, vibrant market with a lot of developers. And those developers create AI technology that’s exported from China all over the world. And so, to the extent that American tech stack can run and operate those AI models, it’s good for the United States and around the world.

REPORTER: So, would you want the Blackwell to be sold in China?

JENSEN HUANG: I hope so. I hope so. But that’s a decision for President Trump to make.

AMY GOODMAN: So, Professor Ramesh Srinivasan, if you can explain what he is saying there? And also, this whole issue of the so-called Chinese spy, what evidence do we have of this? Is it other competing companies saying this? Is there a big division within the U.S. government in the intelligence community who had informed Trump of this months and months ago?

RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. It’s not clear what the evidence is as of this point. You could even see in the story, in the introduction to this story, that even the Attorney General Todd Blanche is, you know, very elusive and vague in his comments about, you know, what is — what exactly occurred here.

But I do think it’s very important to note a couple things that were already mentioned here. First of all, the AI industry, there’s incredible amount of concern that this is an overspeculated bubble. That’s because many of the revenues are occurring in the circular way that your other guest just described. So the revenues seem to be inflated here.

And talking about China, as we actually discussed before, Amy, back, you know, about almost two years ago, Chinese models around AI are performing nearly as well as the top American so-called frontier models. I mean, the question of what we’re building all these models for is a worthwhile question, I think a big elephant in the room. But they’re doing it at a fraction of the cost. So, we have to really consider what’s occurring here and what’s really occurring here, right?

So, the president’s response around all these concerns is often to say that the economy is super healthy. And when he says that, what he’s talking about — Trump, I’m saying — is he’s talking about the S&P 500. But the vast majority of people in America and around the world do not have large amounts of investment capital. Investment capital is how people make money, but there’s a deep amount of concern that these — this is not going to actually produce the type of revenues that even legitimate it for investors.

But what about the rest of us, as workers, as consumers? AI is being pushed out as a technology of replacement, not a technology to augment or expand or help us, you know, create together. It’s not a telescope. It’s not, you know, a microscope. It’s not what Steve Jobs once famously called a “bicycle for the mind.” It’s being — it’s using us. It’s surveilling us. It’s turning us into data. It’s turning life and intelligence into patterns to replace us, to read, write, speak for us. In fact, a CEO in Big Tech told me recently, because I’m from Silicon Valley and I have friends in that industry, “Hey, Ramesh, you don’t even have to do this interview with Democracy Now! Very soon, an AI can do that for you, and better than you.” What does that even mean? So, this is what’s at play here.

And so, this has been cast, as I alluded to earlier, as some sort of flat, you know, geopolitical battle between the U.S. and China, when, in reality, what we need is cooperation between the two nations, and, most importantly, outside of the elites in those two nations, governance by stakeholders, not just in the Global South and around the planet, where I’m part of a Global South AI alliance, but also from workers, consumers and so on, to ensure that a technology that uses patterns to predict the present and construct the future is a technology that’s applied to the right domains. And no one, at the end of the day, has been paid for their data. None of us have equity in any of these companies, but these companies are feeding off us to potentially replace us. And that’s what I would call a parasitic technology. But it doesn’t have to go in that direction.

AMY GOODMAN: Ramesh, can you show us your hands? AI models are notoriously bad at generating the correct number of fingers. I’m only kidding. OK, Paris Marx, Paris, this was from Bloomberg. You have Bloomberg in — let’s see, says, “Jefferies Financial Group Inc.’s Chris Wood said the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the U.S.” Do you see that coming now?

PARIS MARX: It’s hard to say when exactly that would come. You know, I think that there are multiple moments over the past few years where it looked like, you know, maybe — maybe the bubble is going to start bursting, and then, you know, it has continued. I think that it is facing a serious threat in this moment, and not just because of the resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia.

And to be clear, you know, Nvidia was a company that was really like Jensen Huang’s fiefdom. You know, it was not set up to have a lot of kind of people who could easily take over from him if he were to leave the company. You know, a number of his family members are also executives within the company. And so, you know, I think that there’s real concern about what this is going to mean for Nvidia’s future — right? — as such a key player in the AI market, you know, again, one of the most valuable companies in the world, supplying the key technology that these companies need, but also providing a lot of financing to other companies.

But we’ve also been seeing, through this year, a lot of major companies kind of pulling back on their generative AI spending, because they’re finding they’re not getting the return on investment from what they’re doing there. There was just a report at the end of October from an analyst at Apollo called Torsten Slok, and he basically looked at the S&P 500 to see, you know, whether companies had really been benefiting from this rollout of generative AI, and found that with the big seven tech companies, you could clearly see an increase in profit margins and in revenue per employee, you know, from rolling out generative AI products, but for those other 493 companies within the S&P 500, he did not see, you know, kind of like a notable difference or that generative AI had really benefited them.

So, there are growing questions there about the economic benefits of actually using this technology, not to mention, you know, kind of the many social harms that your other guest was talking about that need to be addressed and reined in. And so, you know, there are already — there’s already kind of skepticism and questions about all the money that has been put into these AI models, into these data centers in order to power them, whether they’re actually going to be as useful or whether the market for them is actually going to be as big as the companies are promising. And so, on top of those existing concerns, now these issues at Nvidia are kind of adding on top of that, which means that there is a potential kind of greater risk there, you know, of a collapse of some sort coming in the near future. But I certainly wouldn’t want to go as far as to call that this is the moment that it’s all going to happen.

AMY GOODMAN: And, Paris Marx, as you look down on us in the United States from Toronto, and across, of course, at Alaska, I wanted to get your comment on the midterms. You’ve written extensively about the anti-data center movement in the United States. It certainly fueled a lot of people, might have driven a lot of people to the polls. If you can also talk about the possibility of Democrats investigating tech CEOs? And, of course, right now we have the demand of Democrats and Republicans to investigate Jensen Huang.

PARIS MARX: Yeah, I would love to see it. Let’s bring on more investigations of the tech CEOs. Start with Jensen, and we can go from there.

But I do think that the midterms were not just a repudiation of the Republican Party and Donald Trump, but also of these tech CEOs that have been wielding so much power over, you know, our societies collectively for such a long period of time. And especially it feels like they really took this to a new level with what they’ve been doing the past few years — right? — not just the rollout of this generative AI technology that, as I was saying, is not as beneficial as they promised, but also had a lot of negative social and environmental consequences that came along with it, but then, paired with that, trying to push these massive hyperscale data centers into so many communities across the United States and around the world.

And so, what we saw is voters really push back against that. You know, so many races in the United States had a data center component to them. And if we look at key states like, say, Texas or Georgia or Ohio, we can see that data centers were really consequential in the battles that played out there, and that Democratic lawmakers recognized that, you know, going against data centers, promising moratoriums, was going to win the votes.

I think now the question is where this goes from here, right? Are we actually going to see those Democrats follow through on those promises? Is the pressure going to keep up? Or is the tech industry, which I’m sure it is, you know, about to pivot at this moment, hiring a ton of lobbyists to try to find a way to shape some of what Democrats are going to try to do, try to shape that kind of tech regulation, data center regulation agenda to make sure it’s not going to be as biting as it might otherwise appear? And so, I think that’s what I’ll be watching, you know, going forward, how this is going to play out.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, Paris Marx, I want to thank you for being with us, author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, speaking to us from Toronto, and Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, today speaking to us from Germany. Thanks so much, both, for being with us.

Coming up, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Gaza has killed at least six people, including a surgeon. We’ll speak to Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, who volunteered at Nasser and worked with Dr. Abu Shaira. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Garden” by Nicolás Jaar.

author: Golnar Nikpour
title: To End Iran War, Democrats Need New Leadership — and a New Approach
content:
Democrats must now reject Schumer and Jeffries’s hawkish status quo on Iran and fully embrace diplomacy.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Tens of millions of voters across the United States issued an unequivocal rebuke to the administration of Donald J. Trump this November by voting for Democratic candidates, including dozens of democratic socialists. The so-called blue tsunami was so thorough that Republican strongholds like Texas and Georgia and Mississippi flipped key offices, while swing states and districts from Pennsylvania to Arizona to Michigan moved comprehensively leftward.

As pundits and politicians have rushed to explain the electoral sea change, one interesting point of consensus has emerged: The U.S.’s and Israel’s war of choice against the Islamic Republic of Iran — an unpopular effort that has spiked gas prices and exacerbated inflation — has proven disastrous for the Republican Party.

On election night, Trump himself stated that “Iran was a piece of” the GOP’s midterm drubbing. Vice President JD Vance echoed this point, calling Iran “the real reason” for the electoral bloodbath. Exit polls confirmed this, showing that 74 percent of voters called the war a “crucial” or the “major” factor behind their vote.

Meanwhile, numerous Democratic candidates made opposition to the war a key part of their campaign messaging. Democratic socialists including Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros, and Darializa Avila Chevalier campaigned on staunch antiwar platforms. On Election Day, hours after news broke of the U.S. again bombing Iran’s Qeshm Island, Michigan’s soon-to-be Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed stated, “We need less war, not more.” North Carolina’s Annie Andrews shared a similar message, calling for an end to “this illegal, unconstitutional, billion-dollar-a-day war overseas.”

This messaging hasn’t been limited to the left wing of the Democratic coalition. Centrist party stalwarts have also claimed that voters have provided a mandate to end Trump’s folly in Iran. In a post-election interview, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand put it succinctly: “We have to end this war in Iran.”

Despite Democrats’ current antiwar messaging and an electoral mandate to end the war, the hawkish logic that undergirds Trump’s approach to Iran has decades of bipartisan support.

But what would it mean to end this war, and are Democrats currently led by those who would earnestly endeavor to do so? Amid questions over future party leadership, key Democrats have promised to pluck off the lowest-hanging fruit in Trump’s war cabinet, such as “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth. This is welcome news for opponents of a war that has seen Hegseth’s leadership bring an endless litany of alleged war crimes and the mass killing of Iranian civilians.

But ending the war will be more difficult than simply ridding the Trump administration of Hegseth. To halt a standoff that has the potential to spiral into a yearslong slog of pointless violence and global economic devastation, the Democratic Party needs change in its leadership and in its overall approach toward the Islamic Republic.

Despite Democrats’ current antiwar messaging and an electoral mandate to end the war, the hawkish logic that undergirds Trump’s approach to Iran has decades of bipartisan support. This posture was briefly evidenced in unhappy responses to the Trump administration’s short-lived June memorandum of understanding (MOU) to end the war. Even members of the GOP loath to critique Trump lashed out at the MOU upon its release.

Like their Republican counterparts, some powerful Democrats described the terms of the MOU, particularly its financial concessions, as an unacceptable capitulation. While Democratic responses centered Trump’s recklessness in starting a costly war of choice, they nonetheless described Iran in pointedly hostile terms and challenged the wisdom of offering the Islamic Republic diplomatic compromises. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, then the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the MOU a “catastrophically bad outcome for a war that should have never happened.” Shaheen continued, “President Trump has offered concession after concession to the Iranian regime for next to nothing in return.” Problematic concessions, per Shaheen, included “sanctions relief, billions in unfrozen funds, $300 billion in fresh investments facilitated by the United States and a green light for its missile, drone and proxy forces to continue threatening its neighbors.”

Sen. Cory Booker offered a similar critique, arguing in an interview, “When you have Democrats and Republicans, conservatives and progressives, all coming out talking about capitulation, surrender, catastrophe, you know how bad this deal is.” The New Jersey Democrat said, “Iran gets all of the benefits, literally billions and billions of dollars.” This same theme — “giving Iran money” — was taken up by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who opined, “We’re giving them money so they can oppress you further. I mean, it’s amazing. Just unbelievable. I have never seen such a disaster.”

Over the past 25 years, there have been few figures in U.S. politics more hawkish on Iran than Chuck Schumer.

There is an irony in Democrats decrying sanctions relief and the unfreezing of Iranian financial assets: These critiques echo some of the furious Republican (and AIPAC) responses to the Obama administration’s landmark 2015’s Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JPCOA), also known as the Iran nuclear deal. Republicans — including Donald Trump — hammered then-President Barack Obama for giving Iran “pallets of cash” (in reality, Iran’s own frozen assets) as part of the settlement. That any Democrat would today call similar concessions “capitulation, surrender, catastrophe” reveals a self-defeating contradiction to this hawkish line of attack. In decrying the use of financial incentives as a tool of diplomacy with Iran, and in painting the unfreezing of assets or sanctions relief as the U.S. “giving Iran money,” these Democrats delegitimize the very tools their own party may one day need in order to negotiate a durable agreement with the Islamic Republic. The choice that stands before the U.S. today is not a Trump-negotiated “bad deal” or some mythic perfect outcome wherein Iran agrees to surrender terms — or, to put it as Trump boasted in the early days of war, that there would be “no deal with Iran except UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER.” Rather, the decision is between diplomacy or yet another war without end.

Now, after the election, some of the party’s most vocal Iran war hawks are poised to take on more power.

Over the past 25 years, there have been few figures in U.S. politics more hawkish on Iran than Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader and the person who could potentially become the most powerful Democrat in Congress. In June 2025, eight months before the U.S. and Israel launched the current war, Schumer attacked the Trump administration’s own dithering efforts at diplomacy with Iran over the nuclear issue — what Schumer called “negotiating with the terrorist government of Iran” — for being insufficiently tough. In a social media video, Schumer chided the president, stating, “If TACO Trump is already folding on Iran, the American people need to know about it. No side deals.” (TACO stands for “Trump Always Chickens Out,” a reference to Trump’s seeming tendency not to follow through on threats.)

This is hardly the first time Schumer has taken a hawkish position on Iran. In 2010, at a conference held by powerful pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC, Schumer — who voted in favor of war in Iraq and has long advocated for devastating sanctions against Iran — argued against diplomacy with the Islamic Republic. “Diplomacy has failed,” Schumer exclaimed to a room full of AIPAC guests. “Iran is on the verge of becoming nuclear and we can’t afford that.” (Advocates for war against Iran, most prominently Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu, have claimed that Iran is on the verge of nuclearization for more than 30 years.) In 2015, amid the Obama administration’s diplomatic breakthrough with Iran, Schumer was intransigent, outdoing even longtime hawk Hillary Clinton. While Clinton — who in 2008 called Obama “reckless and naïve” for his position on diplomacy with Iran — signaled guarded support for the deal, Schumer remained steadfast in his opposition.

Schumer is hardly the only Iran hawk among current Democratic leadership. In February 2025, a year before the start of this current war, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries — the current House minority leader — outwardly endorsed Israeli military actions in Gaza and seemed to advocate an adversarial approach for taking on Iran, crowing: “[Hamas leader Yahya] Sinwar is gone. Sinwar is gone. And Hamas is on the run … and Iran is at one of its weakest points in decades … We can’t take our foot off the gas pedal until Iran is brought to its knees — for the good of the world.” Jeffries — who like Schumer and Booker has received significant campaign contributions from AIPAC, and has also received donations from weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin — further showed his hand before the election by naming Rep. Jared Moskowitz as ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa. Moskowitz has called himself “to the right” of the approach to Iran taken by Vance and Trump’s Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, likening himself to recently deceased Sen. Lindsey Graham — that avatar of the neocon lust for war — and far right Sen. Tom Cotton, who led Republican efforts to torpedo Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Recently, Moskowitz has not only demanded that Trump get “tougher” on Iran but also that the U.S. more directly support the Saudi war effort in Yemen.

Reaching an agreement with Iran will be even more difficult today than it was under Obama, who faced a bumpy road — including a cacophony of Israeli and GOP scaremongering about a nuclear Iran — on the path to the 2015 agreement. It is likely that a new agreement will have to start from terms similar to those in the MOU, which appeared more favorable to Iran than those of the JPCOA — a result of Iran’s successful wartime throttling of key global economic chokepoints and pummeling of U.S. bases in the region. And although war hawks have once again been proven disastrously wrong in their rosy predictions — Tom Cotton once boasted that it would take only two quick military strikes to defeat Iran: “the first one and the last one” — many are still promising that total victory is just one bombing campaign away.

Overcoming the current crisis — and avoiding an even worse escalation — requires overturning a hawkish status quo represented by Schumer and Jeffries.

All of this means that the U.S. will not be able to end this war as quickly or as unilaterally as it was launched. Islamic Republic leadership has made it clear that Iran is unwilling to agree to a situation that allows for the U.S. (or Israel) to rebuild military capabilities in the region and start bombing again down the road. If, having failed to win quick regime change in Iran, the U.S. or Israel hope to institute a practice of “mowing the lawn” (that is, routine bombing campaigns, as Israel has conducted for decades in Gaza), it is clear that they have not fully considered the extensive economic, military, and political damage that can be caused by a sovereign nation and military capable of mowing right back.

It is also unlikely that the Islamic Republic will simply sit on its hands if the U.S. continues forward with its current “neither war nor peace” strategy of economic strangulation — what Trump’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called an “economic onslaught” — meant to bring the Islamic Republic to heel. Iran’s economy and infrastructure have been clobbered by the war and Tehran likely wants to avoid a resumption of active hostilities, but it will not be inclined to allow the U.S. a status quo where only the Iranian economy suffers, and all other parties get to move on. Without a negotiated end to the war, the entire region and the global economy alike remain on a razor’s edge; the resumption of full-blown war is practically an inevitability in such a scenario.

If the election is clear proof that Americans don’t want to pay the economic cost of war (to Democrats’ recent electoral benefit), Iran’s leadership has been quick to take credit for the GOP’s losses. Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei claimed after the election that, “The Iranian nation has imposed strategic defeats on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz, and now has now imposed a political defeat in Washington.” Rezai’s point is straightforward: If the U.S. insists on punishing Iran through warfare, be it conventional or economic, the Islamic Republic nonetheless will absorb the body blows and inflict meaningful punishment in return. This is a lesson that Democratic leaders — who campaigned on affordability whether or not they took explicit antiwar positions — can scarcely stand to ignore.

Politicians like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries own the myriad failures of decades of war-making across the Middle East, including in Iran. The Democratic Party stands poised to repeat these deadly mistakes by again elevating figures like Schumer and Jeffries to congressional leadership positions, ignoring not only their own voters but also the lessons of the last months and years of endless and devastating war-making across the region. For a genuine and durable end to this war, the Democratic Party needs new leadership as well as a sincerely peace-oriented approach to Iran. Any antiwar coalition must insist on the simple truth that overcoming the current crisis — and avoiding an even worse escalation — requires overturning a hawkish status quo represented by Schumer and Jeffriesand instead taking steps towards meaningful and potentially transformative diplomacy.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Schumer, Who’s More Unpopular Than Trump, Gets a Challenger for Majority Leader
content:
Trump has hit record low approval ratings during his second term, but even fewer Americans approve of Schumer.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) announced on Thursday that he is running for Senate majority leader, posing competition for Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who is one of the most unpopular congressional leaders this century with an approval rating even lower than Donald Trump’s.

Van Hollen announced that he is vying for the seat in an interview with MS NOW on Thursday evening, saying that voters have handed Democrats a “generational opportunity for the Senate to respond to the call of the American people for change.”

In the half-hour interview about his platform, Van Hollen called for a break from the status quo, saying that he backs numerous progressive populist priorities, like “get[ting] rid of super PACs,” refusing AIPAC funding, and “tak[ing] on a broken economic system that’s rigged” against the working class.

Van Hollen and Democratic advocacy groups have called for the process of choosing a leader to be more democratic, creating a space for the caucus to come together to lay out a plan for the new Congress and have debates on what that may look like. Schumer, on the other hand, has spent the last week speaking as though his leadership is a foregone conclusion.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” said Schumer in a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement. “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

It’s currently unclear whether or not Van Hollen has the votes to win. He has the support of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), one of the most popular politicians in the U.S., and numerous freshman senators who have called for new leadership.

However, polling has found that the public is ready for new leadership in the Democratic Party.

Schumer, who has been the Senate Democratic leader for nearly a decade, is extremely unpopular. NBC polling done late last month found that only 13 percent of voters view Schumer positively, compared to 53 percent who view him negatively — a 40-point gap. This is even worse than Trump’s dismal approval ratings, which have hit new lows in his second term; that same poll found that 60 percent of people disapprove of Trump while only 40 percent approve, a 20-point gap.

Other polls have yielded similar results. A poll by The Economist/YouGov found earlier this month that 54 percent of voters view Schumer unfavorably, compared to 23 percent who view him favorably — giving him a -31-point rating. That poll found that more voters disapprove of Trump, but also that more voters approve of him, at 62 percent to 36 percent, respectively, giving him a -26-point rating.

Schumer is also one of the most unpopular congressional leaders in recent history. According to Gallup polling, 67 percent of respondents said they disapproved of Schumer’s performance in December 2025, compared to 28 percent who approved. This is far lower than his approval rating in 2021, when Schumer had 44 percent approval, and 53 percent disapproval.

Between Rep. Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California), Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-California), Sen. John Thune (R-South Dakota), and Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky), only McConnell had worse favorability at any point in his leadership than Schumer, Gallup found. In his last year as leader of the Senate Republicans, McConnell had a 71 percent disapproval rating, compared to 27 percent approval in 2023.

Voters are hungry for change. Polling by Reuters/Ipsos in June 2025 found that the vast majority of Democrats, 62 percent, want the party leaders to be replaced, with only 24 percent saying the leaders should stay the same.

This may be due, in part, to Schumer’s opposition to many of the populist progressive policies that Van Hollen extols. Last year, he taunted Trump for not being more aggressive against Iran and twice folded on a government shutdown while extracting little to no concessions from Republicans on issues like ICE funding. He is a staunch supporter of Israel, including amid its genocide in Gaza, and has not backed proposals like Medicare for All; rather, in recent months, he has backed the pro-data center legislation currently advancing through Congress.

author: Shahad Ali
title: 1.4 Million People in Gaza Live in Tents. Winter Storms Can Be a Death Sentence.
content:
Making unlivable conditions even more dire, flooding in Gaza is just the first disaster of a long winter to come.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The recent deep low-pressure system that struck the Gaza Strip earlier this month resulted in a widespread humanitarian disaster. According to Gaza’s Government Media Office, flooding inundated 70,000 tents, leaving 350,000 people without shelter. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) also stated that more than 26,000 Palestinian families in the Gaza Strip had requested assistance after their shelters and belongings were damaged by rainfall. In addition, Gaza’s Civil Defense reported that a mother and three of her children died after a rain-soaked sand embankment collapsed onto their tent in Deir al-Balah.

Around 1.4 million people in Gaza — roughly 65 percent of the population — are currently living in tents in overcrowded camps after the Israeli assault destroyed 82 percent of residential buildings. Most are living in worn-out tents that they have been using for years but cannot afford to replace or repair to make them more resistant to heavy rainfall. Shelter materials are extremely expensive in Gaza. For example, a single tent costs around $350, while a tarpaulin costs approximately $50.

For the fourth consecutive winter, Israel continues to restrict the entry of essential winter supplies, including blankets, warm clothing, proper tents, tarpaulins, basic materials needed to repair damaged homes, and heavy machinery required to drain floodwater and repair sewage networks. According to the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, approximately 200,000 tents across the Gaza Strip have become completely worn out and can no longer provide even minimal protection against cold and rain. The International Organization for Migration has also confirmed that currently available shelter stocks cover only 17 percent of Gaza’s actual winter needs. The organization has stressed that Palestinians in Gaza need more durable and sustainable shelter solutions, including wooden structures, prefabricated housing units, and caravans.

In addition to this suffering, many families have few options but to pitch their tents in areas near the beach, as Israeli forces still control roughly 70 percent of the Gaza Strip within what is known as the “Yellow Line,” leaving more than 2 million Gazans confined to approximately 30 percent of the territory. These coastal areas are particularly vulnerable to flooding. Strong waves can reach far inland, flooding tents and washing them away. The lack of adequate rainwater drainage systems in these areas makes matters worse, as floodwater often mixes with sewage and accumulates around tents, turning their surroundings into pools of contaminated water.

According to OCHA, approximately 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding, including more than 400,000 in locations considered at extremely high risk of flooding.

Aya Alshami, 25, a mother of two who is now living in a tent near the Gaza City port, told me that when the deep low-pressure system struck the Gaza Strip, her tent and all her belongings were flooded:

The rain was very heavy. I felt the top of the tent starting to sag and lean towards us. I tried to lift it, but the water had made it so heavy that I couldn’t manage on my own.

Then I heard my children shouting from inside, “Water is coming in!” We wondered where it was coming from. We thought we had secured everything, but then we found water seeping in from all sides.

My husband and I desperately tried to push the water out using a squeegee, but all our efforts were in vain. The mattresses were submerged, our belongings were soaked, and everything was flooded, turning the tent into a pool.

Alshami added that after her tent was flooded, she sat with her children in the street, drenched and shivering, with nothing to keep them warm:

These have been the worst days I have ever experienced. Before the war, winter was my favorite season. We lived in a warm home. I used to prepare sahlab and watch the rain falling while wrapped in a warm blanket. Now, I am literally homeless and helpless.

Although I received a new tent from a humanitarian organization after my previous one was flooded, I am certain it will not withstand the next rainfall. No matter how much you try to protect a tent from the rain, it’s all in vain. It’s still just a piece of fabric, the kind people use to enjoy a holiday at the beach in summer. And you’re expecting us to shelter ourselves in one through flooding and heavy rain?

Majdi Aswarki, 31, a father of three, was forced to relocate to a tent in Deir al-Balah after Israeli forces destroyed his home and took over his neighborhood, Al-Shaboura, in Rafah. Aswarki also told me that when he heard about the approaching low-pressure system, he tried to reinforce his tent to withstand the heavy rainfall.

“I sold my share of the cooking gas so I could buy four tarpaulins and wooden poles,” he said. “I also placed sandbags along the sides of my tent and used shovels to build barriers to prevent water from seeping in.”

However, all of Aswarki’s preparations proved futile in the face of the heavy rainfall:

The area where we live is very low-lying. This area is known to flood every winter, even before the war. From the first hour of rainfall, things were already out of control. The rain was so heavy that my tent collapsed and became completely submerged because there were no drainage channels.

All our clothes and blankets were soaked. We did not sleep at all that night. Instead, we spent the entire night trying to salvage whatever belongings we could. The water literally reached our knees, and we had nowhere to shelter from the rain. We were not the only ones affected; all my neighbors in the camp suffered the same fate.

For Aswarki and many others in Gaza, the suffering they experienced during the first rainfall of this winter is far from over. In fact, it is likely to be repeated with every storm, as the world continues to watch our suffering in silence without taking meaningful action to end it.

“It really breaks my heart that we have to keep pleading with the world to hear about our suffering. How much more do we have to tell you?” he said. “We spoke to you while we were being bombed, while we were starving, and while we were being displaced. And now we are speaking to you while we are drowning. Winter has only just begun.”

title: Over 200,000 Debtors and Their Allies Demand Student Loan Repayment Pause
content:
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reports that outstanding student loan debt has hit approximately $1.66 trillion.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

More than 200,000 student borrowers and their allies, as well as a coalition of advocacy groups, demanded Thursday that Democratic congressional leaders seize the moment of their soon-to-be majorities in both houses of Congress to win a student loan repayment pause.

A petition circulated by the Student Debt Crisis Center (SDCC) demanding President Donald Trump act to pause all federal student loan repayments and interest had collected 209,359 signatures as of Thursday afternoon.

The petition accuses the Department of Education under Education Secretary Linda McMahon — who has said she shares Trump’s goal of abolishing the DOE — of having “failed Americans” by moving the student loan portfolio to the US Treasury Department, creating lengthy delays in and “egregious account errors” in application processing, not granting loan forgiveness to qualified borrowers, making repayment less affordable, announcing the end of the Saving on a Valuable Education plan, and restarting interest accrual on SAVE plans. Dozens of Democratic lawmakers last week pressed McMahon to answer for these failures.

“Amid an affordability crisis and the current state of affairs, student loan payments should be the last thing on anyone’s mind,” the petition states. “Student loan payments are an unacceptable source of additional stress for Americans who are already stretched thin.”

Our payment pause petition surpassed 200,000 signatures, but we aren't stopping there. Read the full press release here: www.studentdebtcrisis.org/post/student…Add your name to the petition: actionnetwork.org/petitions/pa…

“We called for a payment pause in 2025, which the Department of Education chose to ignore, but we are resuming our call for a pause right now,” the document adds. “Given the growing economic anxiety and hardship facing Americans, an immediate payment pause is not just necessary; it is imperative.”

SDCC said in a statement announcing the petition:

Following the midterms, affordability is top of mind for millions of Americans. With a new Congress opening the door for real change, beginning with a payment pause would give student loan borrowers necessary relief while the 120th Congress legislates and conducts oversight. Lawmakers are already demanding answers from the Department of Education on their extensive failures managing the federal student loan system. Now, borrowers are holding those in charge accountable.

“The results of the midterm election are undeniable — Americans need relief from the burden of unaffordable living, and they need it now,” said SDCC founder and president Natalia Abrams.

“Implementing an immediate pause on student loan payments and interest wouldn’t just be an effective way of providing relief, it would also free up room in the paychecks of over 43 million borrowers to pay bills, care for their families, and revitalize their local economies,” Abrams added. “It’s a no-brainer.”

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported Tuesday that outstanding student loan debt reached approximately $1.66 trillion in the third quarter of 2026, making it the second-largest category of household debt after mortgages.

Meanwhile, Federal Student Aid, a DOE agency, highlighted earlier this year that more than 42 million people hold federal student loans, with the federally managed portfolio alone exceeding $1.64 trillion.

On Wednesday, around 20 advocacy groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, both New York Democrats, urging them to pressure Trump to sign legislation pausing student loan repayments after Democrats take back control of Congress in January.

We joined nearly 20 orgs in a letter to Senator Schumer and Rep. Jeffries urging them to win a pause on student loan payments in this next Congress.From widespread administrative errors to high monthly payments, Dems must step up for student debtors.www.forbes.com/sites/adammi…

“The student debt system is on the brink of breakdown, and today it functions worse than it did before the COVID-era payment pause,” the groups contended in their letter, referring to the suspension of repayments during the first Trump administration that continued during former President Joe Biden’s tenure before ending in 2023.

“We do not make this request lightly,” the letter continues. “It is grounded in a documented and worsening pattern of administrative failure that is causing real, immediate, and irreparable harm to millions of borrowers.”

“The chaos and disarray in the current system are not the fault of borrowers, and borrowers should not bear the consequences,” the signers asserted. “A pause is the only responsible course until the department can guarantee that the system works as the law requires.”

Groups signing the letter include the American Association of University Professors, Debt Collective, Democratic Socialists of America, Sunrise Movement, SDCC, and the University of California Student Association.

“A historic number of voters sent a clear message to Congress this election that they want mass economic relief and financial breathing room,” Debt Collective co-founder Astra Taylor said on Bluesky. “Trump paused student loans once. Democrats should push him to get it done again.”

Corporate Democrats could also prove to be an obstacle to debt relief. Both Schumer and Jeffries backed legislation that effectively prohibited the Biden administration from extending the pandemic-era payment pause.

Schumer had previously been among the most prominent congressional advocates for student debt relief, repeatedly urging Biden to extend the payment moratorium and cancel as much as $50,000 in debt per borrower.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has moved aggressively to resume collections. In April 2025, the DOE announced that it would restart collections on defaulted federal student loans the following month, and that it would seize federal tax refunds and other payments through the Treasury Offset Program.

The department also announced plans to garnish borrowers’ wages. In July 2025, it notified borrowers that interest would resume accruing on loans enrolled in Biden’s SAVE repayment plan, which had been blocked by a federal court injunction. The administration subsequently announced plans to eliminate SAVE. However, the Trump administration has also twice delayed involuntary collections, including the planned wage garnishments, amid public outcry.

As of September, more than 9.3 million student loan borrowers were in default, owing approximately $234 billion.

title: Jeffries Refuses to Say If He Opposes US-Israeli Military Integration Measure
content:
Jeffries and Schumer are already under scrutiny for their vehement pro-Israel views as calls grow for new leadership.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Thursday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) refused to say whether or not he supports efforts to strip the Pentagon budget bill of a highly controversial provision to integrate the U.S. and Israeli militaries, even as other Democrats unite on the issue.

This week, a group of 12 members of the Senate led by Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) urged congressional leaders to remove the measure mandating the creation of a “U.S.-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” from the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for 2027. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) also said this week that it is one of his top priorities for Congress before the new year.

The issue is time sensitive. The measure is slated for inclusion in the Pentagon budget, which is regarded by many in Congress as a bill that must pass before year’s end.

When asked about the measure and the Van Hollen letter at a press conference on Thursday morning, however, Jeffries dodged the question.

“I haven’t had a conversation with Senator Van Hollen,” Jeffries said. “But what I have said is that things have to dramatically change over in the Middle East.”

“That looks like, as far as I’m concerned, making sure you have a safe and secure Israel, living side by side, as a Jewish and democratic state, with an independent Palestinian state,” he went on. The only legislation that he called out specifically was the West Bank Violence Prevention Act, which has been criticized as insufficient by pro-Palestine advocates, and which Jeffries said he supports.

The military integration measure — Section 219 in the House version and Section 1217 in the Senate — would mandate the creation of an initiative to deeply integrate the U.S. and Israeli military and technology sectors, including in areas like weapons production and autonomous warfare. It is backed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and has faced vehement opposition by critics who say that it inextricably links the U.S. and Israeli military at a time when Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, backing horrific violence in the occupied West Bank, and razing huge swaths of Lebanon.

“As an American, I am outraged by Section 219,” said Khanna. Khanna and Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Kentucky) amendment to remove Section 219 was blocked in committee twice this summer. “Who do they think they are? This needs to be the top priority in the lame duck session.”

Jeffries also called for “dramatic change” with the memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the U.S. and Israel, which is set to expire in 2028. However, he did not address President Donald Trump’s announcement last week that the U.S. would stop sending the roughly $4 billion in annual funding called for by the MOU next year. This announcement was already met with skepticism by advocates for Palestinian rights, who pointed out that Section 219 and other measures are slated to deepen the U.S.-Israel relationship in more secretive ways.

The remarks are likely to fuel yet more criticism of Jeffries, who has been under scrutiny in the past week along with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer amid calls for new Democratic leadership. Both Democratic leaders are staunch supporters of Israel, and have broken with large swaths of their caucuses this year in votes on blocking assistance to Israel.

Their continued support of the apartheid state comes as support for Israel among the public has fallen to all-time lows amid its genocide in Gaza, as Americans grow increasingly incensed over the U.S.’s aid to Israel, polls have found. The military integration measure is also extremely unpopular: An August poll found that 61 percent of Americans oppose the proposal, including 78 percent of Democrats.

This week, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) announced that he is not backing Schumer for Senate leadership when the Democratic caucus votes next month, calling for drastic change. In an interview with The Nation, he cited Schumer’s backing of Israel as a reason to oust him from leadership.

“[I]n this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is. On issue after issue, I think he is just not in tune with where his constituents are at,” Sanders said.

When asked about the issues in which Schumer differs from the base, Sanders said: “You can start off with U.S. military aid to Israel.”

author: Qassam Muaddi
title: Palestinian Opinions Are Divided as Elections Are Now Postponed Until 2027
content:
Although some in Gaza welcomed the prospect of elections, many are looking for solutions to more urgent problems.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On October 10, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a presidential decree postponing the legislative and presidential elections from November 2026, the original scheduled date, until September 2027.

Amid obstacles imposed by the Israeli occupation, the postponement was justified by a need to create appropriate political, security, and on-the-ground conditions for free, fair, and inclusive elections.

According to the official Palestinian news agency WAFA, the decree aims to allow for comprehensive national dialogue to strengthen Palestinian unity, preserve Palestinian territory, safeguard the political system, address challenges that the electoral process is facing, and ensure the participation of Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip while protecting their political and constitutional rights.

While some expected the postponement, in light of the cancellation of Palestinian elections in 2021, it nevertheless came as a surprise to observers.

In the Gaza Strip, reactions to the decision have been divided. Some consider it to be in the national interest, arguing that the current conditions in Gaza do not permit elections. Others believe that postponing the vote, after more than 20 years without elections, undermines the national democratic process and marginalizes the role of Gaza’s residents in determining their political future.

Fadi al-Sheikh Youssef, head of a youth-led electoral list that had been preparing to contest the elections, described the postponement as an unjust and direct denial of the Palestinian people’s democratic right.

“The elections should have continued after nearly 20 years of freezing the democratic process in Palestine,” he said. “If the Israeli occupation has imposed obstacles, the elections should have become a political battle fought by all parties against the occupation. This electoral process should have been a new opportunity to expose the occupation to the world and reveal the falsity of its claims about democratic practices and its supposed respect for freedom of expression and Palestinians’ right to political participation.”

He added that the postponement appeared to reflect an agreement among political parties to reproduce the same political landscape.

“Unfortunately, we see this postponement as part of an effort by the parties to recreate the same political scene. Even the justification of national consensus does not reflect the real wishes of the Palestinian people. If there had truly been national consensus, it should have been achieved over the past 20 years, not now, as the political landscape is being reshaped through a democratic process,” he said.

Al-Sheikh Youssef described the decision as deeply unjust and ill-suited to the current political landscape, arguing that it excluded new groups and political actors seeking to enter the arena and defend what remains of people’s dignity.

In a statement, Hamas said it viewed the decision to postpone the elections until next year as a step in the right direction, given the absence of the political, security, and on-the-ground conditions necessary for free and fair elections throughout the occupied Palestinian territories, including Jerusalem.

Hamas said the postponement should lead to comprehensive, serious and productive national dialogue. It also expressed its readiness to participate in discussions aimed at reaching clear and binding agreements for all parties, including mechanisms to reorganize Palestinian political institutions, particularly the Palestinian National Council and the Palestinian Legislative Council.

Furthermore, some Palestinian political analysts and academics offered a broader assessment of the political calculations behind the postponement and its potential consequences for the Palestinian political system.

Political analyst Adel Shadid told Mondoweiss that “despite the Palestinian demands and European pressure on the Palestinian Authority to hold elections, the PA are afraid of elections, because they know its officials know that there are real possibilities of losing, and despite that, I was surprised by the postponement of elections.”

According to Shadid, the elections were postponed in an unexpected manner. “I expected the Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas to unilaterally call off the elections, like in 2021, but I didn’t expect all the Palestinian factions to meet in Cairo and then come out with a joint statement to call off the elections together,” he said.

Shadid pointed out that although the alliance of Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the dissident Fatah currents led by Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Qudwah had a very high chance of winning, these factions knew that there was still uncertainty regarding Israeli attempts to block Palestinians from voting in east Jerusalem. This would have given the PA the possibility of calling off elections by blaming the decision on Israel, exposing their unwillingness to relinquish control, while the factions wanted to make it clear that it was a Palestinian decision. Shadid also said that “the result of this decision will be that the Palestinian political scene will remain at the current stagnation, which prolongs the overall Palestinian incapacity to face the Israeli offensive.”

Shadid, who twenty years ago ran the elections campaign for Fatah in Hebron, the West Bank’s largest city, today believes that all factions, including the leadership of Fatah in the PA, act on narrow political calculations rather than the overall national interest.

“During the revolutionary years of the PLO, when it was based in exile, political legitimacy came from the role played in the struggle, or as the saying goes, from the barrel of the gun,” Shadid explained. “But since the PA was established as an embryo for a Palestinian state, legitimacy comes from a popular vote, but this transition wasn’t fully and properly made, which has created a rift between the leadership and the people.”

Despite the uncertainty, he remains hopeful for the next generation of Palestinian leaders. “The international solidarity movement today finds more Palestinian partners in civil society, where they can find more Palestinians from the young generations with whom they can cooperate, and eventually, a new Palestinian leadership will emerge and channel all this potential towards Palestinian liberation,” Shadid said.

For Palestinian analyst and academic Akram Atallah, all factions feared the elections, because their performance in the past years, especially during the Gaza genocide, was very poor. This meant that despite the wide opposition alliance, the voting rate would have shown that the popularity of all of them has fallen back.

“I wasn’t surprised by the postponement of elections, because in my opinion, president Abbas believed that Hamas, his main opponent, had lost much of its popularity and capacity of influence, but the formation of the wide opposition alliance changed his calculations, therefore, it was expected from him to postpone elections,” he told Mondoweiss.

Atallah believes that the consequences of calling off elections will be paid by the Palestinian people in general. “Elections for Palestinians meant the possibility to renew their leadership in order to counter the Israeli genocidal and expansionist project, and calling elections off means to remain in the same political weakness experienced by the Palestinian people,” he said.

For Atallah, the entire Palestinian political system is in crisis, from the PA losing influence to Hamas losing capacity to present an opposition, resulting in all factions becoming more concerned with “their share in the political pie” rather than a renewed leadership for Palestine.

Despite this, he insists that “the Palestinian people will produce new leadership, and Palestinians will continue their struggle and resilience despite the political stagnation.”

On the streets of Gaza, opinions remain divided between those who support the postponement and those who oppose it.

Mahmoud al-Dhahir, 41, originally from Rafah and now displaced in Khan Younis, said President Abbas had made the right decision, given the instability of the Gaza Strip’s political and security situation. According to al-Dhahir, people in Gaza are already struggling with severe problems related to food and shelter, leaving them in no position to focus on elections or think clearly about which candidates could meet their needs.

“We are now living in just 30 percent of the Gaza Strip. If elections are to be held, we at least want to be able to return to all parts of Gaza and move freely. Only then can we think about who will serve the interests of the Palestinian people and go to the ballot boxes,” he said.

Al-Dhahir had voted in the 2006 elections, hoping that conditions would improve. However, after Palestinians chose their representatives through the ballot box and Hamas’s list won, he said, Israel imposed a tighter blockade on Gaza and deprived its residents of their rights.

He argued that conditions in the West Bank might be more conducive to elections because its residents are not facing a genocide, but that the situation in Gaza is entirely different.

“The Palestinian people in Gaza have been living through a genocide that has continued for three years and has not yet ended,” he said. “It would be better to look for solutions to end this genocide before thinking about another vote or another election.”

Although some people in Gaza had welcomed the prospect of elections as a democratic process through which residents could choose their representatives, the conditions they face have left many looking for solutions to more urgent problems.

Bassem al-Masri, 51, who was displaced from Beit Hanoun and is now living in Deir al-Balah, said he was delighted when the elections were announced for a near-future date, viewing them as a long-overdue democratic right for the Palestinian people. At the same time, he said the current circumstances in Gaza were not conducive to holding elections.

More pressing priorities include enabling displaced people to return to their homes and rebuilding the houses they have lost. All of this, he argued, requires Palestinian leaders to unite before elections take place.

“Palestinian factions and leaders who want to unite and consolidate their political decisions into a single position should have taken this step to help the Palestinians devastated in Gaza, rather than doing so merely to take part in elections,” al-Masri said.

Critics described the X post as technofascist, as it espoused a pro-war, pro-policing ideology, lamented the post-Holocaust “neutering” of Nazi Germany and Japan, and said that cultures that have “produced vital advances” are superior to those that are “dysfunctional and regressive.”

The tech CEO has been on the record many times branding himself and Palantir as undertaking a far right effort, with Karp calling his company “anti-woke” and praising the Trump administration’s anti-immigration measures.

Karp also appears to have given Republican House candidate Jay Obernolte $7,000 in January, federal disclosures show, though he listed his employer as “Plantatir Technologies” — making it so that his company wouldn’t come up in database search queries for Palantir, spelled correctly.

Karp’s comments represent what is likely a naked attempt to woo Democrats before they take control of Congress in January.
