title: Refugee Groups Sue to Stop Canada From Handing Over Asylum Seekers to ICE
content:
The lawsuit says handing asylum seekers over to the abuse-perpetrating US is a violation of Canada’s constitution.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Canada is violating its own constitution by turning asylum seekers away at the border with the United States, where they face serious threats under U.S. President Donald Trump, Canadian legal experts and rights advocates say.

Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees, and the Canadian Council of Churches are in court this week to challenge a decades-old pact that allows Canadian officials to summarily send most refugees back at the U.S. border.

People rallied in Toronto and Montreal, the two largest cities in Canada, on Monday to show support for the case and call on the Canadian government to rip up the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA).

In Montreal, dozens of protesters held posters that read, “Canada must protect, not send back” and “Humanity has no borders.”

“If Canadians don’t feel safe in the United States, we can be sure that refugees aren’t safe either,” Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, told the crowd.

“The asylum system in the U.S. is failing, and those who flee in search of safety deserve to be protected.”

The Safe Third Country Agreement, which came into force in 2004, is premised on the idea that Canada and the U.S. each offer people access to a robust refugee protection system.

In practice, it means that asylum seekers can seek protection in the first country they arrive in, but not both: someone in the U.S. cannot apply for asylum in Canada, or vice versa.

For years, the restriction applied to asylum claims made at official crossings along the border.

But if people entered Canada irregularly between ports of entry (via farmers’ fields or rural roads, for example), they could circumvent the pact — and as Trump began to crack down on immigration during his first term, tens of thousands of people made dangerous crossings into Canada to request protection.

In 2023, amid public and political pressure to crack down on immigration, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and President Joe Biden closed the loophole, extending the Safe Third Country Agreement to the entire 5,525-mile border.

Now, only people who meet specific conditions — such as unaccompanied minors or individuals with relatives who are already in Canada — are exempt from being turned away under the Safe Third Country Agreement.

The lawsuit being heard in Federal Court in Toronto this week argues that the Safe Third Country Agreement violates equality rights under Section 15 of Canada’s constitution, known as the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

According to the complainants, that’s because the pact disproportionately harms racialized asylum seekers, including women fleeing gender-based violence, children, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Julia Sande, a lawyer at Amnesty International Canada, explained that Section 15 applies to everyone who is physically in the country, including refugee claimants.

“Canada cannot deport people to face torture, harm [and] persecution in another country,” she said. “It would be a violation of their Charter rights, even if it’s another country doing the harm, because it’s Canada’s decision to send them out … [and] to put them in [harm’s way] when harm is reasonably foreseeable.”

While conditions for asylum seekers and refugees in the U.S. have been concerning for a long time, Sande said the situation has deteriorated dramatically under the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump.

She pointed to the expansion of immigration detention as one example. “Things are obviously extremely urgent and extremely harmful,” she said.

“We all act in horror at what’s unfolding in the United States. You hear Canadian citizens talking about being afraid to go there, being afraid of ICE.”

“We all act in horror at what’s unfolding in the United States. You hear Canadian citizens talking about being afraid to go there, being afraid of ICE,” she told Truthout.

“I have a hard time believing that you could find anyone here who would say, ‘Yeah I’d really like my government to hand a child over to ICE to be thrown in detention … and ultimately sent back to a country where they fled gang violence.’”

Canada’s federal immigration ministry — Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada — told Truthout in an email that it can’t comment on matters before the courts.

But it said the Safe Third Country Agreement “is designed to keep the Canada–U.S. border safe and well-managed,” adding: “It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems. This means Canada can keep the border orderly while continuing to offer protection to people who need it.”

The government also says on its website that, “only countries that respect human rights and offer a high degree of protection to asylum seekers may be designated as safe third countries.”

But Yael Schacher, head of the Americas program at humanitarian group Refugees International, said the U.S. “absolutely” does not meet that threshold.

“The U.S. does not have fair procedures for asylum seekers anymore,” she said.

“We have a situation here where people that — by Canadian standards — should be entitled to asylum, entitled to protection, are having their rights violated all the time in the United States in many, many ways.”

“Canada Should Be Thinking Twice”

Schacher told Truthout that the Trump administration is not effectively screening asylum seekers for harm they would face should they be deported from the U.S. It also has purged judges who may have been favorable to asylum cases from U.S. immigration courts, effectively transforming them into “deportation courts.”

At the same time, the U.S. government is detaining people in dire conditions as it pushes to deport them to their home countries or to third countries where they face myriad dangers, including torture and imprisonment.

She described a recent case in which a Haitian man agreed to be deported to Haiti’s capital Port-au-Prince — which has been ravaged by deadly gang-related violence — after eight months in U.S. detention because he could not get sufficient insulin to manage his diabetes.

“He gave up his right to an asylum hearing on the merits because he couldn’t take the detention conditions anymore. He was afraid he was going to die,” Schacher said.

She said there have been cases in which people handed over to U.S. immigration authorities by Canada at the border have been detained and deported without a fair assessment of their asylum claims.

“‘Turning away’ is a way too euphemistic way of describing what Canada is doing, which is giving people to the U.S. immigration authorities, who are then putting them in prison and deporting them,” Schacher said, adding that Canada needs to rethink the STCA altogether.

“The U.S. doesn’t provide asylum anymore, and Canada — like Mexico — needs to rethink how it relates to the United States as a result.”

“The U.S. doesn’t provide asylum anymore, and Canada — like Mexico — needs to rethink how it relates to the United States as a result.”

That was echoed by Sande at Amnesty International Canada, who said that while she expects the legal challenge to the Safe Third Country Agreement to be a long process, the Canadian government “has the power to end this at any time.”

“If you survey people on the street and ask them, based on what you’ve seen unfolding in the United States, do you think the United States is safe for refugees? I think most people would say no,” Sande said.

“A government does not need a court to tell them what is abundantly obvious. They could stop sending people back to the U.S. today.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: Democratic Party Factions Are Competing to Define What Is Possible Right Now
content:
David Sirota points out that a billionaire-backed group is now convening in Denver to try to sculpt the party’s agenda.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the Democratic Senate leader, calling for the party to move in “a new and bold direction.” Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan to govern differently, and several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is considering challenging Schumer. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is facing questions about his leadership of House Democrats after 11 of the party’s members missed a key vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

After “a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, … it would be a betrayal for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership,” says David Sirota, editor-in-chief of The Lever.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: As Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, their current leader, Hakeem Jeffries, is facing questions about his leadership after a vote this week that effectively derailed an effort to impeach Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. On Tuesday, the Republican-led House voted 211 to 204 to send the articles to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively stalling the effort. Eleven Democrats were absent, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. The vote prompted criticism of Jeffries, who is seeking to become House speaker, with some questioning why he had not ensured more Democrats were present.

AMY GOODMAN: The debate over Democratic leadership in the House and Senate is also intensifying in that upper house, in the Senate. Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the party’s leader, calling for Democrats to move in, quote, “a new and bold direction.”

SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: If this campaign was about anything, it was about change and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction. I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.

AMY GOODMAN: That’s Bernie Sanders. Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has also said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan for a different vision. It’s not clear if she would throw her hat in the ring. Several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen says he’s listening to colleagues and has not ruled out a leadership bid.

The debate over who should lead the Democratic Party comes as the party prepares to take control of Congress following its sweeping midterm victories. The question now is what Democrats will do with that power and whether they’ll deliver on the promises they campaigned on.

The Lever has launched a new video and podcast series hosted by David Sirota called Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats — but they’re using the full word. Let’s go to a preview.

DAVID SIROTA: After election night, what comes next? I’m David Sirota, founder of The Lever and host of the award-winning investigative podcast Master Plan. Right now Americans are not politely asking for change. They’re mad. So, as the party looks towards the next Congress and the 2028 presidential election, we’re asking: What would it actually take for Democrats to get it right?

ROBERT REICH: How do Democrats not [bleep] this up again?

DAVID SIROTA: And so, our new series has a title that channels that anger and requires a bleep. It’s called Don’t [bleep] It Up, Democrats. I’m sitting down with politicians, economists, activists, former White House officials, power brokers and thinkers to talk about the big choices facing the party. How do you fight corruption when billionaires bankroll the political system? How do you make life affordable when corporations have so much power? How do you fix a healthcare system that’s bankrupting people? And how do Democrats win back working-class voters who’ve heard promises of change again and again? Winning elections is one thing, but actually delivering on your promises, that’s something else.

ROBERT REICH: Because Democrats do have an extraordinary capacity to grab defeat out of the jaws of victory again and again and again and again.

AMY GOODMAN: And that voice, that last voice, was former Labor Secretary Robert Reich.

Well, for more, we go to Lisbon, Portugal, where we’re joined by David Sirota, founder and editor-in-chief of The Lever, the author of the Master Plan: The Hidden Plot to Legalize Corruption in America.

David, that’s quite a provocative title for your podcast series, Don’t F#*k It Up. Can you talk about what’s just taken place? We’re speaking to you the day after the victory of Scott Colom, the first Black senator — he will be — from Mississippi since Reconstruction. And to say the least, in the last few days, he was very critical of the Democrats who refused to fund him, the leadership, until the very end. Talk about what you’re seeing in the House and the Senate now.

DAVID SIROTA: Look, I think what you’re seeing is, clearly, in the vote across the country, a massive vote for change. And let’s be really clear here: Many of the races that decided this election were won by candidates who were making a very crystal-clear critique of the status quo, of oligarchy, of the endemic corruption. Essentially, the way I see it, you see an election in which the politics, the anti-oligarch politics, that have been championed by people like Bernie Sanders, ended up winning the day, and winning the day in a huge way, particularly in places like red states.

And I think what you’re then seeing now reflected in the leadership races is whether that wave will result in some reflection of change. There would be an irony to have an election with a wave this clear, this anti-oligarch, this populist, a wave that was a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, a wave that is about change — it would be more than ironic — some would argue it would be a betrayal — for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership. So, I think you’ve got a lot of Democrats on Capitol Hill who are caught between knowing what the election was about, and also an existing current leadership, Democratic Party leadership, that doesn’t want the leadership of the party to have to change.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, David, if we could just, you know, go back and see: Why do so many progressives, progressive Democrats, and their supporters — why don’t they want to support Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer? If you could just give us a history of their — basically, their record?

DAVID SIROTA: Yeah, I mean, for sure. I mean, look, Hakeem Jeffries is somebody who, as an example, most recently, right before the election, said that he is not a supporter of Medicare for All. Hakeem Jeffries has promised to stack the House Foreign Affairs Committee with AIPAC — members who are very close to AIPAC, who are very supportive of the existing relationship, U.S.-Israel relationship. You have a steering committee in the House that’s supposed to be writing the Democrats’ AI policy, and it is comprised of lawmakers who are very close, not surprisingly, to the tech industry.

Chuck Schumer has been somebody who has danced around all sorts of issues. For instance, he ended up not supporting a major antitrust bill. He is not somebody who is perceived to have used the Senate, the power in the Senate, to really deliver on or really champion a populist agenda. And so, I think, look, I think with Schumer, there’s some generational change. I mean, Chuck Schumer has been leader for a very long time, through some very, very bad Democratic losses. So, Schumer’s got a generational question here, you know, a demand for new leadership. Jeffries hasn’t been speaker, but Jeffries is juxtaposing himself policy-wise in many ways against the base and against, in some cases, the majority of his own party.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, David, do you have any idea of who the candidates might be to replace Schumer or Jeffries?

DAVID SIROTA: Yeah, I mean, look, Chris Van Hollen, I think, is the most serious challenger, right now, to Chuck Schumer. Chris Van Hollen actually was on The Lever’s podcast just before the election, making a clear line in the sand, saying Democrats should use the upcoming continuing resolution to try to block funding for the Iran war, something that Chuck Schumer has not been willing to do or say. Chris Van Hollen is somebody who has been a serious Iran war critic, a serious critic of war in general, and much closer to the progressive populist base of the Democratic Party than, I think, Chuck Schumer.

Hakeem Jeffries, an official challenger has not emerged yet. There’s been a huge petition, a set of — I think it’s a million signatures at this point — demanding a different leader than Hakeem Jeffries. A single candidate has not happened yet, has not emerged, although there is some talk — there is a push to have it be Ayanna Pressley from Massachusetts.

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to go to Senator Van Hollen, who publicly criticized the Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for refusing to support the campaigns of Democratic candidates who went on to win, like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine.

SEN. CHRIS VAN HOLLEN: We have two members in that room, newly elected senators, who would not be there if Schumer and the DSCC had had their way. And, you know, Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates.

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, this is very interesting. I wanted to get your response to this and to now Mississippi Senator-elect Scott Colom, who was speaking, sharply criticizing national Democrats for writing Mississippi off and failing to invest in his campaign early on. He said, quote, “Mississippi was never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause.” He was speaking on NBC News before the election.

SCOTT COLOM: The reality is, our country does not do well when it ignores places like Mississippi. When America makes sure kids in Mississippi have good education, that teachers got the pay they need to actually teach the students, where we make sure that hospitals are open and that healthcare is accessible, and that we actually live up to our American values, the country does well. When the country ignores places like Mississippi, inevitably it catches up with the country, and we all suffer. So, we have to understand that the math and the morals in Mississippi have to matter. …

You can’t lead with doubt. You have to believe. You have to lead with belief. And that’s where the power is. When you believe things, you can actually achieve it. And there’s some people in the party that they are just treading water. Right? “What’s the path to least resistance to get to 51? Ooh my gosh, we did it.” That’s not the right way to think. In this particular moment, you have to think about how can we win everywhere, because we need to represent working people in a way where we actually deliver.

AMY GOODMAN: So, there you have Scott Colom speaking right before the election on NBC News. Respond to Van Hollen, what he has said, and Colom.

DAVID SIROTA: Yeah, I think — look, I think what they’re talking about is a Democratic Party that has a broader vision than the current Democratic Party. And I think all of this is pointing to not just how Democrats need to try to win, but also how they need to try to compete to deliver. And that is a — that is the biggest question of all right now. Will a Democratic Party, with margins that it has now, really think more transformatively than it has in the past when it has had such majorities?

And that fight is playing out right now in politics. You see factions of the Democratic Party competing to decide and define what is possible right now. You see one faction saying we should demand votes on Medicare for All, we should demand votes on a much — on a really expansive agenda. Then you see the corporate Democrats trying to say, “No, no, no, no. This was essentially a status quo election. So-called moderates won.”

I tend to agree, in one sense, that Bernie Sanders-style anti-oligarch, populist agenda has become and is now being recognized as a moderate centrist agenda, but you have a faction of corporate-friendly Democrats who are trying to already preemptively slow down a push for Democrats to try to deliver in a big way. There’s this big conference that’s coming up in Denver where a billionaire-funded group is convening Democrats right now. This is the same group that has said that Democrats, for instance, should not push for a Medicare for All vote, should not even try to put a Medicare for All or Medicare for All-style bill on Donald Trump’s desk.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, The Lever has been closely reporting on the gathering. On Thursday, Democracy Now! reached The Lever’s Luke Goldstein.

LUKE GOLDSTEIN: There are two things that are really distinct about the Majority Democrats/Bench political operation. For one, they sort of offer the candidates they work with access to a really illustrious and powerful donor network that they control. There’s a lot of dark money that funds these groups, as well as large donors, primarily from Wall Street and Silicon Valley, you know, tech and finance sectors, for the most part.

And then the other additional service that’s more unique is that these groups offer, essentially, a political-operative-for-rent service to candidates. So, they have a setup of real kind of insider political operatives, probably most prominently Lis Smith, who previously worked on the Pete Buttigieg campaign in 2020. And those candidates will work with different campaigns at the same time as they work with these outside PACs, and it allows these groups to really kind of control and have a centralized narrative and political messaging that you’ll see spread out across those candidates.

I think it’s fair to say that these groups have a more kind of moderate political orientation. They definitely don’t support policies, for example, like Medicare for All. I would say that they are uneasy about policies like a data center moratorium. And they’re fairly hostile to the more left-wing climate and immigration groups, certainly.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, that’s The Lever’s Luke Goldstein. And the meeting is happening today. If you could say more, David, about this billionaire-backed group, the Majority Democrats?

DAVID SIROTA: I think it — let’s add some context here. Look, we have seen this is sort of the faction with a thousand faces. People who have watched this show know this faction as the old Democratic Leadership Council. It has become the so-called — the group Third Way. It is the so-called New Democrats. Now it is called Majority Democrats. This is the same faction over and over throughout the generations: corporate-friendly Democrats who believe that winning politics means coddling oligarchs, means incrementalist-at-best policies, means a sort of deal with the corporate class for very small changes. It is essentially the faction that broke the Democratic Party away from its New Deal coalition and its New Deal agenda.

And so, Majority Democrats is a billionaire-backed group that is convening Democrats to negotiate right now at its conference, try to negotiate and sculpt the party’s agenda. I think it’s obviously more than ironic that we had an anti-oligarch, populist election, and the first thing that many major Democrats are doing are rushing to a conference funded by a billionaire, a billionaire-funded group. There’s an irony there. There’s a tension there. And I think the question is: What comes out of it?

AMY GOODMAN: David, we just have 30 seconds, but I want to go back to one of the top headlines this week, and that is that the Democrats, just by not showing up, not by being outvoted by the Republicans, they basically scuttled the possible impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. This goes to Hakeem Jeffries, who would be the majority leader, is the minority leader in the House. What happened?

DAVID SIROTA: I think it raises serious questions about how serious the Democratic leadership is, and some rank-and-file members of Congress, really the party itself. How serious are you about understanding the assignment and understanding the most basic things that need to be done to challenge Donald Trump? And I do think it is a huge question, in particular, as you allude to, for Hakeem Jeffries. Getting members to show up is the most basic, basic job of being a House leader, and certainly a House speaker.

AMY GOODMAN: David Sirota, we want to thank you for being with us, founder and editor-in-chief of The Lever. It has a new series, Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats.

Coming up, as votes are still being counted in Alaska Senate and governor’s race, we’ll speak with Rob Richie of Expand Democracy about how ranked-choice voting could shape the Alaska election, and the growing movement to elect presidents by national popular vote rather than through the Electoral College. Back in 20 seconds.

AMY GOODMAN: “Greed” by Sweet Honey in the Rock in our firehouse studio years ago.

author: Doug Bock Clark
title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead — They Aren’t
content:
After the midterm, a GOP election board member in Georgia challenged dozens of ballots using a controversial data tool.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots.

The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.

But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.

The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices.

The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting.

In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious.

ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.

Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.”

The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica.

In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica.

Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.

“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.”

Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.

In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names.

Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone. The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead.

State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”

Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name.

During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further.

But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.”

Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy.

“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said.

The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter.

Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona.

ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive.

Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why.

“It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said.

Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned.

In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said.

The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.”

The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial.

One voter, Alexander Knight, told ProPublica that he goes by his middle name and that the information in voter records mirrors how Department of Driver Services officials suggested he be identified on his driver’s license.

“I am real,” he told ProPublica.

Four other challenged voters said they, too, abbreviated their first names. A. Joseph Guntherberg confirmed he routinely used the same formulation of his name, adding that blocking his ballot would not help the challengers: “My candidate didn’t win.”

Richards said it was up to county election workers to check ELLY’s data — he merely gathers it to facilitate efforts to maintain accurate voter lists.

But at the meeting, Joel Natt, a Republican board member, said the responsibility lay with challengers to justify their accusations. “This has no relevance to anybody here until” they provide solid evidence, he said, “through the proper channel.”

author: Chris Walker
title: House Democrats Vow to Investigate White House Despite Trump Admin Threats
content:
The counsel to the president claimed that recent statements by Democrats “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The White House has sent a threatening letter to House Democrats, warning that lawmakers could face repercussions if they open investigations into the Trump administration once they take control of Congress.

The letter, sent by Will Scharf in his official role as counsel to the president, was delivered just days after President Donald Trump demanded investigations into Democrats who stated that they were planning inquiries into the administration in the wake of the “blue wave” in this month’s midterm elections. Trump falsely called those statements “illegal” and “criminal.”

Scharf’s letter, first revealed by Punchbowl News, was sent to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) on Monday, according to the date on the letter, though the House Oversight Committee said midweek that it had not yet received an actual copy of the document. Garcia, currently the ranking member of the committee, is likely to become its chair after Democrats take control of the House in January.

Citing several Election Night social media posts by Democrats — including comments from Garcia urging the administration to “lawyer up” — Scharf claimed that there are “foundational” constitutional limits “on congressional investigations and subpoenas,” and accused incoming Democrats of having personal reasons for planning inquiries into the White House.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” Scharf said.

The comments by Democrats “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” Scharf added, though he provided no basis for that claim.

The letter is highly unusual — while past presidents have criticized subpoenas and inquiries into their actions, the ability of the House Oversight Committee to conduct such investigations has long been considered a basic function of its work, and Supreme Court precedent has protected those powers. The statements by both Scharf and Trump are also hypocritical, given that Trump’s predecessor, former President Joe Biden, faced investigations by Republicans into his executive branch actions, including into his family members.

Garcia suggested that the letter indicates the administration has “something to hide.” He added:

The Trump administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. … [We] will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the president’s lawyers.

House Democratic leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House, also criticized Scharf’s letter, describing it as “outrageous” and “factually inaccurate…in terms of the Constitution.”

Peter M. Shane, constitutional legal scholar and adjunct professor at NYU School of Law, agreed that the letter contained false claims about the limits of congressional oversight.

“Our Constitution protects legislators from the threat of criminal prosecution while performing official duties as an essential bulwark to repel executive overreach and defend checks and balances,” Shane told The New York Times. “Congressional oversight and the issuance of subpoenas by definition cannot be the focus of legitimate criminal prosecution. It may be that an occasional subpoena may be quashed as outside the committee’s jurisdiction or for some other reason, but that is not a criminal offense.”

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: ICE’s Own Investigations Reveal Deaths in Custody Caused by Medical Neglect
content:
Internal ICE investigations have found that 23 individuals died in 2025 after a lack of proper medical care.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The San Francisco Chronicle has obtained internal ICE investigations into the deaths of dozens of people in its custody during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, finding that 23 of the 29 individuals died after a lack of proper medical care.

Guards, medical providers, and staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities failed to provide emergency care, failed to send individuals to the emergency room, or ignored other critical warning signs, the report indicates. According to ICE’s own investigations, deficient medical care directly contributed to 20 of 23 of the deaths. The six other individuals who died in 2025 had received care within sufficient limits, the agency claims.

The Chronicle acquired the reports through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. The findings contradict the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s claim that its immigration jails provide “timely and appropriate medical care” and that “the medical care in ICE detention is the best care” that many immigrants “have received in their entire lives.”

The Chronicle previously reported on 48 deaths in ICE custody since Trump’s second term began, finding that delayed medical care and failure to provide critical care contributed to 17 of these deaths and that there was not enough information on at least 15 cases. This report, from April, came before the outlet obtained ICE’s own investigations into the 2025 deaths, which reported an even larger number directly caused by medical neglect.

At least 62 people have died in ICE custody since the start of Trump’s second term, more than double the amount of deaths from the first Trump administration and the highest rate in over a decade.

ICE has not investigated all of the deaths caused by the agency and its immigration jails. For example, Prisciliano Trejo Ricano died shortly after ICE released him from custody while he was in a coma; his name has not been counted among those who died in custody after the agency changed its policy in June to no longer report and investigate deaths of individuals who died within 30 days of release. Similarly, at least two disabled people died in 2026 shortly after ICE released them into freezing weather, and were not counted among ICE’s official death count.

In the second half of October alone, three people died in ICE detention: Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old permanent resident from Mexico who died on October 17 at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, whose family reported that he was denied medication and care; Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old Salvadoran who died on October 23 in ICE detention in Georgia and, according to DHS, died by suicide; and Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old Guatemalan who was found unresponsive on October 24.

In some cases, prison staff mocked individuals who called for help and who later died after their neglect. In others — like the deaths at Camp East Montana in Texas, which have been referred to as suicides — conditions included medical neglect, solitary confinement, and physical and sexual violence.

People imprisoned inside ICE jails have launched hunger strikes in protest of the conditions inside, including medical neglect and unlawful, prolonged detention. In May, over 300 detained people launched a hunger and labor strike at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall, which lasted approximately a month and brought national attention to conditions in immigration jails. In September, immigrants being detained at the El Valle Detention Facility in Texas launched a hunger strike; and in October, at least 73 people launched a hunger strike at a processing center in Georgia. Other hunger strikes have been reported in immigration jails in Pennsylvania, Michigan, California, and Washington — with one immigration jail in Tacoma, Washington, witnessing at least 20 hunger strikes in 2026.

author: Julia Conley
title: Fossil Fuel Giants Have Sued States for Over $443 Billion Under Trade Deals
content:
Critics say the companies are weaponizing provisions to siphon money from public budgets that are already stretched.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Ahead of an official side event at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, campaigners on Thursday released an analysis of UN data regarding secretive deals within trade agreements aimed at protecting the profits of corporations, including fossil fuel giants, which have now claimed at least $443 billion from the legal provisions.

Investor-state dispute settlements (ISDS), which allow corporations to sue governments over their investments and profit losses as the result of laws and regulations, have increasingly been used by the fossil fuel industry as countries have started taking action to regulate planet-heating oil and gas emissions, according to data from the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

The data was analyzed by the British campaign group Global Justice Now and the German research organization PowerShift, which found that based on 987 publicly disclosed ISDS cases, corporate investors have demanded a total of $1.177 trillion up to 2025.

That represents a 37.5% increase, or $321 billion more, from the amount investors were attempting to claim at the end of 2023.

$1.177 trillion is nearly equivalent to the total global climate finance needs, including mitigation costs, for 2021-22, said the campaigners.

The total compensation demanded by fossil fuel investors, $443.8 billion, “is equivalent to the estimated minimum amount of economic losses developing countries will face due to climate change in 2030,” said Global Justice Now and PowerShift.

In fossil fuel cases, the amount demanded rose by $80 billion, or 22%, compared to 2023.

Fabian Flues, investment policy lead at PowerShift, pointed out that by “weaponizing” ISDS, fossil fuel giants are siphoning “money from public budgets that are already stretched,” and Nick Dearden, director of Global Justice Now, compared the ISDS payouts to “the owners of enslaved people being compensated for their grotesque harms following abolition in the early 19th century.”

“We know fossil fuel corporations are making a fortune out of global crises, hitting ordinary people hard,” said Dearden. “But they are also using obscure international agreements to bully governments out of responding and drain money from the public sector. It’s obscene that the very corporations which have created the climate crisis are demanding eye-watering payouts when governments take much needed climate action.”

This week, US company ExxonMobil launched a legal challenge to the European Union’s Net Zero Industry Act, under which the company is required to pay for carbon storage.

The law would saddle Exxon with “unrealistic timelines,” the company said in a statement.

A UK-based mining company and its Singapore-based majority shareholder also sued the UK government last year for £300 million ($398 million) after officials blocked their “unviable” coal mine planned for Cumbria.

“This legal challenge is a last, desperate attempt by investors to make some money out of a project which belonged in the last century,” Niall Toru, a senior lawyer at Friends of the Earth, told Land and Climate Review in May.

According to Global Justice Now and PowerShift, the total amount of compensation awarded to corporate investors through ISDS cases reached $123 billion last year, with fossil fuel investors receiving “the lion’s share of $85.9 billion, representing almost 70% of all payouts to investors.”

$123 billion is “equivalent to the entire bilateral development aid given by [Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development] countries in 2025,” said the campaigners.

The groups are among those calling on leaders at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) to agree to a coordinated phase-out of ISDS.

Next Monday, Global Justice Now and the Netherlands-based group Both ENDS are organizing an official side event in Antalya featuring Vanuatu Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu, representatives from communities at the center of ISDS disputes, and a senior government official from Australia, which announced a new policy in 2022 of excluding ISDS mechanisms from future trade deals.

“Governments need to stop this heist and cancel the international agreements that enable fossil fuel investors to sue over climate policies,” said Flues. “Countries like Australia, South Africa, and Indonesia have taken significant steps to free themselves from ISDS, and others should follow suit.”
