author: Alex Cuadros
title: Bill Gates’ $29B Stake in Landfill Company Tied to Major Methane Emissions
content:
Gates has called on businesses to fight climate change. But his own investments tell a different story.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.

Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.

For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.

“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.

With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.

While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.

One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.

Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.

“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.

As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”

Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.

In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.

A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.

Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.

It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases, he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.

Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but usually from agricultural sources (“cow farts,” in his words). He has rarely mentioned landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office, Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic’s board in 2009. Gates’ stake in the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about something I’m buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea what Cascade owns.” (Gates’ Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in securities filings.)

Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it generates methane. The Gates Foundation has funded research and advocacy aimed at solving that problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest methane into fertilizer. Its product was actually tested last year at a Republic landfill in California, where the pink liquid was sprinkled on the soil covering the top layer of trash.

Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but the startup reportedly ceased operations after a Department of Energy grant was canceled. (Windfall didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.)

On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In 2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science Based Targets Initiative, promising to cut its emissions by 35% by 2030. Not that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its pitch for garbage-collection contracts in progressive cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for businesses that meet certain environmental, social and governance criteria, attracting sustainability-minded investors.

Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates’ vision. As Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You can’t have sustainability without profitability.”

Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to mention the occasional dead pet.

Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under 100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country’s 1,400 active landfills, where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out of mind.

People who live near landfills, though, describe smelling rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning eyes, headaches and nausea. And while methane itself has no scent, those odors indicate that the gas is being released, studies show.

Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before. Open dumping and burning remained widespread until the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like benzene).

Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures. Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to keep that gas from escaping. Managing such a beast is costly, which helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of scale.

Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s historic climate bill — the company invited the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian kind of project.

On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave a tour of the gas-collection system. Like at most other large landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below — five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue, snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it into a salable product.

Most landfills that are required to collect gas simply burn it off. But they can also process it into “renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from decomposing waste, it’s generally considered more climate-friendly. It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.

Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In fact, it may be just the opposite.

In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement alert” saying that landfills across the country were “violating monitoring and maintenance requirements.” While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities targeted belong to Republic.

McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It would soon earn Republic a formal “finding of violation” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” — methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection system as well.

And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with renewable natural gas facilities can actually emit more methane than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some operators may prioritize collecting gas with higher methane content, which is cheaper to process — allowing more of the remaining methane to leak out.

Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”

“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.

The issues aren’t exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since 2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39 of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than 1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells — spewing excessive amounts of methane.

In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.

Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan: “Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying away from true climate leadership.

In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets Initiative, the SBTI made its minimum climate goal much more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.

This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders. Republic has also spent more than $8 billion buying its own stock in the open market, ProPublica’s analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by investors.

The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024, this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime investment manager — whose “insight into sustainability issues” is cited in company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’ dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the corporate-governance expert.

Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is “not an immediate strategic priority.”

Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to submit an updated target. But when ProPublica asked if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.

There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.

In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already cut its landfill emissions by 20% since 2017. But that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports, Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.

This method is based on an industry study that, as the EPA has noted, excluded data from gas-collection systems that were “not working well.” The EPA’s own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to “erroneously report decreasing emissions,” according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year period.

The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the No. 1 and No. 2 emitters among the roughly 70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA. And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn’t in the study, but according to measurements by Carbon Mapper, it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)

In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said, “We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”

He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association, a major trade group, questioning the accuracy of satellite measurements. It is a tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for cleaning up landfills.

“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane emissions,” she said. “There’s a fire alarm going off and instead of getting out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector.”

Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the “doomsday view” of global warming — a striking shift for someone who’d once warned of the failing ecosystems, mass migration and soaring mortality that could result from hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald Trump, to say that Gates had admitted he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to shift his resources, he remained a “climate activist,” he told one audience.

Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas companies because, he later wrote, “I don’t want to profit if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also called on other business leaders to “make sure that they’re not holding back” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into profits.

Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according to securities filings, has never sold a share.

In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among other potential changes, the agency asked for comments on the newer technologies, such as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in monitoring and controlling methane pollution.

Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But they wanted almost all of it to remain voluntary, according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which have Republic executives on their boards.

“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,” the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”

The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes against its climate commitments.

“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.

Gates’ press representatives didn’t respond to questions about whether he’s aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated the source of a fifth of his fortune. But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy, Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity. They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.

“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him, I think he’s very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for him.”

“My theory is that he probably doesn’t have much involvement in those investments,” said another laid-off staffer.

Gates’ investment managers, at least, can’t claim total ignorance. Larson and Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in Republic’s board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level” reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “practices we could do better,” this director said. (Larson didn’t return phone messages left by ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn’t respond to a question about his and Handley’s involvement in Republic.)

It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen, methane is produced.

Properly managing the waste we’ve already buried is only the first step, said Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. “In parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”

This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started phasing out the landfilling of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health benefits would ultimately outweigh the costs.

In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.

But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with dumpster collection, as its most profitable segments. So when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company, along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should be left to the states to decide.

“It’s like you’ve got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard, a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the environmental justice movement. “You’ve got a landfill, and it makes money — big money. So why tinker with it?”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

author: Jesse Hagopian
title: Paulo Freire’s Revolutionary Approach to Literacy Still Threatens Those in Power
content:
The new documentary Reading the World reveals how teaching literacy in Brazil became a struggle for political power.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In 1963, Brazilian educator Paulo Freire helped launch a revolutionary literacy campaign in the impoverished northeastern Brazilian town of Angicos, where hundreds of rural workers learned to read and write in just 40 hours of instruction. Freire’s approach was about much more than literacy. Rather than emphasizing memorization and repetition, he developed “Culture Circles” where participants discussed their experiences, examined the conditions shaping their lives, and developed the critical consciousness to challenge oppression.

The experiment helped lay the groundwork for Freire’s groundbreaking book, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, which would become one of the most influential works in the history of education. But the literacy campaign was violently interrupted when a U.S.-backed military coup overthrew Brazilian President João Goulart in 1964. Freire was imprisoned and forced into exile, while students burned or buried their educational materials to escape persecution.

A powerful new documentary Reading the World (Lendo o Mundo) explores this formative period in Freire’s life, before he became an internationally celebrated educational philosopher. Drawing on rare archival footage of 1960s Brazil and the memories of the farmers, students, and educators who participated in the Culture Circles, the film reveals how Freire’s ideas emerged from grassroots struggles for literacy, land, voting rights, and democracy.

The film, which premiered in New York and aired on PBS WORLD Channel this October, arrives at a time when educators in the United States are confronting renewed censorship, book bans, and political attacks on teaching about racism and inequality.

I spoke with Catherine Murphy, co-director of Reading the World, about the revolutionary potential of literacy, the political forces that sought to destroy Freire’s educational experiment, and why his ideas continue to threaten those in power.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Jesse Hagopian: One of my favorite moments in the film is the opening scene, when Paulo Freire tells his audience that he wants to have a dialogue with them rather than give a lecture. He also promises that if he doesn’t know an answer, he won’t lie. It seems like such a simple statement, but it represents a profound departure from traditional teaching. Who was Freire, and what made his approach so revolutionary?

Catherine Murphy: Paulo Freire was a Brazilian educator born in Recife in 1921. He became one of the world’s most celebrated educational philosophers. His most famous book, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, was published while he was in exile.

I also love that opening quote because it lays the groundwork for the entire film. Freire says that ever since he was a child, he understood that not knowing is part of knowing.

That gets to the essence of Freire’s philosophy: Knowledge belongs to all of us. Knowledge is generated by all of us. Education is a reciprocal, collective process. It’s about sharing what we know, and learning from each other. Freire critiqued what he called “the banking model of education” and favored a “dialogic” process based on horizontal dialogue, problem-posing, and really listening to each other.

As Freire became internationally recognized, he was increasingly invited to speak at conferences and educational institutions around the world. But his collaborators repeatedly told me stories about how he didn’t want to simply deliver lectures. He wanted dialogue with people, to listen.

When Freire visited the Highlander Center in 1987 or attended the Chicago Alternative Schools Network Conference in 1977, he wanted to know what people were doing themselves. What were popular educators doing? What were classroom teachers, community educators, and activists doing? What was working? What were they struggling with?

Freire was willing to share his ideas and experiences, but he also wanted to learn from others.

That is a beautiful lesson for all of us, not only in formal educational spaces, but in life.

Before we get into Freire’s literacy campaign, can you describe the conditions in northeastern Brazil in the early 1960s? How did illiteracy help maintain existing relations of economic and political power?

Brazil in the late 1950s and early 1960s had a highly colonial and feudal social, political, and economic structure. They had highly concentrated landownership, with 1 percent of the population owning the vast majority of the and an agricultural labor system that was only one step removed from legal slavery.

Freire came from this region of northeastern Brazil, a region often compared to the U.S. South because its economy had been based on enslavement. In northeastern Brazil at the time, approximately 70 percent of people could not read or write. Education was almost exclusively reserved for children of the elite. Most formal education was provided through the Catholic Church or elite universities.

Access to education was restricted to a very small segment of society, who would then go on to control the political and economic institutions of the country.

This was not simply a question of individuals lacking educational opportunities. Illiteracy was deeply connected to the concentration of wealth, landownership, and political power.

And the struggle for education was inseparable from the struggle for voting rights, labor organizing, and land reform. The people who had been systematically excluded from education were also excluded from many forms of political participation.

One person in the film gives an important insight that “literacy is achieved through the discussion of political topics.” That struck me because so much contemporary advocacy around what’s called the “science of reading” leaves out the social and political context that makes reading meaningful — for example, the fact that many books are being banned right now. Your film is called Reading the World, which speaks to Freire’s understanding that learning to read words is connected to learning to critically examine society. What did his approach look like in practice?

That wonderful quote is from Marcos Guerra, a leader in the Brazilian student movement, at the time which was playing a major role in struggles for educational reform.

Marcos was recruited [in 1962] by Freire to work with him in Angicos in 1963, and I’ll tell a bit about that history.

Freire began developing his approach to adult literacy in Recife in the late 1950s. Based on that work, he was invited to come work in the neighboring state of Rio Grande do Norte, where adult illiteracy was around 70 percent.

From the very beginning, he wanted the project to be collective and participatory.

He didn’t want the project to be run by the Ministry of Education, where it might get caught up in bureaucracy or become a political photo opportunity. Instead, he wanted to work with university students from different academic disciplines, including student organizers.

Marcos Guerra was one of those students, and was brought in by Freire to be the student coordinator of the Angicos project.

Together with other teachers and learners, they began developing a methodology that broke dramatically from traditional adult literacy instruction.

First, they refused to use children’s books to teach adults. They wanted to honor the tremendous knowledge and wisdom adults already possessed, even if those adults had been excluded from formal education.

They understood students as holders of knowledge and creators of culture.

They gathered vocabulary from the communities themselves, using local language and words connected to people’s everyday lives.

“In the process of learning to read the word, students were also learning to examine and interrogate the world around them, their place within it, and how it could be transformed.”

One of their first words was tijolo, meaning brick. A brick could become a metaphor for constructing words out of letters and syllables, just as workers construct buildings out of bricks.

But the words also included things like people, vote, land, and work.

These words opened conversations about people’s lives and the social conditions they experienced.

So in the process of learning to read the word, students were also learning to examine and interrogate the world around them, their place within it, and how it could be transformed.

One of the most moving parts of the film is hearing people describe what it meant to learn to read and write. One woman remembers, “It was wonderful,” and explains that learning to write your name was an enormous achievement. That made me think of my great-great-grandmother, Laura Lenoir, who was enslaved in Mississippi and became an educator after emancipation. My family recently discovered the plantation where Laura had been enslaved. We also found her signature — evidence that she had learned to write despite being born into a system that made it illegal for Black people to be literate. During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved people organized extraordinary literacy campaigns because they understood that education was essential to making emancipation meaningful. I see my family’s history reflected in the experiences of the Brazilian farmers in your film. What did learning to read mean to them, and why do these memories evoke such powerful emotions more than 60 years later?

I really appreciate the connections you’re drawing between Reconstruction in the United States, the Freedmen’s Bureau schools, and the relationship between emancipation and education.

In Brazil, just as in the long Black freedom struggle in the United States, access to literacy was tied to the struggle for voting rights, land, and self-determination.

People whose labor had been exploited for generations through enslavement and then through forms of quasi-enslavement after emancipation were often locked into those relationships partly because they couldn’t read or write.

Think about the history of people losing their land because they couldn’t read a contract. Someone tells them, “This contract says this. Just sign here.” They put down a thumbprint or an X without having certainty of what they’re signing.

“In Brazil, just as in the long Black freedom struggle in the United States, access to literacy was tied to the struggle for voting rights, land, and self-determination.”

Just as what happened to Black people in the United States, and it happened to people in Brazil.

So literacy was connected to people’s ability to defend their rights, have access to land, and participate in political life. And it began with something that might seem small but was actually enormous: learning to write your name.

Writing your name affirms your humanity. It affirms your dignity.

Freire talked about becoming a subject, becoming a protagonist in your own life. Literacy provided people with greater tools for self-determination. Once people could read and write, they could obtain identification documents. Many of the students in Angicos had never previously had any form of identification. And then they could register to vote.

So people were becoming empowered both personally and collectively to change the world around them.

One of the most haunting details in the film is what happened after Brazil’s 1964 military coup. Farmers burned or buried their notebooks so they wouldn’t get caught with contraband, and Freire himself was arrested, imprisoned, and forced into exile. There’s something extraordinary about a government that considers teaching impoverished farmers to read and write so threatening that it imprisons educators and drives them out of the country. What made Freire’s and his collaborators’ educational approach so dangerous to the dictatorship? And how was it connected to the broader struggle over land, class, democracy, and political power?

When you enter a society with these colonial, feudal, quasi-slavery relationships and begin teaching people who have been systematically excluded from education, you’re putting a crowbar into the existing social structure.

Exclusion from literacy meant exclusion from voting, obtaining identification documents, organizing, and participating in political life. At the time, rural labor organizing was also restricted. There was a powerful movement called the ligas camponesas, or peasant leagues, which was fighting for land reform. Some of the important leaders were Elizabeth Teixeira and Francisco Julião, both of whom are in the film.

These movements were demanding access to education, voting rights, land, and land reform.

The progressive president at the time, João Goulart, was beginning to respond to grassroots demands.

In March 1964, Goulart announced reforms that included expanding voting rights and beginning a limited land redistribution program. The land reform proposal wasn’t even especially radical. It involved allowing landless agricultural workers to use strips of federal land along highways, where they could live, grow food, and sell their produce. For workers trapped in plantation-like conditions, these reforms could begin changing their lives.

And literacy work was a crucial part of that transformation.

In Angicos, approximately 300 newly literate adults could potentially become 300 new voters. At the time, there were only around 700 registered voters in the town. Think about how dramatically that could alter the political balance. President Goulart actually attended the graduation ceremony in Angicos, accompanied by a presidential delegation that included numerous governors and mayors from the northeast, and a group of military officers. Some of those officers would later lead the U.S.-backed military coup that overthrew Goulart’s government in 1964 and ushered in more than two decades of dictatorship.

The military dictatorship understood that this literacy campaign was connected to movements challenging the concentration of economic and political power. So Freire and his collaborators became targets. Marcos Guerra and other members of Freire’s team were arrested the very next day after the coup. They confiscated books. Students in Angicos destroyed their educational materials, burning or burying their notebooks and other records out of fear.

The extraordinary historical footage in our film survived only because people deliberately hid it.

The filmmaker Luiz Lobo, for example, preserved film reels documenting the Angicos experience by hiding them for years, buried in a trunk in his family’s backyard. So the footage we’re able to witness today exists because people recognized the importance of preserving this history, even at considerable personal risk.

Education under capitalism contains a fundamental contradiction. The system needs education to reproduce itself, but education can also give people the knowledge and confidence to challenge the existing order. In 2012, officials in Tucson, Arizona, banned Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed and several other books from the Mexican American Studies curriculum — they actually removed the books in the middle of class! Today, we’re witnessing widespread attacks on teaching Black history and ethnic studies, and on educators who embrace Freire’s approach. Why do Freire’s ideas remain so threatening to those in power, and what do they teach us about education as a force for liberation?

Freire’s ideas, like those of other liberation thinkers, call upon us to question the world and our place in it. His approach is about developing critical consciousness through problem-posing education. It asks us to consider: Why is the world like this? How could it be different?

And, significantly, this kind of education asks us to question power.

What are the structures of power? How do they create inequalities? And how can people become collectively empowered to challenge those structures? Freire’s ideas challenge the false narratives that tell us the world is simply the way it’s supposed to be. They challenge notions of social Darwinism and the mythology of meritocracy — the idea that everyone simply gets what they work for. Instead, liberatory education encourages us to ask: What laws, structures, and institutional injustices hold people back? These are questions we need to raise and examine over and over.

But people who benefit from existing power structures often don’t want those questions asked. That’s why books become threatening. That’s why there are attempts to ban books and suppress discussions. And of course, [this is] connected to the emphasis on standardized testing, the undermining of the humanities, the privatization of education, the underpayment of teachers, and attacks on teachers’ unions.

These conversations are potentially transformative. They give people the opportunity to examine their circumstances and imagine something different.

And those who feel threatened by that possibility want to stop those conversations.

I love the scene in the film where a woman puts on a shirt bearing Freire’s words: “Whoever believes in changing reality must carry out the transformation.” Your film also emphasizes the collective experiences of farmers and educators rather than simply celebrating Freire as a great individual. What lessons should educators and organizers draw from this history today?

What I love about that quote is that Freire calls upon us to do something. It’s a call to action.

“If we know something is wrong, if we recognize injustice, if we believe the world needs to change, then we have a responsibility to be part of that transformation.”

If we know something is wrong, if we recognize injustice, if we believe the world needs to change, then we have a responsibility to be part of that transformation.

And I think that’s especially important for educators today, when we’re living through such a challenging period for people who believe in democracy and want to expand it. Freire also spoke a great deal about hope. In Portuguese and Spanish, Freire had this idea of turning hope into a verb: Esperanzar. Hope isn’t just a passive feeling. It’s something active.

It’s about remaining engaged, continuing to care, and working collectively toward a world that’s better for everyone, not just a tiny, privileged few.

One of our central purposes in making this film was to move beyond understanding Freire simply as a man of ideas. We wanted to understand him as a person of action.

So many of his ideas emerged from concrete experiences working with communities and grassroots movements. We wanted to understand who he was working with, who his closest collaborators were in these early educational experiences. It’s important to recognize the farmers, students, and community organizers as co-creators of this history.

And that legacy is still alive.

People continue this work in Brazil, the United States, and throughout the world. The struggle to expand access to education, develop critical consciousness, and build collective power is ongoing.

Freire’s legacy isn’t simply something to study in books. It’s something people are continuing to create through their struggles today.

author: Derek Seidman
title: WWII Sparked Anti-Fascist Ideas Among War Workers. What Lessons Can We Learn?
content:
Historian Tejasvi Nagaraja explains how wartime mobilization generated wider organizing around labor, race, and empire.

Historian Tejasvi Nagaraja explains how wartime mobilization generated wider organizing around labor, race, and empire.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

World War II was a period of enormous mobilization in U.S. society that brought together tens of millions of “war workers” — soldiers and laborers in war-essential industries, spanning the globe. While mainstream mythologies persist of the World War II years as a period of “consensus,” Black Americans fought in a Jim Crow military while Japanese Americans were interned by the U.S. government. Moreover, the wartime mobilization generated massive conflict and resistance around labor, race, and empire.

Tejasvi Nagaraja is a historian of labor and racial capitalism at Cornell University, and the author of Troop Movements: Labor, Race, and Global Freedom Struggles in America’s World War II. As he shows in this new book, soldiers and defense workers, stationed across much of the world, waged and linked struggles for labor and civil rights and against colonialism and imperialism throughout the 1940s. Furthermore, many World War II veterans and war workers, drawing on wartime political experiences forged in a period of rising anti-fascist consciousness, went on to lead and provide guidance for major postwar U.S. social movements into the 1960s and beyond.

In this exclusive Truthout interview, published on Veteran’s Day, Nagaraja discusses Troop Movements and what lessons its history might hold for organizers and activists today. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Derek Seidman: The military is sometimes imagined as separate from the rest of society, but your book shows how blurred these lines really were during the 1940s. Can you elaborate on this?

Tejasvi Nagaraja: World War II was, at least for the United States, the closest thing to a total war mobilization. Most employment was converted to military service in the armed forces and to working in war-essential industries. Virtually every family and community had members in the military and defense industries.

The story I tell about World War II is about what happened in this realm, where tens of millions of people were in the armed forces and defense industries, and their experiences at home, but also abroad — in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Caribbean.

Labor during World War II was not just working at a Michigan auto factory or Appalachian coal mine, but also cooking and cleaning on a military base in Texas and Mississippi or France, or building the Ledo Road across China, Burma, and India. These were sites of labor experience and labor struggle.

The 1930s and 1940s were a peak period of union membership growth and strike activity in U.S. history. Wildcat strikes were happening in defense industries during World War II. Service members in the Army, Navy, and Air Force engaged in wildcat strikes, hunger strikes, and mutinies to protest labor conditions.

The 1930s and 1940s were a peak period of union membership growth and strike activity in U.S. history. Wildcat strikes were happening in defense industries during World War II.

Black men and women protested labor, policing, and jailing conditions. They experienced race and class struggles — not just in Georgia, but in Massachusetts, as well as in France, India, and the Philippines. Their struggles linked up to global questions.

There was a real blurring of defense industry and service member labor, and civil rights and worker struggles, at home and abroad. It was a time of global anti-fascist struggle and global decolonial possibility, linking the U.S. working class, in some moments, to working people from other regions.

A huge part of the U.S. working class was tied to the war machine during World War II. How did leftists and anti-imperialists who opposed war and militarism engage with this reality?

The 1940s were a crucible through which the longer struggles of economic, racial, and global politics were transformed. In this context, labor, civil rights, and global justice activists navigated a contradictory and double-edged terrain. They sometimes made a devil’s bargain that we can understand as partly a question of choice and political ideology, but also of not making history as we please and having to navigate things bigger than oneself.

Labor unions, for example, embraced a no-strike pledge in exchange for winning union security in some defense industries. Even left-leaning Congress of Industrial Organization (CIO) unions had a seat at the table of the warfare state. In the textile mills of Georgia and North and South Carolina, union activists waged daring campaigns to unionize the very anti-union South, and they gained some openings when the War Department intervened in mid-1940s strikes to keep war production going.

At times, the Pentagon even partnered with CIO unionists to stand up to recalcitrant Jim Crow capitalists. After the war, however, those unions were left to fend for themselves and faced a reactionary push by the region’s Jim Crow capitalists.

As U.S. foreign policy shifted from anti-fascism to anti-communism and Third World interventionism, the military-industrial complex proved durable while the labor openings for more emancipatory possibilities became constrained by that very security state that arose during FDR’s anti-fascist war but then was consolidated in the Cold War anti-communist turn.

Again, you have these double-edged bargains: the civil rights movement navigating openings through defense industries and military service, but also brokering these civil rights possibilities around a U.S. becoming more permanently militarized.

How was this 1940s protest moment expressed within the military?

Service members and veterans themselves debated the postwar stakes for U.S. militarism. Active-duty service members stationed in the Philippines and Calcutta had mass meetings in 1945 and 1946 asking whether the U.S. would become an imperialist power of its own.

These service members debated how they could use their veteran identity to push for a wider vision of social democracy and civil rights in a peaceful United States. Even in a so-called “Good War” with popular support, many of them were critical of militarism and imperialism more generally.

Some service members were actually the first critics of postwar U.S. foreign policy, protesting in 1946 the U.S. aiding European colonial allies and U.S. policy toward the Philippines or Saudi Arabia.

Today, far fewer people work in defense industries. We have an all-volunteer army that has made war-work sectors more invisible and weakened the possibilities for democratic claims that could be made by service members. We think of military service now as a private individual choice — though service member identities would also be contested during the wars in Vietnam and Iraq.

Your book shows how World War II veterans and war industry workers played critical roles in postwar movements around labor, civil rights, and anti-colonialism. Can you elaborate?

I argue that this “greatest generation” of 1930s and 1940s labor, civil rights, and other social movements was also the vanguard of the 1960s movements, serving as middle-aged elders to the younger generation and setting in motion some of their movements. It built a bridge from the 1930s labor movement to the 1960s civil rights and antiwar movement.

A total war brings everybody together in a transformative experience. Before the war, when different people worked for different employers in different settings, it was harder to think about a bigger picture that links a national and international economy and politics.

But when tens of millions of people are working all over the world for this new thing called the Pentagon, directly as service members or indirectly as defense workers, they can see a bigger picture.

For example, Ossie Davis became a famous actor and senior statesman of labor, civil rights, and global justice movements, along with his partner Ruby Dee, from the 1940s to the 1960s. Davis spent most of the World War II years in West Africa, seeing, as a Black working-class American, the U.S. Army projecting power abroad. He saw Firestone Tire and Rubber Company — one of the biggest corporations in the world, with Pentagon war contracts — controlling the biggest rubber plantation in the world in Liberia.

All this was formative for Davis developing a larger vision — seeing how working-class and Black struggles in Georgia or Harlem were linked to global capitalism and global war.

The interracial labor and civil rights movements, and even early queer and feminist movements, of the 1940s would grow into the movements of the 1960s. And many key people in those 1940s movements were formed in this culture of CIO unionism, and of a labor-civil rights-veterans coalition, as active-duty service members, returning veterans, and defense workers in the 1940s. They came into their political life in this moment of anti-fascist consciousness during a global war.

Mainstream commemorations of Veterans Day tend to ignore the robust tradition of GI and veteran organizing for peace and justice. How does your book help us counter the right’s capture of veteran history and identity?

Service member and veteran identity is a contested thing that’s always been fought over.

World War II saw a mass service member experience where people from all walks of life were drafted into the armed forces. CIO union and civil rights organizers went into the Army and Air Force and engaged in civil rights and anti-imperial mutinies and strikes from Indiana to the Philippines.

Many of these people asserted their veteran identity in labor, civil rights, and veterans’ groups from the mid-1940s onward to make a claim on U.S. citizenship to criticize reactionary capitalist, racist, and imperialist trajectories.

CIO union and civil rights organizers went into the Army and Air Force and engaged in civil rights and anti-imperial mutinies and strikes from Indiana to the Philippines.

It was only with the 1950s Red Scare that conservative hegemony asserted itself over veteran identity. But in the 1940s, you had groups like the American Veterans Committee, with a mass membership linked to the NAACP and the CIO unions, advocating for peaceful social democracy.

Some of the first protesters of a U.S. global empire in 1945 and 1946 were CIO organizers in the army mobilizing mass protests in Honolulu, Paris, and Manila, demanding speedy demobilization to go home and criticizing the new U.S. imperialism and aid to European colonialism.

There were bitter conflicts over veteran identity during the Vietnam War. Some mobilized to support the brutal U.S. war, but others engaged in widespread GI and veteran resistance.

It’s different in the post-Vietnam era with the turn to an all-volunteer army. You have groups like About Face using their veteran identity in critiquing U.S. foreign policy, but there’s also much fewer people engaging in military service.

What do you think left organizers and movement activists today can learn from the history you write about?

Bigger lessons from World War II still hold today. How do you stitch together a broader populist base moving in a progressive direction, led by some people who have a more daring and even radical vision?

I write about the “Bring the Boys Home” demobilization movement in 1946. Some participants were not very political and just wanted to go home, but they were mobilized by people with a left-leaning vision.

Today, with Trump’s unpopular war on Iran, you have everyday expressions of service member defiance, like on the USS Gerald Ford, which aren’t necessarily politicized. How could activists connect up with that?

In our moment, there’s widespread defiance against U.S. foreign policy and a broader discontent among even more apolitical working-class people. There’s an opening to challenge the bipartisan foreign policy elite and assert something new — not just what’s good for us, but for the wider world.

Local struggles around labor, race, policing — they’re deeply interconnected with global wars and global capitalism. When people see the foreign and the domestic, the local and the global, as linked, it can embolden a horizon of anti-fascist urgency. In the 1930s and 1940s, this allowed for positive fights for racial and economic justice.

When people see the foreign and the domestic, the local and the global, as linked, it can embolden a horizon of anti-fascist urgency.

Today, as we face neo-fascism in our times, it’s an opportunity to confront not only the worst horrors in the Middle East or ICE at home, but to imagine a positive reconstruction, linking global justice with our local racial and economic justice work. Studying this history has painful lessons — Japanese Americans faced mass incarceration, and Black Americans faced Jim Crow segregation — but also lessons of tremendous success that can help us move in a positive coalitional direction and with a cross-issue vision for our own times.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $47,000 in the next 8 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

Under her watch, the Civil Rights Division shifted considerably to the right, ignoring violations of civil rights that have traditionally been defended by the DOJ and focusing instead on conservative priorities.

Dhillon’s office, for example, oversaw investigations into supposed instances of antisemitism on college and university campuses — and led the DOJ’s aggressive crackdown on student organizing against Israel’s genocide of Palestinians in Gaza.

content:

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A political and economic battle against today’s robber barons — the billionaire and trillionaire class of tech bosses — is unfolding on many fronts as tech workers agitate against these oligarchs’ complicity with the U.S. military, the cops, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Israeli occupation of Palestine.

In their new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine recount the emergence of the tech workers’ movement over the last two decades, from the political campaigns they have launched to the heroic strikes they have staged against companies like Kickstarter and The New York Times.

No armchair analysts, Tan and Redwine are tech worker leaders who have been at the heart of many of these fights. In this interview, they discuss the rise of the movement, the workers’ turn to unionization, and the oligarchs’ adoption of authoritarianism and austerity to crush it. And they draw lessons from this struggle not only for tech workers, but for the entire labor movement.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

title: Extreme Flooding in US Southwest May Foreshadow a Disastrous El Niño Winter
content:
Historically, the phenomenon boosts precipitation in the southern US. This may be a glimpse at the pain to come.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Southwest just got way too much of a good thing. Last weekend, a ferocious storm inundated communities and killed at least four people. Though precipitation is an essential component of Arizona’s desert climate, the state got two or three months’ worth of it in just a few days — far more than human infrastructure could handle all at once. Since September 20, an astonishing 28.84 inches of rain has fallen on Clovis, New Mexico, compared to its historical average of just 3.3 inches.

“This weekend was just adding more on the rough times that those communities in Southwest Colorado and Arizona and Utah and New Mexico have been having recently,” said Russ Schumacher, director of the Colorado Climate Center at Colorado State University, who’s also the state climatologist. “I think the El Niño connection is pretty clear.”

Indeed, that band of warm water in the Pacific could be priming much of the southern United States for a winter of increased precipitation, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook. “Could an event like this have happened in a non-El Niño year?” asked Michael A. title: The Navajo Nation Just Elected Its First Woman President
content:
The Navajo Nation isn’t alone. The Seneca Nation of Indians also elected its first woman president this week.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Crystalyne Curley is set to become the first woman president of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation by land mass in the country.

Curley, who also held the distinction of being the first woman to serve as the Nation’s council speaker — the head of its legislative branch —when she was voted by council members to fill that role in 2023, has worked on issues related to water rights, uranium contamination and voter rights.

In another first for tribal governments, the Seneca Nation of Indians in New York also elected its first woman president, Tina Abrams. She previously served two terms on the Nation’s council.

While Native women made history for their tribes in this election, it is not uncommon for women to hold top positions in tribal nations. Activist Wilma Mankiller was appointed as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1985, the largest tribe in the country by tribal enrollment numbers. Though there is no official data on women’s representation in tribal governments, the nonprofit RepresentWomen found that in 2020 at least 78 tribal nations had reached or exceeded gender parity in their legislatures.

Donnelly, a member of the AI working group in the Chicago Teachers Union, says Google is one of many tech companies that are centrally motivated by profit, despite purporting to serve other aims. As AI developers like Microsoft and OpenAI push to integrate their products into U.S. schools and pupils’ lives more broadly, Donnelly said she believes that students are entitled to a clear understanding of the forces shaping their education.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has lost dozens of races in which it backed a candidate in this year’s midterm elections, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable political lobbying group, in a sign of its waning influence.

Politico found in a report on Thursday that more than 30 of the group’s candidates lost their elections this week. This marks “defeat for AIPAC in over three-fourths of the competitive races that have been called so far where it backed an incumbent,” Politico reported.

This includes candidates like Republican Representatives Mike Lawler (New York), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), and Max Miller (Ohio), as well as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who fell to progressive Israel critic Troy Jackson, and Mike Rogers in Michigan.

Collins has been a staunch defender of Israel in the Senate, and AIPAC was her biggest outside donor by a massive margin during the race. California has more people sentenced to capital punishment than any other state, but for years there has been a moratorium on carrying out the death penalty. Newsom’s action ensures that the moratorium is permanent for those 548 individuals.

The action doesn’t abolish the death penalty in the state, meaning that future convictions could result in death sentences. It also commutes all capital punishment sentences to lifetime imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that ensures these individuals will still face death by incarceration.

But the move is being praised as a step in the right direction — one that could result in other states following suit.

Newsom said that he made the decision to commute the sentences of everyone on death row “because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”

Voters in Montana on Tuesday delivered a major blow to big moneyed interests by overwhelmingly passing a ballot initiative barring corporate cash from political campaigns in the state.

With 87% of votes counted as of Wednesday morning, Montana Constitutional Initiative 194 has received support from more than 65% of voters, with just 35% registering opposition.

The initiative prohibits what it describes as “artificial persons” — which includes corporations, nonprofits, trusts, partnerships, and trade associations — from giving money to political campaigns.

Supporters of the initiative have billed it as a way to strike a blow against the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which opened the door to unlimited campaign spending in US politics.

Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump.

It was 3:00 am when Doug George-Kanentiio first arrived at the Mohawk Institute Residential School in Brantford, Ontario, in 1967.

He was 11 years old, and he would go on to spend 18 months at the abusive institution, which was Canada’s longest-running residential school. The notorious school operated for more than 140 years before it closed in 1970.

“They weren’t places of learning, they were places of confinement,” George-Kanentiio said.

Decades later, he still remembers the hunger, fear, and brutality that he and the other Indigenous children who were forced to attend the Mohawk Institute endured there every day.

“Anything you could imagine [being done] to a child, when it comes to abuse, that’s what these individuals did,” said George-Kanentiio, who is from Akwesasne, a Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) community on the U.S.-Canada border, between New York state and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

“It was physically painful and extraordinarily cruel,” he told Truthout.

content:

Immigrant rights and labor icon Dolores Huerta died Wednesday at the age of 96. Huerta co-founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962 and then the United Farm Workers of America, working with Cesar Chavez. From 1965 to 1970, the union organized the historic Delano grape strike, which ended in major gains for farmworkers’ labor rights.

In the years that followed, Huerta became heavily involved in the women’s liberation and immigrant rights movements and became a major supporter of the Democratic Party. In March, The New York Times published an investigation into Cesar Chavez’s history of sexual abuse of women and girls in the farmworkers’ movement, prompting Huerta to reveal that she, too, had been raped by Chavez. Huerta said the assaults led to the births of two of her children.

Dolores Huerta appeared on Democracy Now! many times over the years. A broadly democratic socialist organization, COPE ran on a bold platform demanding full rent control, an end to data center construction, and taxing the rich to fund social housing, schools, parks, and libraries. All 12 COPE candidates swept into office, constituting the single largest party bloc. Now with those dozen seats on the three boards — out of 27 total seats — COPE is poised to advance a bold, socialist-inspired agenda for one of Canada’s major cities.

The president was also in the state to hold rallies for Ken Paxton in his race for U.S. Senate against Democrat James Talarico.

“We took over Venezuela very successfully, and they sent me, as a gift, a boatload of — a million barrels of oil. And I’m giving that to the United States of America,” Trump said in remarks before his flight.

title: Far Right Influencer James O’Keefe Charged With Voter Fraud in Minnesota
content:
O’Keefe used a racist accent and wore what he dubbed “Muslim garb” in his failed attempt to expose “fraud.”

Right-wing provocateur James O’Keefe is facing charges in Minnesota relating to his attempts to illegally register to vote as part of an online stunt that attempted but failed to expose flaws in the state’s registration process.

There are numerous methods of registering to vote in Minnesota. One process, called “vouching,” is used by people who don’t yet have proof of residence in the state. The person seeking to register to vote can get an individual who knows them to vouch for them by signing a document affirming that they live at the address listed.

The process doesn’t end there — the person who is attempting to register has to provide other forms of identity, including their driver’s license number or part of their Social Security number.

Vouching is considered a secure method of confirming a potential voter’s place of residence. It’s also rare, with the process being used in only about 0.6 percent of all registration applications.

title: High Palestinian Turnout in Israeli Elections Came Down to Matters of Survival
content:
“We fear that if we do not get this government out of power, we will lose everything,” one Palestinian voter said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Jaffa, Israel — Outside of Ahva Elementary School in Ajami, a historic Palestinian neighborhood just south of central Tel Aviv, the mood was defiant on October 27, the day of Israel’s national elections. “We fear that if we do not get this government out of power, we will lose everything,” one Palestinian voter told me after casting her ballot.

It came as no surprise that she, like most of the Palestinian citizens of Israel I interviewed on Election Day, asked not to be named. Since October 7, 2023, more than 400 Palestinian citizens of Israel have been investigated by police for “incitement,” often over social media posts, according to the legal rights group Adalah.

During the 1948 war, which Palestinians call the Nakba, most of Jaffa’s nearly 100,000 Palestinian residents fled or were expelled. The fewer than 4,000 who remained were concentrated in Ajami, fenced in with barbed wire, where they lived under Israeli military rule until 1949.

title: Trump Welcomes Bolsonaro to US, Echoes His Unsubstantiated Election Fraud Claims
content:
Bolsonaro and his family reportedly arrived in Miami on Wednesday.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a far right politician from Brazil who recently lost a narrow election against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has fled the country, and is reportedly set to receive visas from the State Department to remain in the U.S. for an indeterminate amount of time.

Bolsonaro and his family left Brazil following his defeat and amid an investigation into his involvement in a money-laundering scheme, in which police had asked him to surrender his passports to prevent him from leaving the country. They reportedly exited Brazil by land, traveling to Argentina and then to Ecuador. It’s unclear if they traveled to the U.S. directly from there, but Bolsonaro and his family reportedly arrived in Miami on Wednesday morning.

In an unusual move, the State Department is planning to issue visas to Bolsonaro and his wife and two daughters, allowing them to stay in the U.S. for an indefinite amount of time. It’s likely that the administration’s decision to grant Bolsonaro the right to stay in the U.S. will further escalate tensions between the Trump and Lula administrations.

author: Katheryn Houghton
title: Hospitals Nationwide Are Closing Intensive Care Units for Critically Ill Kids
content:
Pediatricians expect more cutbacks in the wake of federal Medicaid cuts.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Hospital units dedicated to treating the nation’s sickest kids are disappearing nationwide. In the past year alone, hospitals have closed pediatric intensive care units for critically ill kids in Montana, Oregon, and Missouri. Overnight hospital wings for kids have also shuttered in Illinois and California.

Depending on the hospital, pediatric units — which are separate from neonatal intensive care units — can serve patients ranging from a few weeks old to well into their teens or early adulthood. As hospitals look to cut costs, many are converting those beds into more services for newborns or adults. As a result, pediatric intensive care has become centralized in medical hubs, requiring critically ill children to travel farther for lifesaving care.

“You can’t expect that people will be fine if the next-closest children’s hospital is a flight away or an eight-hour drive,” said Elizabeth Mack, a pediatric critical care doctor and spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.

content:

On Tuesday, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the Federal Police to investigate suspected foreign financing of Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign. Bolsonaro lost to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the runoff. The investigation will also need to determine whether any connection exists between political support for the senator and foreign interests in Brazil’s rare earth and strategic mineral resources.

Dino issued the 38 page ruling as part of ADPF 1178, a constitutional challenge originally filed by the Brazilian Mining Institute (Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração/Ibram). He ordered that an investigation be opened under the Supreme Court’s direct supervision, due to the possible involvement of members of Congress, whose parliamentary immunity can only be overridden in the nation’s highest court, in the alleged crimes under investigation.
